senses.evidence: those characters which are transmitted entire, or almost unchanged in the hybridization, and therefore in themselves constitute the characters of the hybrid, are termed the dominant, and those which become latent in the process recessive

senses.label: consensus - as measured in the literature: the share of papers taking a position that endorse one explanation
senses.head: consensus
senses.gloss: as measured in the literature: the share of papers taking a position that endorse one explanation
senses.evidence: The peer-reviewed scientific literature provides a ground-level assessment of the degree of consensus among publishing scientists.

senses.label: consensus - as measured by asking scientists directly, which earlier surveys put at 97–98%
senses.head: consensus
senses.gloss: as measured by asking scientists directly, which earlier surveys put at 97–98%
senses.evidence: Surveys of climate scientists have found strong agreement (97–98%) regarding AGW amongst publishing climate experts (Doran and Zimmerman 2009 , Anderegg et al 2010 ).

senses.label: consensus - as perceived by the public, which is that scientists disagree, and which the paper treats as the thing to be corrected
senses.head: consensus
senses.gloss: as perceived by the public, which is that scientists disagree, and which the paper treats as the thing to be corrected
senses.evidence: Despite numerous indicators of a consensus, there is wide public perception that climate scientists disagree over the fundamental cause of global warming (GW; Leiserowitz et al 2012 , Pew 2012 ).

senses.label: `the 97% consensus` - A NUMBER MADE BY A DENOMINATOR CHOICE, AND THE PAPER PRINTS BOTH: `66.4% OF ABSTRACTS EXPRESSED NO POSITION on AGW, 32.6% endorsed AGW, 0.7% rejected AGW ... AMONG ABSTRACTS EXPRESSING A POSITION on AGW, 97.1% ENDORSED the consensus position.` The famous figure is computed on the third of the sample that took a position; two thirds are excluded BY DEFINITION, not by data.
senses.head: `the 97% consensus`
senses.gloss: A NUMBER MADE BY A DENOMINATOR CHOICE, AND THE PAPER PRINTS BOTH: `66.4% OF ABSTRACTS EXPRESSED NO POSITION on AGW, 32.6% endorsed AGW, 0.7% rejected AGW ... AMONG ABSTRACTS EXPRESSING A POSITION on AGW, 97.1% ENDORSED the consensus position.` The famous figure is computed on the third of the sample that took a position; two thirds are excluded BY DEFINITION, not by data.
senses.evidence: We find that 66.4% of abstracts expressed no position on AGW, 32.6% endorsed AGW, 0.7% rejected AGW and 0.3% were uncertain about the cause of global warming. Among abstracts expressing a position on AGW, 97.1% endorsed the consensus position that humans are causing global warming

senses.label: Degree of endorsement - seven-level code ranging from explicit quantified endorsement through no position to explicit quantified rejection
senses.head: Degree of endorsement
senses.gloss: seven-level code ranging from explicit quantified endorsement through no position to explicit quantified rejection
senses.evidence: We classified each abstract according to the type of research (category) and degree of endorsement. Written criteria were provided to raters for category (table 1 ) and level of endorsement of AGW (table 2 ). Explicit endorsements were divided into non-quantified (e.g., humans are contributing to global warming without quantifying the contribution) and quantified (e.g., humans are contributing more than 50% of global warming, consistent with the 2007 IPCC statement that most of the global warming since the mid-20th century is very likely due to the observed increase in anthropogenic greenhouse gas concentrations)

senses.label: Explicit quantified endorsement - statement that humans are the primary cause of recent global warming
senses.head: Explicit quantified endorsement
senses.gloss: statement that humans are the primary cause of recent global warming

Written criteria were provided to raters for category (table 1 ) and level of endorsement of AGW (table 2 ). Explicit endorsements were divided into non-quantified (e.g., humans are contributing to global warming without quantifying the contribution) and quantified (e.g., humans are contributing more than 50% of global warming, consistent with the 2007 IPCC statement that most of the global warming since the mid-20th century is very likely due to the observed increase in anthropogenic greenhouse gas concentrations)

senses.label: Explicit unquantified endorsement - statement of human causation without a percentage contribution
senses.head: Explicit unquantified endorsement

Explicit endorsements were divided into non-quantified (e.g., humans are contributing to global warming without quantifying the contribution) and quantified (e.g., humans are contributing more than 50% of global warming, consistent with the 2007 IPCC statement that most of the global warming since the mid-20th century is very likely due to the observed increase in anthropogenic greenhouse gas concentrations)

senses.label: Implicit endorsement - assumed human causation even when the abstract does not state it explicitly
senses.head: Implicit endorsement
senses.gloss: assumed human causation even when the abstract does not state it explicitly
senses.evidence: Implicit endorsement Implies humans are causing global warming. E.g., research assumes greenhouse gas emissions cause warming without explicitly stating humans are the cause

senses.label: Implicit rejection - natural-main-cause implication that minimizes human impact
senses.head: Implicit rejection
senses.gloss: natural-main-cause implication that minimizes human impact
senses.evidence: Implicit rejection Implies humans have had a minimal impact on global warming without saying so explicitly E.g., proposing a natural mechanism is the main cause of global warming ‘…anywhere from a major portion to all of the warming of the 20th century could plausibly result from natural causes according to these results’ (6) Explicit rejection without quantification Explicitly minimizes or rejects that humans are causing global warming ‘…the global temperature record provides little support for the catastrophic view of the greenhouse effect’ (7) Explicit rejection with quantification Explicitly states that humans are causing less than half of global warming

senses.head: Explicit unquantified rejection
senses.gloss: explicit minimization or rejection of human causation
senses.evidence: Implicit rejection Implies humans have had a minimal impact on global warming without saying so explicitly E.g., proposing a natural mechanism is the main cause of global warming ‘…anywhere from a major portion to all of the warming of the 20th century could plausibly result from natural causes according to these results’ (6) Explicit rejection without quantification Explicitly minimizes or rejects that humans are causing global warming ‘…the global temperature record provides little support for the catastrophic view of the greenhouse effect’ (7) Explicit rejection with quantification Explicitly states that humans are causing less than half of global warming

senses.label: Explicit quantified rejection - claim that humans caused less than half of global warming
senses.head: Explicit quantified rejection

senses.label: Blind abstract rating - web-distributed title and abstract with author, affiliation, journal, and date hidden
senses.head: Blind abstract rating
senses.gloss: web-distributed title and abstract with author, affiliation, journal, and date hidden
senses.evidence: Abstracts were randomly distributed via a web-based system to raters with only the title and abstract visible. All other information such as author names and affiliations, journal and publishing date were hidden. Each abstract was categorized by two independent, anonymized raters

senses.label: Rating reconciliation - anonymous comparison and revision followed by third-party adjudication
senses.head: Rating reconciliation
senses.gloss: anonymous comparison and revision followed by third-party adjudication
senses.evidence: Initially, 27% of category ratings and 33% of endorsement ratings disagreed. Raters were then allowed to compare and justify or update their rating through the web system, while maintaining anonymity. Following this, 11% of category ratings and 16% of endorsement ratings disagreed; these were then resolved by a third party

senses.label: Four endorsement metrics - shares among all papers, positioned papers, all scientists, and positioned scientists
senses.head: Four endorsement metrics
senses.gloss: shares among all papers, positioned papers, all scientists, and positioned scientists
senses.evidence: To simplify the analysis, ratings were consolidated into three groups: endorsements (including implicit and explicit; categories 1–3 in table 2 ), no position (category 4) and rejections (including implicit and explicit; categories 5–7). We examined four metrics to quantify the level of endorsement: (1) The percentage of endorsements/rejections/undecideds among all abstracts. (2) The percentage of endorsements/rejections/undecideds among only those abstracts expressing a position on AGW. (3) The percentage of scientists authoring endorsement/ rejection abstracts among all scientists. (4) The same percentage among only those scientists who expressed a position on AGW

senses.label: Abstract-only categorization - method that underestimates how many full papers take an AGW position
senses.head: Abstract-only categorization
senses.gloss: method that underestimates how many full papers take an AGW position
senses.evidence: Another potential area of uncertainty involved the text of the abstracts themselves. In some cases, ambiguous language made it difficult to ascertain the intended meaning of the authors. Naturally, a short abstract could not be expected to communicate all the details of the full paper. The implementation of the author self-rating process allowed us to look beyond the abstract. A comparison between self-ratings and abstract ratings revealed that categorization based on the abstract alone underestimates the percentage of papers taking a position on AGW

senses.label: Scientific reticence / least-drama bias - possible pressure toward a no-position abstract classification
senses.head: Scientific reticence / least-drama bias
senses.gloss: possible pressure toward a no-position abstract classification
senses.evidence: Two sources of rating bias can be cited: first, given that the raters themselves endorsed the scientific consensus on AGW, they may have been more likely to classify papers as sharing that endorsement. Second, scientific reticence (Hansen 2007 ) or ‘erring on the side of least drama’ (ESLD; Brysse et al 2012 ) may have exerted an opposite effect by biasing raters towards a ‘no position’ classification

senses.label: Consensus gap - public under-perception of overwhelming scientific agreement on human-caused warming
senses.head: Consensus gap
senses.gloss: public under-perception of overwhelming scientific agreement on human-caused warming
senses.evidence: Contributing to this ‘consensus gap’ are campaigns designed to confuse the public about the level of agreement among climate scientists. In 1991, Western Fuels Association conducted a $510 000 campaign whose primary goal was to ‘ reposition global warming as theory (not fact) ’. A key strategy involved constructing the impression of active scientific debate using dissenting scientists as spokesmen

senses.label: Equal-attention media norm - opposing-side balance that amplifies a vocal minority
senses.head: Equal-attention media norm
senses.gloss: opposing-side balance that amplifies a vocal minority
senses.evidence: The situation is exacerbated by media treatment of the climate issue, where the normative practice of providing opposing sides with equal attention has allowed a vocal minority to have their views amplified

senses.label: Systematic literature review - quantitative counter-evidence to claims that scientific rejection is growing
senses.head: Systematic literature review
senses.gloss: quantitative counter-evidence to claims that scientific rejection is growing
senses.evidence: A systematic, comprehensive review of the literature provides quantitative evidence countering this assertion. The number of papers rejecting AGW is a miniscule proportion of the published research, with the percentage slightly decreasing over time

senses.label: bias - as a rate of unwarranted positives produced by design, analysis and reporting choices; a property of how research is done
senses.head: bias
senses.gloss: as a rate of unwarranted positives produced by design, analysis and reporting choices; a property of how research is done
senses.evidence: First, let us define bias as the combination of various design, data, analysis, and presentation factors that tend to produce research findings when they should not be produced.

senses.label: bias - explicitly NOT chance variability, which produces false findings even under a perfect design
senses.head: bias
senses.gloss: explicitly NOT chance variability, which produces false findings even under a perfect design
senses.evidence: Bias should not be confused with chance variability that causes some findings to be false by chance even though the study design, data, analysis, and presentation are perfect.

senses.label: negative - a term the paper calls a misnomer, because a study that fails to find a relationship is informative rather than empty
senses.head: negative
senses.gloss: a term the paper calls a misnomer, because a study that fails to find a relationship is informative rather than empty
senses.evidence: “Negative” is actually a misnomer, and the misinterpretation is widespread.

senses.label: pre-study probability - the probability that a relationship is true before testing, equal to R divided by R plus one
senses.head: pre-study probability
senses.gloss: the probability that a relationship is true before testing, equal to R divided by R plus one
senses.evidence: The pre-study probability of a relationship being true is R /( R + 1).

senses.label: Type II error rate - beta, whose complement is the power to find a true relationship
senses.head: Type II error rate
senses.gloss: beta, whose complement is the power to find a true relationship
senses.evidence: The probability of a study finding a true relationship reflects the power 1 - β (one minus the Type II error rate).

senses.label: Type I error rate - alpha, governing a claimed relationship when none exists
senses.head: Type I error rate
senses.gloss: alpha, governing a claimed relationship when none exists
senses.evidence: The probability of claiming a relationship when none truly exists reflects the Type I error rate, α.

senses.label: Proteus phenomenon - rapidly alternating extreme claims and extremely opposite refutations
senses.head: Proteus phenomenon
senses.gloss: rapidly alternating extreme claims and extremely opposite refutations
senses.evidence: The term Proteus phenomenon has been coined to describe this phenomenon of rapidly alternating extreme research claims and extremely opposite refutations [ 29 ].

senses.label: null field - a field with no true findings, where unbiased effects vary by chance around the null
senses.head: null field
senses.gloss: a field with no true findings, where unbiased effects vary by chance around the null
senses.evidence: Let us suppose that in a research field there are no true findings at all to be discovered. History of science teaches us that scientific endeavor has often in the past wasted effort in fields with absolutely no yield of true scientific information, at least based on our current understanding. In such a “null field,” one would ideally expect all observed effect sizes to vary by chance around the null in the absence of bias.

senses.label: data dredging - using data-mining procedures to yield statistically significant results
senses.head: data dredging
senses.gloss: using data-mining procedures to yield statistically significant results

senses.head: confirmatory designs

senses.evidence: Thus, research findings are more likely true in confirmatory designs, such as large phase III randomized controlled trials, or meta-analyses thereof, than in hypothesis-generating experiments.

senses.head: hypothesis-generating experiments

senses.head: selective outcome reporting
senses.gloss: manipulation of reported outcomes and analyses, common even in randomized trials

senses.head: Virtual screening
senses.gloss: computationally assaying large libraries and experimentally testing selected leads
senses.evidence: Virtual screening can be used to speed up this search. 3 − 6 Virtual libraries containing thousands to hundreds of millions of candidates can be assayed with first-principles simulations or statistical predictions based on learned proxy models, and only the most promising leads are selected and tested experimentally.

senses.head: encoder network

senses.label: decoder network - converts vectors back into molecular strings
senses.head: decoder network
senses.gloss: converts vectors back into molecular strings
senses.evidence: The autoencoder in comprised of two deep networks: an encoder network to convert each string into a fixed-dimensional vector, and a decoder network to convert vectors back into strings ( Figure 1 a).

senses.label: property prediction task - predicts molecular properties from the latent vector during joint training
senses.head: property prediction task
senses.gloss: predicts molecular properties from the latent vector during joint training
senses.evidence: This autoencoder was then trained jointly on the reconstruction task and a property prediction task; an additional multilayer perceptron (MLP) was used to predict the property from the latent vector of the encoded molecule.

senses.label: latent space - the encoder's vector space, functioning as a continuous molecular representation
senses.head: latent space
senses.gloss: the encoder's vector space, functioning as a continuous molecular representation
senses.evidence: Starting from a discrete molecular representation, such as a SMILES string, the encoder network converts each molecule into a vector in the latent space, which is effectively a continuous molecular representation.

senses.label: dead areas - sparse latent-space regions that decode into invalid SMILES strings
senses.head: dead areas
senses.gloss: sparse latent-space regions that decode into invalid SMILES strings
senses.evidence: Without this constraint, the latent space learned by the autoencoder may be sparse and may contain large “dead areas”, which decode to invalid SMILES strings.

senses.label: doubly probabilistic model - stochastic in both encoding noise and decoder output sampling
senses.head: doubly probabilistic model
senses.gloss: stochastic in both encoding noise and decoder output sampling
senses.evidence: The variational autoencoder is a doubly probabilistic model. In addition to the Gaussian noise added to the encoder, which can be turned off by simply sampling the mean of the encoding distribution, the decoding process is also nondeterministic, as the string output is sampled from the final layer of the decoder. This implies that decoding a single point in the latent space back to a string representation is stochastic.

senses.label: spherical interpolation - follows a circular arc to remain in high-probability latent-space regions
senses.head: spherical interpolation
senses.gloss: follows a circular arc to remain in high-probability latent-space regions
senses.evidence: Interpolating linearly between two points might pass by an area of low probability, to keep the sampling on the areas of high probability we utilize spherical interpolation 35 ( slerp ). With slerp , the path between two points is a circular arc lying on the on the surface of a N -dimensional sphere.

senses.head: slerp
senses.gloss: the paper's short form for spherical interpolation

senses.label: synthetic accessibility score - SAS, a property used to compare generated molecule sets
senses.head: synthetic accessibility score
senses.gloss: SAS, a property used to compare generated molecule sets
senses.evidence: We compare the water–octanol partition coefficient (logP), the synthetic accessibility score (SAS), 37 and Quantitative Estimation of Drug-likeness (QED), 38 which ranges in value between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating that the molecule is more drug-like.

senses.label: Quantitative Estimation of Drug-likeness - QED, ranging from zero to one with higher values more drug-like
senses.head: Quantitative Estimation of Drug-likeness
senses.gloss: QED, ranging from zero to one with higher values more drug-like
senses.evidence: We compare the water–octanol partition coefficient (logP), the synthetic accessibility score (SAS), 37 and Quantitative Estimation of Drug-likeness (QED), 38 which ranges in value between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating that the molecule is more drug-like.

senses.label: Gaussian process model - a lightweight smooth-function model used to smooth the optimization landscape
senses.head: Gaussian process model
senses.gloss: a lightweight smooth-function model used to smooth the optimization landscape
senses.evidence: In order to create a smoother landscape to perform optimizations, we used a Gaussian process model to model the property predictor model. Gaussian processes can be used to predict any smooth continuous function 41 and are extremely lightweight, requiring only a few minutes to train on a dataset of a few thousand molecules.

senses.label: joint training for property prediction - organizes latent-space molecules by property value
senses.head: joint training for property prediction
senses.gloss: organizes latent-space molecules by property value
senses.evidence: With joint training for property prediction, the distribution of molecules in the latent space is organized by property values.

senses.label: teacher forcing - feeds the previous sampled character to the GRU, improving valid outputs but complicating training
senses.head: teacher forcing
senses.gloss: feeds the previous sampled character to the GRU, improving valid outputs but complicating training
senses.evidence: The output GRU layer had one additional input, corresponding to the character sampled from the softmax output of the previous time step and was trained using teacher forcing. 54 This increased the accuracy of generated SMILES strings, which resulted in higher fractions of valid SMILES strings for latent points outside the training data, but also made training more difficult, since the decoder showed a tendency to ignore the (variational) encoding and rely solely on the input sequence.

senses.label: Big Data - as a comparison class of domains, each with its own acquisition architecture, rather than as a property a dataset has
senses.head: Big Data
senses.gloss: as a comparison class of domains, each with its own acquisition architecture, rather than as a property a dataset has
senses.evidence: Projecting to the year 2025, we compared genomics with three other major generators of Big Data: astronomy, YouTube, and Twitter.

senses.label: data volume - as ACQUIRED, which for particle physics is enormous
senses.head: data volume
senses.gloss: as ACQUIRED, which for particle physics is enormous
senses.evidence: Particle physics also produces massive quantities of raw data, although the footprint is surprisingly limited since the vast majority of data are discarded soon after acquisition using the processing power that is coupled to the sensors [ 8 ].

senses.label: data volume - as STORED, which for genomics is a small fraction of what is produced and for particle physics is smaller still
senses.head: data volume
senses.gloss: as STORED, which for genomics is a small fraction of what is produced and for particle physics is smaller still
senses.evidence: However, the 3.6 petabases represent a small fraction of the total produced; most of it is not yet in these archives.

senses.label: Storage / distribution / analysis - three lifecycle components alongside acquisition
senses.head: Storage / distribution / analysis
senses.gloss: three lifecycle components alongside acquisition
senses.evidence: To compare these four disparate domains, we considered the four components that comprise the “life cycle” of a dataset: acquisition, storage, distribution, and analysis

senses.label: Compressive genomics - storage reduction constrained by decompression time and fidelity
senses.head: Compressive genomics
senses.gloss: storage reduction constrained by decompression time and fidelity
senses.evidence: These needs can be diminished with effective data compression [ 27 ], but decompression times and fidelity are a major concern in compressive genomics

senses.label: Long-read sequencing - mature technology that may remove the need to retain raw reads
senses.head: Long-read sequencing
senses.gloss: mature technology that may remove the need to retain raw reads
senses.evidence: Are the emerging “third-generation” single-molecule sequencing technologies with much longer reads, such as those from Pacific Biosciences and Oxford Nanopore, a computational panacea? Though error rates currently are higher and throughput lower than short-read technologies, as they mature, these technologies are starting to be used to sequence and assemble nearly entire chromosomes [ 29 ]. This will minimize the need to oversample as much, and eventually, the raw sequence data may not need to be stored at all

senses.label: Delta encoding - retention of reference-relative variant lists instead of complete genomes
senses.head: Delta encoding
senses.gloss: retention of reference-relative variant lists instead of complete genomes
senses.evidence: More significant reductions in storage demand will come when improvements in sequencing accuracy and database comprehensiveness reach the point at which genome sequences themselves do not need to be stored, just the list of variants relative to a reference collection (“delta encoding”)

senses.label: Streaming omics analysis - real-time inference performing at least as well as nonstreaming methods
senses.head: Streaming omics analysis
senses.gloss: real-time inference performing at least as well as nonstreaming methods
senses.evidence: In contrast, we do see great opportunities for data reduction and real-time analysis of other ‘omics analysis. For example, once sequencing becomes fast enough and the methods mature enough to correctly infer transcript expression levels in real time, we anticipate that raw RNA-seq reads will no longer be stored, except for specific research purposes. Already several such “streaming” algorithms have been published for this purpose, performing as well as or superior to their nonstreaming counterparts

senses.label: Hierarchical genomic archive - data and summaries exposed at multiple compression and latency levels
senses.head: Hierarchical genomic archive
senses.gloss: data and summaries exposed at multiple compression and latency levels
senses.evidence: To make it practical to search and query through such vast collections, the data will be stored in hierarchical systems that make data and their statistical summaries available at different levels of compression and latency

senses.label: Cloud genomic analysis - code moves to remote machines already holding the data
senses.head: Cloud genomic analysis
senses.gloss: code moves to remote machines already holding the data
senses.evidence: For large-scale analysis, cloud computing is particularly suited to decreasing the bandwidth for distribution of genomic data [ 37 ] so that applications can run on remote machines that already have data [ 38 ]. Only small segments of code are uploaded and highly processed outputs are downloaded, thus significantly reducing the computing resources necessary for distribution

senses.label: Homomorphic encryption - controlled analysis of encrypted data without revealing raw genomes
senses.head: Homomorphic encryption
senses.gloss: controlled analysis of encrypted data without revealing raw genomes
senses.evidence: new methods of data reliability and security are required to ensure privacy, much more so than for the other three domains. A serious breach of medically sensitive genomic data would have permanent consequences and could seriously hinder the development of genomic medicine. Homomorphic encryption systems, in which encrypted data can be analyzed and manipulated for certain controlled queries without disclosing the raw data, are currently too computationally expensive for widespread use, but these and related cryptographic techniques are promising areas of research

senses.label: Variant calling - computationally intensive identification of variants in each individual genome
senses.head: Variant calling
senses.gloss: computationally intensive identification of variants in each individual genome
senses.evidence: For population and medical genomics, identifying the genomic variants in each individual genome is currently one of the most computationally complex phases

senses.label: Whole-genome alignment - comparative method for phylogeny reconstruction and genome annotation
senses.head: Whole-genome alignment
senses.gloss: comparative method for phylogeny reconstruction and genome annotation
senses.evidence: Whole genome alignment is another important form of genomic data analysis, used for a variety of goals, from phylogeny reconstruction to genome annotation via comparative methodologies. Just a single whole genome alignment between human and mouse consumes ~100 CPU hours [ 43 ]. Aligning all pairs of the ~2.5 million species expected to be available by 2025 amounts to 50–100 trillion such whole genome alignments, which would need to be six orders of magnitude faster than possible today

senses.label: I/O bottleneck - data shuttling between storage and processors rather than CPU arithmetic
senses.head: I/O bottleneck
senses.gloss: data shuttling between storage and processors rather than CPU arithmetic
senses.evidence: Improvements to CPU capabilities, as anticipated by Moore’s Law, should help close the gap, but trends in computing power are often geared towards floating point operations and do not necessarily provide improvements in genome analysis, in which string operations and memory management often pose the most significant challenges. Moreover, the bigger bottleneck of Big Data analysis in the future may not be in CPU capabilities but in the input/output (I/O) hardware that shuttles data between storage and processors [ 44 ], a problem requiring research into new parallel I/O hardware and algorithms that can effectively utilize them

senses.label: Genomic data sharing - protection against isolated collections too underpowered for subtle signals
senses.head: Genomic data sharing
senses.gloss: protection against isolated collections too underpowered for subtle signals
senses.evidence: If we do not commit as a scientific community to sharing now, we run the risk of establishing thousands of isolated, private data collections, each too underpowered to allow subtle signals to be extracted

senses.label: modular - the ecological sense: species grouped by where and when they are active, so interaction frequency tracks group membership
senses.head: modular
senses.gloss: the ecological sense: species grouped by where and when they are active, so interaction frequency tracks group membership
senses.evidence: Ecological communities are structured both in space, as in a stratified lake and in time, as for migratory birds.

senses.label: modular - the formal sense: a value of Q above what an Erdos-Renyi reference model would give by chance
senses.head: modular
senses.gloss: the formal sense: a value of Q above what an Erdos-Renyi reference model would give by chance
senses.evidence: Values of Q >0 ( Q <0) mean that we observe within-subsystem interactions more (less) frequently than expected by chance.

senses.label: stability - local: recovery from a small perturbation around an equilibrium, as against persistence or robustness to species loss
senses.head: stability
senses.gloss: local: recovery from a small perturbation around an equilibrium, as against persistence or robustness to species loss
senses.evidence: In ecology, the idea that a modular organization would be beneficial for the local stability of ecological communities (that is, their ability to recover from small perturbations) dates back to work on complexity and stability by May 20 , where he suggested ‘that our model multi-species communities [...] will do better if the interactions tend to be arranged in blocks'.

senses.label: quaternionic parameterization - the parameterization of the cavity method used for the paper's random-matrix results
senses.head: quaternionic parameterization
senses.gloss: the parameterization of the cavity method used for the paper's random-matrix results
senses.evidence: Here we study the effect of modularity on the local stability of ecological dynamical systems, by presenting new results in random matrix theory, which are obtained using a quaternionic parameterization of the cavity method.

senses.label: cavity method - the method used with quaternions to obtain the new random-matrix-theory results
senses.head: cavity method
senses.gloss: the method used with quaternions to obtain the new random-matrix-theory results
senses.evidence: Here we study the effect of modularity on the local stability of ecological dynamical systems, by presenting new results in random matrix theory, which are obtained using a quaternionic parameterization of the cavity method.

senses.head: Hadamard (element-by-element) product

senses.evidence: In both cases, the matrix M is obtained via the Hadamard (element-by-element) product of W and the adjacency matrix K .

senses.head: adjacency matrix
senses.gloss: K, combined element by element with W to obtain M
senses.evidence: In both cases, the matrix M is obtained via the Hadamard (element-by-element) product of W and the adjacency matrix K .

senses.label: spectrum of M - a bulk plus up to two real outliers in the two-subsystem case
senses.head: spectrum of M
senses.gloss: a bulk plus up to two real outliers in the two-subsystem case
senses.evidence: when there are two subsystems the spectrum of M is composed of a ‘bulk' of eigenvalues, and up to two ‘outlier', real eigenvalues.

senses.label: bulk - the main body of eigenvalues in M's spectrum
senses.head: bulk
senses.gloss: the main body of eigenvalues in M's spectrum
senses.evidence: when there are two subsystems the spectrum of M is composed of a ‘bulk' of eigenvalues, and up to two ‘outlier', real eigenvalues.

senses.label: outlier eigenvalue - one of up to two real outliers outside the spectral bulk
senses.head: outlier eigenvalue
senses.gloss: one of up to two real outliers outside the spectral bulk
senses.evidence: when there are two subsystems the spectrum of M is composed of a ‘bulk' of eigenvalues, and up to two ‘outlier', real eigenvalues.

senses.label: cascade model - a size-ordered food web in which species consume only smaller species
senses.head: cascade model
senses.gloss: a size-ordered food web in which species consume only smaller species
senses.evidence: We therefore analysed matrices constructed using a variation of the cascade model, where we assign a ‘size' to each species and each species can only consume smaller species, and has a preference for those in the same subsystem ( Q >0), or for those in the other subsystem ( Q <0).

senses.label: universality property - distribution choice does not alter the large-system result once moments are fixed and fourth moments bounded
senses.head: universality property
senses.gloss: distribution choice does not alter the large-system result once moments are fixed and fourth moments bounded
senses.evidence: We do not need to specify the exact form of the distributions and , given that, as for many results in random matrix theory, our findings are consistent with the ‘universality' property 38 39 : once fixed the mean and covariance matrices of and , and provided that the fourth moment of each is bounded, any choice of distributions yields the same result, for S →∞.

senses.label: elliptic law - B's large-system eigenvalues are approximately uniform in an ellipse
senses.head: elliptic law
senses.gloss: B's large-system eigenvalues are approximately uniform in an ellipse
senses.evidence: In this case, the eigenvalues of B follow the ‘elliptic law' 39 , and for S large, are approximately uniformly distributed in an ellipse, centred at (− μ w , 0), and with horizontal semi-axis and vertical semi-axis .

senses.label: feasible equilibrium point - the point around which M represents population dynamics
senses.head: feasible equilibrium point
senses.gloss: the point around which M represents population dynamics
senses.evidence: M is the S × S community matrix, representing the population dynamics of an unknown dynamical system around a feasible equilibrium point.

senses.label: local asymptotic stability - the system property on which block structure can have an effect
senses.head: local asymptotic stability
senses.gloss: the system property on which block structure can have an effect
senses.evidence: Block structure can have an effect on the local asymptotic stability of the underlying system.

senses.label: risk of bias - study-level: a property of how the whole study was designed and run, e.g. adequacy of allocation concealment
senses.head: risk of bias
senses.gloss: study-level: a property of how the whole study was designed and run, e.g. adequacy of allocation concealment
senses.evidence: For studies included in a systematic review, a thorough assessment of the risk of bias requires both a “study-level” assessment (e.g., adequacy of allocation concealment) and, for some features, a newer approach called “outcome-level” assessment.

senses.label: risk of bias - outcome-level: assessed separately per outcome, because quality can differ within one study between a primary efficacy measure and the recording of harms
senses.head: risk of bias
senses.gloss: outcome-level: assessed separately per outcome, because quality can differ within one study between a primary efficacy measure and the recording of harms
senses.evidence: The quality of evidence may differ across outcomes, even within a study, such as between a primary efficacy outcome, which is likely to be very carefully and systematically measured, and the assessment of serious harms [39] , which may rely on spontaneous reports by investigators.

senses.label: reporting bias - publication bias: whole studies going unreported
senses.head: reporting bias
senses.gloss: publication bias: whole studies going unreported
senses.evidence: Selective reporting of complete studies (e.g., publication bias) [28] as well as the more recently empirically demonstrated “outcome reporting bias” within individual studies [40] , [41] should be considered by authors when conducting a systematic review and reporting its results.

senses.label: reporting bias - outcome reporting bias: outcomes going unreported within a study that was itself published
senses.head: reporting bias
senses.gloss: outcome reporting bias: outcomes going unreported within a study that was itself published
senses.evidence: as well as the more recently empirically demonstrated “outcome reporting bias” within individual studies

senses.label: the unit of counting - record: what the search returns, before anything is screened
senses.head: the unit of counting
senses.gloss: record: what the search returns, before anything is screened
senses.evidence: Before including studies and providing reasons for excluding others, the review team must first search the literature. This search results in records.

senses.label: the unit of counting - article versus study: not interchangeable, because one article can report several studies and one study can appear in several articles
senses.head: the unit of counting
senses.gloss: article versus study: not interchangeable, because one article can report several studies and one study can appear in several articles
senses.evidence: The number of included articles might be smaller (or larger) than the number of studies, because articles may report on multiple studies and results from a particular study may be published in several articles.

senses.label: conduct versus reporting: nominally distinct, but for systematic reviews a failure to report can itself be read as a marker of poor conduct
senses.evidence: For example, the failure of a systematic review to report the assessment of the risk of bias in included studies may be seen as a marker of poor conduct, given the importance of this activity in the systematic review process [37] .

senses.label: Systematic review - explicit question, systematic identification and appraisal, and collection and analysis of included-study data
senses.head: Systematic review
senses.gloss: explicit question, systematic identification and appraisal, and collection and analysis of included-study data
senses.evidence: The terminology used to describe a systematic review and meta-analysis has evolved over time. One reason for changing the name from QUOROM to PRISMA was the desire to encompass both systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We have adopted the definitions used by the Cochrane Collaboration [9] . A systematic review is a review of a clearly formulated question that uses systematic and explicit methods to identify, select, and critically appraise relevant research, and to collect and analyze data from the studies that are included in the review. Statistical methods (meta-analysis) may or may not be used to analyze and summarize the results of the included studies. Meta-analysis refers to the use of statistical techniques in a systematic review to integrate the results of included studies

senses.label: Meta-analysis - statistical integration used within a systematic review, but not required for every systematic review
senses.head: Meta-analysis
senses.gloss: statistical integration used within a systematic review, but not required for every systematic review
senses.evidence: The terminology used to describe a systematic review and meta-analysis has evolved over time. One reason for changing the name from QUOROM to PRISMA was the desire to encompass both systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We have adopted the definitions used by the Cochrane Collaboration [9] . A systematic review is a review of a clearly formulated question that uses systematic and explicit methods to identify, select, and critically appraise relevant research, and to collect and analyze data from the studies that are included in the review. Statistical methods (meta-analysis) may or may not be used to analyze and summarize the results of the included studies. Meta-analysis refers to the use of statistical techniques in a systematic review to integrate the results of included studies

senses.label: Iterative systematic review - protocol changes may be appropriate when included-study scope or quality changes
senses.head: Iterative systematic review
senses.gloss: protocol changes may be appropriate when included-study scope or quality changes
senses.evidence: Completing a Systematic Review Is an Iterative Process The conduct of a systematic review depends heavily on the scope and quality of included studies: thus systematic reviewers may need to modify their original review protocol during its conduct. Any systematic review reporting guideline should recommend that such changes can be reported and explained without suggesting that they are inappropriate. The PRISMA Statement (Items 5, 11, 16, and 23) acknowledges this iterative process. Aside from Cochrane reviews, all of which should have a protocol, only about 10% of systematic reviewers report working from a protocol [22] . Without a protocol that is publicly accessible, it is difficult to judge between appropriate and inappropriate modifications

senses.label: Conduct / reporting distinction - nominally separate but closely intertwined for systematic reviews
senses.head: Conduct / reporting distinction
senses.gloss: nominally separate but closely intertwined for systematic reviews
senses.evidence: Conduct and Reporting Research Are Distinct Concepts This distinction is, however, less straightforward for systematic reviews than for assessments of the reporting of an individual study, because the reporting and conduct of systematic reviews are, by nature, closely intertwined. For example, the failure of a systematic review to report the assessment of the risk of bias in included studies may be seen as a marker of poor conduct, given the importance of this activity in the systematic review process

senses.label: Study-level / outcome-level risk of bias - whole-study design assessment plus outcome-specific reliability and validity
senses.head: Study-level / outcome-level risk of bias
senses.gloss: whole-study design assessment plus outcome-specific reliability and validity
senses.evidence: Study-Level Versus Outcome-Level Assessment of Risk of Bias For studies included in a systematic review, a thorough assessment of the risk of bias requires both a “study-level” assessment (e.g., adequacy of allocation concealment) and, for some features, a newer approach called “outcome-level” assessment. An outcome-level assessment involves evaluating the reliability and validity of the data for each important outcome by determining the methods used to assess them in each individual study [38] . The quality of evidence may differ across outcomes, even within a study, such as between a primary efficacy outcome, which is likely to be very carefully and systematically measured, and the assessment of serious harms [39] , which may rely on spontaneous reports by investigators. This information should be reported to allow an explicit assessment of the extent to which an estimate of effect is correct

senses.label: Essential checklist item - retained or added only when the consensus group judged it essential
senses.head: Essential checklist item
senses.gloss: retained or added only when the consensus group judged it essential
senses.evidence: Only items deemed essential were retained or added to the checklist. Some additional items are nevertheless desirable, and review authors should include these, if relevant [10] . For example, it is useful to indicate whether the systematic review is an update [11] of a previous review, and to describe any changes in procedures from those described in the original protocol

senses.label: Review registration - transparency precedent with a possible role in reducing duplicate reviews
senses.head: Review registration
senses.gloss: transparency precedent with a possible role in reducing duplicate reviews
senses.evidence: Although no direct evidence was found to support retaining or adding some items, evidence from other domains was believed to be relevant. For example, Item 5 asks authors to provide registration information about the systematic review, including a registration number, if available. Although systematic review registration is not yet widely available [12] , [13] , the participating journals of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) [14] now require all clinical trials to be registered in an effort to increase transparency and accountability [15] . Those aspects are also likely to benefit systematic reviewers, possibly reducing the risk of an excessive number of reviews addressing the same question [16] , [17] and providing greater transparency when updating systematic reviews

senses.label: PRISMA instrument - 27-item checklist and four-phase flow diagram for reporting improvement
senses.head: PRISMA instrument
senses.gloss: 27-item checklist and four-phase flow diagram for reporting improvement
senses.evidence: The PRISMA Statement consists of a 27-item checklist ( Table 1 ; see also Text S1 for a downloadable Word template for researchers to re-use) and a four-phase flow diagram ( Figure 1 ; see also Figure S1 for a downloadable Word template for researchers to re-use). The aim of the PRISMA Statement is to help authors improve the reporting of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We have focused on randomized trials, but PRISMA can also be used as a basis for reporting systematic reviews of other types of research, particularly evaluations of interventions. PRISMA may also be useful for critical appraisal of published systematic reviews. However, the PRISMA checklist is not a quality assessment instrument to gauge the quality of a systematic review

senses.label: PRISMA scope - randomized-trial focus, extensible to other research and critical appraisal, but not a review-quality scale
senses.head: PRISMA scope
senses.gloss: randomized-trial focus, extensible to other research and critical appraisal, but not a review-quality scale
senses.evidence: The PRISMA Statement consists of a 27-item checklist ( Table 1 ; see also Text S1 for a downloadable Word template for researchers to re-use) and a four-phase flow diagram ( Figure 1 ; see also Figure S1 for a downloadable Word template for researchers to re-use). The aim of the PRISMA Statement is to help authors improve the reporting of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We have focused on randomized trials, but PRISMA can also be used as a basis for reporting systematic reviews of other types of research, particularly evaluations of interventions. PRISMA may also be useful for critical appraisal of published systematic reviews. However, the PRISMA checklist is not a quality assessment instrument to gauge the quality of a systematic review

senses.label: PRISMA flow units - records become articles after screening and eligibility, while article and study counts can diverge
senses.head: PRISMA flow units
senses.gloss: records become articles after screening and eligibility, while article and study counts can diverge
senses.evidence: The flow diagram has also been modified. Before including studies and providing reasons for excluding others, the review team must first search the literature. This search results in records. Once these records have been screened and eligibility criteria applied, a smaller number of articles will remain. The number of included articles might be smaller (or larger) than the number of studies, because articles may report on multiple studies and results from a particular study may be published in several articles. To capture this information, the PRISMA flow diagram now requests information on these phases of the review process

senses.label: Explanation and Elaboration - companion exemplars, rationales, and evidence bases for checklist items
senses.head: Explanation and Elaboration
senses.gloss: companion exemplars, rationales, and evidence bases for checklist items
senses.evidence: In addition to the PRISMA Statement, a supporting Explanation and Elaboration document has been produced [18] following the style used for other reporting guidelines [19] – [21] . The process of completing this document included developing a large database of exemplars to highlight how best to report each checklist item, and identifying a comprehensive evidence base to support the inclusion of each checklist item. The Explanation and Elaboration document was completed after several face to face meetings and numerous iterations among several meeting participants, after which it was shared with the whole group for additional revisions and final approval. Finally, the group formed a dissemination subcommittee to help disseminate and implement PRISMA

senses.label: Bias-assessment reporting - imperfect evidence that nevertheless marks thorough review conduct
senses.head: Bias-assessment reporting
senses.gloss: imperfect evidence that nevertheless marks thorough review conduct
senses.evidence: The quality of reporting of systematic reviews is still not optimal [22] – [27] . In a recent review of 300 systematic reviews, few authors reported assessing possible publication bias [22] , even though there is overwhelming evidence both for its existence [28] and its impact on the results of systematic reviews [29] . Even when the possibility of publication bias is assessed, there is no guarantee that systematic reviewers have assessed or interpreted it appropriately [30] . senses.label: Cross-domain PRISMA - general concepts persist across review questions while concrete bias items and flow diagrams require adaptation
