senses.evidence: Continuous vector representation, as a distributed representation for words, has been recently established in natural language processing (NLP) as an efficient way to represent semantic/syntactic units with many applications.

senses.label: word - biological: three consecutive amino acids, defined outright as the unit that plays the role a word plays in text
senses.head: word
senses.gloss: biological: three consecutive amino acids, defined outright as the unit that plays the role a word plays in text
senses.evidence: The same procedure is applied on all 546,790 sequences in Swiss-Prot, thus at the end we obtain a corpus consisting of 546,790 × 3 = 1,640,370 sequences of 3-grams (3-gram is a “biological” word consisting of 3 amino acids).

senses.label: family - the broad sense: a set of evolutionarily related proteins, which is what the classification task means by it
senses.head: family
senses.gloss: the broad sense: a set of evolutionarily related proteins, which is what the classification task means by it
senses.evidence: A protein family is a set of proteins that are evolutionarily related, typically involving similar structures or functions.

senses.label: family - the Pfam sense: one of four sibling categories, so that a Pfam 'family' is a species of the very thing the word names
senses.head: family
senses.gloss: the Pfam sense: one of four sibling categories, so that a Pfam 'family' is a species of the very thing the word names
senses.evidence: In Pfam, a family can be classified as a “family”, “domain”, “repeat”, or “motif”.

senses.label: accuracy - per-family binary: one classifier per family with equal positives and negatives, which is what every number in Table 2 is
senses.head: accuracy
senses.gloss: per-family binary: one classifier per family with equal positives and negatives, which is what every number in Table 2 is
senses.evidence: In order to evaluate the strength of ProtVec, we performed classifications of 7,027 protein families and obtained a weighted average accuracy of 93 ± 0.06%, which exhibits a more reliable result than the existing methods.

senses.label: smoothness - measured against a shuffled control rather than in absolute terms, so the reported figure is a ratio and not a value
senses.head: smoothness
senses.gloss: measured against a shuffled control rather than in absolute terms, so the reported figure is a ratio and not a value
senses.evidence: The results suggest that the protein-space is on average 2-times smoother in terms of physical and chemical properties than a random space.

senses.label: Language of life - conceptual analogy mapping biological sequences to human language
senses.head: Language of life
senses.gloss: conceptual analogy mapping biological sequences to human language
senses.evidence: Nature uses certain languages to describe biological sequences such as DNA, RNA, and proteins. Much like humans adopt languages to communicate, biological organisms use sophisticated languages to convey information within and between cells. Inspired by this conceptual analogy, we adopt existing methods in natural language processing (NLP) to gain a deeper understanding of the “language of life” with the ultimate goal to discover functions encoded within biological sequences

senses.label: Content-addressable representation - nearby storage of items and properties enabling partial-cue recall
senses.head: Content-addressable representation
senses.gloss: nearby storage of items and properties enabling partial-cue recall
senses.evidence: The main idea in this approach is encoding and storing information about an item within a system through establishing its interactions with other members. Distributed representation was originally inspired by the structure of human memory, where the items are stored in a “content-addressable” fashion. Content-based storing allows for efficiently recalling items from partial descriptions. Since the content-addressable items and their properties are stored within a close proximity, such a system provides a viable infrastructure to generalize features attributed to an item

senses.label: Embedding context - neighboring words that characterize a word’s meaning
senses.head: Embedding context
senses.gloss: neighboring words that characterize a word’s meaning
senses.evidence: The basic idea behind training such vectors is that the meaning of a word is characterized by its context, i.e. neighboring words. Thus, words and their contexts are considered to be positive training samples. Such vectors can be trained using large amounts of textual data in a variety of ways, e.g. neural network architectures like the Skip-gram model

senses.label: Shifted 3-gram construction - three non-overlapping offset tokenizations per protein
senses.head: Shifted 3-gram construction
senses.gloss: three non-overlapping offset tokenizations per protein
senses.evidence: The next step in training distributed representations is to break the sequences into sub sequences (i.e. biological words). The simplest and most common technique in bioinformatics to study sequences involves fixed-length overlapping n-grams [ 32 – 34 ]. However, instead of using n-grams directly in feature extraction, we utilize n-gram modeling for training a general purpose distributed representation of sequences. This so-called embedding model needs to be trained only once and may then be adopted in feature extraction part of specific problems. In n-gram modeling of protein informatics, usually an overlapping window of 3 to 6 residues is used. Instead of taking overlapping windows, we generate 3 lists of shifted non-overlapping words

senses.label: ProtVec training corpus - 1,640,370 shifted 3-gram sequences derived from Swiss-Prot
senses.head: ProtVec training corpus
senses.gloss: 1,640,370 shifted 3-gram sequences derived from Swiss-Prot
senses.evidence: In order to prepare the training data, each protein sequence will be represented as three sequences (1, 2, 3) of 3-grams. The same procedure is applied on all 546,790 sequences in Swiss-Prot, thus at the end we obtain a corpus consisting of 546,790 × 3 = 1,640,370 sequences of 3-grams (3-gram is a “biological” word consisting of 3 amino acids)

senses.label: Negative sampling - observed pairs pulled together and incorrect pairs used to prevent vector collapse
senses.head: Negative sampling
senses.gloss: observed pairs pulled together and incorrect pairs used to prevent vector collapse
senses.evidence: In Eq (2) , the positive samples maximize the probabilities of the observed (w, c) pairs in the training data, while the negative samples prevent all vectors from having the same value by disallowing some incorrect (w, c) pairs

senses.label: Protein sequence vector - sum of all overlapping 3-gram representations
senses.head: Protein sequence vector
senses.gloss: sum of all overlapping 3-gram representations
senses.evidence: Each sequence is represented as the summation of the vector representation of overlapping 3-grams. Thus, each sequence is presented as a vector of size 100

senses.label: Balanced one-family classifier - equal positive and randomly sampled negative instances
senses.head: Balanced one-family classifier
senses.gloss: equal positive and randomly sampled negative instances
senses.evidence: For each family type, the same number of instances from Swiss-Prot are selected randomly to form the negative examples. Support vector machine classifiers are used to evaluate the strength of ProtVec in the classification of protein families through 10 × fold cross-validations

senses.label: Specificity / sensitivity - true-negative and true-positive family-classification rates
senses.head: Specificity / sensitivity
senses.gloss: true-negative and true-positive family-classification rates
senses.evidence: For the evaluation we report specificity (true negative rate), sensitivity (true positive rate), and the accuracy of family classifications

senses.label: Sequence-only feature learning - contrast with methods requiring extensive engineered properties
senses.head: Sequence-only feature learning
senses.gloss: contrast with methods requiring extensive engineered properties
senses.evidence: Besides the primary sequence, the existing methods typically require extensive information for feature extraction, e.g. hydrophobicity, normalized Van der Waals volume, polarity, polarizability, charge, surface tension, secondary structure and solvent accessibility. The reported accuracies of a previous study on family classification have been in the range of 69.1–99.6% for 54 protein families [ 16 ]. In another study, researchers used motifs from protein interactions for detecting Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) [ 19 ] families for 368 proteins, and obtained a classification accuracy of 75% at sensitivity of 10% [ 20 ]. In contrast, our proposed approach is trained based solely on primary sequence information, yet achieving high accuracy

senses.label: Best Lipschitz constant - smallest bound quantifying continuity of embedding-space properties
senses.head: Best Lipschitz constant
senses.gloss: smallest bound quantifying continuity of embedding-space properties
senses.evidence: we required a quantitative approach to measure the continuity of these properties in the protein-space. To do so, we calculated the best Lipschitz constant

senses.label: Scrambled space - control created by randomly shuffling 3-gram property labels
senses.head: Scrambled space
senses.gloss: control created by randomly shuffling 3-gram property labels
senses.evidence: To evaluate this result we made an artificial space called “scrambled space” by randomly shuffling the labels of 3-grams in the 100 dimensional space

senses.label: ill-posedness - LINEAR, and only that: the theorem is about the linearization around solutions with non-degenerate critical points, so the bare claim 'the Prandtl equation is ill-posed' drops the word that bounds the result
senses.head: ill-posedness
senses.gloss: LINEAR, and only that: the theorem is about the linearization around solutions with non-degenerate critical points, so the bare claim 'the Prandtl equation is ill-posed' drops the word that bounds the result
senses.evidence: This theorem expresses strong linear ill-posedness of the Prandtl equation in the Sobolev framework. It is a consequence of an instability process, that holds at high tangential frequencies

senses.label: the expected answer - STATED AND THEN OVERTURNED: the paper records that the inviscid result made well-posedness the reasonable bet, and then proves the opposite in this framework
senses.head: the expected answer
senses.gloss: STATED AND THEN OVERTURNED: the paper records that the inviscid result made well-posedness the reasonable bet, and then proves the opposite in this framework
senses.evidence: On the basis of the inviscid result, it seems reasonable to bet for well-posedness of the Prandtl equation (1.3) in Sobolev type spaces. The aim of this paper is to show that it is actually linearly ill-posed in this framework

senses.label: the source of instability - VISCOSITY, which is the term usually read as stabilising: the paper names viscosity and critical points in the base profile as the two ingredients
senses.head: the source of instability
senses.gloss: VISCOSITY, which is the term usually read as stabilising: the paper names viscosity and critical points in the base profile as the two ingredients
senses.evidence: As we shall see later on, the reason for illposedness is a strong destabilization mechanism due to two ingredients: viscosity, and critical points in the base velocity profile

senses.label: Inviscid-limit difficulty - no uniform vorticity bound as viscosity vanishes, corresponding physically to a boundary layer
senses.head: Inviscid-limit difficulty
senses.gloss: no uniform vorticity bound as viscosity vanishes, corresponding physically to a boundary layer
senses.evidence: One challenging open problem of fluid dynamics is to understand the inviscid limit of the Navier-Stokes equations ∂tuν + uν uν + pν ∇ − · ∇   ν∆uν = 0, x uν = 0, x |∂Ω = 0, ∇ · uν Ω, Ω, ∈ ∈ (1.1)  in a domain Ω with boundaries, endowed with a no-slip boundary condition. Mathematically, the main difficulty is the lack of uniform bounds on the vorticity field, as the viscosity ν goes to zero. In terms of fluid dynamics, this corresponds to a boundary layer phenomenon near

senses.label: Prandtl asymptotics - formally natural but not uniformly valid because boundary-layer separation can occur
senses.head: Prandtl asymptotics
senses.gloss: formally natural but not uniformly valid because boundary-layer separation can occur
senses.evidence: Although this formal asymptotics is very natural, its validity is not clear. As emphasized by physicists, including Prantdl himself, it may not hold uniformly in space and time. One reason is the so-called boundary layer separation, which is observed for flows around obstacles, see [7]. Nevertheless, the description (1.2) fits with many experiments, upstream from the separation zone. In any case, to understand the relevance and limitations of the Prandtl model is a crucial issue

senses.label: Tangential regularity obstacle - one derivative is lost without horizontal diffusion to balance it
senses.head: Tangential regularity obstacle
senses.gloss: one derivative is lost without horizontal diffusion to balance it
senses.evidence: These two problems depend crucially on the choice of the underlying functional spaces, especially on the regularity that is required in the tangential variable x. Indeed, the main mathematical difficulty is the lack of control of the x derivatives. For example, v is recovered in (1.3) through the divergence condition, and in terms of x-regularity, behaves broadly like ∂xu. This loss of one derivative is not balanced by any horizontal diffusion term, so that standard energy estimates do not apply

senses.label: Analytic setting - sufficient for local boundary-layer justification but filters instability mechanisms
senses.head: Analytic setting
senses.gloss: sufficient for local boundary-layer justification but filters instability mechanisms
senses.evidence: Various instability mechanisms, that are filtered out in an analytic framework, become a huge source of trouble. For example, when the viscosity is small, the Navier-Stokes equation admits exponentially growing solutions which are both small-scale and isotropic in x, y. Their evolution is lost in the anisotropic Prandtl description. This remark was used by Emmanuel Grenier in [6], who relied on the so-called Rayleigh instability for inviscid flows to show that the asymptotics (1.2) does not (always) hold in the Sobolev space H 1 (see [6] for a precise statement). However, the relevance of this asymptotics in Lp, or its relevance in the absence of Rayleigh instabilities, are still open issues

senses.label: Inviscid Cauchy problem - characteristic solution with finite tangential derivative loss and weak well-posedness
senses.head: Inviscid Cauchy problem
senses.gloss: characteristic solution with finite tangential derivative loss and weak well-posedness
senses.evidence: Interestingly, for a smooth initial data, this equation turns out to have an explicit solution through the method of characteristics. In particular, starting from a smooth data, one recovers locally in time a smooth data. More precisely, there is only a finite loss of x-derivatives, so that the Cauchy problem is (weakly) well-posed

senses.label: Viscous destabilization - viscosity and non-degenerate critical points jointly underlie the Sobolev failure
senses.head: Viscous destabilization
senses.gloss: viscosity and non-degenerate critical points jointly underlie the Sobolev failure
senses.evidence: the reason for illposedness is a strong destabilization mechanism due to two ingredients: viscosity, and critical points in the base velocity profile. In particular, it does not contradict the positive results obtained in the inviscid case and for monotonic data

senses.label: Strong linear ill-posedness - high-frequency perturbations grow on a square-root-frequency timescale
senses.head: Strong linear ill-posedness
senses.gloss: high-frequency perturbations grow on a square-root-frequency timescale
senses.evidence: This theorem expresses strong linear ill-posedness of the Prandtl equation in the Sobolev framework. It is a consequence of an instability process, that holds at high tangential frequencies. We will show that some perturbations with tangential frequency k 1 grow like

senses.label: Spectral reduction - PDE ill-posedness is reduced to a condition on a lower-dimensional ODE
senses.head: Spectral reduction
senses.gloss: PDE ill-posedness is reduced to a condition on a lower-dimensional ODE
senses.evidence: Thanks to this analysis, we show that ill-posedness for the PDE (1.6) comes down to a “spectral condition” for a reduced ODE

senses.label: Spectral-condition problem - existence of a heteroclinic orbit for the reduced ordinary differential equation
senses.head: Spectral-condition problem
senses.gloss: existence of a heteroclinic orbit for the reduced ordinary differential equation
senses.evidence: We need to study the existence of heteroclinic orbits for the ODE (1.7)

This gives access to the function z0. Then, a Newton-Raphson procedure allows to find a ∂zX (τ, 0). Using such a procedure, we have found zero

senses.head: Direct numerical test
senses.gloss: finite differences on a stretched grid and Crank-Nicholson time stepping from random data
senses.evidence: We have discretized this equation in space using finite differences on a stretched grid, and in time through a Crank-Nicholson scheme. Starting from initial random data (i.e. with random 1 ranging values at each gridpoint), we have computed its time evolution for values of k = ε− from 1 to 3

senses.label: Numerical confirmation - eigenvalue and eigenmode comparisons agree with theory and show the mechanism dominates linear dynamics
senses.head: Numerical confirmation
senses.gloss: eigenvalue and eigenmode comparisons agree with theory and show the mechanism dominates linear dynamics
senses.evidence: Again, we obtain an excellent agreement. This confirms that the instability mechanism we have described is indeed effective, and moreover dominates the linear dynamics

senses.label: training samples - AS RAW COUNT: around 350,000, being 40 years of hourly data
senses.head: training samples
senses.gloss: AS RAW COUNT: around 350,000, being 40 years of hourly data
senses.evidence: Another potential issue is the limited amount of training data available. 40 years of hourly data amounts to around 350,000 samples.

senses.label: training samples - AS EFFECTIVE COUNT: around 15,000, once temporal correlation is taken into account under the assumption of one new weather situation per day
senses.head: training samples
senses.gloss: AS EFFECTIVE COUNT: around 15,000, once temporal correlation is taken into account under the assumption of one new weather situation per day
senses.evidence: If one assumes that a new weather situation occurs every day, then the number of samples is reduced to around 15,000.

senses.label: success on this benchmark - defined by a SINGLE metric over two fields, which the paper presents as a virtue of the design
senses.head: success on this benchmark
senses.gloss: defined by a SINGLE metric over two fields, which the paper presents as a virtue of the design
senses.evidence: Clear metric for success: We defined a single metric (RMSE) for two fields (500 hPa geopotential and 850 hPa temperature). These scores provide a simple measure of success

senses.label: primary metric - chosen for computational convenience and for matching the ML community's loss function, not for meteorological importance; the paper states both reasons
senses.head: primary metric
senses.gloss: chosen for computational convenience and for matching the ML community's loss function, not for meteorological importance; the paper states both reasons
senses.evidence: We chose the root mean squared error (RMSE) as our primary metric because it is easy to compute and mirrors the loss used for most ML applications

senses.label: `extremes` - LEFT UNDEFINED ON PURPOSE, AND THE BENCHMARK DROPS THE PHENOMENON RATHER THAN PICK A DEFINITION: `DEFINING EXTREMES IS AMBIGUOUS WHICH IS WHY THERE IS NO STANDARD METRIC for evaluating extremes ... we decided to OMIT EXTREMES FOR NOW but users are encouraged to chose their own verification`. THE AMBIGUITY IS UPSTREAM OF THE METRIC AND THE MISSING METRIC IS UPSTREAM OF THE BENCHMARK'S SCOPE - a definitional problem propagating into what a whole field will be measured on.
senses.head: `extremes`
senses.gloss: LEFT UNDEFINED ON PURPOSE, AND THE BENCHMARK DROPS THE PHENOMENON RATHER THAN PICK A DEFINITION: `DEFINING EXTREMES IS AMBIGUOUS WHICH IS WHY THERE IS NO STANDARD METRIC for evaluating extremes ... we decided to OMIT EXTREMES FOR NOW but users are encouraged to chose their own verification`. THE AMBIGUITY IS UPSTREAM OF THE METRIC AND THE MISSING METRIC IS UPSTREAM OF THE BENCHMARK'S SCOPE - a definitional problem propagating into what a whole field will be measured on.
senses.evidence: But defining extremes is ambiguous which is why there is no standard metric for evaluating extremes. The goal of this benchmark is to provide a simple, clear problem. Therefore, we decided to omit extremes for now but users are encouraged to chose their own verification of extremes.

senses.label: Post-processing - ML correction of physical-model output bias
senses.head: Post-processing
senses.gloss: ML correction of physical-model output bias
senses.evidence: ML can be applied to weather prediction in many different ways. Two long-standing applications of ML are post-processing – the correction of statistical biases in the output of physical models – and statistical forecasting – the prediction of variables not directly output by the physical model. Traditionally, this has been done using simple linear techniques but more recently modern machine learning approaches like random forests or neural networks have been explored (Gagne et al., 2014; Taillardat et al., 2016; McGovern et al., 2017; Lagerquist et al., 2017; Rasp and Lerch, 2018). Typically, these approaches target very specific variables or locations whereas the general evolution of the atmosphere is still predicted by a physical model

senses.label: Statistical forecasting - ML prediction of variables absent from physical-model output
senses.head: Statistical forecasting
senses.gloss: ML prediction of variables absent from physical-model output
senses.evidence: ML can be applied to weather prediction in many different ways. Two long-standing applications of ML are post-processing – the correction of statistical biases in the output of physical models – and statistical forecasting – the prediction of variables not directly output by the physical model. Traditionally, this has been done using simple linear techniques but more recently modern machine learning approaches like random forests or neural networks have been explored (Gagne et al., 2014; Taillardat et al., 2016; McGovern et al., 2017; Lagerquist et al., 2017; Rasp and Lerch, 2018). Typically, these approaches target very specific variables or locations whereas the general evolution of the atmosphere is still predicted by a physical model

senses.label: Nowcasting - radar-only precipitation extrapolation up to six hours
senses.head: Nowcasting
senses.gloss: radar-only precipitation extrapolation up to six hours
senses.evidence: Another application that has recently been explored using ML is nowcasting, which describes the short range (up to 6 hours) prediction of precipitation by directly extrapolating radar observation without a physical model involved

senses.label: Hybrid weather model - physical dynamics with selected uncertain or expensive components replaced by ML emulators
senses.head: Hybrid weather model
senses.gloss: physical dynamics with selected uncertain or expensive components replaced by ML emulators
senses.evidence: Yet another direction for ML research is hybrid modeling, in which a physical model is combined with data-driven components, for example replacing heuristic cloud or radiation parameterizations (Chevallier et al., 1998; Krasnopolsky et al., 2005; Rasp et al., 2018; Brenowitz and Bretherton, 2018; Yuval and O’Gorman, 2020). The key idea behind these approaches is to only replace uncertain (e.g. clouds) or computationally expensive (e.g. line-by-line radiation) model components with machine learning emulators and leave other model components (e.g. large-scale dynamics) untouched

senses.label: WeatherBench medium range - direct global atmospheric-flow prediction at three- and five-day leads
senses.head: WeatherBench medium range
senses.gloss: direct global atmospheric-flow prediction at three- and five-day leads
senses.evidence: Here we focus on purely-data driven prediction of the global atmospheric flow in the medium-range. Specifically, we select lead times of 3 and 5 days, for which the atmosphere is still reasonably deterministic but also exhibits complex nonlinear behaviour, such as baroclinic instabilities and tropical cyclogenesis. This forecast range is important from a societal point of view because it delivers crucial information for disaster preparation, for example for flooding, cold and hot spells or damaging winds (Lazo et al., 2009). Creating a good medium-range forecast requires understanding complex atmospheric dynamics and the interplay between several variables across a range of scales. This sets this challenge apart from post-processing and statistical forecasting, in which the large-scale dynamics are predicted by a physical model, and nowcasting, in which the considered evolution is univariate and short-term. In other words, this benchmark closely emulates the task performed by physical NWP models

senses.label: ERA5 reanalysis - forecast-model and observation synthesis used as atmospheric truth proxy
senses.head: ERA5 reanalysis
senses.gloss: forecast-model and observation synthesis used as atmospheric truth proxy
senses.evidence: For the proposed benchmark, we use the ERA5 reanalysis dataset (Hersbach et al., 2020) for training and testing. Reanalysis datasets provide the best guess of the atmospheric state at any point in time by combining a forecast model with the available observations. The raw data is available hourly for 40 years from 1979 to 2018 on a 0.25°latitude-longitude grid (721×1440 grid points) with 37 vertical levels

senses.label: Train / validation / test - fitting data, tuning data, and held final-evaluation data
senses.head: Train / validation / test
senses.gloss: fitting data, tuning data, and held final-evaluation data
senses.evidence: However, there is the danger that through continued tuning of hyperparameters one unwillingly overfits to the validation dataset. Therefore it is advisable to keep a third, testing, dataset for final evaluations of model performance

senses.label: Persistence forecast - tomorrow’s field set equal to today’s field
senses.head: Persistence forecast
senses.gloss: tomorrow’s field set equal to today’s field
senses.evidence: The two simplest possible forecasts are a) a persistence forecast in which the fields at initialization time are used as forecasts ("tomorrow’s weather is today’s weather"), and b) a climatological forecast

senses.label: Direct / iterative forecast - lead-specific model versus recursively applied short-lead model
senses.head: Direct / iterative forecast
senses.gloss: lead-specific model versus recursively applied short-lead model
senses.evidence: As a first purely data-driven baseline we fit a simple linear regression model. For the direct predictions a separate model was trained for each of the four variables. For this purpose the 2D fields were flattened from 32×64 → 2048. This was done for 3 d and 5 d forecast time. In addition an iterative model for Z500 and T850 was trained. Here we use a single linear regression to predict 6 hours ahead where the two fields are concatenated (2×32×64 → 4096). The advantage of iterative forecasts is that a single model is able to make predictions for any forecast time rather than having to train several models. For iterative forecasts the model takes its previous output as input for the next step. To create a 5 day iterative forecast the model trained to predict 6 hour forecasts is called 20 times

senses.label: CNN weather baseline - fully convolutional Z500/T850 model with longitude-periodic kernels
senses.head: CNN weather baseline
senses.gloss: fully convolutional Z500/T850 model with longitude-periodic kernels
senses.evidence: As our deep learning baseline we chose a simple fully-convolutional neural network. CNNs are the natural choice for spatial data since they exploit translational invariances in images/fields. Here we train a CNN with 5 layers. Each hidden layer has 64 channels with a convolutional kernel of size 5 and ELU activations (Clevert et al., 2015). The input and output layers have two channels, representing Z500 and T850. The model was trained using the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2014) and a mean squared error loss function. The total number of trainable parameters is 313,858. We implemented periodic convolutions in the longitude direction but not the latitude direction

senses.label: Transfer learning - pretrain on related simulations, then fine-tune on target observations
senses.head: Transfer learning
senses.gloss: pretrain on related simulations, then fine-tune on target observations
senses.evidence: Should overfitting be a problem, one could try transfer learning. In transfer learning, the network is pretrained on a similar task or dataset, for example, climate model simulations, and then finetuned on the actual data. This is common practice in computer vision and has been successfully applied to seasonal ENSO forecasting

senses.label: Physical-field augmentation - overfitting control constrained by non-interchangeable spatial directions
senses.head: Physical-field augmentation
senses.gloss: overfitting control constrained by non-interchangeable spatial directions
senses.evidence: Another common method to prevent overfitting is data augmentation, which in traditional computer vision is done by e.g. randomly rotating or flipping the image. However, many of the traditional data augmentation techniques are questionable for physical fields. Random rotations, for example, will likely not work for this dataset since the x and y directions are physically distinct. Thus, finding good data augmentation techniques for physical fields is an outstanding problem

senses.label: Probabilistic forecast - ensemble or parametric distribution expressing uncertainty
senses.head: Probabilistic forecast
senses.gloss: ensemble or parametric distribution expressing uncertainty
senses.evidence: One important aspect that is not currently addressed by this benchmark is probabilistic forecasting. Because of the chaotic evolution of the atmosphere, it is very important to also have an estimate of the uncertainty of a forecast. In physical NWP this is done by running several forecasts, called an ensemble, from slightly different initial conditions and potentially with different or stochastic model physics (Palmer, 2019). From this Monte Carlo forecast one can then estimate a probability distribution. A different approach, which is often taken in statistical post-processing of NWP forecasts, is to directly estimate a parametric distribution

senses.label: Forecast reliability - uncertainty accurately indicates error
senses.head: Forecast reliability
senses.gloss: uncertainty accurately indicates error
senses.evidence: For a probabilistic forecast to be reliable the forecast uncertainty has to be an accurate indicator of the error. A good first order approximation for this is the spread (ensemble standard deviation) to error (RMSE) ratio which should be one (Leutbecher and Palmer, 2008). A more stringent test is to use a proper probabilistic scoring rule, for example the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS)

senses.label: Weather / climate prediction - future state before the horizon versus long-term statistics
senses.head: Weather / climate prediction
senses.gloss: future state before the horizon versus long-term statistics
senses.evidence: Even though weather and climate deal with the same underlying physical system, they pose different forecasting challenges. In weather forecasting the goal is to predict the state of the atmosphere at a specific time into the future. This is only possible up to the prediction horizon of the atmosphere, which is thought to be at roughly two weeks. Climate models, on the other hand, are evaluated by comparing long-term statistics to observations

senses.label: Climate-change extrapolation - future states outside the historical training manifold
senses.head: Climate-change extrapolation
senses.gloss: future states outside the historical training manifold
senses.evidence: future climates will produce atmospheric states that lie outside of the historical manifold of states. Plain neural networks are very bad at extrapolating to climates beyond what they have seen in the training dataset (Rasp et al., 2018). For this reason, climate change simulations with current data-driven methods are likely not a good idea

senses.label: upper limit on Λ(1.4 M⊙) - UNDER THE LOW-SPIN PRIOR: 800, the value obtained when component spins are restricted to the range seen in known binary neutron stars
senses.head: upper limit on Λ(1.4 M⊙)
senses.gloss: UNDER THE LOW-SPIN PRIOR: 800, the value obtained when component spins are restricted to the range seen in known binary neutron stars
senses.evidence: which gives Λð1.4M⊙Þ ≤ 1400 for the high-spin prior and Λð1.4M⊙Þ ≤ 800 for the lowspin prior.

senses.label: upper limit on Λ(1.4 M⊙) - UNDER THE HIGH-SPIN PRIOR: 1400, the value obtained when the spin range is left wide, which is the same measurement under a weaker assumption
senses.head: upper limit on Λ(1.4 M⊙)
senses.gloss: UNDER THE HIGH-SPIN PRIOR: 1400, the value obtained when the spin range is left wide, which is the same measurement under a weaker assumption
senses.evidence: we place a 90% upper limit of ~Λ ≤ 800 in the low-spin case and ~Λ ≤ 700 in the high-spin case.

senses.label: direct evidence - in this paper, strain measured in an interferometer, defined against the INDIRECT evidence of 1974: orbital energy loss in PSR B1913+16
senses.head: direct evidence
senses.gloss: in this paper, strain measured in an interferometer, defined against the INDIRECT evidence of 1974: orbital energy loss in PSR B1913+16
senses.evidence: Observations of PSR B1913+16 found that its orbit was losing energy due to the emission of gravitational waves, providing the first indirect evidence of their existence

senses.label: GW170817 detection - SNR 32.4, extremely low estimated false-alarm rate, 28-square-degree localization, and about 40 Mpc distance
senses.head: GW170817 detection
senses.gloss: SNR 32.4, extremely low estimated false-alarm rate, 28-square-degree localization, and about 40 Mpc distance
senses.evidence: On August 17, 2017 at 12∶41:04 UTC the Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo gravitational-wave detectors made their first observation of a binary neutron star inspiral. The signal, GW170817, was detected with a combined signal-to-noise ratio of 32.4 and a false-alarm-rate estimate of less than one per 8.0 × 104 years. We infer the component masses of the binary to be between 0.86 and 2.26 M⊙, in agreement with masses of known neutron stars. Restricting the component spins to the range inferred in binary neutron stars, we find the component masses to be in the range 1.17–1.60 M⊙, with the total mass of the system 2.74+0.04 −0.01 M⊙. The source was localized within a sky region of 28 deg2 (90% probability) and had a luminosity distance of 40+8 −14 Mpc, the closest and most precisely localized gravitational-wave signal yet. The association with the γ-ray burst GRB 170817A, detected by Fermi-GBM 1.7 s after the coalescence, corroborates the hypothesis of a neutron star merger and provides the first direct evidence of a link between these mergers and short γ-ray bursts. Subsequent identification of transient counterparts across the electromagnetic spectrum in the same location further supports the interpretation of this event as a neutron star merger. This unprecedented joint gravitational and electromagnetic observation provides insight into astrophysics, dense matter, gravitation, and cosmology

senses.label: Binary inspiral - gravitational radiation removes orbital energy, shrinking and accelerating the orbit while luminosity rises
senses.head: Binary inspiral
senses.gloss: gravitational radiation removes orbital energy, shrinking and accelerating the orbit while luminosity rises
senses.evidence: Observations of PSR B1913+16 found that its orbit was losing energy due to the emission of gravitational waves, providing the first indirect evidence of their existence [2]. As the orbit of a the gravitational-wave luminosity BNS system shrinks, increases, accelerating the inspiral. This process has long been predicted to produce a gravitational-wave signal observable by ground-based detectors [3–6] in the final minutes before the stars collide

senses.label: Low-latency identification - post-Newtonian template search first saw Hanford alone because Livingston saturated and Virgo transfer lagged
senses.head: Low-latency identification
senses.gloss: post-Newtonian template search first saw Hanford alone because Livingston saturated and Virgo transfer lagged
senses.evidence: GW170817 was initially identified as a single-detector event with the LIGO-Hanford detector by a low-latency binary-coalescence search [81–83] using template waveforms computed in post-Newtonian theory [11,13,36,84]. The two LIGO detectors and the Virgo detector were all taking data at the time; however, the saturation at the LIGO- Livingston detector prevented the search from registering a simultaneous event in both LIGO detectors, and the lowlatency transfer of Virgo data was delayed

senses.label: Detection statistic / background - candidate signal ranking against the frequency with which noise reaches the same score
senses.head: Detection statistic / background
senses.gloss: candidate signal ranking against the frequency with which noise reaches the same score
senses.evidence: Events are assigned a detection-statistic value that ranks their probability of being a gravitational-wave signal. Each search uses a different method to compute this statistic and measure the search background—the rate at which detector noise produces events with a detection-statistic value equal to or higher than the candidate event

senses.label: Chirp mass - component-mass combination dominating low-frequency chirp evolution
senses.head: Chirp mass
senses.gloss: component-mass combination dominating low-frequency chirp evolution
senses.evidence: At early times, for low orbital and gravitational-wave frequencies, the chirplike time evolution of the frequency is determined primarily by a specific combination of the component masses m1 and m2, the chirp mass M ¼ ðm1m2Þ3=5ðm1 þ m2Þ−1=5. As the orbit shrinks and the gravitational-wave frequency grows rapidly, the gravitational-wave phase is increasingly influenced by relativistic effects related to the mass ratio q ¼ m2=m1, where m1 ≥ m2, as well as spin-orbit and spin-spin couplings

senses.label: Waveform phase - progressively influenced by mass ratio and spin couplings as the orbit shrinks
senses.head: Waveform phase
senses.gloss: progressively influenced by mass ratio and spin couplings as the orbit shrinks
senses.evidence: At early times, for low orbital and gravitational-wave frequencies, the chirplike time evolution of the frequency is determined primarily by a specific combination of the component masses m1 and m2, the chirp mass M ¼ ðm1m2Þ3=5ðm1 þ m2Þ−1=5. As the orbit shrinks and the gravitational-wave frequency grows rapidly, the gravitational-wave phase is increasingly influenced by relativistic effects related to the mass ratio q ¼ m2=m1, where m1 ≥ m2, as well as spin-orbit and spin-spin couplings

senses.label: Source-property inference - Bayesian matching of detector data to predicted waveforms with calibration uncertainty included
senses.head: Source-property inference
senses.gloss: Bayesian matching of detector data to predicted waveforms with calibration uncertainty included
senses.evidence: The properties of gravitational-wave sources are inferred by matching the data with predicted waveforms. We perform a Bayesian analysis in the frequency range 30–2048 Hz that includes the effects of the 1σ calibration uncertainties on the received signal [135,136] (< 7% in amplitude and 3° in phase for the LIGO detectors [137] and 10% and 10° for Virgo at the time of the event)

senses.label: Glitch-mitigation validation - recovered-parameter bias remains within uncertainty after subtraction
senses.head: Glitch-mitigation validation
senses.gloss: recovered-parameter bias remains within uncertainty after subtraction
senses.evidence: After applying the glitch subtraction technique, we found that the bias in recovered parameters relative to their known values was well within their uncertainties. This can be understood by noting that a small time cut out of the coherent integration of the phase evolution has little impact on the recovered parameters

senses.label: Three-detector localization - timing, phase, and amplitude jointly restrict the event to one small region
senses.head: Three-detector localization
senses.gloss: timing, phase, and amplitude jointly restrict the event to one small region
senses.evidence: The source was localized to a region of the sky 28 deg2 in area, and 380 Mpc3 in volume, near the southern end of the constellation Hydra, by using a combination of the timing, phase, and amplitude of the source as observed in the three detectors [138,139]. The third detector, Virgo, was essential in localizing the source to a single region of the sky, as shown in Fig. 3. The small sky area triggered a successful follow-up campaign that identified an electromagnetic counterpart

senses.label: Distance / inclination degeneracy - independent host distance sharpens the source viewing angle
senses.head: Distance / inclination degeneracy
senses.gloss: independent host distance sharpens the source viewing angle
senses.evidence: The distance measurement is correlated with the inclination angle cos θJN ¼ ˆJ · ˆN, where ˆJ is the unit vector in the direction of the total angular momentum of the system and ˆN is that from the source towards the observer [140]. We find that the data are consistent with an antialigned source: cos θJN ≤ −0.54, and the viewing angle Θ ≡ minðθJN; 180° − θJNÞ is Θ ≤ 56°. Since the luminosity distance of this source can be determined independently of the gravitational wave data alone, we can use the association with NGC 4993 to break the distance degeneracy with cos θJN

senses.label: Mass / spin prior dependence - well-constrained chirp mass coexists with component masses sensitive to admissible spin
senses.head: Mass / spin prior dependence
senses.gloss: well-constrained chirp mass coexists with component masses sensitive to admissible spin
senses.evidence: While the chirp mass is well constrained, our estimates of the component masses are affected by the degeneracy between mass ratio q and the aligned spin components χ1z and χ2z [38,146–150]. Therefore, the estimates of q and the component masses depend on assumptions made about the admissible values of the spins

senses.label: Equation-of-state constraint - recovered deformabilities disfavor less compact stars, while a shared-EOS assumption should improve bounds
senses.head: Equation-of-state constraint
senses.gloss: recovered deformabilities disfavor less compact stars, while a shared-EOS assumption should improve bounds
senses.evidence: We find that our constraints on Λ1 and Λ2 disfavor equations of state that predict less compact stars, since the mass range we recover generates Λ values outside the 90% probability region. This is consistent with radius constraints from x-ray observations of neutron stars [162–166]. Analysis methods, in development, that a priori assume the same EOS governs both stars should improve our constraints

senses.label: Tidal-deformability systematics - current post-Newtonian limits are treated as conservative pending improved models
senses.head: Tidal-deformability systematics
senses.gloss: current post-Newtonian limits are treated as conservative pending improved models
senses.evidence: Therefore, based on our current understanding of the physics of neutron stars, we consider the post-Newtonian results presented in this Letter to be conservative upper limits on tidal deformability. Refinements should be possible as our knowledge and models improve

senses.label: Postmerger remnant - neutron-star or black-hole outcomes whose high-frequency radiation is difficult to observe
senses.head: Postmerger remnant
senses.gloss: neutron-star or black-hole outcomes whose high-frequency radiation is difficult to observe
senses.evidence: Binary neutron star mergers may result in a shortor longlived neutron star remnant that could emit gravitational waves following the merger [184–190]. The ringdown of a black hole formed after the coalescence could also produce gravitational waves, at frequencies around 6 kHz, but the reduced interferometer response at high frequencies makes their observation unfeasible

senses.label: Multi-messenger gravity test - 1.7-second GW/GRB delay constrains propagation speed, Lorentz symmetry, and equivalence
senses.head: Multi-messenger gravity test
senses.gloss: 1.7-second GW/GRB delay constrains propagation speed, Lorentz symmetry, and equivalence
senses.evidence: GRB 170817A was observed 1.7 s after GW170817. Combining this delay with the knowledge of the source luminosity distance, strong constraints are placed on the fundamental physics of gravity. The observed arrival times are used to investigate the speed of gravity, Lorentz invariance, and tests of the equivalence principle through the Shapiro time delay, as reported in [45]. We also expect the much longer duration of the BNS signal compared to previous BBH gravitational-wave sources to yield significantly improved constraints when testing for waveform deviations from general relativity using a parametrized waveform expansion [194], especially at low post-Newtonian orders. Placing these bounds requires a deep understanding of the systematic uncertainties resulting from waveform modeling and data conditioning, and is the subject of ongoing investigations

senses.label: Standard-siren cosmology - gravitational-wave distance plus host redshift measures H0 without the cosmic distance ladder
senses.head: Standard-siren cosmology
senses.gloss: gravitational-wave distance plus host redshift measures H0 without the cosmic distance ladder
senses.evidence: The gravitational-wave signal gives a direct measurement of the luminosity distance of the source, which, along with a redshift measurement, can be used to infer cosmological parameters independently of the cosmic distance ladder

senses.label: GW170817 interpretation - joint gravitational and electromagnetic analyses inform compact binaries, dense matter, gravitation, and cosmology
senses.head: GW170817 interpretation
senses.gloss: joint gravitational and electromagnetic analyses inform compact binaries, dense matter, gravitation, and cosmology
senses.evidence: Subsequent observations have determined the location of the source and followed its evolution through the electromagnetic spectrum [50]. Detailed analyses of the gravitational-wave data, together with observations of electromagnetic emissions, are providing new insights into the astrophysics of compact binary systems and γ-ray bursts, dense matter under extreme conditions, the nature of gravitation, and independent tests of cosmology. Less than two years after the debut of gravitational-wave astronomy, GW170817 marks the beginning of a new era of discovery

senses.label: concept - BACKGROUND: everything the term has meant across the literature, contested and changing
senses.head: concept
senses.gloss: BACKGROUND: everything the term has meant across the literature, contested and changing
senses.evidence: The background concept comprises the full and diverse set of meanings that might be associated with a particular term.

senses.label: concept - SYSTEMATIZED: the one definition this study adopts, chosen for its question and framework
senses.head: concept
senses.gloss: SYSTEMATIZED: the one definition this study adopts, chosen for its question and framework
senses.evidence: That definition, in turn, represents the systematized concept: the formulation that is adopted for the study.

senses.label: accuracy - as VALIDITY: what it is usually presented as, and what it cannot be without an objective standard
senses.head: accuracy
senses.gloss: as VALIDITY: what it is usually presented as, and what it cannot be without an objective standard
senses.evidence: Accuracy, as well as other measures such as precision, recall and F-score, are sometimes presented as a measure of validity, but if we do not have a genuinely objective determination of what something is supposed measure—as is often the case in text analysis—then accuracy is perhaps a better indication of reliability than of validity.

senses.label: accuracy - as RELIABILITY: consistency against a human sample, which is what it actually measures when no ground truth exists
senses.head: accuracy
senses.gloss: as RELIABILITY: consistency against a human sample, which is what it actually measures when no ground truth exists
senses.evidence: In NLP and machine learning, most models are primarily evaluated by comparing the machine-generated labels against an annotated sample.

senses.label: ambiguity - in computational linguistics: a problem to be solved, on the assumption that one correct interpretation exists
senses.head: ambiguity
senses.gloss: in computational linguistics: a problem to be solved, on the assumption that one correct interpretation exists
senses.evidence: In Computational Linguistics [.] ambiguity is almost uniformly treated as a problem to be solved; the focus is on disambiguation, with the assumption that one true, correct interpretation exists .

senses.label: ambiguity - in literary criticism: prized, alongside interpretation and argumentation, above definitive conclusions
senses.head: ambiguity
senses.gloss: in literary criticism: prized, alongside interpretation and argumentation, above definitive conclusions
senses.evidence: interpretation, ambiguity, and argumentation are prized far above ground truth and definitive conclusions.

senses.label: annotator disagreement - as NOISE: a failure of the scheme or the coders, to be reduced
senses.head: annotator disagreement
senses.gloss: as NOISE: a failure of the scheme or the coders, to be reduced
senses.evidence: Disagreement between annotators can signal weaknesses of the annotation scheme, or highlight the inherent ambiguity in what we are trying to measure.

senses.label: annotator disagreement - as SIGNAL: a property of the concept, which can be carried into the analysis rather than resolved away
senses.head: annotator disagreement
senses.gloss: as SIGNAL: a property of the concept, which can be carried into the analysis rather than resolved away
senses.evidence: Disagreement itself can be meaningful and can be integrated in subsequent analyses (Aroyo and Welty, 2013 ; Demeester et al., 2016 ).

senses.label: Insight-driven analysis - describes or explains a phenomenon rather than optimizing a prediction task
senses.head: Insight-driven analysis
senses.gloss: describes or explains a phenomenon rather than optimizing a prediction task
senses.evidence: Computational analysis of text motivated by these questions is insight driven: we aim to describe a phenomenon or explain how it came about. For example, what can we learn about how and why hate speech is used or how this changes over time? Is hate speech one thing, or does it comprise multiple forms of expression? Is there a clear boundary between hate speech and other types of speech, and what features make it more or less ambiguous? In these cases, it is critical to communicate high-level patterns in terms that are recognizable. This contrasts with much of the work in computational text analysis, which tends to focus on automating tasks that humans perform inefficiently. These tasks range from the annotation of linguistic features that constitute the backbone of natural language processing (NLP), such as part-of-speech tagging (assigning parts of speech to words), to tasks such as spam filtering and sentiment detection, which are motivated by applications like online content moderation. Success, then, is often measured by performance, and communicating why a certain prediction was made—for example, why a document was labeled as positive sentiment, or why a word was classified as a noun—has traditionally been less important than the accuracy of the prediction itself. While more recent research has focused on building systems whose predictions are “explainable” (Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) or whose workings are “interpretable” (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017 ; Lipton, 2018 ), such approaches still center the task of prediction, rather than the generation of insights about relationships between theoretically-motivated constructs

senses.label: Dual use - a protective hate-speech method may also be adapted to suppress marginalized speech or dissent
senses.head: Dual use
senses.gloss: a protective hate-speech method may also be adapted to suppress marginalized speech or dissent
senses.evidence: Questions about potential “dual use” may also arise. Returning to our introductory example, Chandrasekharan et al. ( 2017 ) started with a deceptively simple question: if an internet platform eliminates forums for hate speech, does this impact hate speech in other forums? The research was motivated by the belief that a rising tide of online hate speech was (and is) making the internet increasingly unfriendly for disempowered groups, including minorities, women, and LBGTQ individuals. Yet the possibility of dual use troubled the researchers from the onset. Could the methodology be adopted to target the speech of groups like Black Lives Matter? Could it be adopted by repressive governments to minimize online dissent? While these concerns remained, they concluded that hypothetical dual use scenarios did not outweigh the tangible contribution this research could offer toward making the online environment more equal and just

senses.label: Born-digital evidence - massive and unobtrusive, yet ethically constrained by contextual privacy and absent consent
senses.head: Born-digital evidence
senses.gloss: massive and unobtrusive, yet ethically constrained by contextual privacy and absent consent
senses.evidence: The use of born-digital data raises ethical concerns. Although early studies often treated privacy as a binary construct, many now acknowledge its complexity (danah boyd and Crawford, 2012 ). Conversations on private matters can be posted online, visible for all, but social norms regarding what should be considered public information may differ from the data's explicit visibility settings. Often no informed consent has been obtained, raising concerns and challenges regarding publishing content and potentially harmful secondary uses (Salganik, 2017 ; Williams et al., 2017 ). Recently, concerns about potential harms stemming from secondary uses have led a number of digital service providers to restrict access to born-digital data. Facebook and Twitter, for example, have reduced or eliminated public access to their application programming interfaces (APIs) and expressed hesitation about allowing academic researchers to use data from their platforms

senses.label: Black-box collection - commercial APIs can introduce unknown biases into research inference
senses.head: Black-box collection
senses.gloss: commercial APIs can introduce unknown biases into research inference
senses.evidence: Working with data that someone else has acquired presents additional problems related to provenance and contextualization. It may not always be possible to determine the criteria applied during the creation process. For example, why were certain newspapers digitized but not others, and what does this say about the collection? Similar questions arise with the use of born-digital data. For instance, when using the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine to gather data from archived web pages, we need to consider what pages were captured, which are likely missing, and why. We must often repurpose born-digital data (e.g., Twitter was not designed to measure public opinion), but data biases may lead to spurious results and limit justification for generalization (Olteanu et al., 2019 ). In particular, data collected via black box APIs designed for commercial, not research, purposes are likely to introduce biases into the inferences we draw, and the closed nature of these APIs means we rarely know what biases are introduced, let alone how severely they might impact our research

senses.label: Restricted generalization - biased data can support within-population comparison when claims stay within that population
senses.head: Restricted generalization
senses.gloss: biased data can support within-population comparison when claims stay within that population
senses.evidence: These biases limit the generalizability of the findings, which cannot be extrapolated to other languages, other types of hate speech, and other demographic groups. However, because the findings are based on measurements on the same sort of hate speech and the same population of writers, as long as the collected data are representative of this specific population, these biases do not pose an intractable validity problem if claims are properly restricted

senses.label: Counterfactual control - matched untreated forums estimate what would have happened without platform closure
senses.head: Counterfactual control
senses.gloss: matched untreated forums estimate what would have happened without platform closure
senses.evidence: Chandrasekharan et al. used a matching design, populating the control group with forums that were as similar as possible to the treatment group, but were not banned from Reddit. The goal is to estimate the counterfactual scenario: in this case, what would have happened had the site not taken action against these specific forums? An ideal control would make it possible to distinguish the effect of the treatment—closing the forums—from other idiosyncratic properties of texts that were treated

senses.label: Discretization tradeoff - categories facilitate nonlinear analysis but overly broad bins threaten validity
senses.head: Discretization tradeoff
senses.gloss: categories facilitate nonlinear analysis but overly broad bins threaten validity
senses.evidence: Discretization—converting a continuous variable to a discrete variable—can facilitate quantitative analysis when the relationship of interest is non-linear. For example, research in both natural language processing and sociolinguistics has often modeled age as a categorical variable (Eckert, 1997 ; Nguyen et al., 2016 ). But any discretization raises questions: How many categories? Where to place the boundaries? Fine distinctions might not always be meaningful for the analysis we are interested in, but categories that are too broad can threaten validity

senses.label: Supervised versus unsupervised learning - labels learned from annotated data versus structure learned from unlabeled data
senses.head: Supervised versus unsupervised learning
senses.gloss: labels learned from annotated data versus structure learned from unlabeled data
senses.evidence: Supervised and unsupervised learning are the most common approaches to learning from data. With supervised learning, a model learns from labeled data (e.g., social media messages labeled by sentiment) to infer (or predict) these labels from unlabeled texts. In contrast, unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data

senses.label: Annotation disagreement - can reveal either scheme weaknesses or inherent ambiguity and may itself be retained as signal
senses.head: Annotation disagreement
senses.gloss: can reveal either scheme weaknesses or inherent ambiguity and may itself be retained as signal
senses.evidence: Disagreement between annotators can signal weaknesses of the annotation scheme, or highlight the inherent ambiguity in what we are trying to measure. Disagreement itself can be meaningful and can be integrated in subsequent analyses

senses.label: Preprocessing provenance - operationally consequential choices should be documented like editorial or biomedical protocols
senses.head: Preprocessing provenance
senses.gloss: operationally consequential choices should be documented like editorial or biomedical protocols
senses.evidence: Preparing the data can be a complex and time-consuming process, often involving working with partially or wholly unstructured data. The pre-processing steps have a big impact on the operationalizations, subsequent analyses and reproducibility efforts (Fokkens et al., 2013 ), and they are usually tightly linked to what we intend to measure. Unfortunately, these steps tend to be underreported, but documenting the pre-processing choices made is essential and is analogous to recording the decisions taken during the production of a scholarly edition or protocols in biomedical research

senses.label: Tokenization - seemingly basic segmentation that can fail on creative orthography and transform multi-word patterns
senses.head: Tokenization
senses.gloss: seemingly basic segmentation that can fail on creative orthography and transform multi-word patterns
senses.evidence: One step that almost everyone takes is to tokenize the original character sequence into the words and word-like units. Tokenization is a more subtle and more powerful process than people expect. It is often done using regular expressions or scripts that have been circulating within the NLP community. Tokenization heuristics, however, can be badly confused by emoticons, creative orthography (e.g., U$A, sh!t), and missing whitespace. Multi-word terms are also challenging. Treating them as a single unit can dramatically alter the patterns in text. Many words that are individually ambiguous have clear, unmistakable meanings as terms, like “black hole” or “European Union.” However, deciding what constitutes a multi-word term is a difficult problem. In writing systems like Chinese, tokenization is a research problem in its own right

senses.label: Word-piece segmentation - effective for prediction but potentially unsuitable when linguistic-unit interpretation matters
senses.head: Word-piece segmentation
senses.gloss: effective for prediction but potentially unsuitable when linguistic-unit interpretation matters
senses.evidence: Current state-of-the-art techniques in NLP address these issues by applying statistical segmentation techniques to whitespace-delimited tokens, yielding a sequence of “word pieces” to be used for all downstream processing (Kudo and Richardson, 2018 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ). Word pieces do not necessarily correspond to linguistically meaningful units such as inflectional affixes; furthermore, languages like Arabic employ systems of morphology that cannot be captured by segmentation (Soudi et al., 2007 ). Thus, while this style of segmentation is sufficient for highly accurate prediction in many tasks, it may not be suitable in cases where interpretability of specific linguistic units is essential

senses.label: Domain dictionary construction - automation proposes candidates and human theory filters spurious features
senses.head: Domain dictionary construction
senses.gloss: automation proposes candidates and human theory filters spurious features
senses.evidence: Corpus- or domain-specific dictionaries can overcome limitations of general-purpose dictionaries. The dictionaries are often manually compiled, but increasingly they are constructed semi-automatically (e.g., Fast et al., 2016 ). When we semi-automatically create a word list, we use automation to identify an initial word list, and human insight to filter it. By automatically generating the initial words lists, words can be identified that human annotators might have difficulty intuiting. By manually filtering the lists, we use our theoretical understanding of the target concept to remove spurious features

senses.label: Post-hoc explanation - interprets individual predictions without guaranteeing fidelity to the underlying model
senses.head: Post-hoc explanation
senses.gloss: interprets individual predictions without guaranteeing fidelity to the underlying model
senses.evidence: One way would be to only use models that are already somewhat interpretable, for example models that use a small number of human-interpretable features. Rather than imposing such restrictions, there is also work on generating post-hoc explanations for individual predictions (e.g., Ribeiro et al. ( 2016 )), even when the underlying model itself is very complex. However, a concern with post-hoc explanations is that they may not faithfully reflect the behavior of the original model

senses.label: Topic count - a user-selected analytical scale like map scale or microscope magnification, not an intrinsic truth
senses.head: Topic count
senses.gloss: a user-selected analytical scale like map scale or microscope magnification, not an intrinsic truth
senses.evidence: One of the most common questions about topic models is how many topics to use, usually with the implicit assumption that there is a “right” number that is inherent in the collection. We prefer to think of this parameter as more like the scale of a map or the magnification of a microscope. The “right” number is determined by the needs of the user, not by the collection. If the analyst is looking for a broad overview, a relatively small number of topics may be best. If the analyst is looking for fine-grained phenomena, a larger number is better

senses.label: Content revalidation - jointly interrogates concept, indicators, and scores and may force recoding or method replacement
senses.head: Content revalidation
senses.gloss: jointly interrogates concept, indicators, and scores and may force recoding or method replacement
senses.evidence: Along similar lines, we can subject both the machine-generated output and the human annotations to another round of content validation. That is, take a stratified random sample, selecting observations from the full range of scores, and ask: Do these make sense in light of the systematized concept? If not, what seems to be missing? Or is something extraneous being captured? This is primarily a qualitative process that requires returning to theory and interrogating the systematized concept, indicators, and scores together. This type of validation is rarely done in NLP, but it is especially important when it is difficult to assess what drives a given machine learning model. If there is a mismatch between the scores and systematized concept at this stage, the codebook may need to be adjusted, human coders retrained, more training data prepared, algorithms adjusted, or in some instances, even a new analytical method adopted

senses.label: Computational and qualitative analysis - complementary scales for trends and individual stories
senses.head: Computational and qualitative analysis
senses.gloss: complementary scales for trends and individual stories
senses.evidence: Computational text analysis is not a replacement for but rather an addition to the approaches one can take to analyze social and cultural phenomena using textual data. By moving back and forth between large-scale computational analyses and small-scale qualitative analyses, we can combine their strengths so that we can identify large-scale and long-term trends, but also tell individual stories

senses.label: PRIMING AS PROCESSING SKIPPED, NOT PROCESSING SPED UP. `A direct association forms between the stimulus presented and the response made to it. On a subsequent encounter with the stimulus, this association automatically cues the response, BYPASSING the various processing stages that were required to select that response during its first presentation.` That is a different claim from facilitation and from sharpening, and it makes a prediction neither does: change the response and the saving disappears
senses.evidence: According to this view, a direct association forms between the stimulus presented and the response made to it. On a subsequent encounter with the stimulus, this association automatically cues the response, bypassing the various processing stages that were required to select that response during its first presentation

senses.label: REPETITION SUPPRESSION IS NOT ONE THING, and this is the record that splits it: `a dissociation between RS within the PFC, which may be sensitive to retrieval of stimulus-response associations, and RS within posterior perceptual regions, which may reflect facilitation of perceptual pr[ocessing]`. Two regions, two mechanisms, one name. Gotts2012 reviews four candidate mechanisms as though the phenomenon were unitary; here it is divided by anatomy and each half takes a different explanation
senses.evidence: In contrast, RS within ventral temporal regions (such as the fusiform cortex), which are usually associated with perceptual processing, is shown to be robust to response changes. The present study therefore suggests a dissociation between RS within the PFC

senses.label: THE ACCOUNT Humphries2018 TESTED AND DID NOT REPLICATE, and the two records are three hours apart in this corpus. Humphries changed the RESPONSE HAND - a manipulation the binding account predicts should break the saving - and found a negligible effect, noting that the study which did find one contrasted VERBAL with KEYPRESS responses. That is this paper. So the corpus holds the account, its confirmation, and a null against it at a smaller manipulation, with both papers' own hedges attached
senses.head: THE ACCOUNT Humphries2018 TESTED AND DID NOT REPLICATE, and the two records are three hours apart in this corpus. Humphries changed the RESPONSE HAND
senses.gloss: a manipulation the binding account predicts should break the saving - and found a negligible effect, noting that the study which did find one contrasted VERBAL with KEYPRESS responses. That is this paper. So the corpus holds the account, its confirmation, and a null against it at a smaller manipulation, with both papers' own hedges attached
senses.evidence: Recent research has suggested that both behavioural priming and RS can be largely determined by previously learned stimulus–response associations. According to this view, a direct association forms between the stimulus presented and the response made to it

senses.label: Component-process view - priming follows faster or more efficient processing in separate supporting brain regions
senses.head: Component-process view
senses.gloss: priming follows faster or more efficient processing in separate supporting brain regions
senses.evidence: RS is normally found in a number of cortical regions, depending on the nature of the stimulus and the manner in which it is processed (which is normally a function of the experimental task). For example, for tasks involving decisions about familiar visual objects, RS is normally found in higher parts of the ventral visual processing stream and in inferior frontal regions ( Koutstaal et al., 2001 ; Simons, Koutstaal, Prince, Wagner, & Schacter, 2003 ; van Turennout, Ellmore, & Martin, 2000 ; Vuilleumier, Henson, Driver, & Dolan, 2002 ). The former is often attributed to facilitation of perceptual identification, while the latter is often attributed to facilitation of controlled semantic or name retrieval. This common “component-process” view of priming ( Henson, 2003 ) thus assumes that behavioural priming is a consequence of faster or more efficient processing in a number of brain regions that support separate, component processes

senses.label: Two-route account - retrieval of a prior stimulus-response instance races re-engagement of the algorithmic route
senses.head: Two-route account
senses.gloss: retrieval of a prior stimulus-response instance races re-engagement of the algorithmic route
senses.evidence: However, repetition of a stimulus in a specific task may also entail the formation of a more direct association between the stimulus and the response given. These associations can allow the response to be cued by the recurrence of the stimulus, without necessarily requiring repetition of all the processing stages engaged during its prior presentation ( Fig. 1 C). For example, Logan (1990) proposed a race between these two possible routes to the response – i.e., retrieval of a previous stimulus–response “instance” or reengagement of the “algorithmic” route – with the behavioural response being determined by the faster. Retrieval of the associated response could completely by-pass, or at least curtail, processing within the stages involved in determining the initial response

senses.label: Same condition - repeats the bigger-than-a-shoebox task at test
senses.head: Same condition
senses.gloss: repeats the bigger-than-a-shoebox task at test
senses.evidence: The purposes of the present study were therefore to reproduce and extend the findings of Dobbins et al. We replicated the basic paradigm, using the same type of stimuli (a superset of those used by Dobbins et al.) and the same “bigger/smaller than a shoebox” task. However, we switched to a “study-test” design, in which the lag between initial and repeated presentations was matched across the three critical conditions. In the study phases, the task was always “is the object bigger than a shoebox?”, to which participants responded “yes” or “no” using finger presses ( Fig. 1 D). For the Same condition, this task was repeated at test. For the Reverse condition, the task was switched to “is the object smaller than a shoebox?” (maintaining the mapping of “yes”/“no” to finger press). Finally, we added a third condition – the Orthogonal condition – in which the test task was “is the object man-made?”. 2 Importantly, the stimuli were selected so that one half of those man-made were bigger than a shoebox, and one half of those not man-made were bigger than a shoebox, so on average the response required for a stimulus at study would not apply to the response required at test. The reason for this third condition was to provide a “baseline” measure of priming/RS, against which any facilitation owing to response repetition (in the Same condition) or any interference owing to response reversal (in the Reverse condition) could be assessed. This condition was also analogous to previous fMRI studies that used classification tasks in which responses were uncorrelated for initial and repeated presentations

senses.label: Reverse condition - switches to smaller-than-a-shoebox while preserving the yes/no key mapping
senses.head: Reverse condition
senses.gloss: switches to smaller-than-a-shoebox while preserving the yes/no key mapping
senses.evidence: The purposes of the present study were therefore to reproduce and extend the findings of Dobbins et al. We replicated the basic paradigm, using the same type of stimuli (a superset of those used by Dobbins et al.) and the same “bigger/smaller than a shoebox” task. However, we switched to a “study-test” design, in which the lag between initial and repeated presentations was matched across the three critical conditions. In the study phases, the task was always “is the object bigger than a shoebox?”, to which participants responded “yes” or “no” using finger presses ( Fig. 1 D). For the Same condition, this task was repeated at test. For the Reverse condition, the task was switched to “is the object smaller than a shoebox?” (maintaining the mapping of “yes”/“no” to finger press). Finally, we added a third condition – the Orthogonal condition – in which the test task was “is the object man-made?”. 2 Importantly, the stimuli were selected so that one half of those man-made were bigger than a shoebox, and one half of those not man-made were bigger than a shoebox, so on average the response required for a stimulus at study would not apply to the response required at test. The reason for this third condition was to provide a “baseline” measure of priming/RS, against which any facilitation owing to response repetition (in the Same condition) or any interference owing to response reversal (in the Reverse condition) could be assessed. This condition was also analogous to previous fMRI studies that used classification tasks in which responses were uncorrelated for initial and repeated presentations

senses.label: Orthogonal condition - switches to a man-made judgment so study and test responses are uncorrelated on average
senses.head: Orthogonal condition
senses.gloss: switches to a man-made judgment so study and test responses are uncorrelated on average
senses.evidence: The purposes of the present study were therefore to reproduce and extend the findings of Dobbins et al. We replicated the basic paradigm, using the same type of stimuli (a superset of those used by Dobbins et al.) and the same “bigger/smaller than a shoebox” task. However, we switched to a “study-test” design, in which the lag between initial and repeated presentations was matched across the three critical conditions. In the study phases, the task was always “is the object bigger than a shoebox?”, to which participants responded “yes” or “no” using finger presses ( Fig. 1 D). For the Same condition, this task was repeated at test. For the Reverse condition, the task was switched to “is the object smaller than a shoebox?” (maintaining the mapping of “yes”/“no” to finger press). Finally, we added a third condition – the Orthogonal condition – in which the test task was “is the object man-made?”. 2 Importantly, the stimuli were selected so that one half of those man-made were bigger than a shoebox, and one half of those not man-made were bigger than a shoebox, so on average the response required for a stimulus at study would not apply to the response required at test. The reason for this third condition was to provide a “baseline” measure of priming/RS, against which any facilitation owing to response repetition (in the Same condition) or any interference owing to response reversal (in the Reverse condition) could be assessed. This condition was also analogous to previous fMRI studies that used classification tasks in which responses were uncorrelated for initial and repeated presentations

senses.label: Repetition priming measure - mean reaction time for Novel stimuli minus mean reaction time for Repeated stimuli
senses.head: Repetition priming measure
senses.gloss: mean reaction time for Novel stimuli minus mean reaction time for Repeated stimuli
senses.evidence: Given the interest in response learning, RTs for Primed items in the Same condition were calculated only from “consistent” trials, where the same “yes” or “no” response was given for that object at both Study and Test (note that this could include trials that were “incorrect” according to the prior norms, but that were likely “correct” according to that participant's idiosyncratic view).
