Likewise, for the Reverse condition, RTs for Primed items were calculated only for trials in which the response at Study was the opposite of that given at Test. The proportions of trials excluded by this procedure are shown in Table 1 . Repetition priming was then calculated as the difference in mean RTs between Novel and Repeated stimuli

senses.label: Switch cost - within-participant difference in priming between Same and Reverse tasks
senses.head: Switch cost
senses.gloss: within-participant difference in priming between Same and Reverse tasks
senses.evidence: Finally, a further simple regression was performed to test whether RS in the Same condition for each region correlated with a behavioural measure of “switch cost”, the difference in each participant's priming between the Same and Reverse tasks

senses.label: Regional dissociation - PFC repetition suppression is task-modulated while fusiform suppression is task-resilient
senses.head: Regional dissociation
senses.gloss: PFC repetition suppression is task-modulated while fusiform suppression is task-resilient
senses.evidence: The present data provide evidence for a dissociation between RS in the PFC, which is significantly modulated by task changes, and RS in the fusiform cortex, which appears resilient to changes in task. RS in the PFC seems to be related to some form of stimulus–response learning. RS in the PFC also plays a clear role in behavioural priming, whereas the role of the fusiform is unclear. It should be noted however that these conclusions may be a consequence of the specific paradigm used here (and by others), in which perceptual demands are low (at least for complete objects) and semantic and/or executive demands are high (given the rather ad hoc classification, viz. object size relative to a shoebox). Paradigms with greater perceptual demands (e.g., object-fragments) and fewer semantic/executive demands (e.g., naming, or more basic-level categorisations) may reveal a stronger correlation between fusiform RS and behavioural measures of priming, and less influence of stimulus–response learning

senses.label: Response representation - learning may bind a size-judgement decision rather than a finger press or yes/no response
senses.head: Response representation
senses.gloss: learning may bind a size-judgement decision rather than a finger press or yes/no response
senses.evidence: The finding that priming was greater in the Reverse condition than the Orthogonal condition suggests that response learning does not occur solely at the level of a specific finger press, or even at the level of a specific decision, i.e., “yes” or “no”. This is because retrieval of such responses would help on one half of trials in the Orthogonal condition, but none of the trials in the Reverse condition. Rather, the response associated with stimuli may be at the level of a size-judgement decision, e.g. “bigger than”. Retrieval of this decision would help in the Reverse condition, despite a switch in yes/no response, but would be irrelevant in the Orthogonal condition (see Horner & Henson, in preparation , for further data and discussion concerning multiple levels of response representation, and the role of semantic overlap)

senses.label: THE artifact IS TIME-LOCKED TO THE BEHAVIOURAL VARIABLE OF INTEREST: lick-response-induced brain motion was the major obstacle, and licking happens at reward, which happens after the target
senses.evidence: A major obstacle in our early efforts developing two-dimensional calcium imaging during behavior involved systematic, lick response-induced brain motion artifacts. To overcome this problem, we modified previous techniques (Göbel et al., 2007 ) to achieve rapid, trapezoidal vertical movement of the microscope objective (Figure 1 B, Section ‘ Materials and Methods ’), generating complete local volumes at sufficiently fast rates to correct for rapid brain motion (and slow drift) in three dimensions.

senses.label: and it is measured in a channel where the signal CANNOT exist - a calcium-INSENSITIVE dye that generates a constant fluorescence in the absence of brain motion
senses.head: and it is measured in a channel where the signal CANNOT exist
senses.gloss: a calcium-INSENSITIVE dye that generates a constant fluorescence in the absence of brain motion
senses.evidence: A local volume was loaded with a green synthetic calcium indicator (OGB1-AM), and astrocytes were co-loaded with sulforhodamine (SR101; Nimmerjahn et al., 2004 ), a red, calcium-insensitive fluorescent dye that generates a constant average fluorescence level in the absence of brain motion

senses.label: up to 15 micrometers of sinking as the animal opens its jaw, which a single plane would have recorded as an artifactual fluorescence change
senses.evidence: This cell demonstrated up to 15 μm of ‘sinking’ Z-displacement as the mouse adjusted his posture, opened his jaw and began to lick – a displacement that is well-corrected by 3D co-registration methods (Figure 5 B, bottom ; see also Figure S2B in Supplementary Material). By monitoring fluorescence in a single plane (Figure 5 A, orange square), one can observe artifactual effects of brain motion on SR101 signal that would occur using 2D imaging

senses.label: THE CORRECTION DECIDES THE FINDING: standard two-dimensional correction removes the motion that is NOT lick-related, and only three-dimensional correction removes the motion that is
senses.evidence: Brain motion artifacts not related to licking were mostly corrected using standard 2D motion correction techniques, (Figure 5 C, middle ), consistent with previous studies (Dombeck et al., 2007 ; Greenberg and Kerr, 2009 ). However, adequate correction of lick-related motion artifacts required 3D motion correction (Figure 5 C, bottom ). Further, 3D motion correction also reduced motion contamination not related to licking (Figure 5 C, histograms), likely caused by body motion, chewing, breathing, and the heart beat

senses.label: A CLASS ASSIGNED BY A PROXY FEATURE, CRITICISED BY NAME: the few studies that related behavioral modulation to cell type all inferred cellular identity from extracellular spike waveforms, WHICH HAS LIMITED SCOPE AND RELIABILITY
senses.evidence: Although considerable anatomical, neurochemical, and physiological diversity exists in nearby neurons, only a small number of in vivo electrophysiological studies have correlated behavioral modulation of neural responses with information about cell type (Swadlow and Weyand, 1987 ; Mitchell et al., 2007 ; Chen et al., 2008 ). These studies have all inferred cellular identity from extracellular spike waveforms, which has limited scope and reliability.

senses.label: and the motivating problem is that the modulation of nearby neurons is heterogeneous IN MAGNITUDE AND EVEN IN DIRECTION, so a population average hides opposite effects
senses.evidence: A poorly understood feature of most studies, however, is that behavioral modulation of responses in nearby neurons is heterogeneous, both in magnitude and even in sign.

senses.label: THE THRESHOLD IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE ANIMAL ALONE: absolute orientation thresholds likely depend on the incidence of presentation of each stimulus, and on the task structure
senses.evidence: Within ten sessions, mice were able to discriminate orientations as little as 10–20° apart, consistent with previous observations in freely moving mice (Reuter, 1987 ). Absolute orientation thresholds likely depend on incidence of presentation of each stimulus (Figure 4 B, legend), and task structure (e.g., GO–NOGO vs. 2-AFC).

senses.label: and the ceiling of the discriminability measure is set by truncating the rates at 0.01 and 0.99, giving a maximum of 4.65 that belongs to the arithmetic and not to the mouse
senses.evidence: A useful measure of behavioral discriminability of targets from non-targets is given by d ′ = norminv(HR) − norminv(FA), where norminv() is the inverse of the cumulative normal function (Green and Swets, 1966 ). Values for HR and FA were truncated between 0.01 and 0.99. Higher d ′ values indicate better discriminability (maximum d ′ = 4.65).

senses.label: THE DEMONSTRATION SESSION IS NOT THE TYPICAL SESSION, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: the performance in the two imaging figures was below the trained level, in that mouse and even in that session
senses.evidence: While these data clearly illustrate the strength of our 3D imaging techniques for obtaining clean neural traces during active discrimination (including during lick responses), the behavioral performance demonstrated in Figures 6 A and 7 A was below the level achieved during training (Table 1 ), due to an increase in spurious licking compared to other mice (see Figure 3 B), and even compared to other imaging sessions from the same mouse

senses.label: with about half the mice tested learning the task at all
senses.evidence: About half of the mice tested (13/25) learned to perform the visual discrimination task, but with variable learning rates. Training proceeded as follows: First, mice were rewarded for licking in response to drifting target stimuli, using an inter-stimulus interval that was gradually increased from 2 to 5–8 s. Subsequent training involved gradually increasing the similarity of target and non-target stimuli in 5–15 sessions by presenting non-target stimuli that were (1) orthogonal to target and stationary, (2) orthogonal and of increasingly similar speed to target, (3) of increasingly similar orientation to target gratings and of identical speed.

senses.label: THE SAMPLED POPULATION DEPENDS ON THE LABEL: the synthetic dye loads every cell in a local volume, while the genetically encoded indicator labels only a subset
senses.evidence: The choice of whether to use synthetic dyes or GECIs depends on the research question at hand. For example, neurons bulk-loaded with OGB1-AM dye are typically brighter than neurons expressing GECIs, and thus can be imaged with less laser power and potentially less cell damage. Further, OGB1-AM loads every cell in a local volume (∼300 × 300 × 300 μm 3 ), thus providing greater yield than GECI experiments where only a subset of neurons are been labeled using viral or electroporation techniques.

senses.label: and the animal's motivation is a controlled variable with the arithmetic shown - a 25 gram mouse at a 90% hit rate earns about 0.65 cc against a daily minimum of 0.625
senses.head: and the animal's motivation is a controlled variable with the arithmetic shown
senses.gloss: a 25 gram mouse at a 90% hit rate earns about 0.65 cc against a daily minimum of 0.625
senses.evidence: Because the mean number of active discrimination trials per session was ∼300 (Table 1 ), and ∼40% of trials were target trials, then a 25-g mouse with a 90% hit rate (HR) would receive, on average, ∼0.65 cc of water during a session (minimum total daily water for a mouse of this weight: 0.625 cc).

senses.label: A behaviorAL CONTROL THAT SHOWS THE ASSOCIATION IS NOT REFLEXIVE: mice stop licking when the spout is withdrawn, and the discrimination does not extinguish when it returns
senses.evidence: We varied task engagement using interleaved blocks of 43 trials in which mice either actively discriminated target and non-target stimuli, or passively viewed these same stimuli (Figure 3 A). During passive viewing, a solenoid removed the lickspout from reach (Figure 1 B), and mice quickly learned to stop licking in response to target stimuli until the following ‘engaged’ block began, suggesting that the learned stimulus association is not purely reflexive (Figure 3 C). Presentation of stimuli during passive viewing, or of novel stimuli during orientation mapping, did not lead to extinction of subsequent discrimination behavior (e.g., Figures 3 B,C and 4 D), allowing for comparison of neural responses obtained during behavior with receptive field mapping obtained during passive viewing.

senses.label: and the same neurons give the same orientation preference during the behavior and during passive viewing, which is what licenses comparing the two
senses.evidence: The relative response strength of neurons to different stimulus orientations during behavior (Figures 6 A and 6 E, top left ) was consistent with orientation tuning curves obtained during passive viewing

senses.label: THE MEASURE IS A LOSS OF PRIMING, AND THAT IS THE INSTRUMENT. Modify a feature of the prime image and see how much priming survives: `a REDUCTION IN PRIMING for COLOR-modified NATURAL entities and ORIENTATION-modified ARTIFICIAL entities`. The size of the loss reads off how integral the broken feature is to the concept - so the informative quantity is the effect's ABSENCE, and a corpus that records only that priming occurred would lose the finding entirely
senses.head: THE MEASURE IS A LOSS OF PRIMING, AND THAT IS THE INSTRUMENT. Modify a feature of the prime image and see how much priming survives: `a REDUCTION IN PRIMING for COLOR-modified NATURAL entities and ORIENTATION-modified ARTIFICIAL entities`. The size of the loss reads off how integral the broken feature is to the concept
senses.gloss: so the informative quantity is the effect's ABSENCE, and a corpus that records only that priming occurred would lose the finding entirely
senses.evidence: Reaction time analysis indicated a reduction in priming for color-modified natural entities and orientation-modified artificial entities. Standard event-related potentials (ERP) analysis was performed, in addition to linear classification. For natural entities, a N400 effect at central channel sites was observed for the color-modified condition

senses.label: PRIMING AS AN INSTRUMENT, IN A LITERATURE THAT IS NOT ABOUT PRIMING. The question is which features a semantic category depends on - a question about conceptual structure and about category-specific deficits in patients - and priming is borrowed to answer it. This is the distinction pickering2008 asks its own field to keep (Q-744): an investigation USING priming rather than ABOUT it. Here the borrowing is complete enough that the conclusion mentions categorization and not priming at all
senses.head: PRIMING AS AN INSTRUMENT, IN A LITERATURE THAT IS NOT ABOUT PRIMING. The question is which features a semantic category depends on
senses.gloss: a question about conceptual structure and about category-specific deficits in patients - and priming is borrowed to answer it. This is the distinction pickering2008 asks its own field to keep (Q-744): an investigation USING priming rather than ABOUT it. Here the borrowing is complete enough that the conclusion mentions categorization and not priming at all
senses.evidence: These findings provide strong evidence that color is an integral property to the categorization of fruits/vegetables, thus substantiating the claim that feature-based processing guides as a function of semantic category

senses.label: THE HYPOTHESIS IS WRITTEN WITH BOTH ARMS AND ITS ALTERNATIVE, BEFORE THE RESULTS: `if color and orientation are asymmetrically important for natural and manmade objects, respectively, then color-modified primes should render a more severe priming reduction for fruits/vegetables, while orientation-modified primes would shrink priming for tools` - and then the rival, that if fruits and vegetables overlap with the artificial category, orientation-modified primes should ALSO reduce priming there. Two distinguishable predictions, stated in advance, with the data able to separate them
senses.head: THE HYPOTHESIS IS WRITTEN WITH BOTH ARMS AND ITS ALTERNATIVE, BEFORE THE RESULTS: `if color and orientation are asymmetrically important for natural and manmade objects, respectively, then color-modified primes should render a more severe priming reduction for fruits/vegetables, while orientation-modified primes would shrink priming for tools`
senses.gloss: and then the rival, that if fruits and vegetables overlap with the artificial category, orientation-modified primes should ALSO reduce priming there. Two distinguishable predictions, stated in advance, with the data able to separate them
senses.evidence: Our hypothesis is as follows: if color and orientation are asymmetrically important for natural (fruits/vegetables) and manmade (tools) objects, respectively, then color-modified primes should render a more severe priming reduction for fruits/vegetables, while orientation-modified primes would shrink priming for tools

senses.label: THE NEURAL INDEX IS A SEMANTIC-VIOLATION MARKER, WHICH IS A STRONGER CLAIM THAN A SLOWDOWN: a colour-modified fruit `should yield a SEMANTIC VIOLATION as indexed by an increase in N400 amplitude`, and it does. The behavioural half says the concept is harder to reach; the N400 says the modified image is treated as semantically WRONG for its category, which is what distinguishes an integral feature from a merely useful one
senses.evidence: These findings are in line with our hypothesis that a color-modification for fruits/vegetables should yield a semantic violation as indexed by an increase in N400 amplitude

senses.label: number sense has no agreed definition - the paper opens by saying cognitive psychologists and math educators define it differently, then adopts a six-part working list
senses.head: number sense has no agreed definition
senses.gloss: the paper opens by saying cognitive psychologists and math educators define it differently, then adopts a six-part working list
senses.evidence: Although cognitive psychologists and math educators have different definitions of number sense ( Gersten et al., 2005 ), most of them agree that it is an ability to subitize small quantities, discern number patterns, compare numerical magnitudes, estimate quantities, count, and perform simple number transformations

senses.label: P2 and P2p are DIFFERENT components separated in time and space, despite names differing by one letter; P2p indexes the DE and P2 does not
senses.evidence: The next positive wave, P2p, was initially described by Dehaene (1996) as reflecting the DE (right parietal–occipital–temporal positive waveform to close numbers compared to far numbers) and was seen as an index of the approximate magnitude representation ( Hyde and Spelke, 2011 ). This component, simultaneous with N1, is clearly separated in time and space from the earlier broad fronto-central positivity wave, which is classically known as P2

senses.label: anterior N1 and posterior N1 are different components with different generators; this study evokes the anterior one where the cited precedent evoked the posterior
senses.evidence: According to the time and brain regions of occurrence, this component was the anterior N1. This result was inconsistent with a previous study (i.e., Dehaene, 1996 ) in which the posterior N1 was evoked by the number comparison task.

senses.label: LPC may or may not be the P3b - the identification is attributed to some researchers and not settled here
senses.head: LPC may or may not be the P3b
senses.gloss: the identification is attributed to some researchers and not settled here
senses.evidence: The last positive component is the late positive component (LPC), which is characterized by later onset (usually after 300 ms) and central–parietal distribution ( Friedman and Johnson, 2000 ). Some researchers suggested that this component was the P3b, which indicated the amount of context updating and also reflected the DE

senses.label: SES is a composite score built from parental education, occupation and household resources by item response theory and principal components, not a single measured quantity
senses.evidence: The SES criteria consisted of parental education, occupation, and family resources, which together represented SES better than any of these alone

senses.label: spatial ability (SA) - the broad literature term, used loosely and often for measures that are actually narrower
senses.head: spatial ability (SA)
senses.gloss: the broad literature term, used loosely and often for measures that are actually narrower
senses.evidence: Very broadly, spatial ability (SA) refers to “the ability to generate, retain, and manipulate abstract visual images” [ 19 ].

senses.label: spatial visualization (SV) - the specific factor measured here, and the authors' stated convention is to say SV for their own work and SA when reporting prior research
senses.head: spatial visualization (SV)
senses.gloss: the specific factor measured here, and the authors' stated convention is to say SV for their own work and SA when reporting prior research
senses.evidence: Since previous studies have often used the broad term SA even when measures were of SV, we use the term SA when referring to previous research in this field.

senses.label: threshold - the general claim: above some ability level, further differences stop predicting anything
senses.head: threshold
senses.gloss: the general claim: above some ability level, further differences stop predicting anything
senses.evidence: Overall, our data clearly showed that ability differences in this high-ability population are relevant to achievement prediction, corroborating previous findings against a ‘threshold’ view of cognitive abilities [ 34 , 44 , 48 , 49 ].

senses.label: threshold - per ability and per domain: each ability has its own level that suffices for a given subject, and spatial ability's is low for mathematics
senses.head: threshold
senses.gloss: per ability and per domain: each ability has its own level that suffices for a given subject, and spatial ability's is low for mathematics
senses.evidence: Apparently, when it comes to predicting mathematics achievements, SV seems to have a lower threshold than numerical and verbal abilities (i.e., a lower level is sufficient for success).

senses.label: what a spatial test measures - as named: spatial-visual processing
senses.head: what a spatial test measures
senses.gloss: as named: spatial-visual processing
senses.evidence: The most studied type of SA in the context of STEM is spatial visualization (SV), which is the ability to “…apprehend a spatial form, shape or scene in order to match it with another spatial form, shape or scene, often with the necessity of rotating it in two or three dimensions one or more times” [ 24 ].

senses.label: what a spatial test measures - in practice: also executive function, and analytic strategies that substitute for visualising altogether
senses.head: what a spatial test measures
senses.gloss: in practice: also executive function, and analytic strategies that substitute for visualising altogether
senses.evidence: Research showed that solving SA tests involves not only strictly spatial-visual processes, but also a variety of non-spatial components.

senses.label: THE TITLE SAYS `IMPAIRS` AND THE RESULT IS A REVERSAL. `Participants in the UST group chose the faces that were shown 12 times significantly more, WHILE THOSE IN THE IMT GROUP WERE MORE LIKELY TO CHOOSE FACES PRESENTED ONCE.` Told the choice is unspecified, people pick what they have seen most; told it matters, they pick what they have seen LEAST. An instruction that inverts a preference is a stronger finding than one that removes it, and the abstract's verb understates the result
senses.evidence: Participants in the UST group chose the faces that were shown 12 times significantly more, while those in the IMT group were more likely to choose faces presented once (Fig. 1 C). Response Time (RT), analysed by Generalised Linear Models, in the experimental trials was significantly lower in the UST group

senses.label: ONE INSTRUCTION, TWO PRIMING TYPES, ONLY ONE MOVES. The design crosses repetition priming (mere frequency of exposure) with emotional priming (valenced phrases attached to faces), and the importance instruction reverses the repetition effect while `positive faces were equally chosen by both groups`. So top-down control does not turn priming down as a whole - it reaches the frequency-based effect and not the affective one
senses.head: ONE INSTRUCTION, TWO PRIMING TYPES, ONLY ONE MOVES. The design crosses repetition priming (mere frequency of exposure) with emotional priming (valenced phrases attached to faces), and the importance instruction reverses the repetition effect while `positive faces were equally chosen by both groups`. So top-down control does not turn priming down as a whole
senses.gloss: it reaches the frequency-based effect and not the affective one
senses.evidence: Our working hypothesis is that mere repetition of an option (repetition priming) or its emotional valence (emotional priming) would prime the choice preference, but this susceptibility to priming could be impaired by the task for which it is chosen

senses.label: `priming susceptibility` as a construct in its own right - the paper measures not the effect but the OPENNESS to it, which is what allows an instruction to be the independent variable and priming to be the dependent one. Most records in this corpus put priming on the causal side; here it is the thing being caused to happen or not
senses.head: `priming susceptibility` as a construct in its own right
senses.gloss: the paper measures not the effect but the OPENNESS to it, which is what allows an instruction to be the independent variable and priming to be the dependent one. Most records in this corpus put priming on the causal side; here it is the thing being caused to happen or not
senses.evidence: The aim of the present research is to evaluate the priming susceptibility on decisions. Our working hypothesis is that mere repetition of an option (repetition priming) or its emotional valence (emotional priming) would prime the choice preference, but this susceptibility to priming could be impaired by the task for which it is chosen (top-down modulation)

senses.label: THE SECOND STUDY IS A NATIONAL ELECTION. 3,673 surveys during the 2019 Argentine presidential campaign plus a count of news mentions: familiarity and trust explain voting probability and correlate with how often each candidate appeared in the press and with the actual result. The laboratory's repetition variable becomes MEDIA FREQUENCY, and the choice becomes a vote - an ecological check that most priming records in this corpus do not attempt
senses.head: THE SECOND STUDY IS A NATIONAL ELECTION. 3,673 surveys during the 2019 Argentine presidential campaign plus a count of news mentions: familiarity and trust explain voting probability and correlate with how often each candidate appeared in the press and with the actual result. The laboratory's repetition variable becomes MEDIA FREQUENCY, and the choice becomes a vote
senses.gloss: an ecological check that most priming records in this corpus do not attempt
senses.evidence: The familiarity and trust to each candidate explained the voting-probability for most of them, as well as correlated with their frequency of mentions in the news, their positive associations, and election results

senses.label: THE REVIEW EXISTS BECAUSE OF WHAT THE STRUCTURE IS NAMED FOR, AND SAYS SO IN ITS FIRST SENTENCE: GIVEN THE TWO MOST WELL-KNOWN FUNCTIONS OF THE HIPPOCAMPUS - SUPPORTING EPISODIC MEMORY IN HUMANS AND SPATIAL NAVIGATION IN ANIMALS - A REVIEW OF THIS STRUCTURE IN RELATION TO SOUND MAY SEEM AN UNLIKELY EXERCISE. What is not looked for in a structure is decided by what the structure is known for
senses.head: THE REVIEW EXISTS BECAUSE OF WHAT THE STRUCTURE IS NAMED FOR, AND SAYS SO IN ITS FIRST SENTENCE: GIVEN THE TWO MOST WELL-KNOWN FUNCTIONS OF THE HIPPOCAMPUS
senses.gloss: SUPPORTING EPISODIC MEMORY IN HUMANS AND SPATIAL NAVIGATION IN ANIMALS - A REVIEW OF THIS STRUCTURE IN RELATION TO SOUND MAY SEEM AN UNLIKELY EXERCISE. What is not looked for in a structure is decided by what the structure is known for
senses.evidence: Given the two most well-known functions of the hippocampus – supporting episodic memory in humans ( Scoville and Milner, 1957 , Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991 ) and spatial navigation in animals ( O’Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971 ) – a review of this structure in relation to sound may seem an unlikely exercise.

senses.label: and the anatomy points away too: IN HUMANS, CORTICAL CIRCUITS UNDERLYING AUDITORY PERCEPTION AND COGNITION ARE LARGELY FOUND IN LATERAL, RATHER THAN MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE STRUCTURES
senses.evidence: In humans, cortical circuits underlying auditory perception and cognition are largely found in lateral, rather than medial temporal lobe structures

senses.label: THE QUESTION BECOMES ASKABLE ONLY BY WIDENING THE JOB DESCRIPTION: THEORIES OF HIPPOCAMPAL FUNCTION HAVE LONG EXTENDED BEYOND EPISODIC MEMORY AND SPATIAL NAVIGATION - THE HIPPOCAMPUS IS IMPORTANT FOR THE BINDING OF ARBITRARY RELATIONS AND MEDIATING THEIR FLEXIBLE EXPRESSION. Widen the function and the evidence that was always there becomes relevant
senses.head: THE QUESTION BECOMES ASKABLE ONLY BY WIDENING THE JOB DESCRIPTION: THEORIES OF HIPPOCAMPAL FUNCTION HAVE LONG EXTENDED BEYOND EPISODIC MEMORY AND SPATIAL NAVIGATION
senses.gloss: THE HIPPOCAMPUS IS IMPORTANT FOR THE BINDING OF ARBITRARY RELATIONS AND MEDIATING THEIR FLEXIBLE EXPRESSION. Widen the function and the evidence that was always there becomes relevant
senses.evidence: However, theories of hippocampal function have long extended beyond episodic memory and spatial navigation ( Kimble, 1968 , Papez, 1937 ). One idea is that the hippocampus is important for the binding of arbitrary relations and mediating their flexible expression ( Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993 , Lisman et al., 2017 ). This extended job description encompasses linking multimodal objects with a spatiotemporal, environmental, or cognitive context to form episodic memories ( Yonelinas et al., 2019 ), supporting short-term memory ( Hannula and Ranganath, 2008 , Pertzov et al., 2013 ), associating disparate elements of a scene ( Graham et al., 2010 , Maguire and Mullally, 2013 , Olsen et al., 2012 ), structuring conceptual knowledge ( Behrens et al., 2018 ), and forming predictions

senses.label: and the conclusion follows from the widening rather than from new data: IN LIGHT OF THIS EXTENDED PROPOSED FUNCTIONAL SCOPE, A FULL ACCOUNT OF THE AUDITORY SYSTEM SHOULD AT LEAST CONSIDER THE HIPPOCAMPUS
senses.evidence: In light of this extended proposed functional scope, a full account of the auditory system should at least consider the hippocampus.

senses.label: THE POOLING ACROSS SPECIES IS ARGUED FOR, NOT ASSUMED: RECOGNIZING THE RELATIVE PRESERVATION OF HIPPOCAMPAL ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY ACROSS SPECIES, AND THE ADVANCES IN UNDERSTANDING FUNCTION THIS AFFORDS, WE INCLUDE STUDIES FROM RODENTS TO PRIMATES - ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL AND NEUROIMAGING DATA ARE CONSIDERED ALONGSIDE NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL AND ANIMAL LESION WORK
senses.head: THE POOLING ACROSS SPECIES IS ARGUED FOR, NOT ASSUMED: RECOGNIZING THE RELATIVE PRESERVATION OF HIPPOCAMPAL ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY ACROSS SPECIES, AND THE ADVANCES IN UNDERSTANDING FUNCTION THIS AFFORDS, WE INCLUDE STUDIES FROM RODENTS TO PRIMATES
senses.gloss: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL AND NEUROIMAGING DATA ARE CONSIDERED ALONGSIDE NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL AND ANIMAL LESION WORK
senses.evidence: Recognizing the relative preservation of hippocampal anatomy and physiology across species, and the advances in understanding function this affords ( Buffalo, 2015 , Clark and Squire, 2013 , Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993 , Witter and Amaral, 2021 ), we include studies from rodents to primates. Electrophysiological and neuroimaging data are considered alongside neuropsychological and animal lesion work.

senses.label: A DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN STUDIES ATTRIBUTED TO ONE PARAMETER OF THE ANALYSIS: DIFFERENCES ACROSS THE RESULTS OF THESE STUDIES MAY RELATE TO THE THRESHOLDS USED IN THE PROBABILISTIC TRACTOGRAPHY PROCEDURE
senses.evidence: Differences across the results of these studies may relate to the thresholds used in the probabilistic tractography procedure. Complementing structural approaches like DTI that identify anatomical tracts, functional-connectivity analysis defines correlated time series between areas, from which direct or indirect connections can be inferred.

senses.label: A DEFINITION WIDENED, EXPLICITLY: A BROADER DEFINITION OF CONTEXT IS ADOPTED IN THE CONTEXTUAL BINDING THEORY OF HUMAN EPISODIC MEMORY - IT HOLDS THAT NOT ONLY BACKGROUND ELEMENTS OF THE PHYSICAL ENVIRONMENT, BUT ALSO SLOWLY CHANGING COGNITIVE STATE OR MOOD AS WELL AS TEMPORAL CONTEXT, ARE BOUND TOGETHER IN THE HIPPOCAMPUS. The same word, a larger set, and the older findings are now about the new one
senses.head: A DEFINITION WIDENED, EXPLICITLY: A BROADER DEFINITION OF CONTEXT IS ADOPTED IN THE CONTEXTUAL BINDING THEORY OF HUMAN EPISODIC MEMORY
senses.gloss: IT HOLDS THAT NOT ONLY BACKGROUND ELEMENTS OF THE PHYSICAL ENVIRONMENT, BUT ALSO SLOWLY CHANGING COGNITIVE STATE OR MOOD AS WELL AS TEMPORAL CONTEXT, ARE BOUND TOGETHER IN THE HIPPOCAMPUS. The same word, a larger set, and the older findings are now about the new one
senses.evidence: A broader definition of context is adopted in the contextual binding theory of human episodic memory ( Yonelinas et al., 2019 ; see also Section 13 ). It holds that not only background elements of the physical environment, but also slowly changing cognitive state or mood as well as temporal context, are bound together in the hippocampus with items and events as they are encountered or experienced

senses.label: AND A DEFINITION IMPORTED FROM ANOTHER SENSE: AN AUDITORY PERCEPTUAL OBJECT, LIKE ITS VISUAL COUNTERPARTS, IS DEFINED BY THE BINDING OF MULTIPLE SENSORY FEATURES, REPRESENTS A SOURCE DISTINCT FROM OTHERS IN THE SCENE, AND IS INVARIANT OVER DIFFERENT SENSORY INSTANCES
senses.evidence: An auditory perceptual object, like its visual counterparts, is defined by the binding of multiple sensory features, represents a source distinct from others in the scene, and is invariant over different sensory instances

senses.label: OPPOSITE SINGLE-UNIT FINDINGS IN ONE STRUCTURE: single unit recordings from human hippocampus REVEAL NEURONS THAT RESPOND PREFERENTIALLY TO REPEATED WORDS ALONGSIDE THOSE DRIVEN BY WORD NOVELTY - a `hippocampus signals novelty` tag and a `hippocampus signals repetition` tag are both true of the same recordings
senses.head: OPPOSITE SINGLE-UNIT FINDINGS IN ONE STRUCTURE: single unit recordings from human hippocampus REVEAL NEURONS THAT RESPOND PREFERENTIALLY TO REPEATED WORDS ALONGSIDE THOSE DRIVEN BY WORD NOVELTY
senses.gloss: a `hippocampus signals novelty` tag and a `hippocampus signals repetition` tag are both true of the same recordings
senses.evidence: The novelty of both a word ( Davis et al., 2009 ) and its category ( Dolan and Fletcher, 1997 ) can drive hippocampal activity during memory encoding. However single unit recordings from human hippocampus reveal neurons that respond preferentially to repeated words alongside those driven by word novelty

senses.label: A STRUCTURAL CORRELATION WHOSE CAUSAL READING IS WITHHELD: LONGITUDINAL STUDIES, SIMILAR TO THOSE IN TAXI DRIVERS, WILL BE IMPORTANT TO ESTABLISH CAUSALITY IN ANY OF THE ABOVE RELATIONSHIPS
senses.evidence: Longitudinal studies, similar to those in taxi drivers ( Woollett and Maguire, 2011 ), will be important to establish causality in any of the above relationships.

senses.label: and it does not generalize beyond experts: FOR SPATIAL NAVIGATION AND OTHER HIPPOCAMPUS-DEPENDENT TASKS, THE GENERALIZABILITY OF A VOLUME-FUNCTION RELATIONSHIP TO A NON-EXPERT POPULATION HAS NOT BEEN DEMONSTRATED
senses.evidence: For spatial navigation and other hippocampus-dependent tasks, the generalizability of a volume-function relationship to a non-expert population has not been demonstrated

senses.label: THE FINDING CITED FOR A STRUCTURE WAS MEASURED IN A DIFFERENT ONE, AND THE REVIEW SAYS SO IN A PARENTHESIS: THE VOLUME OF PARAHIPPOCAMPAL GYRUS (HIPPOCAMPUS WAS NOT TESTED) WAS FOUND TO CORRELATE POSITIVELY WITH AN INDEX OF MUSICAL SOPHISTICATION IN A GROUP OF 73 OLDER ADULTS AFTER CONTROLLING FOR INTRACRANIAL VOLUME
senses.evidence: However with respect to music, the volume of parahippocampal gyrus (hippocampus was not tested) was found to correlate positively with an index of musical sophistication in a group of 73 older adults after controlling for intracranial volume

senses.label: and the positive associations that do exist are with training time: POSITIVE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN YEARS OF TRAINING AND ANTERIOR HIPPOCAMPAL GRAY MATTER VOLUME IN MUSICIANS AND PIANO-TUNERS
senses.evidence: Such associations have been found, with positive relationships between years of training and anterior hippocampal gray matter volume in musicians ( Groussard et al., 2014 , Groussard et al., 2010a ) and piano-tuners

senses.label: A CLINICAL EFFECT THAT DEPENDS ON THE TIMING AND NOT THE SOUND: CLICK TRAINS PRESENTED AT THIS RATE (BUT NOT WITH RANDOM TIMING) REDUCED SIGNS OF ALZHEIMER'S PATHOLOGY (AMYLOID LOAD AND TAU PHOSPHORYLATION) IN THE HIPPOCAMPUS OF THIS MOUSE MODEL AND BOOSTED MEMORY FOR THE IDENTITY AND LOCATION OF OBJECTS
senses.evidence: Remarkably, click trains presented at this rate (but not with random timing) reduced signs of Alzheimer's pathology (amyloid load and tau phosphorylation) in the hippocampus of this mouse model and boosted memory for the identity and location of objects.

senses.label: and the effect is larger when a second modality is added: EFFECTS WERE LARGER WHEN THE AUDITORY STIMULUS WAS PAIRED WITH VISUAL FLICKER AT THE SAME RATE - THIS COMBINED STIMULATION ALSO INDUCED AN INCREASE IN 40 Hz POWER AND A CLUSTERING EFFECT OF MICROGLIA AROUND AMYLOID DEPOSITS
senses.head: and the effect is larger when a second modality is added: EFFECTS WERE LARGER WHEN THE AUDITORY STIMULUS WAS PAIRED WITH VISUAL FLICKER AT THE SAME RATE
senses.gloss: THIS COMBINED STIMULATION ALSO INDUCED AN INCREASE IN 40 Hz POWER AND A CLUSTERING EFFECT OF MICROGLIA AROUND AMYLOID DEPOSITS
senses.evidence: Effects were larger when the auditory stimulus was paired with visual flicker at the same rate - this combined stimulation also induced an increase in 40 Hz power and a clustering effect of microglia around amyloid deposits.

senses.label: THE MECHANISM OF THE HEADLINE RESULT IS NOT UNDERSTOOD, AND HUMAN TRIALS ARE ALREADY RUNNING: WORK IS ONGOING TO TEST THE SAME APPROACH IN HUMAN TRIALS - THE MECHANISM IS NOT YET UNDERSTOOD
senses.head: THE MECHANISM OF THE HEADLINE RESULT IS NOT UNDERSTOOD, AND HUMAN TRIALS ARE ALREADY RUNNING: WORK IS ONGOING TO TEST THE SAME APPROACH IN HUMAN TRIALS
senses.gloss: THE MECHANISM IS NOT YET UNDERSTOOD
senses.evidence: The implications for dementia treatment are considerable, and work is ongoing to test the same approach in human trials ( Chan et al., 2021 ). The mechanism is not yet understood but networks of inhibitory interneurons generate peaks at this low-gamma frequency, which may also be involved in coupling CA3 and CA1 during memory retrieval

senses.label: A CONFOUND REMOVED BY MOVING THE RESPONSE: BY HAVING SUBJECTS REPORT TARGET COUNTS AT THE END OF A TRIAL OR BLOCK, EXPLICIT MOTOR CONFOUNDS ARE REMOVED
senses.evidence: In human subjects, behavioral relevance can be instilled in the absence of explicit reward through task instructions, such as to count particular target sounds or to make certain judgments. By having subjects report target counts at the end of a trial or block, explicit motor confounds are removed.

senses.label: and the review names what is still not known: IT REMAINS TO BE DETERMINED WHETHER SOUNDS PREDICTED ON THE BASIS OF ASSOCIATIONS LEARNED IN THE SHORT-TERM OR THROUGH SEMANTIC CONTEXT CAN BE DECODED FROM HIPPOCAMPAL ACTIVITY BEFORE THEY ARE HEARD
senses.evidence: It remains to be determined whether sounds predicted on the basis of associations learned in the short-term (such as the next note in a melody learned in an experiment) or through semantic context (such as the sound of a bark following a picture of a dog) can be decoded from hippocampal activity before they are heard.

senses.label: AN APPARENTLY MULTISENSORY SIGNAL EXPLAINED AWAY BY behavior: neural activity that is apparently multisensory MAY SIMPLY ARISE from low-dimensional signals associated with internal state and behavior
senses.evidence: Sensory cortices can be affected by stimuli of multiple modalities and are thus increasingly thought to be multisensory. For instance, primary visual cortex (V1) is influenced not only by images but also by sounds. Here we show that the activity evoked by sounds in V1, measured with Neuropixels probes, is stereotyped across neurons and even across mice. It is independent of projections from auditory cortex and resembles activity evoked in the hippocampal formation, which receives little direct auditory input. Its low-dimensional nature starkly contrasts the high-dimensional code that V1 uses to represent images. Furthermore, this sound-evoked activity can be precisely predicted by small body movements that are elicited by each sound and are stereotyped across trials and mice. Thus, neural activity that is apparently multisensory may simply arise from low-dimensional signals associated with internal state and behavior.

senses.label: and the account being replaced is stated first, with its evidence - suppression by inhibiting auditory cortex, mimicry by stimulating auditory fibers
senses.head: and the account being replaced is stated first, with its evidence
senses.gloss: suppression by inhibiting auditory cortex, mimicry by stimulating auditory fibers
senses.evidence: Many studies suggest that all cortical sensory areas, including primary ones, are multisensory 1 . For instance, mouse’s primary visual cortex (V1) is influenced by sounds. Sounds may provide V1 with global inhibition 2 , modify the neurons’ tuning 3 , 4 , boost detection of visual events 5 or even provide tone-specific information, reinforced by prolonged exposure 6 or training 7 . This sound-evoked activity is thought to originate from direct projections from the auditory cortex 2 , 3 , 5 , 7 —it may be suppressed by inhibition of the auditory cortex 2 , 5 , and it may be mimicked by stimulation of auditory fibers 2 , 3 .

senses.label: THE HYPOTHESIS IS TURNED INTO FOUR ADVANCE PREDICTIONS: low dimension, a broad footprint beyond the cortex, independence from auditory input, and predictability from behavior
senses.evidence: This hypothesis predicts that sound-evoked activity in V1 should have the typical attributes of behavioral signals: low dimension 13 and a broad footprint 14 , 21 , 22 that extends beyond the cortex 13 . Moreover, sound-evoked activity should be independent of direct inputs from auditory cortex and should be predictable from the behavioral effects of sounds.

senses.label: THREE MODELS, AND THE RANKING IS THE FINDING: one from sound identity alone, one from movement alone, one from both - and the behavioral model performs JUST AS WELL as the full model
senses.head: THREE MODELS, AND THE RANKING IS THE FINDING: one from sound identity alone, one from movement alone, one from both
senses.gloss: and the behavioral model performs JUST AS WELL as the full model
senses.evidence: This analysis revealed that the sounds themselves were unnecessary to predict sound-evoked activity in visual cortex, whereas the body movements elicited by sounds were sufficient. As expected, the auditory model was able to capture much of this activity. However, it performed worse than the full model and the behavioral model ( P = 0.0078, Wilcoxon two-sided paired signed rank test; Fig. 4l,m ). These models captured not only the average responses to the sounds (see Extended Data Fig. 1a for time courses across all sounds), but also the fine differences in neural activity between the train and test set, which the auditory model cannot predict (because the two sets share the same sounds). Remarkably, the behavioral model performed just as well as the full model ( P = 0.25, Wilcoxon two-sided paired signed rank test; Fig. 4n ), indicating that the sounds themselves were unnecessary to predict sound-evoked activity.

senses.label: with the auditory model's built-in advantage disclosed - it is equivalent to a test-retest prediction and would fit perfectly with infinite trials, so it performs well REGARDLESS of the origin of the activity
senses.head: with the auditory model's built-in advantage disclosed
senses.gloss: it is equivalent to a test-retest prediction and would fit perfectly with infinite trials, so it performs well REGARDLESS of the origin of the activity
senses.evidence: We then asked to what extent body movements could predict sound-evoked neural activity in V1. We fitted three models to the sound-related single-trial responses (projected onto the full auditory subspace) and used the models to predict trial averages of these sound responses on a different test set (Fig. 4k and Supplementary Fig. 3 ). The first was a purely auditory model where the time course of neural activity depends only on sound identity. This model is equivalent to a test–retest prediction, so it will perform well regardless of the origin of sound-evoked activity; it would fit perfectly with an infinite number of trials. The second was a purely behavioral model where neural activity is predicted by pupil area, eye position and motion, and facial movements. This model would perform well only if behavioral variables observed in individual trials do predict the trial-averaged sound-evoked responses. The third was a full model where activity is due to the sum of both factors, auditory and behavioral.

senses.label: THE MANIPULATION WAS CHOSEN FOR WHAT IT DOES NOT DISTURB: silencing or stimulating auditory cortex would interfere with auditory processing and could affect the sound-evoked behavior, so the fibres were cut instead
senses.evidence: This result contrasts those of studies that ascribed the activity evoked by sounds in V1 to a direct input from auditory cortex. These studies used multiple methods: silencing of auditory cortex 2 , 5 , stimulation of its projections to visual cortex 2 , 3 or transectomy of these projections 2 . However, the first two methods would interfere with auditory processing, and thus could affect sound-evoked behavior. We thus opted for transectomy 2 , which is less likely to modify behavior, and we performed bilateral recordings to have an internal control—the uncut side—within the same mice and with the same behavior.

senses.label: and the control is INSIDE the animal - bilateral recording, the uncut side, the same mouse and the same behavior
senses.head: and the control is INSIDE the animal
senses.gloss: bilateral recording, the uncut side, the same mouse and the same behavior
senses.evidence: The activity evoked by sounds in visual cortex was similar on the cut and the uncut side. Indeed, the time course of the activity projected along auditory PC1 on the side of the cut (Fig. 3d,e ) was essentially identical to the time course of auditory PC1 in the opposite hemisphere ( r = 0.9, Fig. 3f,g ) and barely distinguishable from the one measured in the control mice (cut, r = 0.62 and uncut, r = 0.56; Fig. 3h,i ). Their relative timing was also identical, with a cross-correlation (measured at 1-ms resolution) that peaked at 0 delays. The distribution of the variance explained by the first auditory PCs and the distribution of neuronal weights on the auditory PC1 were similar on the two sides (Fig. 3e versus g ). The total variance of the activity related to sounds on the cut side was on average equal to the sound-related variance on the uncut side (Fig. 3j and see Extended Data Fig. 2c for all eigenspectra) and was significantly larger than expected from the few auditory fibers that were spared by the transectomies ( P = 0.031, Wilcoxon two-tailed paired signed rank test, n = 6 experiments across three mice). Furthermore, decoding accuracy was similar across sides for both sounds (cut, 27 ± 3% and uncut, 24 ± 2%; P = 0.016 for both, Wilcoxon right-tailed signed rank test; comparison: P = 0.44, Wilcoxon two-sided paired signed rank test) and videos (cut, 90 ± 4% and uncut, 85 ± 6%; P = 0.016 for both, Wilcoxon right-tailed signed rank test; comparison: P = 0.31, Wilcoxon two-sided paired signed rank test; Fig. 3k ). These results indicate that the activity evoked by sounds in visual cortex in our experiments cannot be explained by direct inputs from auditory cortex.

senses.label: THREE METHOD DIFFERENCES ENUMERATED WHERE THE RESULT CONTRADICTS THE STUDY THAT INTRODUCED THE SAME CUT: intracellular in layers 2/3 against extracellular in layers 4-6, hours against days after surgery, and anesthetized against awake
senses.evidence: This result contrasts with the original study that introduced the transectomy 2 , and the difference in results may be due to differences in methods. First, the previous study was conducted intracellularly and mostly in layers 2/3 (where sounds hyperpolarized cells, unlike in other layers where sounds increased spiking), whereas we recorded extracellularly mainly in layers 4-6 (and observed mainly increases in spiking). Second, the previous study performed recordings hours after the transectomy, whereas we performed them days later. Third, the previous study anesthetized the mice, whereas we did not, a difference that can profoundly affect V1 activity

senses.label: AND A THRESHOLD AGAINST A FRACTION: the earlier whisking study used a hard threshold to call a response auditory or movement-related, where this one estimated the fraction explained
senses.evidence: An exception is a study 20 that explored the contribution of whisking to sound-evoked activity V1 neurons in layer 1. In agreement with our results, this study found that whisking explains a fraction of those neurons’ sound-evoked activity. However, it did not explain all the neural activity. This discrepancy could be due to differences in recording methods (two-photon imaging versus electrophysiology) in cortical layers (layer 1 versus layers 4–6) or in the analyses. For instance, the previous study relied on a hard threshold to call a response auditory versus movement-related, whereas we estimated the fraction of sound-evoked activity explained by movement.

senses.label: THE DIMENSIONALITY OF THE RESPONSE IS USED TO CLASSIFY WHAT KIND OF SIGNAL IT IS: four significant components for sounds against seventy-nine for videos, and zero for their interaction
senses.evidence: To determine if a cvPCA dimension had variance significantly above 0, we used a shuffling method. The shuffling was done by changing the labels of both the videos and the sounds for each repeat. We performed this randomization 1,000 times and chose a component to be significant if its test–retest covariance value was above the 99th percentile of the shuffled distribution. We defined the dimensionality as the number of significant components. For the video-related activity, we found an average of 79 significant components (±23 s.e., n = 8 mice). As expected, this number grew with the number of recorded neurons 15 (data not shown). For the sound-related activity, instead, we found only four significant components on average (±1 s.e., n = 8 mice). For the interactions between videos and sounds, finally, we found zero significant components (0 ± 0 s.e., n = 8 mice) indicating that the population responses did not reflect significant interactions between videos and sounds.

senses.label: with a between-animal correlation reported against its own within-animal ceiling - 0.34 across mice against a test-retest of 0.44 within them
senses.head: with a between-animal correlation reported against its own within-animal ceiling
senses.gloss: 0.34 across mice against a test-retest of 0.44 within them
senses.evidence: Indeed, the correlation of auditory PC1 time courses evoked in different mice was 0.34, close to the test–retest correlation of 0.44 measured within individual mice

senses.label: A SELECTION STEP CHECKED AGAINST THE RESULT IT COULD HAVE PRODUCED: the reliability of auditory responses did not correlate with the spike-contamination score, and if anything went the other way
senses.evidence: Because spike contamination is a key source of bias 29 , we took particular care in selecting cells with few or no violations in interspike interval (ISI), and we confirmed that a key measure used in our study, the reliability of auditory responses, did not correlate with the ISI violations score. In fact, it showed a slightly negative correlation, indicating that the best-isolated neurons tended to have the highest reliability.

senses.label: A WHOLE LITERATURE'S CONTROLS DECLARED INADEQUATE: distinguishing auditory signals from state and behavior requires careful and systematic controls, WHICH ARE RARELY PERFORMED in passively listening mice
senses.evidence: Distinguishing putative auditory signals from the large contribution of internal state and behavior will require careful and systematic controls, which are rarely performed in passively listening mice. Some studies have controlled for eye movements 5 or for overt behaviors such as licking 7 . However, even these studies may have overlooked the types of movement that we observed to correlate with neuronal activity, which were subtle twitches of the whiskers or the snout

senses.label: and the correlation is not claimed as causation - cortical activity and body movements may BOTH arise from changes in the internal state
senses.head: and the correlation is not claimed as causation
senses.gloss: cortical activity and body movements may BOTH arise from changes in the internal state
senses.evidence: Our results do not imply that cortical activity is directly due to body movements; instead, cortical activity and body movements may both arise from changes in the internal state. Consistent with this view, we found that sound-evoked activity in V1 is low-dimensional, and thus different from the high-dimensional representation of visual stimuli 13 . This interpretation would explain some of the sound-evoked activity in visual cortex under anesthesia 2 , 3 , where movements are not possible, but state changes are common and difficult to control and monitor

senses.label: with the same suspicion extended outward - stereotyped movements are elicited by images and odors too, so other multisensory findings may have the same origin
senses.head: with the same suspicion extended outward
senses.gloss: stereotyped movements are elicited by images and odors too, so other multisensory findings may have the same origin
senses.evidence: Finally, these observations suggest that changes in states or behavior may also explain other aspects of neural activity that have been previously interpreted as being multisensory 9 . Stereotyped body movements can be elicited not only by sounds 16 – 19 but also by images 32 – 36 and odors 33 , 37 . For instance, in our experiments, the videos evoked visual responses in both V1 and in hippocampal formation, and the latter could be largely explained by video-evoked body movements. Such movements may be even more likely in response to natural stimuli 19 , which are increasingly common in the field. Given the extensive correlates of body movement observed throughout the brain 13 , 14 , 21 , 27 , 38 , these observations reinforce the importance of monitoring behavioral state and body movement when interpreting sensory-evoked activity.

senses.label: AND THE AUTHORS RE-RAN IT: the reported statistic was replaced with a paired Wilcoxon sign-rank test on the same data, and the conclusion survived
senses.evidence: To address this concern, we performed a paired Wilcoxon sign-rank test on the laser on vs laser off firing rate of each unit. We still observe significant increases in firing rate with ChR2 activation of AC-IC feedback.

senses.label: SAMPLE SIZE DECIDED WHAT EXISTED: earlier work found no feedback effect in central IC; recording more neurons revealed a subset there
senses.evidence: In our study we were able to record from a larger neuronal population, revealing a subset of neurons in central IC that were modulated by feedback.

senses.label: AN ASYMMETRY BETWEEN DRIVING AND SILENCING is the paper's central result, and it is read as a claim about the resting state rather than as a failed manipulation
senses.evidence: This result suggests that AC-IC inputs at rest do not contribute to IC responses, but rather modulate collicular activity only when activated.

senses.label: MORE FIRING, LESS TUNING: the feedback is described as reducing selectivity rather than sharpening it, against the expectation the earlier stimulation literature set
senses.evidence: Overall our findings imply that direct cortico-collicular feedback can modulate responses to simple (pure tones) and more complex (DRCs) auditory stimuli by reducing, rather than increasing, sound selectivity.

senses.label: THE SAME RESULT SAID PLAINLY, in the authors' own restatement
senses.evidence: In other words, neuronal firing increases overall, but selective responses to specific frequency bands decrease.

senses.label: AN EFFECT SMALLER THAN EXPECTED IS REPORTED AS SUCH, and read as evidence that the target population inside IC is small
senses.evidence: Whereas the direction of the effect was consistent with our prior expectations, the magnitude of the effect was unexpectedly small.

senses.label: A NEGATIVE RESULT ABOUT INHIBITION: changes made by PV interneurons in cortex do not reach the colliculus
senses.evidence: This suggests that the changes in cortical activity driven by manipulation of PV activity does not propagate to the inferior colliculus.

senses.label: SST IS NOT PV: suppressing SST interneurons moves spontaneous activity in IC where PV manipulation moves nothing — a dissociation between two inhibitory subtypes
senses.head: SST IS NOT PV: suppressing SST interneurons moves spontaneous activity in IC where PV manipulation moves nothing
senses.gloss: a dissociation between two inhibitory subtypes
senses.evidence: SST suppression resulted in an increase in spontaneous, but not tone-evoked activity in IC, which suggests that inhibitory modulation of sound responses in AC does not propagate to IC

senses.label: THE FIELD'S DEFAULT IS ASCENDING: descending feedback is described as routinely overlooked
senses.evidence: Information processing is typically studied as a set of computations ascending along a hierarchy of sensory areas, often overlooking the role of descending feedback between these nuclei.

senses.label: A ROBUSTNESS CHECK AGAINST A SELECTION ARTEFACT: the DCIC result is re-run on rate-matched units in case a few high-firing units carried it
senses.evidence: To verify that these results were not due to a select few high firing rates of units in DCIC, we repeated the analysis comparing only units with spontaneous activity in the laser OFF condition less than 40 Hz.

senses.label: TWO MECHANISMS FOR ONE OBSERVATION ARE LEFT OPEN: direct activation and disinhibition are not equivalent, which is offered as why the interneuron result differs
senses.evidence: feedback is not exactly equivalent to disinhibition. Direct activation causes synchronized activation of cells, while disinhibition allows for asynchronous activation. This difference may explain the different results. Furthermore,

senses.label: OCD here is EITHER a professional diagnosis OR a self-report with OCI-r above 18 - one of the two entry routes involves no clinician at all
senses.head: OCD here is EITHER a professional diagnosis OR a self-report with OCI-r above 18
senses.gloss: one of the two entry routes involves no clinician at all
senses.evidence: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

senses.label: the analysed effect sample is conditioned on the dependent variable: respondents answering No to having experienced any change were sent straight to the end of the survey
senses.evidence: The first question was “ Have you experienced a change in your OCD as a result of taking a psychedelic? ” Participants answering No were redirected toward the end of the survey, whereas participants answering Yes had to select the substance that induced the strongest changes in OCD symptoms, among the list presented in part III.

senses.label: dose is a self-recalled quantity converted by a fixed factor - grams of dried mushroom multiplied by 0.0063 to give milligrams of psilocybin - so it carries both recall error and a species assumption
senses.head: dose is a self-recalled quantity converted by a fixed factor
senses.gloss: grams of dried mushroom multiplied by 0.0063 to give milligrams of psilocybin - so it carries both recall error and a species assumption
senses.evidence: For psilocybin mushrooms, most of the doses were expressed as grams of dried mushrooms, which we converted into milligrams of psilocybin by multiplying by a 0.0063 factor (appropriate for Psilocybe cubensis type of mushrooms according to 30 ). Following this transformation, the mean(SD) dose of psilocybin was 20.30 (16.74)mg, ranging from 1 to 88 and the mean(SD) dose of LSD was 131.56 (69.85)μg, ranging from 10 to 250 (Fig. 3 B).

senses.label: improvement is a single retrospective cursor position from -100 to +100, not a repeated clinical measure, and the OCI-r was collected only at survey time
senses.evidence: Each item was scored by moving a cursor on a 100-point scale (2-point step) starting at midpoint (0: no change ) and ranging from -100 ( Worsening ) to + 100 ( Improvement ).

senses.label: classic psychedelics is a category that behaves inhomogeneously here - LSD and psilocybin drive the result while DMT and mescaline do not
senses.head: classic psychedelics is a category that behaves inhomogeneously here
senses.gloss: LSD and psilocybin drive the result while DMT and mescaline do not
senses.evidence: Similarly, DMT and mescaline were not selected as effective for OCD symptoms. Despite being categorized as serotoninergic hallucinogens, DMT and mescaline have phenomenological and pharmacological profiles that seem to differ from LSD or psilocybin 33 . Among other differences, DMT has no affinity for the serotoninergic receptor 2C, as well as a lower hallucinogenic potency and duration of action in human 34 . Mescaline on the other side, seems to have combined psychedelic and entactogenic properties 35 and does not act on raphe neurons

senses.label: A DEFINING CRITERION THAT SURVIVED ITS OWN REFUTATION: the pre-categorical nature is one of the three characteristics that define iconic memory, and evidence has since shown the system is NOT entirely pre-categorical
senses.evidence: Finally, regarding its pre-categorical nature, Sperling considered the information contained in this storehouse as physical information that maintains the raw data that is not related to the meaning of stimuli. Subsequently, evidence has been obtained that this system is not entirely pre-categorical ( Loftus et al., 1992 ) since the task improves when the stimuli to remember are letters or numbers instead of meaningless forms.

senses.label: with the three characteristics - large capacity, short duration, pre-categorical nature - still given as the definition
senses.head: with the three characteristics
senses.gloss: large capacity, short duration, pre-categorical nature - still given as the definition
senses.evidence: Subsequent research on visual persistence from Coltheart ( Coltheart, 1983 ) and Sperling’s studies ( Sperling, 1960 ) on the persistence of information led to the definition of three characteristics pertaining to iconic memory: a large capacity, a short duration, and a pre-categorical nature.

senses.label: A CAPACITY THAT WAS NEVER OBSERVED, ONLY EXTRAPOLATED: subjects recalled three or four letters in the full report and about 75% of a cued row, and the large capacity follows by EXTRAPOLATING the partial report to the total
senses.evidence: Sperling (1960) demonstrated this large capacity after presenting the results of his total and partial reports. The full report consisted in presenting a 3 × 3 or 3 × 4 matrix of alphanumeric characters for a short period of time to subjects and later asking them which characters they remembered. On the other hand, in the partial report, subjects were directed to remember the characters in a row specifically assigned to them in the instructions. The total report’s results showed that subjects were only able to recall between 3 or 4 letters of the total number. However, in the partial report, subjects remembered around 75% of those that were asked. In extrapolating the partial report’s data to the total, it follows that individuals could report 9 of the 12 letters contained in the instructions (80% of the total), thus demonstrating a large capacity.

senses.label: THE CLASS IS characterizeD BY ITS BEST-STUDIED MEMBER: research focused on iconic memory, the other two sensory types are comparatively scarce, and iconic memory is therefore presented as the paradigm of the class
senses.evidence: Scientific research has focused mainly on iconic memory; information on echoic and haptic memory is comparatively scarce. Thus, taking into account the goals of this article and that it is aimed at a higher education audience, presenting iconic memory as a paradigm of sensory memory is sufficient for an introductory overview.

senses.label: ONE REFERENT, TWO NAMES, WRITTEN AS A PARENTHESIS: declarative memory (explicit) and non-declarative memory (implicit/procedural)
senses.evidence: In the 1980s, the differences between declarative and non-declarative memories were consolidated and disseminated. This, together with contributions from Tulving and others, such as Di Lollo or Graf and Schacter, enabled a more precise classification of different types of memory. To date, Di Lollo’s model of iconic memory ( Di Lollo, 1980 ) has been the most widely accepted and studied of the three existing types of sensory memory. As discussed in the next section, Di Lollo considered iconic memory a storage unit consisting of two components: the persistence of vision and information. Graf and Schacter (1985) proposed a general difference between declarative memory (explicit) and non-declarative memory (implicit/procedural). This stems from the distinction that Tulving (1972) proposed between the aforementioned episodic memory and semantic memory (both, as we will see, are currently included in declarative memory).

senses.label: and the same pair again in the glossary heading itself - Explicit/declarative memory - so the slash IS the synonymy
senses.head: and the same pair again in the glossary heading itself
senses.gloss: Explicit/declarative memory - so the slash IS the synonymy
senses.evidence: Explicit/declarative memory : refers to conscious memories of previously stored experiences, facts and concepts that are verifiable through a verbal reporting of them

senses.label: and a third - Conceptual short-term memory/episodic buffer - for a component named twice in twenty-six years
senses.head: and a third
senses.gloss: Conceptual short-term memory/episodic buffer - for a component named twice in twenty-six years
senses.evidence: Conceptual short-term memory/episodic buffer : This is a temporary storage system capable of integrating information from different sources that is probably controlled by the central executive. It is episodic in that it has episodes in which information is integrated through space and, potentially, extended through time.

senses.label: A DISTINCTION RENAMED ACROSS A CENTURY: James in 1890 distinguished primary from secondary memory, THEREBY REFERRING TO short- and long-term memory
senses.evidence: As Squire (2004) points out, the first theoretical approaches relevant to current neuroscience come from the 19th century. These include Maine de Biran (1804/1929) ( Maine de Biran, 1929 ) who, at the beginning of the century, wrote of mechanical memory, sensitive memory, and representative memory. The philosopher James, and his book The Principles of Psychology ( James, 1890 ), is also especially worth highlighting. Therein, James distinguishes between primary and secondary memory, thereby referring to short- and long-term memory, respectively.

senses.label: and a type named retroactively - Pavlov's studies are related to a type of memory that LATER WOULD BE CALLED associative memory
senses.head: and a type named retroactively
senses.gloss: Pavlov's studies are related to a type of memory that LATER WOULD BE CALLED associative memory
senses.evidence: The importance of Pavlov (1927) and Fitts and Posner (1967) are especially noteworthy during the first two thirds of the 20th century. Pavlov’s studies are related to a type of memory that later would be called associative memory. Meanwhile, Fitts and Posner’s studies are considered the first model to explain procedural memory.

senses.label: THE FIELD'S FIRST RESPONSE TO A FALSIFYING CASE WAS TO QUARANTINE IT: the patient learned a skill without remembering the task, and discussions at the time SET ASIDE motor skills as a special case, keeping the rest of memory of one piece
senses.evidence: The experimental modern era arguably began when Milner (1962) demonstrated, with HM experiments, that a seriously ill patient could acquire a new skill (hand-eye coordination) without any memory of having encountered the task before. “While this finding showed that memory is not unitary, discussions at the time tended to set aside motor skills as a special case representing a less cognitive form of memory. The suggestion was that the rest of memory is of one piece and is dependent on medial temporal lobe structures

senses.label: A GLOSSARY THAT DISCLAIMS ITSELF: the commentary is NOT INTENDED AS AN EXHAUSTIVE DEFINITION, only enough to situate the reader in a complex panorama
senses.evidence: Finally, the following glossary includes commentary about the terminology that, in our opinion, is essential for an introductory overview, enabling interested students and professionals to effectively approach the latest memory-related discoveries. This commentary is not intended as an exhaustive definition, but rather collects relevant information to situate the reader within a complex panorama.

senses.label: and the model that dominated short-term memory was criticised by a specific prediction that failed - that longer residence makes transfer to long-term storage more likely
senses.head: and the model that dominated short-term memory was criticised by a specific prediction that failed
senses.gloss: that longer residence makes transfer to long-term storage more likely
senses.evidence: Despite the explanatory power of Atkinson and Shiffrin’s model, there were a number of issues that this model could not resolve, causing criticism of it. For example, this model implies that the longer an item remains in memory, the more likely it is to be transferred to long-term storage. But studies like those of Tulving and Pearlstone (1966) and Craik and Watkins (1973) show that said relationship does not exist.

senses.label: A DOUBLE DISSOCIATION BORROWED FROM TWO GENETIC SYNDROMES: Williams patients keep language and Down patients keep more spatial capacity, and each does better on the matching task
senses.evidence: Wang and Bellugi (1994) presented a genetically based test that supports the functional and anatomical separation of Baddeley’s model with phonological and visuospatial storehouses. They compared two genetic syndromes (Williams and Down) with different brain morphology. Williams syndrome patients, despite having widespread mental handicaps, preserve their language skills, while Down syndrome patients preserve more partial capacities, but have very limited language skills. It was therefore assumed that the former would be better at verbal tasks related to operative memory, and that the latter would be better at visuospatial tasks related to operative memory. As expected, subjects with Williams syndrome performed better at phonological tasks, while subjects with Down syndrome, in turn, performed better at spatial tasks.

senses.label: and the dissociation that made priming a separate type - severely amnesic patients show COMPLETELY INTACT priming on the same test items they cannot recognise
senses.head: and the dissociation that made priming a separate type
senses.gloss: severely amnesic patients show COMPLETELY INTACT priming on the same test items they cannot recognise
senses.evidence: Several authors ( Tulving et al., 1982 ) had already mentioned the idea of priming as a separate type of memory, but it was not until the 90’s that experiments were conducted to show it ( Hamann and Squire, 1997 ; Stark and Squire, 2000 ; Levy et al., 2004 ). These studies show that severely amnesic patients can exhibit completely intact priming while performing memory tests that include conventional recognition of the same test items

senses.label: ONE EVENT LAID DOWN TWICE: the same childhood accident consolidates as a declarative memory of the event and crystallises separately as a phobia
senses.evidence: In the 90’s, a classification of the types of memory emerged, but the way they act and their interrelation was still unclear. In order to clarify its operation, Packard and McGaugh (1996) proposed that memory systems operate independently and in parallel. For example, an adverse event in childhood (e.g., seeing your grandfather being run over by a combine) can, on the one hand, consolidate as a stable declarative memory for the event itself (the sound of a combine always makes you remember that moment-episodic memory) and, on the other hand, can crystallize in non-declarative memory and result in a phobia experienced as a personality trait rather than as a mere memory (being near a combine will always produce panic and induces a desire to escape that situation-associative memory).

senses.label: priming measured as SENSITIVITY (d'), not as speed - and the alternative explicitly refused. The claim is that the auditory cue helps the picture BREAK THROUGH INTO AWARENESS `rather than simply giving rise to some sort of criterion change`: the participant sees more, rather than becoming readier to say yes. A signal-detection design used for exactly what it is for, which is rare in this corpus
senses.head: priming measured as SENSITIVITY (d'), not as speed
senses.gloss: and the alternative explicitly refused. The claim is that the auditory cue helps the picture BREAK THROUGH INTO AWARENESS `rather than simply giving rise to some sort of criterion change`: the participant sees more, rather than becoming readier to say yes. A signal-detection design used for exactly what it is for, which is rare in this corpus
senses.evidence: the presentation of either a naturalistic sound or spoken word enhances the sensitivity ( d' ) of visual object detection (Chen & Spence, 2011 ; Lupyan & Ward, 2013 ). Such results suggest that the meaning of the auditory cue facilitates visual processing and boosts the breakthrough of the visual stimulus into awareness cross-modally rather than simply giving rise to some sort of criterion change

senses.label: TIME COURSE AS THE INDIVIDUATING PROPERTY - two primes carrying the same meaning, producing the same effect on the same measure, told apart only by WHEN. Naturalistic sounds prime at 350 ms and not at 1,000; spoken words at 1,000 and not at 350. If the effect were named by what it does, these would be one thing; the paper's title insists they are two, and the difference is a latency
senses.head: TIME COURSE AS THE INDIVIDUATING PROPERTY
senses.gloss: two primes carrying the same meaning, producing the same effect on the same measure, told apart only by WHEN. Naturalistic sounds prime at 350 ms and not at 1,000; spoken words at 1,000 and not at 350. If the effect were named by what it does, these would be one thing; the paper's title insists they are two, and the difference is a latency
senses.evidence: The cross-modal semantic priming effects elicited by the presentation of naturalistic sounds versus spoken words can therefore be dissociated in terms of their differing time courses. Furthermore, naturalistic sounds consistently primed the visual pictures at the short SOA; in contrast, the priming effect elicited by spoken words was significantly modulated by the SOA tested beforehand

senses.label: the word effect is CONDITIONED BY THE ORDER OF TESTING, and the paper reports both halves: meet the 1,000-ms SOA first and priming carries over to 350 ms; meet the 350-ms SOA first - where nothing happens - and the 1,000-ms effect is eliminated too. **A priming effect that depends on what the participant was tested on beforehand** is partly a fact about the paradigm rather than about the mind, and a corpus of priming records should be able to find the papers that said so
senses.head: the word effect is CONDITIONED BY THE ORDER OF TESTING, and the paper reports both halves: meet the 1,000-ms SOA first and priming carries over to 350 ms; meet the 350-ms SOA first
senses.gloss: where nothing happens - and the 1,000-ms effect is eliminated too. **A priming effect that depends on what the participant was tested on beforehand** is partly a fact about the paradigm rather than about the mind, and a corpus of priming records should be able to find the papers that said so
senses.evidence: when the 350-ms SOA (where no priming effect was observed) was tested first, the priming effect at the 1,000-ms SOA was eliminated as well. Finally, higher sensitivity in the 350-ms than in the 1,000-ms SOA was observed in both experiments

senses.label: `via cross-modal associations` and `short lived` - the abstract's own characterisation of the sound effect, and both halves matter. The route is associative rather than lexical, and the duration is explicitly limited, which is what distinguishes this from the long-lasting perceptual priming other records in this corpus describe
senses.head: `via cross-modal associations` and `short lived`
senses.gloss: the abstract's own characterisation of the sound effect, and both halves matter. The route is associative rather than lexical, and the duration is explicitly limited, which is what distinguishes this from the long-lasting perceptual priming other records in this corpus describe
senses.evidence: visual picture processing can be rapidly primed by naturalistic sounds via cross-modal associations, and this effect is short lived. In contrast, spoken words prime visual picture processing over a wider range of prime-target intervals, though this effect was conditioned by the prior context

senses.label: A CLAIM ABOUT A STRUCTURE, EVIDENCED ONLY IN THE PART THAT WAS STUDIED: the midbrain is GENERALLY THOUGHT TO BE BRAIN STATE INDEPENDENT - and the conclusion MAY NOT HOLD TRUE when different subregions are considered
senses.head: A CLAIM ABOUT A STRUCTURE, EVIDENCED ONLY IN THE PART THAT WAS STUDIED: the midbrain is GENERALLY THOUGHT TO BE BRAIN STATE INDEPENDENT
senses.gloss: and the conclusion MAY NOT HOLD TRUE when different subregions are considered
senses.evidence: In contrast to findings in the ACx, neuronal activity in the auditory midbrain or inferior colliculus (IC) is generally thought to be brain state independent. For example, the spectral and temporal tunings of IC neurons in the awake animals are very similar to those in the anesthetized animals 10 , 11 .
