Activity in AC is not only related to processing the sounds and the other context-relevant stimuli but also to mental processes associated with performing a task such as selection of and preparation for behavioral actions, and expectation of rewards ( Brosch et al., 2011 ).

senses.label: with the scope of the conclusion bounded at the end: whether persistent activity changes ALSO SUPPORT STORAGE FOR EVEN LONGER PERIODS and other WM processes IS NOT CLEAR AND IS UNDER DEBATE
senses.evidence: Whether persistent activity changes in AC also support the storage of information for even longer periods and other WM processes, including spatial aspects and processes requiring modifications of stored information, is not clear and is under debate ( Fritz et al., 2005 ; Scott and Mishkin, 2016 ).

senses.label: THREE NULLS, ALL OF THEM LOAD-BEARING - which is unusual enough to record. Priming magnitude is comparable across a word task and an arithmetic task; changing the stimulus COLOUR does nothing; changing the RESPONSE HAND does nothing. Each absence is used as evidence rather than reported as a failure: together they say the effect is indifferent to the surface and to the domain
senses.head: THREE NULLS, ALL OF THEM LOAD-BEARING
senses.gloss: which is unusual enough to record. Priming magnitude is comparable across a word task and an arithmetic task; changing the stimulus COLOUR does nothing; changing the RESPONSE HAND does nothing. Each absence is used as evidence rather than reported as a failure: together they say the effect is indifferent to the surface and to the domain
senses.evidence: The results show that the magnitude of RP was comparable between the two tasks and that changing the color or the response hand had a negligible effect on priming in either task

senses.label: the two accounts of repetition priming, set out as alternatives: FACILITATION OF COMPONENT PROCESSES (repetition tunes the pathway that produces the response) against DIRECT STIMULUS-RESPONSE BINDING retrieved from episodic memory (instance theory, event file theory, action-trigger theory). The difference is whether anything is STORED about the pairing, or whether the machinery simply runs better the second time
senses.evidence: There are two main theoretical perspectives that account for RP. The first perspective emphasizes the role of facilitation of component processes that give rise to a response when a stimulus is repeated. The facilitation can be due to changes in neural responses related to stimulus, task, and/or response features, enabling more efficient processing when the same or a similar stimulus is subsequently presented (see Grill-Spector et al., 2006 , for a review). The second perspective emphasizes direct binding between a stimulus and response during encoding, and the role of episodic memory during retrieval. RP is explained as the result of a match (or mismatch) between a retrieving cue upon perceiving a stimulus and the context in which that same stimulus, or a similar one, was encountered previously

senses.label: THE RESPONSE-HAND NULL AS A THEORY TEST, and this is why it is in the title. A binding account has the RESPONSE bound to the stimulus at encoding, so changing the hand that responds should disturb the retrieved match. It did not - the effect was `negligible`. The paper does not declare the binding account dead, and neither does this record; what is recorded is that the manipulation its logic predicts should matter, did not
senses.head: THE RESPONSE-HAND NULL AS A THEORY TEST, and this is why it is in the title. A binding account has the RESPONSE bound to the stimulus at encoding, so changing the hand that responds should disturb the retrieved match. It did not
senses.gloss: the effect was `negligible`. The paper does not declare the binding account dead, and neither does this record; what is recorded is that the manipulation its logic predicts should matter, did not
senses.evidence: The results show that the magnitude of RP was comparable between the two tasks and that changing the color or the response hand had a negligible effect on priming in either task

senses.label: PRIMING IS INDEXED TO THE LEVEL THE TASK IS DIRECTED AT - the principle offered to explain why surface changes do nothing: `when a task at test required only conceptual processing, priming occurred at a SEMANTIC LEVEL rather than at the level of perceptual features ... priming operates at the level of processing at which the task is directed` (Schacter, 1990). The effect does not live in the stimulus; it lives at whatever depth the task made the participant work
senses.head: PRIMING IS INDEXED TO THE LEVEL THE TASK IS DIRECTED AT
senses.gloss: the principle offered to explain why surface changes do nothing: `when a task at test required only conceptual processing, priming occurred at a SEMANTIC LEVEL rather than at the level of perceptual features ... priming operates at the level of processing at which the task is directed` (Schacter, 1990). The effect does not live in the stimulus; it lives at whatever depth the task made the participant work
senses.evidence: when a task at test required only conceptual processing, priming occurred at a semantic level rather than at the level of perceptual features. This indicates that priming operates at the level of processing at which the task is directed

senses.label: AND THE PAPER DOUBTS ITS OWN NULL, in as many words: `It is possible that our manipulation of response hand was NOT SUFFICIENTLY SENSITIVE to elicit the effect of a change in motor action on RP`. It notes that the comparison which did find an effect (Horner and Henson) contrasted verbal with keypress responses, while this one contrasted left with right hand - a smaller change. A null reported with the reason it might be an artifact of the manipulation's size
senses.head: AND THE PAPER DOUBTS ITS OWN NULL, in as many words: `It is possible that our manipulation of response hand was NOT SUFFICIENTLY SENSITIVE to elicit the effect of a change in motor action on RP`. It notes that the comparison which did find an effect (Horner and Henson) contrasted verbal with keypress responses, while this one contrasted left with right hand
senses.gloss: a smaller change. A null reported with the reason it might be an artifact of the manipulation's size
senses.evidence: It is possible that our manipulation of response hand was not sufficiently sensitive to elicit the effect of a change in motor action on RP between study and test. It is conceivable that a change in motor action requires more attentional resources when the change is large (e.g., from a hand response to a verbal response) than when it is small

senses.label: the same task across species is an EQUIVALENCE CLAIM resting on declared adjustments: reward volume scaled to each species' normal consumption, tubing gauge changed, sound levels set above each species' own threshold
senses.evidence: The volume of water reward was scaled according to the normal consumption for each species

senses.label: similar performance here means failure to reject a difference at n=10 per species, not a demonstrated equivalence - the paper's own phrasing is that no major differences were found
senses.head: similar performance here means failure to reject a difference at n=10 per species, not a demonstrated equivalence
senses.gloss: the paper's own phrasing is that no major differences were found
senses.evidence: We found that both species achieved similarly high performance levels. On average, rats learned the task faster than mice, although some mice were as fast as the average rat. No major differences in subjective categorization boundaries or the speed of adaptation between the two species were found.

senses.label: subjective category boundary is the 50% point of a fitted logistic, distinct from the experimenter's boundary, and it is what shifts between blocks
senses.evidence: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

senses.label: speed of switching is measured as the trial at which an exponential fit crosses chance, not as trials to criterion
senses.evidence: We estimated the speed of switching to a new sound-action association by averaging performance for each trial from several sessions, and calculating when an exponential fit crossed the 50% chance performance level

senses.label: valid trials exclude early withdrawals, so every performance figure is conditioned on the animal having waited out the sound
senses.evidence: If animals withdrew before the end of the stimulus, the trial was aborted and denoted as invalid. Only valid trials were used in calculations of the fraction of correct trials.

senses.label: NON-UNIQUENESS IS DECLARED IN THE METHODS, BEFORE ANY RESULT: with many interacting parameters, alternative sets could reproduce similar results, and no model can be shown to provide a unique solution
senses.evidence: Since HNN is a complex model with a large number of parameters, many of which interact, we cannot rule out that some alternative parameter sets could not reproduce similar results (see “ Discussion ” section). HNN was designed to be a hypothesis development and testing tool. The hypothesis testing here was motivated from our prior studies of sensory evoked responses, which provided the baseline assumptions for the pattern of exogenous proximal and distal drives underlying an evoked response, and prior literature on neural mechanisms underlying hemispheric dominance (see “ Introduction ” section). While we cannot show that any given model provides a unique solution, it is important to note that the dipole shape produced by HNN depends crucially on the underlying assumptions and we can examine the dipole response under alternative hypotheses. To illustrate this, we show models using alternative assumptions for two of our examples

senses.label: and again in the discussion - no given waveform has a unique way in which to model it, because the parameters interact and trade off, which is why the tool is called a hypothesis-testing tool
senses.head: and again in the discussion
senses.gloss: no given waveform has a unique way in which to model it, because the parameters interact and trade off, which is why the tool is called a hypothesis-testing tool
senses.evidence: It is important to note that, since HNN is a large-scale model with thousands of differential equations and parameters, we cannot claim that any given waveform has a unique way in which to model it. With large numbers of parameters, many of which interact and trade off, HNN is primarily a hypothesis testing tool as it is not feasible to test the entire parameter space. However, a large proportion of the model, including cell morphologies and physiologies, and local connectivity patterns were fixed based on a large body of animal models, introducing biologically realistic constraints (Jones et al. 2007 ; Neymotin et al. 2020 ). Further, we drastically limited the number of parameters free to vary, by making the assumption that many basic features of the network are preserved across sensory areas, which allowed us to fix the vast majority of parameters to values previously established for somatosensory response models

senses.label: TWO RIVAL MECHANISMS REPRODUCE THE TARGET AND BREAK THE REST OF THE WAVEFORM: weakening inhibitory connections, or cutting layer V calcium density by 94%, both produce the smaller N100m - and both wreck the P200m, at RMSE 7.84 and 6.57 against 1.96
senses.head: TWO RIVAL MECHANISMS REPRODUCE THE TARGET AND BREAK THE REST OF THE WAVEFORM: weakening inhibitory connections, or cutting layer V calcium density by 94%, both produce the smaller N100m
senses.gloss: and both wreck the P200m, at RMSE 7.84 and 6.57 against 1.96
senses.evidence: However, this manipulation also impacted the subsequent P200m peak, which was significantly larger when the local connections to the inhibitory neurons were decreased due to increased pyramidal neuron firing (data not shown), and hence a larger RMSE between the model and recorded data were observed; RMSE = 7.84 compared to RMSE = 1.96 in Fig. 4 . Similarly, we found that the N100m amplitude decrease could also be reproduced by a simulation in which the calcium channel density in the soma and along the dendrites of the layer V pyramidal neurons (Table S2), was decreased by approximately 94% from the right hemisphere AEF parameters (Fig. 5 b). In this case, the subsequent P200m amplitude was smaller than recorded data due to decreased pyramidal neuron firing (data not shown), and hence the RMSE between the model and recorded data was again larger than before; RMSE = 6.57 compared to RMSE = 1.96. These results suggest that initial manipulations of the strength of the distal input as in Fig. 4 ; Table 1 , was more effective at reproducing multiple features of the empirical data and we therefore used the initial left AEF model for all following analyses.

senses.label: which is only visible because the alternatives were built and reported rather than assumed away
senses.evidence: While our initial testing of the hypothesis that strength of the exogenous distal inputs would be essential to defining the amplitude of the AEF peaks confirmed that alteration in this parameter can reproduce the observed differences, we cannot rule out that alternative mechanisms could reproduce similar results. To address this issue, we also tested two alternative models that could logically account for N100m amplitude differences through alteration of local network features, rather than inputs into the network. Since simulations show that both somatic inhibition and layer V calcium activity can lead to current flow down the dendrite (i.e. larger N100m amplitudes), we decreased the parameter values representing each one at a time to test if these changes could also lead to less current flow down the dendrite and therefore smaller N100m amplitudes as seen in left hemisphere AEFs.

senses.label: TWO RESULTS FROM ONE MODEL WITH DIFFERENT EVIDENTIAL STATUS, AND THE PAPER GRADES THEM: for the hemispheric difference the parameter space was narrowed after the fact, and for the contralateral difference there were clear prior hypotheses predicting the parameters AND the direction, enabling much clearer conclusions
senses.evidence: In the case of interpreting the difference between left and right hemispheres, we attempted to narrow down the parameter space of interest by identifying which changes made the largest contribution to the difference in waveform shape. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that other parameter values could account for the finding in a different way. In the case of contralateral compared to ipsilateral AEFs on the other hand, we had clear hypotheses predicting not only the parameters of interest, but also the direction of their adjustment, enabling much clearer conclusions.

senses.label: and the contralateral model changed only four parameters, chosen from the literature rather than from the data, against 28 hand-tuned and optimized for the other
senses.evidence: However, note that the contralateral models were established by hand-tuning and then optimizing all 28 input parameters (Table 1 ), while the ipsilateral model was generated by adjusting only four parameters, three of which by a fixed value. Importantly, the four parameters, as well as the directions in which to adjust them (i.e. increasing the time of each of three inputs by a fixed amount and decreasing the network scale), were chosen based on predictions from the literature, not on the patterns identified in our data, and no further steps were taken to fit the model simulations to the empirical AEFs. In view of this procedure, we consider the ipsilateral models to reproduce the corresponding AEFs remarkably well.

senses.label: with the hemispheric interpretation labelled model-derived predictions, because there were no clear pre-defined hypotheses
senses.evidence: However, the functional lateralization of auditory processing continues to be debated (e.g. Boemio et al. 2005 ), and its relation to biophysical mechanisms is unknown. Additionally, our interpretations are model-derived predictions, since we did not have clear pre-defined hypotheses regarding the mechanisms underlying the differences in left and right AEFs.

senses.label: THE FITTED PARAMETER MAY BE ABSORBING AN ANATOMICAL artifact: cortical folding in the left hemisphere increases signal cancelation, so the parameter differences may be compensating for structure rather than reflecting function
senses.evidence: For example, macroanatomical differences not captured in HNN between left and right hemispheres could contribute to, if not fully account for, waveform differences observed in AEFs (Galaburda et al. 1978 ; Rademacher et al. 1993 ; Penhune et al. 1996 ; Howard and Poeppel 2009 ). In fact, Shaw et al. ( 2013 ) argued that what may appear as a functional asymmetry in auditory processing is, at least partially, caused by structural asymmetries, as increased cortical folding in the left auditory regions results in increased MEG/EEG signal cancelation. Here, we do not account for these anatomical differences since HNN has been developed to account for the microanatomical principles underlying electrophysiological recordings, and does not include cortical folding in its parameters. As such, we cannot rule out the possibility that the parameter differences between left and right hemisphere AEFs we found in our model are simply compensating for the effect of structural differences, and do not accurately reflect underlying functional mechanisms.

senses.label: A QUANTITY THAT WAS NOT FITTED IS USED AS VALIDATION: firing rates were not part of the fitting procedure and land within physiological ranges, which is offered as further support
senses.evidence: We also calculated the simulated firing rates of each neuronal population by averaging the number of action potentials over trials and cells. We found the highest firing rates in basket cells (layer V = 13.97 spikes/s; layer II/III = 13.46 spikes/s), followed by layer V pyramidal neurons (10.60 spikes/s), and low firing rates in layer II/III pyramidal neurons (1.85 spikes/s, cf. Fig. 4 f). Although firing rates were not considered as part of the model fitting procedures, these firing rates appear to be within physiological ranges (Wallace and Palmer 2008 ; Atencio and Schreiner 2010 ), further supporting the model-derived predictions.

senses.label: THE SAME TEST ON SIMULATED AND ON RECORDED DATA IS NOT THE SAME OBJECT: the reduced variability of simulations means the statistics are not directly comparable, and they are reported anyway for the qualitative features
senses.evidence: We applied the same ANOVAs to the model simulation (see below), by running 10 simulations per modelled condition as a source of variability. While the reduced variability of simulations compared to human MEG data means that these statistics are not directly comparable to those of the empirical data, they nevertheless give insight into whether specific qualitative features, such as differences in slopes or latencies, are reproduced by the model.

senses.label: and the simulations are smoothed specifically so that a comparison can be made at all, a transform applied to one side of it
senses.evidence: To assess the correspondence between averaged evoked responses and modelled dipoles, simulations are smoothed (30 ms Hamming window, see Table S2). There are many more sources of variability in the larger network contributing to the recorded human data, such as spike variability across the network and individual subject differences. We assume high-frequency components created by this variability are more likely to average out in the larger network and multi-subject averages contributing to the recorded AEFs than in model simulations. We therefore apply smoothing to model simulations to allow for a direct comparison between simulation and data

senses.label: A NON-SIGNIFICANT TREND BECOMES A MODELLED MECHANISM: latency differences did not reach significance, and a 5 ms shift was put into the model and captured the trend well
senses.evidence: Although latency differences between contralateral and ipsilateral AEFs were not statistically significant in our data, N100m latencies were slightly but consistently larger in ipsilateral AEFs (Fig. 3 ). This trend was captured well by simulations incorporating this 5 ms shift.

senses.label: with an explanation offered for why the effect keeps failing to replicate - it is small enough to be swamped by individual differences at those latencies
senses.head: with an explanation offered for why the effect keeps failing to replicate
senses.gloss: it is small enough to be swamped by individual differences at those latencies
senses.evidence: Since this is a fairly small difference in latency, it may overlap with individually differing factors that influence AEF measures at these latencies, and may not be easily demonstrated. We speculate that this may explain why other studies, like our own, have not been able to confirm latency differences between ipsilateral and contralateral AEFs

senses.label: THE CANONICAL ASSUMPTION IS GRANTED WITH ITS EXCEPTION STATED: auditory connectivity is less well understood, laminar differences are less prominent than in visual or somatosensory cortex, and layer IV may play a different role
senses.evidence: It is important to note that the connectivity within the auditory cortex is not as well understood as in other sensory regions, and that focusing solely on similarities between cortical regions is likely an oversimplified description of auditory cortical activation. There are known differences between auditory cortex and other sensory regions, as for example, laminar differences are less prominent than in visual or somatosensory regions, and there is some evidence to suggest that the functional role of auditory layer IV may differ from those in other sensory regions

senses.label: and a parameter value is converted into a physical count - 240,000 pyramidal neurons against 300,000 - which reads as a measurement and is a scaling factor
senses.head: and a parameter value is converted into a physical count
senses.gloss: 240,000 pyramidal neurons against 300,000 - which reads as a measurement and is a scaling factor
senses.evidence: As such, the model results predict that a smaller network with on the order of 240,000 pyramidal neurons (1200 × 200 PN per layer) generated the ipsilateral response compared to 300,000 (1500 × 200 PN per layer) for the contralateral response

senses.label: planum temporale - bounded at the horizontal sylvian fissure versus extending to the ascending ramus and into parietal lobe; no consensus exists and the choice is stipulated per study
senses.head: planum temporale
senses.gloss: bounded at the horizontal sylvian fissure versus extending to the ascending ramus and into parietal lobe; no consensus exists and the choice is stipulated per study
senses.evidence: The markers for the posterior boundary of PT are not well established, because in most cases the posterior end of the sylvian fissure bifurcates into ascending and descending rami, the pattern of which varies across subjects [ 21 ]. There is no consensus on whether the posterior end of PT is limited to the posterior end of the horizontal portion of sylvian fissure [ 22 , 23 ] or extends all the way up to the end-point of the ascending ramus (which could cover a part of the parietal lobe [ 21 ]). In this study, we chose the latter option.

senses.label: learning - explicit and reportable versus implicit; probed here with one debriefing question, and the conclusion hedged to some cases
senses.head: learning
senses.gloss: explicit and reportable versus implicit; probed here with one debriefing question, and the conclusion hedged to some cases
senses.evidence: Subjective reports from the participants after the experiment showed that most were not aware of any stimulus re-occurring during the experiment, suggesting that in some cases the learning occurred implicitly.

senses.label: the same acoustic structure - as a repeated stimulus within a trial versus as the same exemplar recurring across trials; the second is what produces learning and the first is the control
senses.head: the same acoustic structure
senses.gloss: as a repeated stimulus within a trial versus as the same exemplar recurring across trials; the second is what produces learning and the first is the control
senses.evidence: Without the subjects’ knowledge, however, one exemplar of a repeated tone cloud (reference tone cloud, RefTC) remained the same from trial to trial. That is, for the RefTC stimulus not only the same burst of tone cloud was repeated (three times) within a trial, but also the exact same exemplar reoccurred over several trials. The trials consisting of RefTC stimuli were presented randomly among trials of RTC and NTC. A RefTC stimulus was drawn from the same statistical process as any other RTC; the only difference was that the same exemplar of RefTC was presented across different trials.

senses.label: an analysis result - as absent under mean activation versus present under distributed pattern classification, on the same scans
senses.head: an analysis result
senses.gloss: as absent under mean activation versus present under distributed pattern classification, on the same scans
senses.evidence: We initially used standard univariate analyses to interrogate the data, but did not find any significant difference in the mean activity evoked by the three RefTC stimuli in any part of the brain. We therefore focused on using MVPA which we believed would have increased sensitivity in our experimental context.

senses.label: a representation of a sound - as a sensory or timbre code versus as a memory trace; the second is preferred on parsimony rather than measurement
senses.head: a representation of a sound
senses.gloss: as a sensory or timbre code versus as a memory trace; the second is preferred on parsimony rather than measurement
senses.evidence: The most parsimonious explanation for our data is a unique memory trace in PT and HC that is formed for each of the three RefTCs, although more work will be needed to probe this point further.

senses.label: SUSTAINED ACTIVITY IS NOT WORKING MEMORY: a region can hold information in subthreshold patterns without elevated activity, and elevated activity can reflect sustained attention instead
senses.evidence: However, a number of recent studies ( Harrison and Tong, 2009 ; Serences et al., 2009 ; Riggall and Postle, 2012 ) have shown that although a brain region may not show elevated activity during the delay period, patterns of subthreshold activity within the same area may nevertheless contain information about the remembered stimulus. Moreover, sustained activity does not imply that the activity is related to WM per se (e.g., it may be related to sustained attention).

senses.label: the maintenance regressor is only interpretable because its correlation with the encoding regressor was MEASURED at 0.04 - the phases are adjacent in time and the BOLD response is lagged
senses.head: the maintenance regressor is only interpretable because its correlation with the encoding regressor was MEASURED at 0.04
senses.gloss: the phases are adjacent in time and the BOLD response is lagged
senses.evidence: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

senses.label: the classifier sees only the middle 10.5 s of the delay, with 4 s trimmed at each end, because the probe tone belonged to the same category and could otherwise leak into the decoding
senses.evidence: In our experiment, the probe tone presented at the retrieval phase was of the same category that was cued for the maintenance phase. It is, therefore, likely that the probe tone could aid in the classification of tones during the maintenance phase (because of the common variance captured by maintenance and recall phase regressors). To ensure that this was not so, only the middle 10.5 s of the maintenance period was modeled, leaving 4 s on either side based on recommendations by Zarahn et al. (1997) .

senses.label: connectivity is never compared with rest, because heart rate and other physiological variables differ between task and rest and are known to confound functional connectivity
senses.evidence: We compared the encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions against each other instead of comparing each of these against baseline. This is because physiological variables such as heart rate during cognitive tasks (here, working memory) are different from the rest condition ( Middleton et al., 1999 ), and changes in physiological variables are known to confound functional connectivity in fMRI ( Birn, 2012 ). Since the physiological parameters will be similar across encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions compared with any of these conditions against baseline, to minimize the effect of physiological noise on the connectivity analysis, we report the comparison in connectivity among the three conditions.

senses.label: the inclusion criteria differ BY ANALYSIS and each difference is justified: poor performers are excluded from classification to reduce noise and retained in the univariate analysis because the brain-behaviour correlation requires the spread
senses.evidence: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

senses.label: d-PRIME is d', the signal-detection sensitivity index, and not a priming prime despite carrying the word: it is the per-subject detection measure (0.89, 0.99, 1.16) used as the exclusion criterion for the pattern analysis
senses.evidence: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

senses.label: THE HEADLINE MECHANISM IS DECLARED UNTESTED, IN THE PAPER'S OWN DISCUSSION: ALTHOUGH THE CAUSALITY OR EVEN THE CONTRIBUTION OF THE PROPOSED ROLES OF PVs, SOMs, AND VIPs AND RECOVERED A1 SOUND PROCESSING WERE NOT TESTED HERE, THEY WILL BE EVALUATED IN FUTURE WORK
senses.evidence: Although the causality or even the contribution of the proposed roles of PVs, SOMs, and VIPs and recovered A1 sound processing were not tested here, they will be evaluated in future work.

senses.label: a second time, for the quantity the argument rests on: ALTHOUGH WE DO NOT PRESENT A MEASURE OF NETWORK STABILITY - and `stabilizer` is the role the paper assigns to PVs
senses.head: a second time, for the quantity the argument rests on: ALTHOUGH WE DO NOT PRESENT A MEASURE OF NETWORK STABILITY
senses.gloss: and `stabilizer` is the role the paper assigns to PVs
senses.evidence: Although we do not present a measure of network stability, future studies could utilize optogenetic perturbations to further investigate our proposed roles of PVs, SOMs, and VIPs while also evaluating how network stability changes after NIHL.

senses.label: and a third time, inside the sentence that states the conclusion: OUR OBSERVATIONS ARE CONSISTENT WITH THE NOTION, ALBEIT NOT TESTED HERE, THAT PVs ACT AS THE STABILIZERS, WHEREAS SOMs ACT AS THE MODULATORS OF A1 PLASTICITY. Three declarations of the same limit, in three places, on the claim the title carries
senses.evidence: Taken together, our observations are consistent with the notion, albeit not tested here, that PVs act as the stabilizers, whereas SOMs act as the modulators of A1 plasticity.

senses.label: THE MODEL'S OWN MECHANISM WAS LOOKED FOR AND NOT FOUND: WE MODELED RECOVERY AS EITHER DEPOLARIZATION OR HYPERPOLARIZATION OF THE RESTING MEMBRANE POTENTIAL INDUCED BY CURRENT INJECTION - HOWEVER, OUR RESULTS DID NOT SHOW A CHANGE IN RESTING MEMBRANE POTENTIAL AFTER NIHL. The model's variable is not the measured one, and the paper says so
senses.head: THE MODEL'S OWN MECHANISM WAS LOOKED FOR AND NOT FOUND: WE MODELED RECOVERY AS EITHER DEPOLARIZATION OR HYPERPOLARIZATION OF THE RESTING MEMBRANE POTENTIAL INDUCED BY CURRENT INJECTION
senses.gloss: HOWEVER, OUR RESULTS DID NOT SHOW A CHANGE IN RESTING MEMBRANE POTENTIAL AFTER NIHL. The model's variable is not the measured one, and the paper says so
senses.evidence: At the neuronal level, we modeled recovery as either depolarization or hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential induced by current injection. After peripheral injuries, such as in NIHL, it is possible that intrinsic or synaptic mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity could lead to such changes in the membrane potential. However, our results did not show a change in resting membrane potential after NIHL.

senses.label: and the regime that makes the model's conclusions follow is an assumption whose truth is open: THE ASSUMPTION THAT CORTICAL INHIBITION IS NEEDED TO PREVENT PATHOLOGIC ACTIVITY PLACES THE MODEL IN THE ISN (ISN) REGIME, and IT REMAINS AN OPEN QUESTION WHETHER THE CORTEX LIES IN THE ISN REGIME WITH INHIBITION ACTIVELY PREVENTING UNSTABLE DYNAMICS BY BALANCING EXCITATION OR IS SIMPLY WIRED TO RESIST INSTABILITY
senses.evidence: However, it remains an open question whether the cortex lies in the ISN regime with inhibition actively preventing unstable dynamics by balancing excitation or is simply wired to resist instability.

senses.label: AN ABSENCE USED AS A CONSTRAINT: THE ABSENCE OF SUCH PATHWAYS IN OUR EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS IMPLIES THAT THE DYNAMICS OBSERVED IN THE ISN REGIME CONSTRAIN THE MECHANISMS UTILIZED IN RECOVERY - the alternatives the model allows were not seen, and that is the argument
senses.head: AN ABSENCE USED AS A CONSTRAINT: THE ABSENCE OF SUCH PATHWAYS IN OUR EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS IMPLIES THAT THE DYNAMICS OBSERVED IN THE ISN REGIME CONSTRAIN THE MECHANISMS UTILIZED IN RECOVERY
senses.gloss: the alternatives the model allows were not seen, and that is the argument
senses.evidence: Yet, the absence of such pathways in our experimental results implies that the dynamics observed in the ISN regime constrain the mechanisms utilized in recovery.

senses.label: THE SAME CELL TYPE, OPPOSITE SIGN AT TWO TIMES: THE INCREASED PV SOUND-EVOKED ACTIVITY 10 DAYS AFTER NIHL MAY STABILIZE THE INCREASED PN ACTIVITY - HOWEVER, 1 DAY AFTER NIHL, WE OBSERVED REDUCED SOUND-EVOKED PV ACTIVITY. A tag reading `PV activity increases after noise trauma` is true of one time point and false of the other
senses.head: THE SAME CELL TYPE, OPPOSITE SIGN AT TWO TIMES: THE INCREASED PV SOUND-EVOKED ACTIVITY 10 DAYS AFTER NIHL MAY STABILIZE THE INCREASED PN ACTIVITY
senses.gloss: HOWEVER, 1 DAY AFTER NIHL, WE OBSERVED REDUCED SOUND-EVOKED PV ACTIVITY. A tag reading `PV activity increases after noise trauma` is true of one time point and false of the other
senses.evidence: Our results suggest that the increased PV sound-evoked activity 10 days after NIHL (Fig. 4d, k , cyan) may stabilize the increased PN activity (Fig. 2 ). However, 1 day after NIHL, we observed reduced sound-evoked PV activity

senses.label: and the early reduction is given a role of its own: SINCE PVs INITIATE CORTICAL PLASTICITY IN JUVENILE AND ADULT BRAIN, AN INITIAL REDUCTION IN PV ACTIVITY AFTER NIHL MAY INITIATE CORTICAL PLASTICITY - so the two signs are two stages, not a contradiction
senses.head: and the early reduction is given a role of its own: SINCE PVs INITIATE CORTICAL PLASTICITY IN JUVENILE AND ADULT BRAIN, AN INITIAL REDUCTION IN PV ACTIVITY AFTER NIHL MAY INITIATE CORTICAL PLASTICITY
senses.gloss: so the two signs are two stages, not a contradiction
senses.evidence: Since PVs initiate cortical plasticity in juvenile and adult brain 83 an initial reduction in PV activity after NIHL may initiate cortical plasticity. Consistent with this notion, a rapid drop in PV-mediated PN inhibition as early as 1 day after cochlear denervation precedes the recovery of cortical sound processing

senses.label: A DISAGREEMENT WITH THREE CANDIDATE CAUSES NAMED, AND ONE OF THEM IS THE SAMPLE SIZE: a recent study REPORTED THAT THE PV SOUND-EVOKED ACTIVITY WAS REDUCED AFTER COCHLEAR DENERVATION AND REMAINED REDUCED FOR TWO WEEKS - the differences offered are the damage model (OUABAIN, WHICH ELIMINATES ~95% OF THE TYPE 1 SGNs), THE SOUND-STIMULI USED (BROADBAND VS. 12 kHz PURE TONES) AND THE NUMBER OF PVs TRACKED (82 VS. 29)
senses.head: A DISAGREEMENT WITH THREE CANDIDATE CAUSES NAMED, AND ONE OF THEM IS THE SAMPLE SIZE: a recent study REPORTED THAT THE PV SOUND-EVOKED ACTIVITY WAS REDUCED AFTER COCHLEAR DENERVATION AND REMAINED REDUCED FOR TWO WEEKS
senses.gloss: the differences offered are the damage model (OUABAIN, WHICH ELIMINATES ~95% OF THE TYPE 1 SGNs), THE SOUND-STIMULI USED (BROADBAND VS. 12 kHz PURE TONES) AND THE NUMBER OF PVs TRACKED (82 VS. 29)
senses.evidence: A recent study 11 reported that the PV sound-evoked activity was reduced after cochlear denervation and remained reduced for two weeks. However, unlike our model of noise-induced cochlear damage, cochlear denervation was induced with bilateral cochlear application of ouabain, which eliminates ~95% of the type 1 SGNs. Since the type and the severity of peripheral organ damage may result in heterogeneous cortical plasticity 7 , 10 , 16 , 21 , 30 , 93 – 99 , noise- and ouabain-induced damage to the cochlea may trigger different trajectories of plasticity in A1 neuronal subtypes. Another explanation for the observed differences could arise from differences in the experimental design, such as the sound-stimuli used (broadband vs. 12 kHz pure tones 11 ) and the number of PVs tracked (82 vs. 29 11 ).

senses.label: TWO IMAGING METHODS, SAME RULE, DIFFERENT SIZE: WIDE-FIELD IMAGING SHOWED LARGER SHIFTS AND REDUCED RECOVERY IN THE RESPONSE THRESHOLDS COMPARED TO THE 2P IMAGING, because WIDE-FIELD IMAGING ASSESSES RESPONSES FROM DIFFERENT NEURONAL COMPARTMENTS (SOMATA AND DENDRITES) AND DIFFERENT CORTICAL LAYERS
senses.evidence: Although we found overall similar plasticity rules via 2P and wide-field imaging after NIHL, wide-field imaging showed larger shifts and reduced recovery in the response thresholds compared to the 2P imaging. The main reason that likely explains these differences is that wide-field imaging assesses responses from different neuronal compartments (somata and dendrites) and different cortical layers, whereas 2P imaging assesses only L2/ 3 somatic responses

senses.label: THE CLASS NAMES ARE NOT THE CLASSES: ONE LIMITATION OF OUR STUDY IS THAT WE STUDIED CELLULAR MECHANISMS BASED ON DISTINGUISHING PNs, PVs, SOMs, AND VIPs - HOWEVER, THESE NEURONAL SUBTYPES ARE NOT A HOMOGENEOUS POPULATION
senses.head: THE CLASS NAMES ARE NOT THE CLASSES: ONE LIMITATION OF OUR STUDY IS THAT WE STUDIED CELLULAR MECHANISMS BASED ON DISTINGUISHING PNs, PVs, SOMs, AND VIPs
senses.gloss: HOWEVER, THESE NEURONAL SUBTYPES ARE NOT A HOMOGENEOUS POPULATION
senses.evidence: In this context, one limitation of our study is that we studied cellular mechanisms based on distinguishing PNs, PVs, SOMs, and VIPs; however, these neuronal subtypes are not a homogeneous population 35 , 36 . Moreover, our 2P studies were only limited to L2/3.

senses.label: WHAT RECOVERS IS NOT WHAT MATTERS: COMPENSATORY A1 PLASTICITY LIKELY SUPPORTS THE RECOVERY OF THE PERCEPTUAL SOUND-DETECTION THRESHOLD BUT DOES NOT SUPPORT SOUND PROCESSING ENCODED BY PRECISE SPIKE TIMING, SUCH AS MODULATED NOISE OR SPEECH, AND RESTRICTS HEARING IN A NOISY ENVIRONMENT
senses.evidence: Compensatory A1 plasticity after peripheral damage likely supports the recovery of the perceptual sound-detection threshold but does not support sound processing encoded by precise spike timing, such as modulated noise or speech, and restricts hearing in a noisy environment

senses.label: and the cell that carries that ability is the one that goes down: A1 SOMs, WHICH ARE CRITICALLY IMPORTANT FOR SOUND PROCESSING ENCODED BY PRECISE SPIKE TIMING OF NEURONAL FIRING, SHOWED REDUCED SOUND-EVOKED ACTIVITY AFTER NIHL
senses.evidence: Interestingly, A1 SOMs, which are critically important for sound processing encoded by precise spike timing of neuronal firing 38 , 46 , 89 , 90 , showed reduced sound-evoked activity after NIHL

senses.label: A COMPOSITE MEASURE WHOSE PARTS ARE NAMED: ABR THRESHOLD AND GAIN REPRESENT THE COMBINED FUNCTIONALITY OF INNER HAIR CELLS (IHCs), OHCs, TYPE-I SGNs, AND SYNAPSES BETWEEN THE IHCs AND TYPE-I SGN DENDRITES CALLED RIBBON SYNAPSES - four things behind one number, and the paper goes on to separate them anatomically
senses.head: A COMPOSITE MEASURE WHOSE PARTS ARE NAMED: ABR THRESHOLD AND GAIN REPRESENT THE COMBINED FUNCTIONALITY OF INNER HAIR CELLS (IHCs), OHCs, TYPE-I SGNs, AND SYNAPSES BETWEEN THE IHCs AND TYPE-I SGN DENDRITES CALLED RIBBON SYNAPSES
senses.gloss: four things behind one number, and the paper goes on to separate them anatomically
senses.evidence: ABR threshold and gain represent the combined functionality of inner hair cells (IHCs), OHCs, type-I SGNs, and synapses between the IHCs and type-I SGN dendrites called ribbon synapses

senses.label: and it does separate them: NOISE EXPOSURE SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCED THE NUMBER OF RIBBON SYNAPSES PER IHC IN THE HIGH-FREQUENCY REGION (16-32 kHz) OF THE COCHLEA, WITHOUT AFFECTING THE SURVIVAL OF EITHER IHCs OR OHCs
senses.evidence: We found that noise exposure significantly reduced the number of ribbon synapses per IHC in the high-frequency region (16–32 kHz) of the cochlea (Fig. 1l, m ), without affecting the survival of either IHCs or OHCs

senses.label: THE CIRCUIT THE INTERPRETATION RESTS ON IS IMPORTED, NOT MEASURED HERE: BASED ON THE KNOWN SEQUENTIALLY ORGANIZED INHIBITORY CORTICAL NETWORK, WHERE VIPs NEURONS INHIBIT SOMs, SOMs INHIBIT PVs AND PNs, AND PVs INHIBIT OTHER PVs AND PNs
senses.evidence: Based on the known sequentially organized inhibitory cortical network 35 , where VIPs neurons inhibit SOMs, SOMs inhibit PVs and PNs, and PVs inhibit other PVs and PNs

senses.label: and the reason one class rather than another is cast as the stabiliser is an argument from symmetry: PNs AND PVs ARE EMBEDDED INTO VERY SIMILAR SYNAPTIC ENVIRONMENTS... THIS SYMMETRY PLACES PVs IN A STRATEGIC POSITION FOR MONITORING AND STABILIZING PN ACTIVITY
senses.evidence: PNs and PVs are embedded into very similar synaptic environments. Both receive the excitatory drive from upstream areas 35 , 36 , and both receive strong recurrent excitation, as well as PV- and SOM-mediated inhibition 66 . This symmetry places PVs in a strategic position for monitoring and stabilizing PN activity

senses.label: THE FINDING IS PROPOSED AS A RULE ACROSS SENSORY CORTICES: THE REDUCED CORTICAL SOM ACTIVITY AFTER PERIPHERAL ORGAN DAMAGE MAY BE A COMMON MECHANISM ACROSS SENSORY CORTICES THAT PERMITS THE INCREASED PN GAIN - supported by the somatosensory case where SELECTIVE SOM ACTIVATION AFTER NERVE INJURY WAS SUFFICIENT TO PREVENT THE INCREASED PN ACTIVITY
senses.head: THE FINDING IS PROPOSED AS A RULE ACROSS SENSORY CORTICES: THE REDUCED CORTICAL SOM ACTIVITY AFTER PERIPHERAL ORGAN DAMAGE MAY BE A COMMON MECHANISM ACROSS SENSORY CORTICES THAT PERMITS THE INCREASED PN GAIN
senses.gloss: supported by the somatosensory case where SELECTIVE SOM ACTIVATION AFTER NERVE INJURY WAS SUFFICIENT TO PREVENT THE INCREASED PN ACTIVITY
senses.evidence: Together, these results suggest that the reduced cortical SOM activity after peripheral organ damage may be a common mechanism across sensory cortices that permits the increased PN gain.

senses.label: and the peripheral damage persists while the cortex recovers: NOISE EXPOSURE SIGNIFICANTLY INCREASED THE ABR RESPONSE THRESHOLDS FOR 8-32 kHz TONES, WHICH REMAINED ELEVATED EVEN 10 DAYS AFTER NOISE EXPOSURE
senses.evidence: Further, we found that noise exposure significantly increased the ABR response thresholds for 8–32 kHz tones, which remained elevated even 10 days after noise exposure (Fig. 1h–j ), suggesting persistent and widespread cochlear damage across the tested frequencies.

senses.label: THE TERM HAS NO AGREED REFERENT, SAID IN THE FIRST SENTENCE: PREFRONTAL CORTEX MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE - and the paper then measures it four ways rather than arguing about it
senses.head: THE TERM HAS NO AGREED REFERENT, SAID IN THE FIRST SENTENCE: PREFRONTAL CORTEX MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE
senses.gloss: and the paper then measures it four ways rather than arguing about it
senses.evidence: Prefrontal cortex (PFC) means different things to different people. In recent years, there has been a major increase in publications on the PFC, especially using mice. However, inconsistencies in the nomenclature and anatomical boundaries of PFC areas has made it difficult for researchers to compare data and interpret findings across species. We conducted a meta-analysis of publications on the PFC of humans and rodents and found dramatic differences in the focus of research on these species. In addition, we compared anatomical terms and criteria across several common rodent brain atlases and found inconsistencies among, and even within, leading atlases. To assess the impact of these issues on the research community, we conducted a survey of established PFC researchers on their use of anatomical terms and found little consensus.

senses.label: AND THE RULE IS STATED AS A RULE: confusion arises when the same anatomic term applies to different areas in different species, and ANATOMIC TERMS SHOULD MEAN THE SAME THING ACROSS SPECIES
senses.evidence: The anatomic term “prefrontal” means different things to different people. For neuroscientists studying humans and nonhuman primates, prefrontal cortex (PFC) typically means the granular and orbital parts of the frontal cortex. These researchers often use variations of the term anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) to refer to agranular areas in the medial frontal cortex. By contrast, researchers studying rodents tend to use the term PFC to refer to the same medial frontal areas that are often called ACC in primates. Confusion can arise when the same anatomic term applies to different areas in different species. Anatomic terms should mean the same thing across species.

senses.label: THE JOIN IS ALREADY BEING MADE WRONG, IN PRINT: it is NOT UNCOMMON for researchers to use information about one prefrontal area in a rodent to understand A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT prefrontal area in a primate - and it is EASY TO DISMISS THIS AS MERE SEMANTICS
senses.head: THE JOIN IS ALREADY BEING MADE WRONG, IN PRINT: it is NOT UNCOMMON for researchers to use information about one prefrontal area in a rodent to understand A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT prefrontal area in a primate
senses.gloss: and it is EASY TO DISMISS THIS AS MERE SEMANTICS
senses.evidence: It is easy to dismiss this issue as one of “mere” semantics or terminology, but it has significant, long-term consequences for our field. For instance, it is not uncommon for researchers to use information about one prefrontal area in a rodent species to understand a completely different prefrontal area in a primate species

senses.label: WITH THE GOVERNANCE GAP NAMED: there is NO ACCEPTED CODE OF CONDUCT FOR REPORTING ANATOMIC RESULTS - and, in parentheses, PERHAPS THERE SHOULD BE
senses.head: WITH THE GOVERNANCE GAP NAMED: there is NO ACCEPTED CODE OF CONDUCT FOR REPORTING ANATOMIC RESULTS
senses.gloss: and, in parentheses, PERHAPS THERE SHOULD BE
senses.evidence: That said, we are well aware of disagreements throughout the history of neuroscience about anatomic terms (e.g., V5 vs MT: Zeki, 2004 ) and the fact that there is no accepted “Code of Conduct” for reporting anatomic results. (Perhaps there should be.)

senses.label: THE WHOLE CONTROVERSY IS ABOUT WORDS, AND THEY SAY SO: three reasons, ALL OF WHICH REFLECT CONFUSION ABOUT ANATOMIC NOMENCLATURE AND NOT ACTUAL PHYSICAL OR PHYSIOLOGIC ISSUES
senses.evidence: We think that controversy about rodent PFC has persisted for three reasons, all of which reflect confusion about anatomic nomenclature and not actual physical or physiologic issues. First, the core areas that compose the rodent PFC are characterized using two different nomenclatures (mPFC and ACC). Second, multiple terms and acronyms are used in prominent brain atlases, and the boundaries for the named areas are inconsistent across atlases. Third, hybrid terms, such as prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex, have recently emerged in the literature, which are not used in human or non-human primate studies.

senses.label: MEASUREMENT ONE - THE VOCABULARY IS THE MOST DIVERGENT PART: anatomic terms were THE MOST DIVERSE, needing 22 terms to cover four species, where disease terms needed only 12
senses.head: MEASUREMENT ONE
senses.gloss: THE VOCABULARY IS THE MOST DIVERGENT PART: anatomic terms were THE MOST DIVERSE, needing 22 terms to cover four species, where disease terms needed only 12
senses.evidence: This approach revealed that anatomic terms were the most diverse, with 22 terms needed to account for all four species. By contrast, disease-related terms were least diverse, with just 12 terms needed to account for the ten most common terms across species.

senses.label: and the two literatures use different words for the same object - the most common term in rodents was mPFC and in primates dlPFC, with prelimbic and infralimbic LARGELY ABSENT from the primate literature
senses.head: and the two literatures use different words for the same object
senses.gloss: the most common term in rodents was mPFC and in primates dlPFC, with prelimbic and infralimbic LARGELY ABSENT from the primate literature
senses.evidence: The plots revealed interesting insights into the use of specific terms within and among species. For example, several anatomic terms were quite common in the monkey literature (e.g., FEF, OFC, parietal, vlPFC) and not so common in the other species, including the human PFC literature. In a similar way, the common rodent terms prelimbic and infralimbic were largely absent from the monkey and human literature. The most common term in rodents was “mPFC” and the most common term in primates was “dlPFC.”

senses.label: with the conclusion drawn in the plainest possible form - the word PREFRONTAL REALLY DOES MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS to human and rodent researchers
senses.head: with the conclusion drawn in the plainest possible form
senses.gloss: the word PREFRONTAL REALLY DOES MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS to human and rodent researchers
senses.evidence: Our meta-analysis suggests that the word “prefrontal” really does mean different things to human and rodent researchers.

senses.label: MEASUREMENT TWO - DUAL CITIZENSHIP: TWO DISTINCT ANATOMIC TERMS, ACC AND mPFC, CAN BE USED TO DESCRIBE THE SAME THREE CORTICAL REGIONS, so a functional difference between them may be a difference between naming schemes
senses.head: MEASUREMENT TWO
senses.gloss: DUAL CITIZENSHIP: TWO DISTINCT ANATOMIC TERMS, ACC AND mPFC, CAN BE USED TO DESCRIBE THE SAME THREE CORTICAL REGIONS, so a functional difference between them may be a difference between naming schemes
senses.evidence: Rodent studies are considered to be “prefrontal” when they report data from three cytoarchitectonically defined parts of the frontal cortex: the prelimbic, infralimbic, and anterior cingulate areas. Studies in humans and monkeys consider these regions to be part of the mPFC, which also includes Walker’s area 10 ( Walker, 1940 ) and the medial parts of area 9, which do not exist in rodents ( Semendeferi et al., 2001 ). A second scheme for cortical nomenclature considers the three rodent medial frontal areas as part of the anterior cingulate cortex ( Vogt and Gabriel, 1993 ). As such, two distinct anatomic terms, ACC and mPFC, can be used to describe the same three cortical regions.

senses.label: AND THREE ACRONYMS FOR ONE AREA: PL, PrL and Cg3 all name the prelimbic cortex, with the paper wishing A SINGLE SET OF ANATOMIC TERMS were used
senses.evidence: However, a wide range of terms and acronyms have been used to describe these areas. For example, three different acronyms have been used to describe the prelimbic cortex: PL, PrL, and Cg3 ( Fig. 4 ). Similar to our comments above about the use of the word “prefrontal” across species and dual membership in the mPFC and ACC nomenclatures, it would be ideal if a single set of anatomic terms, and associated acronyms, were used to define these cortical regions.

senses.label: THE ATLAS ITSELF ADMITS IT, ON PAGE XV: THE NOMENCLATURE OF THE RODENT CINGULATE CORTEX AND RELATED AREAS HAS BEEN A MAJOR PROBLEM FOR SOME DECADES
senses.evidence: The most recent version of the commonly used Paxinos and Watson (2014) rat atlas stated “The nomenclature of the rodent cingulate cortex and related areas has been a major problem for some decades

senses.label: AND THE PUBLISHED FIX WAS IGNORED, WITH THE RATIO COUNTED: 279 publications use the superseded term in their title and FOUR use the corrected one
senses.evidence: Unfortunately, a PubMed search reveals that the latest editions of the Paxinos atlases ( Paxinos and Franklin, 2012 ; Paxinos and Watson, 2014 ) have not been used in many recent studies, and labs still use terms from earlier versions of the Paxinos atlases (e.g., 279 publications with “prelimbic” and four papers with “area 32” in the title of studies using rats or mice, based on a PubMed search in October, 2018).

senses.label: with the disagreement traced to descent rather than to evidence - the atlases stem from two different original atlases, so differences in nomenclature are OFTEN DUE TO USING EITHER ONE OR THE OTHER
senses.head: with the disagreement traced to descent rather than to evidence
senses.gloss: the atlases stem from two different original atlases, so differences in nomenclature are OFTEN DUE TO USING EITHER ONE OR THE OTHER
senses.evidence: It is also worth noting that there are two different sets of rodent atlases which stem from either the Paxinos or Swanson initial rat atlas. The terminology and structures found in Paxinos and Franklin (2012) mouse atlas are based off of Paxinos and Watson (1998) rat atlas, while the Allen Brain mouse reference atlas is largely based off of the Swanson (2004) rat atlas (see Appendix 3 in Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2008 ; Lein et al., 2007 ). Therefore, differences in rodent PFC nomenclature are often due to using either the Paxinos or Swanson atlases.

senses.label: AND HYBRID TERMS COMPOUND IT: prelimbic prefrontal cortex and prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex are REDUNDANT, DO NOT ADD CLARITY, and MAKE IT MORE DIFFICULT TO TRACK NEW FINDINGS and incorporate them into the existing literature
senses.evidence: In recent years, two sets of hybrid terms have emerged in the recent literature (since 2005) for denoting prefrontal regions in rodents. These terms combine the names of the cortical fields, prelimbic and infralimbic, with the term prefrontal cortex, e.g., “prelimbic prefrontal cortex” or “prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex.” Together with the various terms and acronyms described above for the Paxinos and Swanson atlases, it is clear that there are too many terms being used to describe the prefrontal parts of the rodent cortex. We hope that these alternative terms can be eliminated from future publications, as they are redundant, do not add clarity, and make it more difficult to track new findings and incorporate them into the existing literature.

senses.label: MEASUREMENT THREE - THE SURVEY: 38 established researchers, and LITTLE CONSENSUS about what constitutes the region or what terms should describe it
senses.head: MEASUREMENT THREE
senses.gloss: THE SURVEY: 38 established researchers, and LITTLE CONSENSUS about what constitutes the region or what terms should describe it
senses.evidence: We recently conducted a crowdsourcing effort to assess usage of anatomic terms for the rodent prefrontal cortex. We reached out directly via email to several leading human, monkey, and rodent PFC researchers and also requested via social media for anyone with an informed opinion on rodent PFC to fill out a survey on the topic. In brief, the survey questions inquired about the functional and anatomic extent of the rodent PFC and the specifics of anatomic terms within PFC. We also allowed survey responders to input their confidence levels on each given topic or question. We received 38 survey responses from a wide range of PFC researchers. Even with this small, self-selected sample of opinions, the survey revealed that there is little consensus among researchers about what constitutes the rodent PFC and what terms should be used to describe this cortical region.

senses.label: with the sharpest single result - only a MINORITY said the most-studied area is part of the scheme the anatomists put it in, and the authors were SHOCKED
senses.head: with the sharpest single result
senses.gloss: only a MINORITY said the most-studied area is part of the scheme the anatomists put it in, and the authors were SHOCKED
senses.evidence: We asked respondents whether the prelimbic area is part of the anterior cingulate cortex in rodents ( Fig. 5 A ). Surprisingly, a minority of respondents indicated that the prelimbic cortex is part of the ACC ( Fig. 5 C ), despite publications by anatomists that support that designation ( Vogt and Gabriel, 1993 ; Vogt et al., 2013 ; Vogt and Paxinos, 2014 ). The prelimbic area has been perhaps the most studied part of the rodent PFC, and we were shocked by this outcome of the survey. One respondent wrote: “Depends on whose definition of the ACC is used.” We are not aware of anatomic studies or reviews on the ACC that do not include the prelimbic cortex (also known as area 32) as a core component of the ACC

senses.label: AND ONE RESPONDENT PUT THE WHOLE PROBLEM IN SIX WORDS: DEPENDS ON WHOSE DEFINITION OF THE ACC IS USED
senses.evidence: The prelimbic area has been perhaps the most studied part of the rodent PFC, and we were shocked by this outcome of the survey. One respondent wrote: “Depends on whose definition of the ACC is used.”

senses.label: with the category boundary failing outright - SIX RESPONDENTS INCLUDED THE SAME AREA IN BOTH the dorsal and the ventral subdivision, and the exclamation mark is theirs
senses.head: with the category boundary failing outright
senses.gloss: SIX RESPONDENTS INCLUDED THE SAME AREA IN BOTH the dorsal and the ventral subdivision, and the exclamation mark is theirs
senses.evidence: There was almost universal agreement that Cg1 is part of the dmPFC (32 of 36 said yes) and IL is part of the vmPFC (33 of 36 said yes). Respondents were divided about how to characterize PL, with 24 of 36 saying it is part of dmPFC and 16 of 36 saying it is part of vmPFC (six respondents included PL in both dmPFC and vmPFC!)

senses.label: THE FIX PROPOSED IS TO STOP USING THE CATEGORY AND STATE THE PLACE: say exactly where the experiment was done - DORSAL HALF OF PRELIMBIC CORTEX INSTEAD OF dmPFC
senses.head: THE FIX PROPOSED IS TO STOP USING THE CATEGORY AND STATE THE PLACE: say exactly where the experiment was done
senses.gloss: DORSAL HALF OF PRELIMBIC CORTEX INSTEAD OF dmPFC
senses.evidence: Respondents were evenly split on what areas comprise the dmPFC and vmPFC ( Fig. 5 D ), with one in six respondents actually including prelimbic cortex in both areas. (A basis for this might be anatomic studies, Gabbott et al., 2005 , which have reported differences in anatomic connections of the dorsal and ventral aspects of the prelimbic cortex.) Rather than using these confusing terms (dmPFC and vmPFC), we suggest that research articles state exactly where the experiment was done (e.g., dorsal half of prelimbic cortex instead of dmPFC).

senses.label: AND THE COST IS MEASURED IN COLLABORATIONS THAT DID NOT HAPPEN: rodent groups have NOT collaborated with human or monkey labs, evidenced by the SMALL NUMBER OF PUBLICATIONS DONE IN THE SAME BEHAVIORAL TASK ACROSS SPECIES - and the one collaboration that did happen had to invent a third term used in fewer than 1% of papers
senses.head: AND THE COST IS MEASURED IN COLLABORATIONS THAT DID NOT HAPPEN: rodent groups have NOT collaborated with human or monkey labs, evidenced by the SMALL NUMBER OF PUBLICATIONS DONE IN THE SAME BEHAVIORAL TASK ACROSS SPECIES
senses.gloss: and the one collaboration that did happen had to invent a third term used in fewer than 1% of papers
senses.evidence: The anatomic issues described above have made it difficult for researchers with expertise on different species to compare their data and, with only a few exceptions ( Narayanan et al., 2013 ; Parker et al., 2015 ; Hyman et al., 2017 ), rodent research groups have not collaborated with human or monkey labs to understand medial PFC function. When such collaborations have been done, it has been difficult to agree on how to characterize the rodent areas in relation to medial areas of the human mPFC. For example, in a study done through collaboration between rodent and human researchers ( Narayanan et al., 2013 ), data from the prelimbic area were characterized as “medial frontal cortex” instead of the ACC or mPFC. Medial frontal cortex has not been commonly used to describe this area in the literature, with just 48 papers (<1% of all medial PFC papers) published using the term for rodent studies.

senses.label: THE PROPOSAL IS A CROSSWALK, NOT A NEW NAME: rotate three rodent points by the measured curvature of the primate callosum and they land on the three primate divisions, which is a mapping table rather than a rebrand
senses.evidence: By measuring the curvature of the primate callosum and applying it to points in space representing the three main parts of the rodent medial PFC, we found that the three rodent areas rotate to the locations associated with the three major functional zones of the primate ACC: the subgenual region (sACC), the pregenual region (pACC), and the mid-anterior cingulate cortex (MCC; compare our Fig. 6 E with Shackman et al., 2011 , their Fig. 1 C ; see Table 1 ). Thinking of rodent PFC in terms of these primate regions of the ACC should help clarify cross-species findings and might motivate human and monkey researchers to add simple behavioral tasks to their studies so that results can be better related across species.

senses.label: AND THE RECOMMENDATIONS ARE ADDRESSED TO THE INFRASTRUCTURE, NOT TO THE AUTHORS ALONE: state the precise location and the coordinates, show the images, drop the hybrid terms - and JOURNAL EDITORS AND MANUSCRIPT REVIEWERS SHOULD SPEAK UP when they appear
senses.head: AND THE RECOMMENDATIONS ARE ADDRESSED TO THE INFRASTRUCTURE, NOT TO THE AUTHORS ALONE: state the precise location and the coordinates, show the images, drop the hybrid terms
senses.gloss: and JOURNAL EDITORS AND MANUSCRIPT REVIEWERS SHOULD SPEAK UP when they appear
senses.evidence: Second, hybrid terms such as “infralimbic medial prefrontal” should not be used, and the community (especially journal editors and manuscript reviewers) should speak up when such unnecessary and confusion-generating terms appear in a preprint or manuscript that is under consideration for publication. Third, and most important, there is a serious need for community engagement to address the lack of clarity and resulting confusion generated by rodent PFC researchers not having adopted strict standards for anatomic details. This might best be addressed through a dedicated workshop to foster consensus on the use of precise anatomic terms for the rodent PFC, involving leading rodent PFC research labs, expert neuroanatomists, funding partners (NIH), foundations with a vested interest in rodent neuroanatomy (e.g., Allen Brain), and editors from leading neuroscience journals.

senses.label: with the question left genuinely open - the phrase IF ANYTHING emphasises that WE ARE NOT SURE IF THERE IS A CLEAR ANSWER, and a term might not need the word prefrontal in it to be a prefrontal area
senses.head: with the question left genuinely open
senses.gloss: the phrase IF ANYTHING emphasises that WE ARE NOT SURE IF THERE IS A CLEAR ANSWER, and a term might not need the word prefrontal in it to be a prefrontal area
senses.evidence: Here, we attempt to address this issue by asking a simple question: What, if anything, is rodent PFC? The phrase “if anything” emphasizes the idea that we are not sure if there is a clear answer to our question. In particular, we do not wish to dispute the idea that rodents have a PFC. However, it may be that a standard set of anatomic terms, based on established cross-species homologies in the frontal cortex ( Vogt and Paxinos, 2014 ), should be used to describe the “rodent PFC.” These terms might or might not include the word “prefrontal” without implying that the area in question is not a prefrontal area.

senses.label: A THEORETICAL BOUND STATED, THEN BEATEN: ANY SIGNAL PROCESSING CAN ONLY INDUCE DISTORTION, and the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission CAN ONLY ADD NOISE - lost spikes, added background, or jitter
senses.head: A THEORETICAL BOUND STATED, THEN BEATEN: ANY SIGNAL PROCESSING CAN ONLY INDUCE DISTORTION, and the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission CAN ONLY ADD NOISE
senses.gloss: lost spikes, added background, or jitter
senses.evidence: Any signal processing can only induce distortion ( Cover and Thomas, 1991 ). In particular, the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission can only add noise in the form of lost spikes, added background activity, or spike time jitter, requiring a neuronal mechanism to minimize and compensate for added noise.

senses.label: AND THE POSTSYNAPTIC CELL IS MORE PRECISE THAN THE CELLS DRIVING IT: instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit HIGHER precision, and their spike trains allow BETTER SIGNAL RECONSTRUCTION - DEMONSTRATING ERROR CORRECTION
senses.head: AND THE POSTSYNAPTIC CELL IS MORE PRECISE THAN THE CELLS DRIVING IT: instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit HIGHER precision, and their spike trains allow BETTER SIGNAL RECONSTRUCTION
senses.gloss: DEMONSTRATING ERROR CORRECTION
senses.evidence: The brain propagates neuronal signals accurately and rapidly. Nevertheless, whether and how a pool of cortical neurons transmits an undistorted message to a target remains unclear. We apply optogenetic white noise signals to small assemblies of cortical pyramidal cells (PYRs) in freely moving mice. The directly activated PYRs exhibit a spike timing precision of several milliseconds. Instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit higher precision with respect to the white noise signal. Compared with directly activated PYRs, postsynaptic interneuron spike trains allow better signal reconstruction, demonstrating error correction.

senses.label: the bound is not broken but redefined - the SIGNAL is carried by a POOL, and the coincidences among its members survive what any single member's jitter destroys
senses.head: the bound is not broken but redefined
senses.gloss: the SIGNAL is carried by a POOL, and the coincidences among its members survive what any single member's jitter destroys
senses.evidence: We found that error correction and precision improvement via CD of multiple weak synaptic inputs are particularly advantageous when failure of a synapse or a presynaptic neuron occurs. As a practical example of how error correction may work under natural conditions, the WN signal can be viewed as an analog of external input encoding specific sensory information to a pool of neurons, which also receives other activity. Then, every neuron will spike differently due to the background “noise,” but some spikes of the neurons in the activated pool will occur sufficiently close in time to drive postsynaptic activity more robustly than any of the elements of the pool.

senses.label: with the simplest mechanism ruled out first - 1:1 transmission CANNOT COMPENSATE for added noise, and most unitary responses FAIL to generate spikes at all
senses.head: with the simplest mechanism ruled out first
senses.gloss: 1:1 transmission CANNOT COMPENSATE for added noise, and most unitary responses FAIL to generate spikes at all
senses.evidence: Perhaps the simplest mechanism for precise and reliable propagation of spiking signals is 1:1 transmission between a source and a target neuron. Indeed, some neurons generate postsynaptic responses that are sufficiently strong to generate postsynaptic action potentials ( Henze et al., 2002 ; Szegedi et al., 2017 ). In particular, pyramidal cells (PYRs) may connect to neighboring neurons with millivolt-scale unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) ( Cossell et al., 2015 ; Pala and Petersen, 2015 ). However, 1:1 transmission cannot compensate for added noise. Furthermore, cortical spike transmission is typically probabilistic and weak: most unitary EPSPs fail to generate spikes in postsynaptic neurons

senses.label: AND LINEAR SUMMATION RULED OUT BY TRYING IT: simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains DID NOT REPLICATE the experimental findings, where nonlinear summation of coincident spikes drove postsynaptic spiking MORE PRECISELY THAN THE DRIVING TRAINS
senses.evidence: Although expected to saturate when driven by correlated noise ( Zohary et al., 1994 ), linear summation may transmit spikes efficiently ( Reich et al., 2001 ). Indeed, increasing the presynaptic pool size experimentally induced higher precision. However, simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains did not replicate the experimental findings. In contrast, nonlinear summation of coincidence spikes ( Stuart and Häusser, 2001 ) was able to drive postsynaptic spiking more precisely than the driving trains.

senses.label: A LONG-STANDING DEBATE DIAGNOSED AS DEFINITIONAL: whether neurons transmit by rate or temporal codes has been discussed extensively, and MUCH OF THE DEBATE IS ROOTED IN DEFINITIONS - a population code can be based on rates and a single neuron code can be temporal
senses.head: A LONG-STANDING DEBATE DIAGNOSED AS DEFINITIONAL: whether neurons transmit by rate or temporal codes has been discussed extensively, and MUCH OF THE DEBATE IS ROOTED IN DEFINITIONS
senses.gloss: a population code can be based on rates and a single neuron code can be temporal
senses.evidence: The question of whether neurons transmit information via rate or temporal codes has been discussed extensively ( König et al., 1996 ; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001 ; Cohen and Kohn, 2011 ), and much of the debate is rooted in definitions. The temporal/rate code differentiation is distinct from the mode by which a population of neurons encodes information: a population code can be based on rates, and a single neuron code can be temporal ( Rieke et al., 1997 ).

senses.label: AND THE AUTHORS DECLARE THEIR OWN DEFINITION AS ONE CHOICE AMONG PLAUSIBLE OTHERS: we OPERATIONALLY DEFINED temporal coding as a reliability profile peaking below the maximal timescale, but IN FACT we placed rate and temporal coding ON A CONTINUOUS SCALE - and CLEARLY, VARIOUS KERNELS AND OTHER DISTANCE METRICS ARE PLAUSIBLE
senses.head: AND THE AUTHORS DECLARE THEIR OWN DEFINITION AS ONE CHOICE AMONG PLAUSIBLE OTHERS: we OPERATIONALLY DEFINED temporal coding as a reliability profile peaking below the maximal timescale, but IN FACT we placed rate and temporal coding ON A CONTINUOUS SCALE
senses.gloss: and CLEARLY, VARIOUS KERNELS AND OTHER DISTANCE METRICS ARE PLAUSIBLE
senses.evidence: One approach is to analyze spike trains from the perspective of a downstream target. Here, we operationally defined temporal coding as a reliability profile that peaks at a timescale shorter than the maximal tested timescale, but in fact, we placed rate/temporal coding on a continuous scale. This approach, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter, is based on a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support ( Schreiber et al., 2003 ). Clearly, various kernels and other distance metrics are plausible ( Victor and Purpura, 1996 ; van Rossum, 2001 ).

senses.label: with the measure's own artefact stated: when the number of spikes is fixed the reliability profile NECESSARILY increases monotonically, and only nonspecific spikes let it show a local peak - so the signature of temporal coding depends on the presence of noise
senses.head: with the measure's own artefact stated: when the number of spikes is fixed the reliability profile NECESSARILY increases monotonically, and only nonspecific spikes let it show a local peak
senses.gloss: so the signature of temporal coding depends on the presence of noise
senses.evidence: When the number of spikes is fixed, the reliability profile necessarily increases monotonically. However, in the presence of spikes due to nonspecific inputs, the reliability profile may exhibit a local peak.

senses.label: THE STANDARD METHOD'S ANSWER IS ABOUT ITS FIRST SPIKE ONLY: a current pulse attenuates over time, EXPLORES ONLY A SUBSET OF THE RESPONSE SPACE, and is influenced by background spiking - the first spike may be millisecond-precise and ADDITIONAL SPIKES ARE LESS PRECISE
senses.head: THE STANDARD METHOD'S ANSWER IS ABOUT ITS FIRST SPIKE ONLY: a current pulse attenuates over time, EXPLORES ONLY A SUBSET OF THE RESPONSE SPACE, and is influenced by background spiking
senses.gloss: the first spike may be millisecond-precise and ADDITIONAL SPIKES ARE LESS PRECISE
senses.evidence: A classic approach for quantifying the precision and reliability of spike generation is to apply a current pulse to the tested neuron and measure latency and jitter of the resultant spiking. The response to a pulse attenuates over time, explores only a subset of the response space, and is influenced by background spiking. Indeed, previous work showed that, while the first spike after a current pulse may exhibit millisecond-timescale precision, additional spikes are less precise

senses.label: and the widely used intervention is called what it is - current injection is used widely to probe spike generation, BUT IS CLEARLY A NON-PHYSIOLOGICAL INTERVENTION
senses.head: and the widely used intervention is called what it is
senses.gloss: current injection is used widely to probe spike generation, BUT IS CLEARLY A NON-PHYSIOLOGICAL INTERVENTION
senses.evidence: In contrast to intracellular current injection, we applied the WN signals to small groups of adjacent neurons using photocurrents. Current injection is used widely to probe spike generation ( Asanuma et al., 1968 ; Mainen and Seinowski, 1995 ; Bacci and Huguenard, 2006 ; Cossell et al., 2015 ; Pala and Petersen, 2015 ), but is clearly a non-physiological intervention.

senses.label: THE ROUTE OF ACTIVATION CHANGES WHAT IS MEASURED: response properties are QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT when neurons are driven directly by photocurrents rather than by synaptic inputs, because direct activation is largely SOMATIC and synaptic activation largely DENDRITIC
senses.evidence: We found that neuronal response properties are qualitatively different when neurons are driven directly via photocurrents, compared with synaptic inputs. The direct optogenetic activation is largely somatic, whereas excitatory synaptic activation is largely mediated via synapses on the dendrites. Dendrites of PV cells support nonlinear summation of coincident inputs

senses.label: A SELECTION BIAS DECLARED THAT WORKS AGAINST THE PAPER'S OWN CONCLUSION: determining connectivity from finite data is NECESSARILY BIASED TOWARD STRONGER CONNECTIONS, and strong connections favour the RIVAL models more than the coincidence one
senses.evidence: There are several limitations that should be emphasized. First, determining connectivity from finite data is necessarily biased toward stronger connections. Strong connections favor the LL and SP models of transmission more than the CD model, in which the effect of as few as two presynaptic spikes is amplified by the nonlinearity.

senses.label: with an assumption named as an assumption - the temporal-coding finding RESTS UPON THE ASSUMPTION that the synaptically and optically driven cells are identical, verified only at the POPULATION level, and MORE WORK IS REQUIRED to test it directly
senses.head: with an assumption named as an assumption
senses.gloss: the temporal-coding finding RESTS UPON THE ASSUMPTION that the synaptically and optically driven cells are identical, verified only at the POPULATION level, and MORE WORK IS REQUIRED to test it directly
senses.evidence: Second, the finding that postsynaptic INTs exhibit temporal coding rests upon the assumption that the cells tested during synaptic activation (IDA INTs) and the cells tested during direct optogenetic activation (DA INTs) are identical. We verified that properties do not differ at the population level, but more work is required to directly test the assumption by synaptic and optogenetic activation of the exact same INTs.

senses.label: AND THE CASE OF GREATEST INTEREST LEFT UNTESTED: the properties of spike transmission between pyramidal cells, WHICH ARE OF GREAT INTEREST, REMAIN UNKNOWN
senses.evidence: Third, the properties of spike transmission between PYRs, which are of great interest, remain unknown. Specifically, the present experiments did not explore the precision and reliability timescale of spike transmission from a presynaptic assembly of PYRs to a postsynaptic target PYR. Based on the present results, we hypothesize that IDA INTs facilitate error correction and precision improvement during the transmission of information from one pool of PYRs to another.

senses.label: TWO REGIONS, WITH THE DIFFERENCES SPLIT INTO METHODOLOGICAL AND FUNCTIONAL: decoding quality and precision were consistently higher in one, and SOME DIFFERENCES MAY BE DUE TO METHODOLOGICAL DETAILS - light power, number of activated cells - WHEREAS OTHERS MAY BE FUNCTIONAL
senses.head: TWO REGIONS, WITH THE DIFFERENCES SPLIT INTO METHODOLOGICAL AND FUNCTIONAL: decoding quality and precision were consistently higher in one, and SOME DIFFERENCES MAY BE DUE TO METHODOLOGICAL DETAILS
senses.gloss: light power, number of activated cells - WHEREAS OTHERS MAY BE FUNCTIONAL
senses.evidence: To allow generalization beyond the well-mapped circuits of initial sensory processing, we studied local networks in associative brain regions, the parietal cortex and CA1.
