We found that some temporal properties of spike generation and transmission are qualitatively similar: DA PYRs exhibited a precision of a few milliseconds, whereas IDA INTs exhibited error correction and improved precision. However, we also observed some differences. First, decoding quality and precision were consistently higher in the neocortex than in CA1. Second, improved precision was consistently higher in the neocortex. Some differences may be due to methodological details (light power, number of activated PYRs), whereas others may be functional (diversity between PYRs, number of presynaptic PYRs). Regardless of the differences, postsynaptic error correction, improved precision, and temporal coding were observed in both brain regions examined, suggesting convergent synaptic transmission as a general mechanism for precise information propagation along the cortical PYR-to-INT interface.

senses.evidence: Importantly, there was no significant difference in success (exerting effort for at least 1 second of a 3-s period, fixed for each trial) between self (mean = 0.97) and other trials (mean = 0.97, Z = −0.88, r = 0.05 [0.00, 0.29], p = 0.38; Table 1 ) and Bayesian evidence for no difference (BF 01 = 4.19, substantial evidence in support of the null).

senses.label: A COMPUTATION WAS ATTRIBUTED TO THE STRUCTURE WHERE IT HAD BEEN LOOKED FOR: contrast gain control is prominent in auditory cortex and less robust in the ferret midbrain, which implies a primary role for cortex - and that is the inference this paper overturns
senses.head: A COMPUTATION WAS ATTRIBUTED TO THE STRUCTURE WHERE IT HAD BEEN LOOKED FOR: contrast gain control is prominent in auditory cortex and less robust in the ferret midbrain, which implies a primary role for cortex
senses.gloss: and that is the inference this paper overturns
senses.evidence: Contrast gain control is a prominent feature of neuronal responses in the auditory cortex of mice 21 and ferrets 9 , but in ferrets it is less robust in the midbrain 6 . Although this implies a primary role for auditory cortex in contrast gain control, other studies have shown that the responses of subcortical neurons are influenced by sensory context 22 – 28 , as well as motor and cognitive demands 29 – 32 . This raises the possibility that subcortical circuits may also contribute to adaptation to stimulus contrast.

senses.label: and it is equally strong in all three, with a Kruskal-Wallis test across CNIC, MGBv and A1 finding no significant difference at all
senses.evidence: Surprisingly, we also found strong compensatory contrast gain control in MGBv (median = 55%, p = 3.6 × 10 −16 , n = 136 units, eight mice) and CNIC (median = 70.8%, p = 1.7 × 10 −64 , n = 499 units, 13 mice; Fig. 3d–e ). A Kruskal–Wallis test between contrast gain control in CNIC, MGBv and A1 revealed no significant differences ( p = 0.31).

senses.label: THE NULL COMES WITH ITS OWN POSITIVE CONTROL: cortical silencing left contrast gain control untouched DESPITE significant effects on excitability, so the manipulation demonstrably worked and simply did not touch this
senses.evidence: Surprisingly, cortical silencing has no effect on subcortical contrast gain control, despite significant effects on neuronal excitability, suggesting that the midbrain and thalamus implement adaptation independently of cortex.

senses.label: and the same silencing moved firing rate, its variability, reliability and linearity, while the receptive field shape and the gain control did not move
senses.evidence: Although cortical silencing alters the excitability, reliability, and linearity of MGBv and CNIC responses, we found no effect on the strength of contrast gain control. This is consistent with the lack of effect of widespread cortical cooling on adaptation to mean level by IC neurons 27 . However, cortical deactivation does prevent the change in the rate of adaptation by IC neurons following repeated exposure to stimuli with different sound level distributions 27 . It is therefore possible that descending corticofugal inputs might play a role in contrast adaptation in rapidly changing acoustic environments.

senses.label: THE SCALE OF THE MANIPULATION DECIDES THE ANSWER: widespread silencing leaves the receptive field unchanged, while focal silencing or activation of frequency-specific cortical regions is known to shift subcortical best frequency
senses.evidence: However, focal silencing or activation of auditory cortical areas can shift the BF of neurons in both the MGBv and CNIC 34 , 35 . Manipulating the activity of frequency-specific regions of auditory cortex may therefore have similar effects on the structure of the STRFs acquired from complex sounds, which would be consistent with a potential role for corticofugal feedback in the task-dependent STRF plasticity of auditory midbrain neurons

senses.label: THE REPORTED NUMBER IS THE MODEL'S LIMIT, NOT THE NEURON'S: a subset of units sit exactly at the 700 ms maximum, which is the longest value estimable from stimuli that switch every 2 s, and is called a ceiling effect
senses.evidence: A subset of units was estimated to have the maximum time constant allowed by the model (700 ms, because longer time constants could not be reliably estimated using stimuli whose contrast switched every 2 s). This is likely to be a ceiling effect, and suggests that a subset of units have time constants that may be longer than this. Units estimated to have these long time constants were most frequently found in A1.

senses.label: TWO QUANTITIES RISE TOGETHER ACROSS LEVELS AND DO NOT CORRELATE WITHIN THEM: temporal bandwidth and adaptation time constant both increase along the pathway, yet within each structure there is no correlation, so bandwidth does not account for the increase
senses.evidence: The progressive increase in time constants might result from differences in the temporal resolution of spectro-temporal representations at different processing levels. Indeed, the temporal bandwidth (estimated as the full-width half-maximum of the temporal kernel in a separable STRF) differed between units recorded at each level (Kruskal–Wallis test, p = 1.1 × 10 −12 ; Fig. 6c ). Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly (Dunn–Sidak corrected) shorter temporal bandwidths in CNIC relative to both A1 ( p < 0.05) and MGBv ( p < 0.05). Units in MGBv had intermediate values between CNIC and A1, but these were not significantly different from A1 ( p > 0.05). However, within each auditory structure, we did not find a correlation between temporal bandwidths and contrast adaptation time constants (Spearman correlation, p > 0.10). Thus, although both parameters increase in value along the auditory pathway, temporal bandwidth does not in itself account for the increase in contrast adaptation time.

senses.label: THE IN VIVO RESULT HAS THE OPPOSITE SIGN TO THE IN VITRO PREDICTION: corticothalamic feedback was proposed to supply synaptic noise that makes integration more linear, and isolating it in vivo shows it DECREASES linearity and reliability
senses.evidence: It has been proposed on the basis of in vitro investigations that corticothalamic feedback provides synaptic noise, which helps thalamic neurons to integrate synaptic inputs more linearly 60 , 61 . However, by isolating the corticofugal contribution to the representation of ongoing stimuli in vivo, our results suggest that corticofugal activity decreases the linear input–output relationship and the reliability of neuronal responses in the CNIC and MGBv. In the CNIC, this effect of cortical silencing on the transfer function of the neurons appears to depend on wakefulness, but in the MGBv was present even under anesthesia, implying that it is not simply a result of trial-to-trial variability in corticofugal synaptic transmission due to changes in cognitive state.

senses.label: A CANONICAL COMPUTATION NEED NOT HAVE A CANONICAL CIRCUIT: contrast normalization can be viewed as canonical, and is unlikely to be implemented by a canonical neural circuit
senses.evidence: The longer adaptation time constants we observe in the cortex suggest that further contrast-related processing happens there. As the representation of sound features changes along the ascending auditory pathway 48 , corresponding changes in contrast adaptation may be required at each successive stage. If that is the case, an important question for future research will be whether contrast gain control is implemented via different neural architectures, as has been shown for other neuromodulatory computations 49 , 50 . Thus, although auditory contrast normalization can be viewed as a canonical computation in the brain, it is unlikely to be implemented by a canonical neural circuit.

senses.label: and the same phenomenon carries two names in one sentence - contrast gain control, or contrast normalization
senses.head: and the same phenomenon carries two names in one sentence
senses.gloss: contrast gain control, or contrast normalization
senses.evidence: Contrast adaptation may affect multiple neuronal response properties, but is accomplished principally by adjustments in response gain that compensate for the distribution of stimulus levels in a given sensory environment. This specific form of contrast adaptation is known as contrast gain control (or contrast normalization).

senses.label: THE PERCENTAGE ONLY MEANS SOMETHING WITH ITS DEFINITION: 100% compensation is DEFINED as a halving of gain when contrast doubles, so a bare 70.2% joins nothing
senses.evidence: Contrast gain control was measured as percentage compensation in response to a doubling of contrast, where complete (100%) compensation is defined as a halving of gain, and no compensation is defined as no change in gain:

senses.label: AND THE TWO CONFOUNDS CANNOT BOTH BE REMOVED: matching the overall level of high- and low-contrast stimuli costs the equality of the individual tone levels, so the control trades one confound for the other
senses.evidence: The overall sound level of high-contrast stimuli was slightly (∼3 dB) higher than that of the low-contrast stimuli, due to the nonlinearity inherent in the logarithmic scale. An additional experiment was therefore carried out in which the overall sound levels of DRCs were matched in low- and high-contrast stimuli, at the expense of equality of sound levels of individual tones in the DRCs, to control for possible effects of this small difference in overall sound amplitude

senses.label: A SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE WAS DELIBERATELY SET ASIDE: receptive field tuning did change systematically with contrast, but a single combined fit predicted as well or better, so one fit was used
senses.evidence: We found that there were significant systematic changes in STRF tuning across the population (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). However, these changes were small enough that the prediction quality of a single combined STRF was either statistically indistinguishable from (CNIC, MGBv) or better than (A1) the prediction quality of within-condition STRFs (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). We therefore fitted a single STRF to all the data from each neuron

senses.label: and the agreement between mouse neurons and human listeners rests on a FAILURE TO REJECT - a one-way ANOVA at p = 0.22
senses.head: and the agreement between mouse neurons and human listeners rests on a FAILURE TO REJECT
senses.gloss: a one-way ANOVA at p = 0.22
senses.evidence: The strength of perceptual contrast adaptation predicted by the model (mean predicted contrast adaptation: awake CNIC: 19.3%; anesthetized CNIC: 20.2%; MGBv: 17.9%; A1: 21.4%) closely resembled that measured in human participants performing the contrast-dependent sound level discrimination task (28.8%, n = 8 participants; Fig. 7b, c ). No differences were found between these values (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.22), suggesting that the gain control measured at each level of the auditory pathway is sufficient to account for the perceptual adaptation exhibited by human listeners.

senses.label: THE CRITERION GUARANTEES THE POPULATION: adaptation time constants were estimated only from units that had already been shown to undergo contrast adaptation
senses.evidence: In addition to the inclusion criteria used in the LN models for contrast adaptation estimation (see below), we further restricted analysis of time constants to units whose activity was better described by a contrast-dependent LN model than a single contrast-independent model. Consequently, we estimated contrast adaptation time constants only from units that underwent contrast adaptation.

senses.label: priming as against framing, THIS FIELD'S VERSION - the two are granted the same function (activating awareness of an issue) and separated by what framing does in addition: attribute meanings. The paper says so outright: it is OFTEN ALSO DEFINED BY NEGATION, with inauthenticity as falsity, externally motivated behaviour, and reciting a script rather than expressing one's own words

senses.label: THE TOOL'S NAME ASSERTS ITS EFFECT, AND THE EFFECT REVERSES INSIDE ONE CELL: activation INHIBITED THE SOMA but UNEXPECTEDLY DEPOLARIZED THE PRESYNAPTIC TERMINALS resulting in neurotransmitter release
senses.evidence: Light-gated chloride channels are emerging as promising optogenetic tools for inhibition of neural activity. However, their effects depend on the transmembrane chloride electrochemical gradient and may be complex due to the heterogeneity of this gradient in different developmental stages, neuronal types, and subcellular compartments. Here we characterized a light-gated chloride channel, GtACR2, in mouse cortical neurons. We found that GtACR2 activation inhibited the soma, but unexpectedly depolarized the presynaptic terminals resulting in neurotransmitter release.

senses.label: AND IT IS THE WHOLE CLASS, NOT ONE PROTEIN: other light-gated chloride channels had similar effects, and reducing chloride in the axon diminished the release - AN EXCITATORY EFFECT OF CHLORIDE CHANNELS IN THESE COMPARTMENTS
senses.head: AND IT IS THE WHOLE CLASS, NOT ONE PROTEIN: other light-gated chloride channels had similar effects, and reducing chloride in the axon diminished the release
senses.gloss: AN EXCITATORY EFFECT OF CHLORIDE CHANNELS IN THESE COMPARTMENTS
senses.evidence: Other light-gated chloride channels had similar effects. Reducing the chloride concentrations in the axon and presynaptic terminals diminished the GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release, indicating an excitatory effect of chloride channels in these compartments.

senses.label: with the textbook expectation spelled out first - typically there are FEWER chloride ions inside the cell than outside, so opening the channel should make the inside more negative and INHIBIT the neuron
senses.head: with the textbook expectation spelled out first
senses.gloss: typically there are FEWER chloride ions inside the cell than outside, so opening the channel should make the inside more negative and INHIBIT the neuron
senses.evidence: Ions flow from high concentration to low concentration areas. Typically, when a neuron is at rest, there are fewer chloride ions inside the cell than outside. Activating a light-gated chloride channel should thus cause these negatively charged ions to enter the neuron. The charge inside of the cell would become more negative relative to the outside: this would inhibit the neuron, making it less likely to fire.

senses.label: AND THE RESULTS WERE NOT AS EXPECTED: it did inhibit the cell body, YET IT HAD THE OPPOSITE EFFECT IN THE AXON
senses.evidence: Here, Messier et al. looked into using a light-gated chlorine channel called GtACR2 to inhibit the activity of neurons in mouse brain slices, but the results were not as expected. Activating the chloride channel did inhibit the cell body, the area of the neuron that contains the nucleus. Yet, it had the opposite effect in the axon, the structure that carries electrical signals away from the cell body.

senses.label: because the gradient itself differs by compartment - the concentration of chloride is HIGHER INSIDE THE AXON than the cell body, so the ions leave and the neuron fires
senses.head: because the gradient itself differs by compartment
senses.gloss: the concentration of chloride is HIGHER INSIDE THE AXON than the cell body, so the ions leave and the neuron fires
senses.evidence: There, activating GtACR2 caused chloride ions to leave the axon, which resulted in the neuron firing. Testing other types of optogenetic chloride channels produced the same result. Further experiments revealed that the concentration of chloride ions is higher inside the axon than the cell body, explaining the observed effects.

senses.label: MUCH TO OUR SURPRISE - the finding was not sought, and the same phenomenon appeared with three other channels
senses.head: MUCH TO OUR SURPRISE
senses.gloss: the finding was not sought, and the same phenomenon appeared with three other channels
senses.evidence: To this end, we investigated the effects of activating GtACR2 in mouse cortical excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Much to our surprise, wide-field light activation of GtACR2 not only inhibited the soma, but also caused neurotransmitter release onto neighboring neurons. A similar phenomenon was observed with GtACR1, iC++, and iChloC.

senses.label: AND IT EXPLAINS RESULTS ALREADY IN THE LITERATURE: these data explain the recent observations that photostimulation of neurons expressing these channels can PARADOXICALLY release neurotransmitters or generate action potentials
senses.evidence: We further showed that GtACR2 activation in the axon and presynaptic terminals directly depolarized the membrane to induce neurotransmitter release due to high chloride concentrations in these compartments. These data explain the recent observations that photostimulation of neurons expressing GtACR1 or GtACR2 can paradoxically release neurotransmitters or generate action potentials

senses.label: THE FIELD ALREADY KNEW THE CLASS OF PROBLEM FOR TWO OTHER TOOLS: one pump transiently changes the reversal potential of the receptors it is meant to leave alone, another raises presynaptic calcium and spontaneous release - AS LONG AS THESE CONFOUNDS ARE UNDERSTOOD AND CONTROLLED
senses.head: THE FIELD ALREADY KNEW THE CLASS OF PROBLEM FOR TWO OTHER TOOLS: one pump transiently changes the reversal potential of the receptors it is meant to leave alone, another raises presynaptic calcium and spontaneous release
senses.gloss: AS LONG AS THESE CONFOUNDS ARE UNDERSTOOD AND CONTROLLED
senses.evidence: This is due to the possibility that these channels or pumps not only modulate membrane potentials but also may affect other processes such as ion homeostasis or neurotransmitter release. For example, activation of a light-driven inward chloride pump, eNpHR3.0, can transiently change the reversal potential of GABA A receptors and alter the inhibitory synaptic inputs ( Raimondo et al., 2012 ). Prolonged activation of a light-driven outward proton pump, eArch3.0, can increase presynaptic calcium concentrations and spontaneous neurotransmitter release ( Mahn et al., 2016 ). Despite these potential confounds, these inhibitory optogenetic molecules become increasingly important tools for targeted silencing of neuronal populations, as long as these confounds are understood and controlled

senses.label: with the reason stated in general form - the effect depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the reversal potential for chloride, BOTH OF WHICH CAN VARY in different neuronal types and subcellular compartments
senses.head: with the reason stated in general form
senses.gloss: the effect depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the reversal potential for chloride, BOTH OF WHICH CAN VARY in different neuronal types and subcellular compartments
senses.evidence: Therefore, it is also crucial to thoroughly characterize light-gated chloride channels, as their effect depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the reversal potential for chloride, both of which can vary in different neuronal types and subcellular compartments

senses.label: AND THE OLDER TOOLS WERE IMMUNE TO EXACTLY THIS: pumps hyperpolarize INDEPENDENT OF THE ELECTROCHEMICAL GRADIENTS, which is the property the channels traded away for sensitivity and conductance
senses.evidence: The widely used light-driven inward chloride pumps and outward proton pumps, such as Natronomonas pharaonis halorhodopsin (NpHR) and Halorubrum sodomense archaerhodopsin (Arch), can hyperpolarize membrane potentials, independent of the electrochemical gradients, to inhibit action potentials with millisecond precision ( Chow et al., 2010 ; Chuong et al., 2014 ; Han and Boyden, 2007 ; Han et al., 2011 ; Zhang et al., 2007 ). However, their efficacies are limited because only one ion is transported per absorbed photon, and their activation does not decrease membrane resistance. Light-gated chloride channels, such as Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin 1 and 2 (GtACR1 and GtACR2), iC++, and iChloC, overcome these limitations ( Berndt et al., 2014 ; Govorunova et al., 2015 , 2017b ; Wietek et al., 2014 ). They are highly sensitive to light, allow multiple ions to cross the membrane per photocycle, and reduce membrane resistance, thereby potently inhibiting action potentials.

senses.label: THE FIX IS SPATIAL, NOT BIOPHYSICAL: a panel of targeting motifs was screened to keep the protein out of the axon, and RESTRICTING THE LOCALIZATION improves the inhibitory efficacy
senses.evidence: To reduce the excitatory effect of GtACR2, we screened a panel of somatodendritic targeting motifs to reduce the trafficking of GtACR2 to the axon and presynaptic terminals. We created a hybrid motif (Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC) that is most effective in concentrating GtACR2 in the somatodendritic domain. Activation of somatodendritically targeted GtACR2 resulted in larger photocurrents at the soma and less neurotransmitter release than wild type GtACR2. Thus, restricting the localization of light-gated chloride channels to the somatodendritic domain improves the inhibitory efficacy of these optogenetic tools.

senses.label: AND THE BROKEN TOOL BECOMES A MEASURING INSTRUMENT FOR WHAT BROKE IT: these channels can be used to study chloride gradients in regions, cell types and subcellular domains THAT ARE OTHERWISE DIFFICULT TO ACCESS, such as small axons and presynaptic terminals
senses.evidence: Our results also suggest that light-gated chloride channels can be a useful tool for studying the physiological functions of chloride electrochemical gradients in specific brain regions, cell types, or subcellular domains that are otherwise difficult to access, such as small axons and presynaptic terminals.

senses.label: THE SIDE EFFECT WAS FOUND BY RECORDING FROM SOMEBODY ELSE: the excitatory current appears in neurons that do NOT express the tool, which is why it was invisible to anyone recording only the targeted cell
senses.evidence: Activation of GtACR2 with a short light pulse (0.5–10 ms) generated inward currents in all recorded GtACR2 – neurons that were voltage clamped at the reversal potential for GABAergic inhibition (−60 mV). The onsets of these inward currents followed the onset of the blue light by 3.19 ± 0.26 ms (mean ± s.e.m., n = 25). These currents were abolished by the glutamatergic receptor antagonists, NBQX and CPP ( Figure 1F ), or the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 1G ), indicating that they were indeed monosynaptic EPSCs caused by the glutamate transmitter released from GtACR2 + neurons.

senses.label: and the tool even produces inhibition it was never meant to produce - disynaptic inhibitory currents, abolished by glutamate blockers, so activating it in pyramidal neurons RECRUITS INHIBITORY INTERNEURONS
senses.head: and the tool even produces inhibition it was never meant to produce
senses.gloss: disynaptic inhibitory currents, abolished by glutamate blockers, so activating it in pyramidal neurons RECRUITS INHIBITORY INTERNEURONS
senses.evidence: Activation of GtACR2 also produced inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in GtACR2 – neurons that were voltage clamped at the reversal potential for glutamatergic excitation (+10 mV). These IPSCs were disynaptic because they were abolished by NBQX and CPP ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ), indicating that activating GtACR2 in pyramidal neurons can release sufficient glutamate to recruit inhibitory interneurons.

senses.label: with the general rule stated as a prerequisite: determining the precise effects of these tools UNDER DEFINED CONDITIONS is a PREREQUISITE to using them to interrogate the functions of neurons and circuits
senses.evidence: Determining the precise effects of light-gated ion channels or pumps under defined conditions is a prerequisite to use them for interrogating the functions of specific neurons and circuits.

senses.evidence: A great majority of participants (78%) agreed that progress has been made in the scientific study of consciousness. This result appears to hold regardless of whether one studies consciousness or not, as we found no dependence between expertise and perceived progress in the field

senses.evidence: To determine the influence of these stage-generated auditory cues, we interleaved the texture trials with ‘Catch’-trials, in which textures were omitted but with all auditory cues present (start and stop tones), including the sounds generated by the stage translation

senses.label: the region called PPC here is identified by intrinsic-signal boundaries and then VALIDATED by tracing its inputs and outputs, rather than assumed from coordinates
senses.evidence: In four mice, we carried out retrograde and anterograde labelling experiments with tracer injections targeted to LPtA. The resulting labelling patterns validated that this region receives axonal projections from known PPC input sites (Fig. 1D ), particularly the thalamic lateral posterior nucleus LP (Fig. 1H,I ) and premotor cortex M2 (Fig. 1E-F ), as well as sends its axons to known PPC output sites, including M2, the dorsal striatum (Fig. 1E–G ) and LP (Fig. 1H,I ) 15 , 32 . Hence, we identify this region between barrel cortex and V1 as part of PPC

senses.label: the auditory cue is not a designed stimulus but a by-product of the apparatus, measured after the fact and confirmed to be looming-like by recording at the animal's head position
senses.evidence: We confirmed that the auditory cue generated by the stage translation was indeed looming-like by performing sound recordings at the location corresponding to the head of the head-fixed mouse

senses.label: response classes here are outputs of a general linear model fit to calcium traces, so cue-responsive, touch-responsive, mixed and suppressed are model categories rather than observed types
senses.evidence: Using a general linear model (GLM) to fit neuronal calcium traces, we classified the trial-active neurons (n = 126) as cue-responsive (22.2%), touch-responsive (11.9%), mixed-responsive (11.9%) and suppressed (17.5%) based on the dynamics of their calcium responses to the trial period; the remaining 36.5% of ‘unclassified’ active neurons responded neither to auditory cues nor to texture presentation

senses.label: the omission response was present on the SECOND trial the animal ever experienced, which is what makes it a fact about the cue rather than about learning
senses.evidence: Furthermore, for all 4 FOVs the first Catch-trial was presented as the second trial in the sequence of trials, suggesting that the PPC is able to rapidly encode the omission of the auditory-cued tactile stimulus.

senses.label: PFC dysfunction is used at two different grains here - a whole-region lesion and the loss of one interneuron class - and the paper's point is that they are NOT the same manipulation
senses.head: PFC dysfunction is used at two different grains here

senses.evidence: We found that PFC lesions produced behavioral alterations in all three symptom categories, whereas selective inactivation of PVIs caused deficits only in the cognitive domain.

senses.label: working memory in this paper spans three tasks with different demands: repeat investigation, spontaneous alternation, and a 60s delayed match-to-place

senses.evidence: Additionally, TeLC expression was found in the cingulate and medial orbital cortices, demonstrating functional removal of PVIs across an area of mouse PFC thought to integrate functions of the dorsolateral, medial and orbital PFC in humans

senses.evidence: As Cre-recombinase is required to flip the reading frame into the correct orientation, transcription of TeLC can only occur in PVIs 26 . Once expressed, TeLC efficiently stops transmitter release by cleaving VAMP2, a protein required for synaptic vesicle docking

senses.label: TWO CELL TYPES AMPLIFY THE SAME INDEX BY OPPOSITE MECHANISMS: PVs AMPLIFY SSA BY PROVIDING NON-SPECIFIC INHIBITION - suppression led to AN EQUAL INCREASE IN RESPONSES TO FREQUENT AND RARE TONES - while SOMs SELECTIVELY REDUCE EXCITATORY RESPONSES TO FREQUENT TONES, with suppression increasing responses TO FREQUENT, BUT NOT TO RARE TONES
senses.head: TWO CELL TYPES AMPLIFY THE SAME INDEX BY OPPOSITE MECHANISMS: PVs AMPLIFY SSA BY PROVIDING NON-SPECIFIC INHIBITION
senses.gloss: suppression led to AN EQUAL INCREASE IN RESPONSES TO FREQUENT AND RARE TONES - while SOMs SELECTIVELY REDUCE EXCITATORY RESPONSES TO FREQUENT TONES, with suppression increasing responses TO FREQUENT, BUT NOT TO RARE TONES
senses.evidence: We found that two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons. Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVs) amplify SSA by providing non-specific inhibition: optogenetic suppression of PVs led to an equal increase in responses to frequent and rare tones. In contrast, somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) selectively reduce excitatory responses to frequent tones: suppression of SOMs led to an increase in responses to frequent, but not to rare tones. A mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory network model accounts for distinct mechanisms by which cortical inhibitory neurons enhance the brain's sensitivity to unexpected sounds.

senses.label: AND THE FIRST MECHANISM MOVES THE INDEX WITHOUT CHANGING SELECTIVITY AT ALL: one type SUPPRESSED RESPONSES TO BOTH FREQUENT AND RARE SOUNDS, and AS THE RESPONSES TO RARE SOUNDS STARTED OFF GREATER, SUPPRESSING BOTH BY AN EQUAL AMOUNT ACTUALLY LED TO AN INCREASE IN THE RELATIVE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM. A ratio moved by a uniform shift, and the paper says so in its own summary
senses.evidence: One of these neuron types, called ‘parvalbumin-positive interneurons’, exerted a general effect on excitatory neurons and suppressed responses to both frequent and rare sounds As the responses to rare sounds started off greater than the responses to frequent sounds, suppressing both by an equal amount actually led to an increase in the relative difference between them.

senses.label: with the arithmetic stated as the hypothesis before it is tested: EQUALLY STRONG INHIBITORY DRIVE WOULD ATTENUATE THE WEAK RESPONSE TO STANDARD TONES RELATIVELY MORE THAN THE STRONG RESPONSE TO DEVIANT TONES, LEADING TO A GREATER DIFFERENTIAL - the effect is predicted from the shape of the index rather than from a property of the cell
senses.head: with the arithmetic stated as the hypothesis before it is tested: EQUALLY STRONG INHIBITORY DRIVE WOULD ATTENUATE THE WEAK RESPONSE TO STANDARD TONES RELATIVELY MORE THAN THE STRONG RESPONSE TO DEVIANT TONES, LEADING TO A GREATER DIFFERENTIAL
senses.gloss: the effect is predicted from the shape of the index rather than from a property of the cell
senses.evidence: PVs, a subset of which receive direct thalamic inputs ( Staiger et al., 1996 ), may amplify SSA in excitatory neurons by providing a constant inhibitory drive; equally strong inhibitory drive would attenuate the weak response to standard tones relatively more than the strong response to deviant tones, leading to a greater differential between standard vs deviant tone spiking response.

senses.label: and the rival mechanism is a property of the synapse: SOMs have excitatory synapses that EXHIBIT FACILITATION UPON REPETITIVE STIMULATION, so their input may be SELECTIVE TO THE STANDARD TONE AND DOES NOT GENERALIZE TO THE DEVIANT - with an ALTERNATIVELY clause naming a second route through differential post-synaptic integration
senses.head: and the rival mechanism is a property of the synapse: SOMs have excitatory synapses that EXHIBIT FACILITATION UPON REPETITIVE STIMULATION, so their input may be SELECTIVE TO THE STANDARD TONE AND DOES NOT GENERALIZE TO THE DEVIANT
senses.gloss: with an ALTERNATIVELY clause naming a second route through differential post-synaptic integration
senses.evidence: SOMs, which target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells ( McGarry et al., 2010 ; Gentet et al., 2012 ), have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation ( Reyes et al., 1998 ; Silberberg and Markram, 2007 ). Therefore, inputs from SOMs may exert a stimulus-specific increase in suppression of excitatory neurons that is selective to the standard tone and does not generalize to the deviant tone. Alternatively, they may contribute to selective adaptation in excitatory neurons through differential post-synaptic integration.

senses.label: THE INDEX IS DEFINED WITH ITS TWO ENDPOINTS: SSA index is 1 WHEN ADAPTATION IS COMPLETE, no response to the standard and significant response to the deviant, AND 0 WHEN THERE IS NO ADAPTATION, the response to the standard and deviant equal
senses.evidence: To quantify the level of adaptation for each neuron, we computed the index of the change in FR to the same tone when it was presented as the deviant vs the standard (SSA index). SSA index is 1 when adaptation is complete (i.e., no response to the standard, and significant response to the deviant), and 0 when there is no adaptation (i.e., the response to the standard and deviant is equal).

senses.label: and written out as a formula whose numerator is a difference and whose denominator is a sum - which is exactly why a uniform multiplicative change moves it
senses.head: and written out as a formula whose numerator is a difference and whose denominator is a sum
senses.gloss: which is exactly why a uniform multiplicative change moves it
senses.evidence: For each neuron, SSA index is a measure of the strength of SSA based on its mean FR with respect to tone probability. FRs to tones A and B were summed according to their standard or deviant probability within each oddball stimulus ( Ulanovsky et al., 2003 ).

senses.label: A BASELINE-DIFFERENCE CONFOUND CONTROLLED BY MATCHING RATHER THAN BY ARGUMENT: restricting the analysis to subpopulations WHICH HAVE MATCHED MEAN AND STANDARD DEVIATION OF FR TO THE STANDARD VS THE DEVIANT TONES preserved the observation
senses.evidence: However, restricting the analysis to two subpopulations of neurons, which have matched mean and standard deviation of FR to the standard vs the deviant tones ( Ulanovsky et al., 2004 ; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010 ), preserved the observed

senses.label: and the same test run on a different contrast: PV AND SOM SUPPRESSION EXHIBITED A SIMILAR EFFECT ON RESPONSES TO THE STRONG AND THE WEAK TONES in neurons that responded differentially to the two tones - so the selectivity is to probability, not to response size
senses.head: and the same test run on a different contrast: PV AND SOM SUPPRESSION EXHIBITED A SIMILAR EFFECT ON RESPONSES TO THE STRONG AND THE WEAK TONES in neurons that responded differentially to the two tones
senses.gloss: so the selectivity is to probability, not to response size
senses.evidence: However, PV and SOM suppression exhibited a similar effect on responses to the strong and the weak tones in neurons that exhibited differential responses to two tones ( Figure 4—figure supplements 5, 6 ).

senses.label: with the normalization choice checked rather than assumed: dividing by the MEAN rather than the MAXIMUM firing rate DID NOT ALTER SIGNIFICANT RESULTS
senses.evidence: FR normalization was carried out separately for each tone, A and B, for each neuron by dividing the response under all conditions by the maximum FR (across 5-ms bins) of the deviant tone, light-off condition. Performing this normalization by dividing response in all conditions by the mean, rather than maximum FR of the deviant tone, light-off condition did not alter significant results ( Figure 4—figure supplement 8 ).

senses.label: A CAVEAT WORKED THROUGH INSTEAD OF LEFT STANDING: THE FR MAY NOT LINEARLY TRANSLATE ONTO SYNAPTIC INPUT STRENGTH because of the SPIKING NON-LINEAR RECTIFICATION - and OUR FINDINGS WOULD STILL HOLD WERE THIS THE CASE, since the actual difference in synaptic drive WOULD THEN BE EVEN GREATER
senses.head: A CAVEAT WORKED THROUGH INSTEAD OF LEFT STANDING: THE FR MAY NOT LINEARLY TRANSLATE ONTO SYNAPTIC INPUT STRENGTH because of the SPIKING NON-LINEAR RECTIFICATION
senses.gloss: and OUR FINDINGS WOULD STILL HOLD WERE THIS THE CASE, since the actual difference in synaptic drive WOULD THEN BE EVEN GREATER
senses.evidence: However, our findings would still hold were this the case: in examining the effect of SOM suppression on response to the deviant, the actual difference in the synaptic drive between the deviant and the standard would then be even greater

senses.label: THE CELL CLASS IS PUTATIVE AND THE INSTRUMENT IS WHY: putative excitatory neurons were identified by response pattern and by THE LACK OF SIGNIFICANT SUPPRESSION due to light, and THE LOW IMPEDANCE OF THE EXTRACELLULAR PROBES PRECLUDED A MORE DETAILED ANALYSIS based on the spike waveform
senses.evidence: Putative excitatory neurons were identified based on their expected response patterns to sounds and the lack of significant suppression of the spontaneous FR due to light ( Lima et al., 2009 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ). While this subpopulation may still contain inhibitory neurons, only 2% of all recorded neurons were significantly photosuppressed at baseline (one-sided paired t-test, significance taken at p < 0.05). The low impedance of the extracellular probes precluded us from conducting a more detailed analysis of cortical subpopulations based on the spike waveform

senses.label: and the state the numbers come from is named with its alternatives: the results were from mice UNDER LIGHT ISOFLURANE ANESTHESIA, and OTHER FORMS OF ANESTHESIA can affect the measurement
senses.evidence: in awake animals, as our results were based on recordings from mice under light isoflurane anesthesia. Other forms of anesthesia, such as pentobarbital-based ( Cheung et al., 2001 ; Gaese and Ostwald, 2001 ), ketamine ( Otazu et al., 2009 ) and high concentrations of isoflurane ( Cheung et al., 2001 ; Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007 ), can affect multiple

senses.label: with the method chosen against its predecessors on a stated ground: optogenetic methods OVERCOME THE LIMITATIONS OF LESION OR PHARMACOLOGICAL STUDIES, WHICH ONLY ALLOW FOR PROLONGED, NON-SELECTIVE INACTIVATION
senses.evidence: optogenetic methods to test the function of inhibitory interneurons in SSA overcomes the limitations of lesion or pharmacological studies ( Elliott and Trahiotis, 1972 ; Duque et al., 2014 ), which only allow for prolonged, non-selective inactivation ( Moore et al., 2001 ).

senses.label: and the behavioural claim is deferred rather than implied: FUTURE EXPERIMENTS WILL EXPLORE WHETHER INTERNEURON-MEDIATED SSA INDEED AFFECTS THE AUDITORY BEHAVIOR OF THE SUBJECT
senses.evidence: By combining optogenetic manipulation of interneuron activity with behavioral measurements, future experiments will explore whether interneuron-mediated SSA indeed affects the auditory behavior of the subject, such as enhanced ability to detect unexpected events.

senses.label: THE INPUT ALREADY ADAPTS, WHICH IS WHAT THE CORTICAL CLAIM HAS TO BE MEASURED AGAINST: the CSD SINK AMPLITUDE WAS LOWER FOR THE STANDARD AS COMPARED TO THE DEVIANT TONES, so THALAMO-CORTICAL INPUTS EXHIBIT SSA
senses.evidence: We compared the amplitude of the CSD sink for each tone when presented as a deviant or standard, and computed their ratio ( Figure 1F ). The sink amplitude was lower for the standard as compared to the deviant tones ( Figure 1F,G ), suggesting that excitatory signals produced by thalamo-cortical inputs exhibit SSA, consistent with previous findings ( Szymanski et al., 2009 ).

senses.label: and the reason cortex was suspected in the first place is a gradient across the pathway: adaptation is WEAK IN THE LEMNISCAL AREAS which project to A1 and STRONGER IN THOSE NON-LEMNISCAL AREAS WHICH RECEIVE FEEDBACK FROM A1 - therefore CORTICAL CIRCUITS ARE PROPOSED TO CONTRIBUTE TO AND AMPLIFY SSA
senses.head: and the reason cortex was suspected in the first place is a gradient across the pathway: adaptation is WEAK IN THE LEMNISCAL AREAS which project to A1 and STRONGER IN THOSE NON-LEMNISCAL AREAS WHICH RECEIVE FEEDBACK FROM A1
senses.gloss: therefore CORTICAL CIRCUITS ARE PROPOSED TO CONTRIBUTE TO AND AMPLIFY SSA
senses.evidence: Whereas SSA has also been found in sub-cortical structures e.g. in the auditory midbrain ( Malmierca et al., 2009 ; Zhao et al., 2011 ; Thomas et al., 2012 ) and the auditory thalamus ( Kraus et al., 1994 ; Anderson et al., 2009 ; Antunes et al., 2010 ; Bauerle et al., 2011 ), it is weak in the lemniscal areas of the auditory pathway, which project to A1, and stronger in those non-lemniscal areas which receive feedback from A1 ( Ulanovsky et al., 2004 , Perez-Gonzalez et al., 2005 , Duque et al., 2012 ). Therefore, cortical circuits are proposed to contribute to and amplify SSA in A1 ( Ulanovsky et al., 2003 , Szymanski et al., 2009 , Bauerle et al., 2011 , Fishman and Steinschneider, 2012 , Escera and Malmierca, 2014 ), through a combination of plastic modulation of thalamocortical inputs and intra-cortical inhibitory circuits, which would allow for selective suppression of neuronal responses to specific stimuli ( Nelken, 2014 ).

senses.label: with the phenomenon nearly universal in the sample: ALMOST ALL NEURONS RECORDED IN A1 EXHIBITED SIGNIFICANT SSA, 138 out of 147
senses.evidence: Almost all neurons recorded in A1 exhibited significant SSA ( Figure 1D , standard tone-evoked FR significantly lower than the deviant tone-evoked FR in N = 138 out of 147 neurons, Wilcoxon rank sum test p < 0.05).

senses.label: THE MODEL EXISTS TO RECONCILE TWO FACTS THAT LOOK INCOMPATIBLE: PVs AND SOMs EXHIBIT SIMILAR MAGNITUDE OF SSA, YET HAVE A DIFFERENTIAL EFFECT ON SSA in putative excitatory neurons - the model is built AS A PROOF-OF-PRINCIPLE that would account for both
senses.head: THE MODEL EXISTS TO RECONCILE TWO FACTS THAT LOOK INCOMPATIBLE: PVs AND SOMs EXHIBIT SIMILAR MAGNITUDE OF SSA, YET HAVE A DIFFERENTIAL EFFECT ON SSA in putative excitatory neurons
senses.gloss: the model is built AS A PROOF-OF-PRINCIPLE that would account for both
senses.evidence: As a proof-of-principle that would account for our findings that PVs and SOMs exhibit similar magnitude of SSA, yet have a differential effect on SSA in putative excitatory neurons, we constructed a simplified model of mutually coupled inhibitory–excitatory neuronal populations

senses.label: and the function being tested was assumed rather than shown before this: different interneuron types HAVE BEEN HYPOTHESIZED TO CARRY OUT SPECIALIZED COMPLEMENTARY FUNCTIONS, but THEIR FUNCTION IN DRIVING CHANGES IN DYNAMIC AUDITORY PROCESSING HAS NOT BEEN PREVIOUSLY ESTABLISHED
senses.evidence: While different interneuron types have been hypothesized to carry out specialized complementary functions in sensory processing ( DeFelipe, 2002 ; Markram et al., 2004 ; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011 ; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014 ; Marlin et al., 2015 ), their function in driving changes in dynamic auditory processing has not been previously established.

senses.label: memory - the passive sensory kind: a high-resolution trace of what was just heard, not manipulable and not under attentional control
senses.head: memory
senses.gloss: the passive sensory kind: a high-resolution trace of what was just heard, not manipulable and not under attentional control
senses.evidence: Thus, ASM is a passive store of just-heard sounds that retains a “synthesized auditory memory” ( Massaro, 1975 )

senses.label: memory - the working kind: active manipulation, rehearsal and reinstatement, able to run without any sound having been heard
senses.head: memory
senses.gloss: the working kind: active manipulation, rehearsal and reinstatement, able to run without any sound having been heard
senses.evidence: These “working” aspects of WM— active mental manipulation, rehearsal, and reinstatement of information— represent an important functional distinction between WM and ASM.

senses.label: short-term memory - used loosely as a synonym for working memory, which the paper identifies as part of how the two constructs got conflated
senses.head: short-term memory
senses.gloss: used loosely as a synonym for working memory, which the paper identifies as part of how the two constructs got conflated
senses.evidence: Auditory sensory memory is qualitatively different from post-sensory memory processes ( Massaro, 1972 ; Crowder, 1982 ), including Atkinson and Shiffrin’s short-term store, which evolved into the working memory (WM) construct (see, e.g., Logie and Cowan, 2015 ).

senses.label: THE SAME QUANTITY, THREE ESTIMATORS, AND THE ABSOLUTE VALUES DISAGREE BY MORE THAN TWICE: the left network time constant is 82 ms by the quasi-Bayesian posterior, 106.1 ms by a trimmed average and 192.9 ms by the median, and all three are reported as consistent because only the DIRECTION of the hemispheric difference is stable
senses.evidence: Our quasi-Bayesian posterior over time constants were consistent with a simple robust average that discarded time constants longer than 300 ms or shorter than 10 ms: 106.1 ms ( n = 13, SEM = 4.03) for the left and 118.8 ms ( n = 14, SEM = 3.71) for the right ACx. It is also consistent with the median values, 192.9 ms ( n = 24) for the left and 250.3 ms ( n = 27) for the right ACx. Note that the medians are biased, since the outliers are not symmetrically distributed, being bounded by 0 ms from below.

senses.evidence: Our quasi-Bayesian posterior over time constants were consistent with a simple robust average that discarded time constants longer than 300 ms or shorter than 10 ms: 106.1 ms ( n = 13, SEM = 4.03) for the left and 118.8 ms ( n = 14, SEM = 3.71) for the right ACx. It is also consistent with the median values, 192.9 ms ( n = 24) for the left and 250.3 ms ( n = 27) for the right ACx. senses.label: so a network time constant is not a number that can be joined across papers without its estimator: the same neurons yield 82 or 193 ms depending on how the unequally informative cells are combined
senses.evidence: To systematically aggregate the unequally informative neurons, we used a quasi-Bayesian method that accounts for the bias and uncertainty in the time constant estimation for each neuron ( Fig 4B , Methods). Neurons with high uncertainty (low SNR estimate) and relatively weak evidence about the network’s time constant, automatically counted for less contribution. Hence, we did not apply arbitrary criteria to discard neurons with weak autocorrelations, low firing rates or very long timescales, and were able to utilize data from all neurons.

senses.label: TWO READINGS OF ONE OBSERVATION, EACH GIVEN A SIGNATURE BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT: more input to the right hemisphere could mean a similar pool of sources with larger events, or a larger pool with the same event sizes, and the amplitude distribution is what separates them
senses.evidence: Several synaptic mechanisms could underlie the observation of more significant hotspots in superficial layers of the right ACx compared to the left. One possibility is that each hemisphere has a similar pool of presynaptic inputs in these layers, but individual synaptic events were larger in the right ACx compared to the left ( Fig 1F left). Another possibility is that the distribution of the synaptic events’ amplitudes is similar between the hemispheres, but there is a larger pool of presynaptic inputs in the right ACx compared to the left ( Fig 1F right).

senses.label: a normalisation is deliberately NOT applied, and the reason is a measurement rather than an assumption - density and photoexcitability were previously shown not to differ, so dividing by them would add noise without removing bias
senses.head: a normalisation is deliberately NOT applied, and the reason is a measurement rather than an assumption
senses.gloss: density and photoexcitability were previously shown not to differ, so dividing by them would add noise without removing bias
senses.evidence: In a previous study, we determined that neuronal density and photoexcitability of individual cells did not significantly differ between the hemispheres; therefore, we did not normalize maps by these factors

senses.label: the standard remedy is stated to fail here: resampling a low signal-to-noise spike train with a biased estimator makes the variance look small and manufactures a confident wrong answer
senses.evidence: Unfortunately, bootstrapping or resampling procedures cannot practically correct for these issues. For example, if there are only a handful of spikes, bootstrap samples may consistently provide very small time constants such that the variance of the estimator is close to zero. However, in this low firing rate regime, the uncertainty of the estimator should be large if we properly accounted for the spiking noise—resampling low SNR data combined with a strongly biased estimator can create an illusion of a (misleading) high SNR conclusion.

Neurons with high uncertainty (low SNR estimate) and relatively weak evidence about the network’s time constant, automatically counted for less contribution. Hence, we did not apply arbitrary criteria to discard neurons with weak autocorrelations, low firing rates or very long timescales, and were able to utilize data from all neurons.

senses.label: a hemisphere here is an entire cortical area treated as one population with one shared time constant, which is the level at which the claim is made even though every measurement is per neuron
senses.evidence: We then integrated the evidence from multiple neurons assuming that each estimated time constant per neuron is a noisy version of a single shared network time constant per hemisphere

senses.label: a PV cell here is a cell staining for parvalbumin at one moment - the paper is explicit that this counts MARKER EXPRESSION and that expression may be regulated up or down independently of cell number

senses.evidence: However, this finding also indicates that some interneuron subtypes may up- or down-regulate expression of certain markers, perhaps compensating for changes in cortical networks resulting from learning or degeneration.

senses.label: the marker categories OVERLAP - percentages across markers sum to more than 100% and individual cells are counted more than once, so PV, SOM, VIP and the rest are not disjoint classes
senses.head: the marker categories OVERLAP
senses.gloss: percentages across markers sum to more than 100% and individual cells are counted more than once, so PV, SOM, VIP and the rest are not disjoint classes
senses.evidence: It is important to note that all neurons taken together, these percentages add up to more than 100%, confirming that individual neurons express multiple markers and that the same neurons may have been were counted more than once for different markers

senses.label: ChAT and VIP colocalise invariably in visual cortex and only about half the time here, so a marker relationship established in one area does not carry to another
senses.evidence: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+

senses.label: GABA positivity is treated as definitional for these markers, with one developmental exception: a quarter of CR cells at P9 are GABA-negative
senses.evidence: We also found that a subset CR+ cells at P9 were GABA− (24 ± 6%) whereas all of them were GABA+ at later ages.

senses.label: all percentages are shares of a shrinking denominator - total GABA cells fall sharply before P20 - so proportional stability and absolute stability come apart
senses.head: all percentages are shares of a shrinking denominator
senses.gloss: total GABA cells fall sharply before P20 - so proportional stability and absolute stability come apart
senses.evidence: Thus, GABA positive cells saw their overall representation in the neuronal pool fall from 16 to 12% over that time period.

senses.label: neural correlate of consciousness - of CONTENT: the minimal activations sufficient for one specific conscious content
senses.head: neural correlate of consciousness
senses.gloss: of CONTENT: the minimal activations sufficient for one specific conscious content
senses.evidence: Although it is rarely debated what we mean with a “neural correlate of consciousness,” most experiments aim to identify the minimal neural activations that are sufficient for a specific content of consciousness (Chalmers, 2000 ).

senses.label: neural correlate of consciousness - AS SUCH: what distinguishes being awake from asleep or dead, not tied to any content
senses.head: neural correlate of consciousness
senses.gloss: AS SUCH: what distinguishes being awake from asleep or dead, not tied to any content
senses.evidence: Contrary to this, other scientists are preoccupied with finding neural correlates of consciousness “as such”—i.e., neural correlates that mark the difference between being dead, asleep, awake, etc., and which are not content-specific in the sense above.

senses.label: measuring consciousness - DIRECT: the subject reports their own experience, with the known limits of self-report
senses.head: measuring consciousness
senses.gloss: DIRECT: the subject reports their own experience, with the known limits of self-report
senses.evidence: Direct approaches, at least intuitively, are the most informative as participating experimental subjects here simply report about their own experiences.

senses.label: measuring consciousness - INDIRECT: performance on a task stands in for experience, which avoids self-report and imports a threshold assumption instead
senses.head: measuring consciousness
senses.gloss: INDIRECT: performance on a task stands in for experience, which avoids self-report and imports a threshold assumption instead
senses.evidence: Experiments on consciousness that are based on objective measures—the “indirect” approach—typically involve asking subjects to choose between alternatives, e.g., in forced-choice tasks.

senses.label: early activations - as the correlate of phenomenal consciousness, which is the currently favoured reading
senses.head: early activations
senses.gloss: as the correlate of phenomenal consciousness, which is the currently favoured reading
senses.evidence: According to most recent reviews and articles, evidence is lending support toward the latter view (Andersen et al., 2016 ; Koch et al., 2016 ; Hurme et al., 2017 ).

senses.label: early activations - as PRECONSCIOUS: information not yet conscious, which is the opposite reading of the same data
senses.head: early activations
senses.gloss: as PRECONSCIOUS: information not yet conscious, which is the opposite reading of the same data
senses.evidence: Nevertheless, proponents of the opposite view—that consciousness is associated with prefrontal cortex activity—argue that “early” activations in fact represent preconscious states—i.e., information that is not yet conscious (e.g., Lau and Rosenthal, 2011 ).

senses.label: TWO PHENOMENA CALLED FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT, THEN SHOWN TO BE ONE RULE AT TWO SETTINGS: from a theoretical standpoint the mechanism generating one is FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT from the other - one is a path through state space, the other a fixed point attractor
senses.head: TWO PHENOMENA CALLED FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT, THEN SHOWN TO BE ONE RULE AT TWO SETTINGS: from a theoretical standpoint the mechanism generating one is FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT from the other
senses.gloss: one is a path through state space, the other a fixed point attractor
senses.evidence: From a theoretical stand point, the mechanism to generate SA is fundamentally different from the one that generates PA. While SA usually corresponds to a path in the state space of the network, PA is identified as a fixed point attractor. Thus, SA has an inherent transient nature while PA is at least linearly stable in a dynamical system sense.

senses.label: with the open question posed exactly - are the learning rules fundamentally different, or can THE SAME RULE produce both depending on the statistics of the inputs?
senses.head: with the open question posed exactly
senses.gloss: are the learning rules fundamentally different, or can THE SAME RULE produce both depending on the statistics of the inputs?
senses.evidence: One unresolved issue is whether the learning rules used by brain networks to learn PA are fundamentally different than the ones used to learn SA, or whether the same learning rule can produce both, depending on the statistics of the inputs to the network. Learning rules employed in theoretical studies to learn PA typically do not contain any temporal asymmetry, while rules used to learn SA need to contain such a temporal asymmetry.

senses.label: AND THE ANSWER IS THE SAME RULE: cortical circuits endowed with A SINGLE LEARNING RULE can learn QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT neural dynamics depending on the stimuli statistics
senses.evidence: Depending on the stimulus parameters, the network is flexible enough to learn selectively both types of activity by repeated exposure to a sequence of stimuli, without need for supervision. This suggests that cortical circuits endowed with a single learning rule can learn qualitatively different neural dynamics (i.e., persistent vs. sequential activity) depending on the stimuli statistics.

senses.label: with the parameter that decides it named: long durations and large delays give persistent activity, long durations and SHORT delays give sequences - PERSISTENT STIMULATION LEADS TO PERSISTENT ACTIVITY WHILE SEQUENTIAL STIMULATION LEADS TO SEQUENTIAL ACTIVITY
senses.head: with the parameter that decides it named: long durations and large delays give persistent activity, long durations and SHORT delays give sequences
senses.gloss: PERSISTENT STIMULATION LEADS TO PERSISTENT ACTIVITY WHILE SEQUENTIAL STIMULATION LEADS TO SEQUENTIAL ACTIVITY
senses.evidence: We found that stimulations with long durations and large delays generically leads to the formation of PA, whereas stimulations with long enough durations and short delays leads to the formation of SA. Thus, persistent stimulation leads to persistent activity while sequential stimulation leads to sequential activity.

senses.label: A CONVENIENCE OF THE MODELLING TRADITION TREATED AS A FACT ABOUT BRAINS: earlier models SEPARATED a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was SHUT DOWN from a retrieval phase in which the connectivity no longer changes - and that separation is called THE DRAWBACK OF THESE MODELS
senses.head: A CONVENIENCE OF THE MODELLING TRADITION TREATED AS A FACT ABOUT BRAINS: earlier models SEPARATED a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was SHUT DOWN from a retrieval phase in which the connectivity no longer changes
senses.gloss: and that separation is called THE DRAWBACK OF THESE MODELS
senses.evidence: The drawback of these models is that they separated a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was shut down in order to form the synaptic connectivity matrix, and a retrieval phase in which the connectivity matrix does not change anymore. Our model removes this artificial separation, since both plasticity rule and recurrent dynamics operate continuously, both during learning and recall. However, we found that there needs to be a mechanism to attenuate recurrent dynamics during learning for it to be stable.

senses.label: with the honest version stated - by compartmentalizing dynamics and learning in time the runaway is prevented, but IT IS UNCLEAR WHETHER SUCH COMPARTMENTALIZATION EXISTS IN CORTICAL NETWORKS
senses.head: with the honest version stated
senses.gloss: by compartmentalizing dynamics and learning in time the runaway is prevented, but IT IS UNCLEAR WHETHER SUCH COMPARTMENTALIZATION EXISTS IN CORTICAL NETWORKS
senses.evidence: Therefore, by compartmentalizing in time dynamics and learning, the network dynamics does not lead to changes in the synaptic weights during retrieval, and conversely, changes in synaptic weights do not lead to changes in the dynamics during learning. This separation prevents the observed runaway of the synaptic weights due to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity. However, it is unclear whether such compartmentalization exists in cortical networks. In this work, we explored the alternative scenario, in which both plasticity and dynamics happen concurrently during learning and retrieval

senses.label: A DISAGREEMENT WITH PRIOR MODELS DIAGNOSED TO ONE PARAMETER: earlier work learned persistent activity WITHOUT any stabiliser, and the key difference is that in those models the persistent rate sits BELOW THE THRESHOLD FOR LTP INDUCTION, where here it is always maximal
senses.evidence: However, previous studies have shown that PA could be learned without additional stabilization mechanisms. In Del Giudice and Mattia ( 2001 ), Del Giudice et al. ( 2003 ), and Mongillo et al. ( 2005 ) PA is learnt without any stabilizing mechanism except for short-term depression. These studies have a number of differences with ours, however, we believe the key difference for stable learning PA is that in these models there is PA (in the absence of inputs to the network) below the threshold for LTP induction - something is not currently present in our model since PA is always at the maximal rate. Therefore, unlike our model, PA after stimulation does not lead to effective changes in the synaptic connections.

senses.label: and the thresholds are SET so that there is no learning when both populations are persistently active - a modelling choice that decides whether a stabiliser is needed at all
senses.head: and the thresholds are SET so that there is no learning when both populations are persistently active
senses.gloss: a modelling choice that decides whether a stabiliser is needed at all
senses.evidence: Importantly, as in the previous models discussed above, the learning thresholds are set in such a way that there is no learning when both populations present PA. Additionally, during learning the presentations of stimuli are far apart, and unlike our model learning feedback and feedforward connections are due to persistent activity in one neuron, and the stimulation in the other, followed by a small increase in the synaptic strengths in each presentation.

senses.label: with the two mechanisms recognised as the same move under different names - short-term depression shuts down high firing rates during stimulation, WHICH RESEMBLES THE EFFECT of the homeostatic rule here
senses.head: with the two mechanisms recognised as the same move under different names
senses.gloss: short-term depression shuts down high firing rates during stimulation, WHICH RESEMBLES THE EFFECT of the homeostatic rule here
senses.evidence: Interestingly, they introduced short term depression to stabilize learning by rapidly shutting down high firing rates during stimulation or PA, which resembles the effect of the generalized homeostatic plasticity rule in our model.

senses.label: AN UNREALISTIC FEATURE DECLARED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the background state is at zero activity, AN UNREALISTIC FEATURE STEMMING FROM THE SIMPLIFIED PIECEWISE LINEAR TRANSFER FUNCTION
senses.evidence: Lastly, another difference with the models above, and with classical models for persistent delay activity (Amit and Brunel, 1997 ), is that in our model the “background state” is at zero activity. This is an unrealistic feature stemming from the simplified piecewise linear transfer function used in our network (see Equation 5).

senses.label: AND THE PRICE OF NO SUPERVISION IS NAMED: the network can learn the TEMPORAL ORDER of the stimuli BUT NOT THEIR PRECISE TIMING - and the model that recovers timing REQUIRES PARAMETERS TO BE PRECISELY RELATED
senses.head: AND THE PRICE OF NO SUPERVISION IS NAMED: the network can learn the TEMPORAL ORDER of the stimuli BUT NOT THEIR PRECISE TIMING
senses.gloss: and the model that recovers timing REQUIRES PARAMETERS TO BE PRECISELY RELATED
senses.evidence: The cost of not having supervision is that the network can only learn the temporal order of the presented stimuli, but not their precise timing. Veliz-Cuba et al. ( 2015 ) have recently provided a model which bear strong similarities with our model (rate model with unsupervised temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule), but includes in addition a short-term facilitation mechanism that allows the network to learn both order and precise timing of a sequence presented in input. However, their mechanisms require parameters to be precisely related.

senses.label: with the other side of that trade priced too - supervised rules reproduce target sequences PERFECTLY, and ARE NOT BIOPHYSICALLY REALISTIC
senses.head: with the other side of that trade priced too
senses.gloss: supervised rules reproduce target sequences PERFECTLY, and ARE NOT BIOPHYSICALLY REALISTIC
senses.evidence: Models with supervised learning can reproduce perfectly target sequences through minimization of a suitable error function (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ), but the corresponding learning rules are not biophysically realistic.

senses.label: THE FIRST STABILISER TRIED DID NOT WORK, AND IS REPORTED: instantaneous synaptic normalization holding the summed input weight constant does NOT give stable learning, and the homeostatic rule does
senses.evidence: First, we found that by adding to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity an instantaneous synaptic normalization mechanism that maintains constant the sum of incoming synaptic weights to each population, PA and SA cannot be stably learned. Second, we found that adding a generalized homeostatic plasticity to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity leads to stable learning of PA and SA.

senses.label: and a third mechanism works too, over DISTINCT sets of parameters - DATA NOT SHOWN
senses.head: and a third mechanism works too, over DISTINCT sets of parameters
senses.gloss: DATA NOT SHOWN
senses.evidence: We have also tried other stabilization mechanisms such as inhibitory to excitatory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011 ) instead of homeostatic plasticity. In this case we found that stable learning of PA and SA is possible, but for distinct sets of network and stimulation parameters (data not shown).

senses.label: AND THE MODEL'S OWN REQUIREMENT IS UNDER DISPUTE IN THE LITERATURE: the compensatory timescale must be as fast as the Hebbian one, and THERE IS CURRENTLY AN ONGOING DEBATE about whether such timescales are consistent with experimental evidence
senses.evidence: As explained in Zenke and Gerstner ( 2017 ) and Zenke et al. ( 2017 ), in order to prevent the runaway of the synaptic weights produced by Hebbian plasticity, the timescale of any compensatory mechanism should be of the same order or faster than the Hebbian timescale. For generalized homeostatic plasticity, the timescale of the homeostatic variable H i is dependent on the firing rate of neuron i and the target firing rate [i.e., ϕ( u i )/ϕ( u 0 )]. When the network firing rate is close to the target firing rate the homeostatic learning rule is slow, and the homeostatic mechanism seldom play a role in the dynamics. On the other hand, for high firing rates the homeostatic plasticity timescale becomes faster, preventing the runaway of the synaptic weights. There is currently an ongoing debate about whether the timescales of compensatory processes used in theoretical studies, as the ones used here, are consistent with experimental evidence

senses.label: with the instability itself traced to a positive feedback loop - more activity gives more average synaptic strength gives more activity, RUNAWAY of the weights
senses.head: with the instability itself traced to a positive feedback loop
senses.gloss: more activity gives more average synaptic strength gives more activity, RUNAWAY of the weights
senses.evidence: Consistent with many previous studies (Dayan and Abbott, 2001 ), we have shown that a network with unsupervised Hebbian plasticity under sequential stimulation leads to a runaway of the synaptic weights. This instability is due to a positive feed-back loop generated by the progressive increase of network activity leading to a progressive increase in average synaptic strength when PA or SA are being learned.

senses.label: and the model chosen for a stated reason - a rate model at the mesoscopic level, with THE ADVANTAGE OF ANALYTICAL TRACTABILITY
senses.head: and the model chosen for a stated reason
senses.gloss: a rate model at the mesoscopic level, with THE ADVANTAGE OF ANALYTICAL TRACTABILITY
senses.evidence: We use a rate model to describe the activity of populations of neurons (Wilson and Cowan, 1972 ). The connectivity in this model represents the average of the synaptic connections between populations of neurons, allowing to investigate at a mesoscopic level the learning mechanisms of PA and SA. This model has the advantage of analytical tractability.

senses.label: THE OBJECT OF STUDY IS NOT AGREED, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: the small size of the mouse brain HAS MADE IT DIFFICULT TO IDENTIFY PRECISE BORDERS between functional areas, PPC's location IS ESSENTIALLY WHERE mapping studies have identified retinotopic areas RL, A and AM, THE DEGREE TO WHICH PPC OVERLAPS WITH THESE SECONDARY VISUAL AREAS IS A MATTER OF DEBATE, and the coordinates used here MOST DIRECTLY OVERLAP WITH AREA AM
senses.evidence: The small size of the mouse brain has made it difficult to identify precise borders between different functional areas. PPC in the rodent, as classically defined by its thalamic inputs 26 , is located in the region between anterior to V1 and posterior to somatosensory cortex. However, this location is essentially where both anatomical 11 , 12 and functional 13 , 14 mapping studies have identified the retinotopically-organized areas RL, A, and AM. The degree to which PPC overlaps with these secondary visual areas is a matter of debate. Some have argued that rodent PPC may have more in common with primate extrastriate cortex, given that inactivation specifically disrupts sensitivity on visual decisions 10 . Indeed, the stereotaxic coordinates used by us 3 and others 4 , 27 to target mouse PPC most directly overlap with area AM, which exhibits directionally-tuned responses even under anesthesia 14 .

senses.label: and the role is contested in the same way - rodent PPC PLAYS A MINIMAL ROLE in auditory and whisker tasks BUT SEE, is CAUSALLY NECESSARY for visual ones, MAY ULTIMATELY BE MORE HOMOLOGOUS TO EXTRASTRIATE CORTEX, or REFLECTS INTERNAL BIASES - and REMOVAL OF INTERNAL BIASES CANNOT FULLY EXPLAIN the deficits
senses.head: and the role is contested in the same way
senses.gloss: rodent PPC PLAYS A MINIMAL ROLE in auditory and whisker tasks BUT SEE, is CAUSALLY NECESSARY for visual ones, MAY ULTIMATELY BE MORE HOMOLOGOUS TO EXTRASTRIATE CORTEX, or REFLECTS INTERNAL BIASES - and REMOVAL OF INTERNAL BIASES CANNOT FULLY EXPLAIN the deficits
senses.evidence: While rodent PPC plays a minimal role in simple auditory 6 and whisker-based 7 decision tasks (but see 8 ), multiple groups have demonstrated that it is causally necessary for make decisions on the basis of visual stimuli 3 , 4 , 9 , 10 . However, the specific role of PPC in visual decision-making remains unclear. Some argue that rodent PPC may ultimately be more homologous to extrastriate cortex in processing sensory signals that are accumulated elsewhere for decision-making 10 . Indeed, both anatomical projection studies 11 , 12 , as well as functional mapping studies 13 , 14 indicate that PPC may overlap with or contain a group of retinotopically-organized extrastriate areas that are rostral to primary visual cortex (V1). Others suggest that PPC reflects internal biases related to the value of past stimuli 8 or actions 9 . However, removal of internal biases cannot fully explain the decision-making deficits induced by inactivation of PPC during visual decision tasks 3 , 4 , 10 .

senses.label: A DEFINITION WIDENED BECAUSE THE DESIGN CANNOT SEPARATE TWO THINGS: DUE TO THE DIFFICULTY IN DISTINGUISHING BETWEEN MOTOR PREPARATION AND DECISION-RELATED SIGNALS WITH OUR GO/NO-GO PARADIGM, WE DEFINE CHOICE SELECTIVITY BROADLY AS ANY PREMOTOR SIGNAL RELATED TO BEHAVIORAL OUTPUT INDEPENDENT OF THE STIMULUS
senses.evidence: Due to the difficulty in distinguishing between motor preparation and decision-related signals with our go/no-go paradigm, we define “choice” selectivity broadly as any premotor signal related to behavioral output independent of the stimulus.

senses.label: and the other central term is hedged where it is introduced: TASK ENGAGEMENT MAY NOT BE ABLE TO FULLY SEPARATE VARIOUS NON-SENSORY SIGNALS - the design is defended as identifying PURE SENSORY RESPONSES robust in both conditions, not as isolating engagement
senses.head: and the other central term is hedged where it is introduced: TASK ENGAGEMENT MAY NOT BE ABLE TO FULLY SEPARATE VARIOUS NON-SENSORY SIGNALS
senses.gloss: the design is defended as identifying PURE SENSORY RESPONSES robust in both conditions, not as isolating engagement
senses.evidence: While “task engagement” may not be able to fully separate various non-sensory signals, we reasoned that this approach could allow us to identify pure sensory responses that were robust during both passive and engaged conditions.

senses.label: THE CATEGORY QUESTION IS ASKED OF ITSELF AND LEFT OPEN: DO THESE RESPONSE TYPES FORM BONA-FIDE CELL CLASSES OR DOES PPC REPRESENT A CATEGORY-FREE POPULATION, AS OTHERS HAVE PROPOSED? - although various properties ARE CORRELATED WITH ONE ANOTHER, MORE WORK NEEDS TO BE DONE TO DETERMINE WHETHER FUNCTIONAL NEURONAL SUBGROUPS ARE TRULY SEPARABLE
senses.head: THE CATEGORY QUESTION IS ASKED OF ITSELF AND LEFT OPEN: DO THESE RESPONSE TYPES FORM BONA-FIDE CELL CLASSES OR DOES PPC REPRESENT A CATEGORY-FREE POPULATION, AS OTHERS HAVE PROPOSED?
senses.gloss: although various properties ARE CORRELATED WITH ONE ANOTHER, MORE WORK NEEDS TO BE DONE TO DETERMINE WHETHER FUNCTIONAL NEURONAL SUBGROUPS ARE TRULY SEPARABLE
senses.evidence: Do these response types form bona-fide cell classes or does PPC represent a category-free population, as others have proposed 5 ? Although we do find that various properties (such as modulation by engagement, contrast, and reversal) are correlated with one another, more work needs to be done to determine whether functional neuronal subgroups are truly separable.

senses.label: with the heterogeneity described in every condition and quantified in overlapping percentages - roughly 30% with passive responses, 20% contrast-modulated, 10% keeping their selectivity after reversal, against 70% task-gated and 70% choice-selective, plus a third group whose responses CANNOT BE EXPLAINED BY PARTIAL GLM MODELS
senses.head: with the heterogeneity described in every condition and quantified in overlapping percentages
senses.gloss: roughly 30% with passive responses, 20% contrast-modulated, 10% keeping their selectivity after reversal, against 70% task-gated and 70% choice-selective, plus a third group whose responses CANNOT BE EXPLAINED BY PARTIAL GLM MODELS
senses.evidence: In every task condition reported here, PPC responses were heterogeneous. A subset of PPC neurons have significant passive visual responses (~30%, Fig. 2f , E + P) and are modulated by contrast in both engaged and passive conditions (~20%, Fig. 6a , contrast). These neurons maintain their stimulus selectivity even after reversal of reward contingency (~10%, Fig. 8a , Stim). These “stimulus” neurons are spatially intermingled with the larger proportion of “choice” neurons that have task-gated responses (~70%, Fig. 2f , E only), weak contrast modulation (~30%, Fig. 6a , engagement), and choice-selective responses after contingency reversal (~70%, Fig. 8a , Go). Furthermore, a third group of neurons have multiplexed selectivity to stimulus, engagement, and motor signals, exhibiting complex responses to combinations of sensory or motor signals in engaged conditions. These cells exhibit modulation to both contrast and engagement (~30%, Fig. 6a , both) and their responses cannot be explained by partial GLM models that only use a subset of the task variables (~35%, Supplementary Fig. 4f ).

senses.label: and no anatomy behind the groups: NO SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE between within-group and across-group distances, so PPC CONTAINS NEURONS WITH DIVERSE VISUOMOTOR RESPONSE PROPERTIES THAT ARE SPATIALLY INTERMINGLED
senses.evidence: We computed the pairwise distance between all target-preferring neurons, and found no significant difference between within-group and across-group distances (Fig. 6f ; within-group, 268 ± 5 µm; across-group 273 ± 5 µm; p = 0.102, clustered Wilcoxon signed-rank test). We also compared the functional properties of pairs of neurons as a function of distance, and found that the difference in contrast modulation or engagement modulation did not depend on distance (Fig. 6g ; Pearson’s correlation with distance, difference in contrast modulation index, r = 0.003, p = 0.660; difference in engagement modulation index, r = 0.001, p = 0.960). Therefore, PPC contains neurons with diverse visuomotor response properties that are spatially intermingled.

senses.label: THE DECISIVE MANIPULATION IS A CHANGE OF MEANING, NOT OF STIMULUS: after reversal of reward contingency the PPC selectivity measure was DRAMATICALLY ALTERED, with THE MAJORITY OF RESPONSIVE NEURONS PREFERRING THE NEW TARGET STIMULUS B
senses.evidence: However, in PPC, this selectivity measure was dramatically altered with reversal of reward contingency (before, 0.513 ± 0.013; after, −0.373 ± 0.013; p = 4.15 × 10 −3 , clustered Wilcoxon signed-rank test), with the majority of responsive neurons preferring the new target stimulus B after reversal.

senses.label: and the two areas separate cleanly in one scatter plot - 74.3% of V1 cells STIMULUS-SELECTIVE in the first and third quadrants, against 66.8% of PPC cells in the fourth, INDICATING A PREFERENCE FOR THE REWARDED TARGET STIMULUS, REGARDLESS OF ITS ACTUAL IDENTITY
senses.head: and the two areas separate cleanly in one scatter plot
senses.gloss: 74.3% of V1 cells STIMULUS-SELECTIVE in the first and third quadrants, against 66.8% of PPC cells in the fourth, INDICATING A PREFERENCE FOR THE REWARDED TARGET STIMULUS, REGARDLESS OF ITS ACTUAL IDENTITY
senses.evidence: V1 neurons were strongly stimulus-selective, with the majority (74.3% ± 5.2% of cells, Fig. 8a , top) of neurons lying within the first and third quadrants (Fig. 7g ).
