First, it eliminates history-dependent learning and reputation effects, leaving a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium that provides a clean theoretical benchmark. Second, recent cross-task evaluations by Mei et al. (2024), who compared large-language-model agents with human subjects on several classic economic games, including the ultimatum game, show that the one-shot ultimatum game exhibits the largest human-AI performance gap. This makes the one-shot ultimatum game a stringent test bed: if generative agents can narrow that gap here, the implication for other interaction settings is even stronger. Third, a single-round design keeps prompts concise and prevents chain-ofthought content from leaking across rounds, which could otherwise induce artificial correlations in multi-round simulations. Taken together, these considerations make the one-shot ultimatum game the most interpretable and demanding environment for assessing whether enhanced reasoning enables LLM agents to approximate human bargaining behavior

senses.label: Human low-offer rejection - payoff sacrifice explained as resistance to perceived unfairness
senses.head: Human low-offer rejection
senses.gloss: payoff sacrifice explained as resistance to perceived unfairness
senses.evidence: Although s2 = accept is the weakly dominant strategy of player 2, in economic experiments it is common to observe decisions of s2 = reject when the value of s1 is low (Güth et al. 1982). A commonly proposed explanation for this phenomenon is that responders may choose to sacrifice their payoffs to resist perceived unfairness, particularly when their potential earnings are lower

senses.label: Generative AI - distribution-learning synthesis rather than classification within existing boundaries
senses.head: Generative AI
senses.gloss: distribution-learning synthesis rather than classification within existing boundaries
senses.evidence: Generative AI refers to a class of models that autonomously produce new, plausible data samples across various modalities—from text and images to audio and beyond. Unlike discriminative models that classify or predict within existing data boundaries, generative models learn the underlying data distribution itself, enabling them to synthesize entirely new outputs (Goodfellow et al. 2020; Ramesh et al. 2022). This paradigm shift—from recognition to generation—has created models that are not just analytical but creative, capable of mimicking the structure of real-world behavior and expression. In this sense, generative AI offers more than technological novelty; it marks a methodological transformation in how we model social phenomena

senses.label: GPT-4 as behavioral model - a statistical knowledge base reflecting norms, heuristics, and communication conventions
senses.head: GPT-4 as behavioral model
senses.gloss: a statistical knowledge base reflecting norms, heuristics, and communication conventions
senses.evidence: From a behavioral modeling standpoint, gpt-4 can be interpreted as a statistical knowledge base constructed from human language and interaction patterns. Its training corpus contains linguistic patterns that reflect social norms, strategic heuristics, and communicative conventions across cultural contexts (Lorè and Heydari 2024). This enables the model to produce responses that are not only linguistically fluent but also behaviorally plausible, a property that has led to its adoption in simulating agents for bargaining, negotiation, and multi-agent coordination (Dell’Acqua et al. 2023; Phelps and Russell 2024; Park et al. 2023). Crucially, this generative capacity enables LLMs to function as foundation models—general-purpose substrates that can be adapted to various downstream tasks without the need for retraining

senses.label: Hallucination - plausible but wrong output arising from association-based rather than grounded modeling
senses.head: Hallucination
senses.gloss: plausible but wrong output arising from association-based rather than grounded modeling
senses.evidence: Nevertheless, several limitations must be addressed when deploying LLMs as behavioral agents. First, hallucinations, plausible but incorrect outputs, can emerge, especially under poorly constrained prompts (Bubeck et al. 2023). These are a byproduct of the model’s reliance on learned statistical associations rather than grounded world models. Second, LLMs inherit biases from their training data, which can affect their decision-making in subtle but impactful ways (e.g., favoring certain persuasion styles, exhibiting implicit demographic stereotypes) (Blodgett et al. 2020; Caliskan et al. 2017). Third, these models remain black boxes in terms of interpretability: while their outputs are analyzable, their internal reasoning processes are not directly accessible

senses.label: Few-shot prompting - annotated examples guiding output style and logic
senses.head: Few-shot prompting
senses.gloss: annotated examples guiding output style and logic
senses.evidence: While these limitations remain open challenges, recent work has shown that prompt design can shape the inferential structure of LLM outputs. We therefore adopt two prompting strategies—(i) few-shot prompting, where the model is shown a small number of annotated examples to guide output style and logic (Brown et al. 2020), and (ii) chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, which explicitly instructs the model to articulate intermediate reasoning steps (Wei et al. 2022)—not as general mitigation techniques, but as scaffolding methods to influence the reasoning quality of agent decisions in structured tasks. These strategies have been shown to enhance coherence, inference depth, and contextual relevance in complex queries

senses.label: Chain-of-thought prompting - explicit instruction to articulate intermediate reasoning steps
senses.head: Chain-of-thought prompting
senses.gloss: explicit instruction to articulate intermediate reasoning steps
senses.evidence: While these limitations remain open challenges, recent work has shown that prompt design can shape the inferential structure of LLM outputs. We therefore adopt two prompting strategies—(i) few-shot prompting, where the model is shown a small number of annotated examples to guide output style and logic (Brown et al. 2020), and (ii) chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, which explicitly instructs the model to articulate intermediate reasoning steps (Wei et al. 2022)—not as general mitigation techniques, but as scaffolding methods to influence the reasoning quality of agent decisions in structured tasks. These strategies have been shown to enhance coherence, inference depth, and contextual relevance in complex queries

senses.label: Reasoning ability - observable coherent multi-step response structure, not a claim about mental models or logical soundness
senses.head: Reasoning ability
senses.gloss: observable coherent multi-step response structure, not a claim about mental models or logical soundness
senses.evidence: In this study, we refer to “reasoning ability” as the model’s capacity to generate contextually coherent, multi-step responses that reflect inferential structure. This is not meant to imply internal mental models or logical soundness, but rather denotes an observable behavioral property elicited through prompt design

senses.label: LLMs as empirical tools - outputs analyzed, compared, and validated like participant data under safeguards
senses.head: LLMs as empirical tools
senses.gloss: outputs analyzed, compared, and validated like participant data under safeguards
senses.evidence: In summary, this study proceeds from a pragmatist perspective: we do not claim that gpt-4 replicates human cognition per se, but we argue that LLMs can approximate certain behavioral patterns observed in economic experiments with a level of fidelity that may justify their use as methodological tools in specific, well-defined simulation contexts. This positioning is consistent with recent proposals in the social sciences and cognitive modeling communities that advocate using LLMs as empirical tools—entities whose outputs can be analyzed, compared, and validated just like those of human participants (Wang et al. 2025b; Xie et al. 2024). With careful prompt design, evaluation protocols, and methodological safeguards, LLMs may be able to offer a promising route to scalable, replicable, and interpretable simulations of human-like behavior

senses.label: Replication success under coarse criteria - aggregate distributions or binary typical-outcome alignment without individual reasoning
senses.head: Replication success under coarse criteria
senses.gloss: aggregate distributions or binary typical-outcome alignment without individual reasoning
senses.evidence: However, these successes may stem from coarse-grained evaluation criteria: both studies assessed behavior at the level of aggregate distributions or binary alignment with typical outcomes, without deeper analysis of underlying reasoning processes or individual-level deviations

senses.label: Latent utility hypothesis - agents may optimize perceived social harmony rather than material self-interest
senses.head: Latent utility hypothesis
senses.gloss: agents may optimize perceived social harmony rather than material self-interest
senses.evidence: Mei et al. (2024) formalized this observation through behavioral Turing tests and proposed that LLMs encode a latent utility function that LLMs may be implicitly optimizing for perceived social harmony rather than material self-interest

senses.label: Isolated reasoning manipulation - vary zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought while holding persona, framing, and temperature outside the focal contrast
senses.head: Isolated reasoning manipulation
senses.gloss: vary zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought while holding persona, framing, and temperature outside the focal contrast
senses.evidence: Taken together, these findings reveal a fragmented and sometimes contradictory landscape, where various agent design parameters interact in complex ways, highlighting the need for more controlled experiments focusing on individual determinants of behavior. Among these, reasoning ability, the capacity of agents to interpret game structures, anticipate responses, and derive optimal strategies, emerges as a foundational component. Yet few studies have systematically isolated reasoning from confounding variables such as persona, payoff framing, or temperature settings

senses.label: Core validity question - convergence toward normative rationality versus divergence from observed human behavior
senses.head: Core validity question
senses.gloss: convergence toward normative rationality versus divergence from observed human behavior
senses.evidence: In particular, we ask whether increasing inferential sophistication in LLMs drives convergence toward normative benchmarks of rationality or divergence from empirically grounded human behavior

senses.label: Simulation sample - 1000 independent decisions balancing statistical resolution against chain-of-thought cost
senses.head: Simulation sample
senses.gloss: 1000 independent decisions balancing statistical resolution against chain-of-thought cost
senses.evidence: The simulation strategy involved generating 1000 independent decisions for each unique combination of role (proposer/responder), prompt type, and temperature. While this number is not derived from a formal power analysis, it was selected based on two main considerations. First, prior work Kitadai et al. (2023) employed the same sample size and demonstrated that it was sufficient to reveal stable and interpretable distributions of agent behavior. Second, to assess the robustness of our findings, we also tested larger sets of examples (15 and 20 samples) to explore the presence or absence of significant differences in the simulation outcomes. Additionally, we investigate the stability of our results by repeating the selection of 10 examples with different random seeds. Through these robustness check, we confirmed the consistency of results across samples of this size (see Sect. 4). Moreover, the use of chain-of-thought prompting with large models incurs substantial computational cost per generation, making higher sample sizes impractical. Thus, 1000 strikes a balance between statistical resolution and feasibility in simulation-based research

senses.label: Prompt engineering - methodological analog of instructions delivered to human experimental participants
senses.head: Prompt engineering
senses.gloss: methodological analog of instructions delivered to human experimental participants
senses.evidence: To situate our approach within existing methodological traditions, we note that our use of LLM-based generative agents as substitutes for human participants builds on the lineage of agent-based modeling in experimental economics, while integrating recent advances in natural language reasoning through prompt engineering. Our simulation methodology also parallels Monte Carlo methods in computational economics, wherein repeated sampling enables inference over agent behavior under controlled conditions. We emphasize that our use of LLM-driven simulations is not intended to replicate human cognition per se, but rather to probe how reasoning abilities, as computational constructs, affect decision outcomes under experimental conditions

senses.label: AD versus KS - overall distributional difference versus maximum cumulative distribution difference
senses.head: AD versus KS
senses.gloss: overall distributional difference versus maximum cumulative distribution difference
senses.evidence: To quantitatively evaluate the effect of improving reasoning ability, we conducted statistical tests using the Anderson-Darling (AD) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) methods to compare the simulated distributions with both theoretical and human distributions under each prompting condition. These tests evaluate the overall distributional differences and maximum cumulative distribution differences, respectively

senses.label: LLMs as human stand-ins - currently unwarranted without explicit social context and methodological scaffolding
senses.head: LLMs as human stand-ins
senses.gloss: currently unwarranted without explicit social context and methodological scaffolding
senses.evidence: Our findings indicate that LLMs, even when endowed with advanced reasoning capabilities, do not naturally exhibit human-like economic behavior unless explicitly guided by prompts that incorporate social context. Consequently, using LLMdriven MAS as stand-ins for real human groups is currently unwarranted. Moreover, as LLMs continue to improve, there is a risk that such systems could misleadingly portray human behavior as excessively rational. Thus, treating LLMs as direct substitutes for human subjects is a flawed approach. This does not preclude the possibility of employing LLMs in economic modeling or behavioral simulation, but doing so effectively will require deliberate methodological scaffolding. If one seeks to explore such potential within the framework of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis by Huh et al. (2024), careful design and contextualization become essential

senses.label: Persona settings - configured cultural, age, and gender context needed because current models do not inherently possess it
senses.head: Persona settings
senses.gloss: configured cultural, age, and gender context needed because current models do not inherently possess it
senses.evidence: Persona settings are known to play a critical role in shaping human-like behavior in simulations because they reflect contextual variables such as culture, age, and gender, which significantly influence human decision-making (Horton 2023; Phelps and Russell 2024; Han et al. 2024). Current LLMs inherently lack these attributes unless explicitly prompted or configured, underscoring the need for future advancements in LLM architecture and experimental design

senses.label: Persona as behavioral proxy - possible embedding of social preferences and bounded rationality
senses.head: Persona as behavioral proxy
senses.gloss: possible embedding of social preferences and bounded rationality
senses.evidence: First, the human tendency to reject low offers is explained by models of inequity aversion, such as those proposed by Fehr and Schmidt (1999) and Bolton and Ockenfels (2000), as well as fairness equilibrium by Rabin (1993). Furthermore, deviations from the subgame perfect equilibrium in human decision-making correspond to the concept of bounded rationality by Simon (1955). This connection is further supported by our earlier observation that persona settings influenced the degree of deviation from human behavior: their inclusion may act as a proxy for embedding social preferences and bounded rationality into in LLM-driven MAS

senses.label: decision-making phases - Simon's naming: Intelligence, Design and Choice
senses.head: decision-making phases
senses.gloss: Simon's naming: Intelligence, Design and Choice
senses.evidence: A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice.

senses.label: decision-making phases - the same three stages under a different naming convention: Identification, Development and Selection
senses.head: decision-making phases
senses.gloss: the same three stages under a different naming convention: Identification, Development and Selection
senses.evidence: propose slightly different terms to name these stages: Identification, Development and Selection. Despite the differences in naming convention, these three following stages of the decision making process consist of very similar activities.

senses.label: Cognitive neuroscience - multidisciplinary study of mind combining psychology and neurobiology with philosophy, linguistics, and other fields
senses.head: Cognitive neuroscience
senses.gloss: multidisciplinary study of mind combining psychology and neurobiology with philosophy, linguistics, and other fields
senses.evidence: Cognitive neuroscience is a new and rapidly developing field of multidisciplinary research. It brings together many different scientific domains, chiefly psychology and neurobiology, but also philosophy, linguistics and many other sciences that incorporate the study of the mind in their programs

senses.label: Cognitive-neuroscience techniques - brain neuroimaging, neurophysiology, nerve-cell examination, and neuropsychology
senses.head: Cognitive-neuroscience techniques
senses.gloss: brain neuroimaging, neurophysiology, nerve-cell examination, and neuropsychology
senses.evidence: The commonly used techniques of cognitive neuroscience can be divided into four main groups (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008; Shiv et al., 2005): – neuroimaging of the brain, – neurophysiological techniques, – examination of individual nerve cells, – neuropsychological techniques (the study of neurological patients with brain damage)

senses.label: Neuroimaging - methods for studying brain structure and function through electrical, magnetic, or indirect tomographic measures
senses.head: Neuroimaging
senses.gloss: methods for studying brain structure and function through electrical, magnetic, or indirect tomographic measures
senses.evidence: Neuroimaging is associated with a group of research methods used to studying the structure and function of the brain. Among them there are electro- and magneto-physiological techniques, exploring the electrical and magnetic activity of neurons, and tomographic methods in which inferences about neuronal activity are made indirectly (Jaśkowski, 2009). Generally, in the area of economic sciences the most applicable methods are: electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)

senses.label: EEG - scalp-electrode measurement of brain electrical activity with high temporal resolution
senses.head: EEG
senses.gloss: scalp-electrode measurement of brain electrical activity with high temporal resolution
senses.evidence: EEG is focused on the measurement of brain electrical activity recorded by electrodes placed on the scalp at specific locations (Purves et al., 2013). Because of its very good temporal resolution, this method is usually used to study changes in brain activity in time and to analyse reactions to external stimuli

senses.label: fMRI - inference of regional brain activity from oxygen delivery
senses.head: fMRI
senses.gloss: inference of regional brain activity from oxygen delivery
senses.evidence: In such applications, fMRI is much better suited. With its help, you can tell how much oxygen is delivered to specific parts of the brain and deduce their activity. This data contributes to the understanding of the biological basis underlying a performed task

senses.label: fNIRS - non-invasive optical estimation of cortical activity
senses.head: fNIRS
senses.gloss: non-invasive optical estimation of cortical activity
senses.evidence: there is another one, quite novel imaging method, i.e. functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) – a non-invasive technique for the optical estimation of cortical activity. It relies on the low optical absorption of the biological tissue of the infrared radiation in the 650–1000 nm wavelength window (Ferrari, Quaresima, 2012). That represents a powerful tool to non-invasively study task-evoked brain activity

senses.label: Neurophysiological techniques - correlating brain functions with physiological sensations
senses.head: Neurophysiological techniques
senses.gloss: correlating brain functions with physiological sensations
senses.evidence: Neurophysiological techniques are based on the correlation of brain functions with physiological sensations (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008). The most frequently used (especially in experiments on the effect of emotions on the actions and cognitive functions of respondents) are the measurements of galvanic skin-response (GSR), heart rate (HR) and eye-tracking (ET). The reason for their popularity is relatively simple, in comparison to neuroimaging, registration and the interpretation of signals

senses.label: GSR measurement - detecting electrical skin changes, usually on the hand or fingers
senses.head: GSR measurement
senses.gloss: detecting electrical skin changes, usually on the hand or fingers
senses.evidence: The GSR measurement is based on detecting electrical changes in the skin (Dawson, Schell, Filion, 2007) and it is mostly performed on the skin of the hand (fingers)

senses.label: Eye-tracking - detecting eye position, gaze direction, movement sequence, and visual adaptation during cognition
senses.head: Eye-tracking
senses.gloss: detecting eye position, gaze direction, movement sequence, and visual adaptation during cognition
senses.evidence: Eye-tracking, on the other hand, is an effective tool for experimental research because of its abilities to detect the eye position, gaze direction, sequence of eye movement and visual adaptation during cognitive activities. With appropriate software, ET provides both a quantitative and qualitative analysis of the gaze, which is very useful in understanding choice and decision making behaviour

senses.label: Decision process - the path from awareness of a decision problem to a final solution among alternatives
senses.head: Decision process
senses.gloss: the path from awareness of a decision problem to a final solution among alternatives
senses.evidence: Generally speaking, a decision-making process (simply called a decision process) begins with the awareness of a decision problem, and ends up with a final solution among finite or infinite alternatives. A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice

senses.label: Intelligence / Identification - gathering and processing information to diagnose decision needs and formulate alternatives
senses.head: Intelligence / Identification
senses.gloss: gathering and processing information to diagnose decision needs and formulate alternatives
senses.evidence: Intelligence (identification) activity involves gathering and processing information, providing cues for recognizing potential decision needs or opportunities (diagnosis), and for formulating alternatives. Design (development) activity involves identifying alternative courses of action in order to determine likely outcomes and whether these outcomes will satisfy the needs or goals associated with the decision. In the choice (selection) activity, decision-makers make judgements and choose among the previously identified alternatives

senses.label: Data heterogeneity - non-IID cross-institutional distributions that challenge federated aggregation and local optimality
senses.head: Data heterogeneity
senses.gloss: non-IID cross-institutional distributions that challenge federated aggregation and local optimality
senses.evidence: Data heterogeneity. Medical data is particularly diverse—not only because of the variety of modalities, dimensionality and characteristics in general, but even within a specific protocol due to factors such as acquisition differences, brand of the medical device or local demographics. FL may help address certain sources of bias through potentially increased diversity of data sources, but inhomogeneous data distribution poses a challenge for FL algorithms and strategies, as many are assuming independently and identically distributed (IID) data across the participants. In general, strategies such as FedAvg9 are prone to fail under these conditions9,57,58, in part defeating the very purpose of collaborative learning strategies. Recent results, however, indicate that FL training is still feasible59, even if medical data is not uniformly distributed across the institutions16,17 or includes a local bias51. Research addressing this problem includes, for example, FedProx57, part-data-sharing strategy58 and FL with domainadaptation18. Another challenge is that data heterogeneity may lead to a situation in which the global optimal solution may not be optimal for an individual local participant. The definition of model training optimality should, therefore, be agreed by all participants before training

senses.head: Privacy-performance trade-off
senses.gloss: stronger federated protections may affect final-model accuracy
senses.evidence: Privacy vs. performance: It is important to note that FL does not solve all potential privacy issues and—similar to ML algorithms in general—will always carry some risks. Privacy-preserving techniques for FL offer levels of protection that exceed today’s current commercially available ML models12. However, there is a trade-off in terms of performance and these techniques may affect, for example, the accuracy of the final model10. Furthermore, future techniques and/or ancillary data could be used to compromise a model previously considered to be low-risk

senses.evidence: Non-trusted—in FL systems that operate on larger scales, it might be impractical to establish an enforceable collaborative agreement. Some clients may deliberately try to degrade performance, bring the system down or extract information from other parties. Hence, security strategies will be required to mitigate these risks such as, advanced encryption of model submissions, secure authentication of all parties, traceability of actions, differential privacy, verification systems, execution integrity, model confidentiality and protections against adversarial attacks

senses.label: Honest-broker administration - trusted intermediary controls the federation and abstracts internal mechanisms from clients
senses.head: Honest-broker administration
senses.gloss: trusted intermediary controls the federation and abstracts internal mechanisms from clients
senses.evidence: The administration of such a federation can be realised in different ways. In situations requiring the most stringent data privacy between parties, training may operate via some sort of “honest broker” system, in which a trusted third party acts as the intermediary and facilitates access to data. This setup requires an independent entity controlling the overall system, which may not always be desirable, since it could involve additional cost and procedural viscosity. However, it has the advantage that the precise internal mechanisms can be abstracted away from the clients, making the system more agile and simpler to update. In a peer-topeer system each site interacts directly with some or all of the other participants. In other words, there is no gatekeeper function, all protocols must be agreed up-front, which requires significant agreement efforts, and changes must be made in a synchronised fashion by all parties to avoid problems. Additionally, in a trustlessbased architecture the platform operator may be cryptographically locked into being honest by means of a secure protocol, but this may introduce significant computational overheads

We propose, therefore, a definition of a biostimulant as “a formulated product of biological origin that improves plant productivity as a consequence of the novel or emergent properties of the complex of constituents and not as a sole consequence of the presence of known essential plant nutrients, plant growth regulators, or plant protective compounds.”

senses.label: biostimulant - the 1991 sense, Russo and Berlyn: “materials of little or no fertilizer value that accelerate plant growth” - defined by what it is worth as a fertiliser
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: the 1991 sense, Russo and Berlyn: “materials of little or no fertilizer value that accelerate plant growth” - defined by what it is worth as a fertiliser
senses.evidence: “Materials of little or no fertilizer value that accelerate plant growth, usually when used at low concentrations.”

senses.label: biostimulant - the 1992 sense, Schmidt: PLANT HORMONE-CONTAINING substances - which the 2017 definition explicitly rules out
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: the 1992 sense, Schmidt: PLANT HORMONE-CONTAINING substances - which the 2017 definition explicitly rules out
senses.evidence: “Plant hormone-containing substances that can stimulate growth when exogenously applied.”

senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: the 2001 sense, McCarty: a term the literature itself calls AMBIGUOUS, covering microbes, hormones, soil conditioners and microbe energy sources
senses.evidence: “An ambiguous term used to encompass non-nutritional growth-promoting substances such as microbes, plant growth hormones, soil conditioners and microbe energy sources.”

senses.label: biostimulant - the 2003 sense, Beard in Schmidt et al.: defined by a RESIDUAL - a response that cannot be attributed to traditional plant nutrients
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: the 2003 sense, Beard in Schmidt et al.: defined by a RESIDUAL - a response that cannot be attributed to traditional plant nutrients
senses.evidence: An organic material that, when applied in small quantities, enhances plant growth and development such that the response cannot be attributed to application of traditional plant nutrients.

senses.label: biostimulant - the 2001 sense quoted by Sharma: a PLANT-PROTECTION product working by stimulating defence or by competing with harmful organisms - a definition the others do not share at all
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: the 2001 sense quoted by Sharma: a PLANT-PROTECTION product working by stimulating defence or by competing with harmful organisms - a definition the others do not share at all
senses.evidence: “Products intended to protect plants against harmful organisms by stimulating defence mechanisms in the plant or by competing with harmful organisms for space and nutrients in the phyllosphere or rhizosphere.”

senses.label: mode of action - the SPECIFIC pathway, which the paper says is hard to establish for a biostimulant and should NOT be required for validation
senses.head: mode of action
senses.gloss: the SPECIFIC pathway, which the paper says is hard to establish for a biostimulant and should NOT be required for validation
senses.evidence: Given the difficulty in determining a “mode of action” for a biostimulant, and recognizing the need for the market in biostimulants to attain legitimacy, we suggest that the focus of biostimulant research and validation should be upon proof of efficacy and safety and the determination of a broad mechanism of action, without a requirement for the determination of a specific mode of action.

senses.label: mechanism of action - the BROAD account, which the paper says validation should require instead. TWO NEAR-SYNONYMS SEPARATED, WITH A REGULATORY CONSEQUENCE ATTACHED TO THE SPLIT
senses.head: mechanism of action
senses.gloss: the BROAD account, which the paper says validation should require instead. TWO NEAR-SYNONYMS SEPARATED, WITH A REGULATORY CONSEQUENCE ATTACHED TO THE SPLIT
senses.evidence: Given the difficulty in determining a “mode of action” for a biostimulant, and recognizing the need for the market in biostimulants to attain legitimacy, we suggest that the focus of biostimulant research and validation should be upon proof of efficacy and safety and the determination of a broad mechanism of action, without a requirement for the determination of a specific mode of action.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE NUTRITIONAL SENSE: it contributes to crop nutrition and healthy development by its mode of action
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE NUTRITIONAL SENSE: it contributes to crop nutrition and healthy development by its mode of action
senses.evidence: Natural or synthetic products of either mineral or organic composition that by their mode of action positively contribute to crop nutrition and the development of healthy plants.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE EXPLICITLY NON-NUTRITIONAL SENSE: the aim is NOT to supply nutrition but to stimulate metabolism
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE EXPLICITLY NON-NUTRITIONAL SENSE: the aim is NOT to supply nutrition but to stimulate metabolism
senses.evidence: Are organic products composed of peptides, amino acids, polysaccharides, peptides, humic acids, and/or phytohormones, etc. for immediate uptake and availability within the plant.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE HORMONE-EXCLUDING SENSE, where phytohormones are PROHIBITED by regulation
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE HORMONE-EXCLUDING SENSE, where phytohormones are PROHIBITED by regulation
senses.evidence: It must be remind that the biostimulant activity does not have to derive from the addition of phytohormones (Attached 6, codicil 4.1).

senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE HORMONE-DEPENDENT SENSE, where the important benefits are said to REST on influencing hormonal activity
senses.evidence: Many important benefits of biostimulants are based on their ability to influence hormonal activity.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE NEGATIVE/REGULATORY SENSE, defined by what it is not: neither a fertilizer nor a pesticide
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE NEGATIVE/REGULATORY SENSE, defined by what it is not: neither a fertilizer nor a pesticide
senses.evidence: Materials that are neither a fertilizer nor a pesticide, but when applied to a plant will enhance their health, growth, and protection.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE MICROORGANISM SENSE, where the biostimulant is a living organism rather than a substance
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE MICROORGANISM SENSE, where the biostimulant is a living organism rather than a substance
senses.evidence: Both biocontrol microorganisms (BCMs) and plant growth-promoting microorganisms (PGPMs) can be defined as “biostimulant microorganisms,” able to foster plant growth and defence against pathogens throughout the crop life cycle, from seed germination to plant maturity.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE STRESS-MITIGATION SENSE, acting through the plant's own innate defence responses
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE STRESS-MITIGATION SENSE, acting through the plant's own innate defence responses
senses.evidence: Single compounds or mixtures of compounds which mitigate the effects caused by abiotic stress agents, through the induction of innate plant defense responses.

senses.label: biostimulant - THE EFFICIENCY SENSE, defined by enhancing nutrient use efficiency alongside an existing fertilisation plan
senses.head: biostimulant
senses.gloss: THE EFFICIENCY SENSE, defined by enhancing nutrient use efficiency alongside an existing fertilisation plan
senses.evidence: Material that, when applied to a plant, seed, soil or growing media - in conjunction with established fertilization plans, enhances the plant’s nutrient use efficiency, or provides other direct or indirect benefits to plant development or stress response.

senses.label: `biostimulant` - DEFINED BY EXCLUSION FROM TWO LEGAL CATEGORIES: `biostimulants CANNOT BY DEFINITION BE PESTICIDES OR FERTILIZERS`, with seven citations behind the exclusion. The category's edges are drawn by its neighbours.
senses.head: `biostimulant`
senses.gloss: DEFINED BY EXCLUSION FROM TWO LEGAL CATEGORIES: `biostimulants CANNOT BY DEFINITION BE PESTICIDES OR FERTILIZERS`, with seven citations behind the exclusion. The category's edges are drawn by its neighbours.
senses.evidence: Likewise, biostimulants cannot by definition be pesticides or fertilizers (Russo and Berlyn, 1991; Karnok, 2000; Hamza and Suggars, 2001; Banks and Percival, 2012; Du Jardin, 2012; Torre et al., 2013, 2016)

senses.label: `biostimulant` - AND THE BOUNDARY WITH PGRs IS AN ATTRIBUTION RULE, NOT A COMPOSITION RULE: `biostimulants CAN CONTAIN traces of natural plant hormones, BUT THEIR BIOLOGICAL ACTION SHOULD NOT BE ASCRIBED TO THEM, OTHERWISE THEY SHOULD BE REGISTERED AS PLANT GROWTH REGULATORS.` The same bottle is one product or the other depending on what its effect is credited to.
senses.head: `biostimulant`
senses.gloss: AND THE BOUNDARY WITH PGRs IS AN ATTRIBUTION RULE, NOT A COMPOSITION RULE: `biostimulants CAN CONTAIN traces of natural plant hormones, BUT THEIR BIOLOGICAL ACTION SHOULD NOT BE ASCRIBED TO THEM, OTHERWISE THEY SHOULD BE REGISTERED AS PLANT GROWTH REGULATORS.` The same bottle is one product or the other depending on what its effect is credited to.
senses.evidence: “From a legal point of view, biostimulants can contain traces of natural plant hormones, but their biological action should not be ascribed to them, otherwise they should be registered as plant growth regulators” (Bulgari et al., 2015)

senses.label: barriers - IN THIS STUDY A PARTICIPANT-REPORTED CATEGORY, not a measured obstacle: what people said stopped them, grouped by thematic analysis - lack of instruction, lack of confidence, health, cost
senses.head: barriers
senses.gloss: IN THIS STUDY A PARTICIPANT-REPORTED CATEGORY, not a measured obstacle: what people said stopped them, grouped by thematic analysis - lack of instruction, lack of confidence, health, cost
senses.evidence: The themes that emerged were related to barriers (i.e., lack of instructions and guidance, lack of knowledge and confidence, health-related barriers, cost); disadvantages and concerns (i.e., too much and too complex technology, feelings of inadequacy, and comparison with younger generations, lack of social interaction and communication, negative features of tablets); advantages (i.e., positive features of tablets, accessing information, willingness to adopt technology); and skepticism about using tablets and technology in general.

senses.label: cost - A BARRIER ONLY FOR THE EXPERIENCED. The paper notices that only participants with prior computer experience raised it, and offers the reading that inexperience means not knowing what the devices cost
senses.head: cost
senses.gloss: A BARRIER ONLY FOR THE EXPERIENCED. The paper notices that only participants with prior computer experience raised it, and offers the reading that inexperience means not knowing what the devices cost
senses.evidence: Interestingly, only participants with previous computer experience brought up the latter in our study. It is possible that cost is not one of the main barriers to using technology for people with less experience; their lack of exposure to technology in general may mean they are less aware of the costs of such devices, or simply that other concerns take priority.

senses.gloss: a life-management theory built from selection, optimization, and compensation
senses.evidence: Selection Optimization Compensation (SOC) Theory which postulates that there are three fundamental life management processes: selection (goals), optimization (goal-related means to achieve desired goals) and compensation (reaction to loss in goal-related means to maintain success or desired goals)

senses.head: compensation

senses.head: Adult Learning Theory
senses.gloss: the account in which adults participate in planning/evaluating instruction and experience grounds learning
senses.evidence: our results are consistent with the Adult Learning Theory (Knowles, 1984 ). One of the principles of this theory is that adults need to be involved in the planning and evaluation of their instruction. Our participants expressed frustration when they requested assistance and other people completed the job for them rather than providing guidance. This is relevant to another principle of the Adult Learning Theory in which experience provides the basis for the learning activities
