senses.evidence: Thabane et al also considered the relationship between pilot and feasibility, suggesting that feasibility should be the main emphasis of a pilot study and that ‘a pilot study is synonymous with a feasibility study intended to guide the planning of a large scale investigation’.

senses.label: `pilot study` / `feasibility study` - SYNONYMOUS TO ONE BODY AND MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE TO ANOTHER, AT THE SAME TIME. Thabane (2010): `a pilot study is SYNONYMOUS WITH a feasibility study`. NIHR, `at about the same time`: definitions `THAT ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE`, with feasibility earlier in the process and a pilot `a version of the main study that is RUN IN MINIATURE`. The same two terms, the same years, opposite relations.
senses.head: `pilot study` / `feasibility study`
senses.gloss: SYNONYMOUS TO ONE BODY AND MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE TO ANOTHER, AT THE SAME TIME. Thabane (2010): `a pilot study is SYNONYMOUS WITH a feasibility study`. NIHR, `at about the same time`: definitions `THAT ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE`, with feasibility earlier in the process and a pilot `a version of the main study that is RUN IN MINIATURE`. The same two terms, the same years, opposite relations.
senses.evidence: However, at about the same time, the UK National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) developed definitions of pilot and feasibility studies that are mutually exclusive, suggesting that feasibility studies occurred slightly earlier in the research process and that pilot studies are ‘a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’

senses.label: `pilot` (the label, as authors use it) - reached for when a study `DOES NOT HAVE THE POWER to test clinically meaningful hypotheses`, in the hope that reviewers `WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL`
senses.head: `pilot` (the label, as authors use it)
senses.gloss: reached for when a study `DOES NOT HAVE THE POWER to test clinically meaningful hypotheses`, in the hope that reviewers `WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL`
senses.evidence: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

senses.label: `pilot study` (NETSCC, recommended here) - `A VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY THAT IS RUN IN MINIATURE to test whether the components of the main study can all work together`; internal if its data join the final analysis, external if set aside
senses.head: `pilot study` (NETSCC, recommended here)
senses.gloss: `A VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY THAT IS RUN IN MINIATURE to test whether the components of the main study can all work together`; internal if its data join the final analysis, external if set aside
senses.evidence: A Pilot Study is a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together. It is focused on the processes of the main study, for example to ensure recruitment, randomisation, treatment, and follow-up assessments all run smoothly. It will therefore resemble the main study in many respects. In some cases this will be the first phase of the substantive study and data from the pilot phase may contribute to the final analysis; this can be referred to as an internal pilot. Alternatively at the end of the pilot study the data may be analysed and set aside, a so-called external pilot.

senses.label: `feasibility study` (NETSCC) - research done before a main study to estimate design parameters, which `CRUCIALLY ... DO NOT EVALUATE THE OUTCOME OF INTEREST`
senses.head: `feasibility study` (NETSCC)
senses.gloss: research done before a main study to estimate design parameters, which `CRUCIALLY ... DO NOT EVALUATE THE OUTCOME OF INTEREST`
senses.evidence: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

senses.label: `pilot work` / `pilot study` / `pilot trial` (Arnold et al) - a three-way split: any background research, a study with hypotheses and methodology, and a stand-alone pilot study with randomisation
senses.head: `pilot work` / `pilot study` / `pilot trial` (Arnold et al)
senses.gloss: a three-way split: any background research, a study with hypotheses and methodology, and a stand-alone pilot study with randomisation
senses.evidence: They made useful distinctions between: pilot work which is any background research to inform a future study, a pilot study which has specific hypotheses, objectives and methodology and a pilot trial which is a stand-alone pilot study and includes a randomization procedure. They excluded feasibility studies from their consideration.

senses.label: `core microbiome` (this paper) - THE 1660 UNIQUE SEQUENCES PRESENT IN ALL THREE SAMPLED INDIVIDUALS, contributing 66% of reads; an intersection, so its size is a function of how many people were sequenced
senses.head: `core microbiome` (this paper)
senses.gloss: THE 1660 UNIQUE SEQUENCES PRESENT IN ALL THREE SAMPLED INDIVIDUALS, contributing 66% of reads; an intersection, so its size is a function of how many people were sequenced
senses.evidence: There was a large overlap in the higher taxa, "species-level" phylotypes and unique sequences among the three microbiomes: 84% of the higher taxa, 75% of the OTUs and 65% of the unique sequences were present in at least two of the three microbiomes. The three individuals shared 1660 of 6315 unique sequences. These 1660 sequences (the "core microbiome") contributed 66% of the reads. The overlapping OTUs contributed to 94% of the reads, while nearly all reads (99.8%) belonged to the shared higher taxa.

senses.label: `species-level phylotype` - `OTUs CLUSTERING SEQUENCES AT A 3% GENETIC DIFFERENCE` in the V5-V6 region only, a convention the authors adopt for comparability while saying it `MAY NOT CORRELATE EXACTLY` with 3% over the whole gene
senses.head: `species-level phylotype`
senses.gloss: `OTUs CLUSTERING SEQUENCES AT A 3% GENETIC DIFFERENCE` in the V5-V6 region only, a convention the authors adopt for comparability while saying it `MAY NOT CORRELATE EXACTLY` with 3% over the whole gene
senses.evidence: Phylotypes were defined as OTUs clustering sequences at a 3% genetic difference. The highest taxon (in most cases, genus)

senses.label: `healthy` (as operationalised here) - no pockets deeper than 3 mm and bleeding at no more than 10% of gingival sites, against a literature convention of `LESS THAN 20-25%`
senses.head: `healthy` (as operationalised here)
senses.gloss: no pockets deeper than 3 mm and bleeding at no more than 10% of gingival sites, against a literature convention of `LESS THAN 20-25%`
senses.evidence: The periodontal health was defined as no periodontal pockets deeper than 3 mm and no bleeding on probing at more than 10% of gingival sites. The sites that were sampled did not show any bleeding. In selecting healthy volunteers for experimental gingivitis studies, gingiva is considered healthy if bleeding on marginal probing is present at less than 20-25% of gingival sites [ 24 , 25 ].

senses.label: `transients` - the low-abundance taxa (5-49 reads) the paper judges `NOT A PART OF THE COMMENSAL ORAL FLORA`; a residue of the abundance filter, given a name
senses.head: `transients`
senses.gloss: the low-abundance taxa (5-49 reads) the paper judges `NOT A PART OF THE COMMENSAL ORAL FLORA`; a residue of the abundance filter, given a name
senses.evidence: However, these taxa were found at a very low abundance (5-49 reads) and most likely were not a part of the commensal oral flora, and should be regarded as "transients".

senses.label: `health literacy` (this paper's synthesis) - `people's KNOWLEDGE, MOTIVATION AND COMPETENCES TO ACCESS, UNDERSTAND, APPRAISE, AND APPLY HEALTH INFORMATION` in healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion, across the life course
senses.head: `health literacy` (this paper's synthesis)
senses.gloss: `people's KNOWLEDGE, MOTIVATION AND COMPETENCES TO ACCESS, UNDERSTAND, APPRAISE, AND APPLY HEALTH INFORMATION` in healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion, across the life course
senses.evidence: Health literacy is linked to literacy and entails people's knowledge, motivation and competences to access, understand, appraise, and apply health information in order to make judgments and take decisions in everyday life concerning healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion to maintain or improve quality of life during the life course . This definition encompasses the public health perspective and can easily be specified to accommodate an individual approach by substituting the three domains of health "healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion" with "being ill, being at risk and staying healthy".

senses.label: `medical` / `patient` / `clinical health literacy` - three names for the individual cognitive-skills tradition, framed by Nutbeam as a `CLINICAL RISK` approach
senses.head: `medical` / `patient` / `clinical health literacy`
senses.gloss: three names for the individual cognitive-skills tradition, framed by Nutbeam as a `CLINICAL RISK` approach
senses.evidence: One perspective is that they refer to a series of individual cognitive skills and abilities applied in a medical context; the other perspective sees a broader range of competencies applied in the social realm. The first is referred to as "medical health literacy" [ 5 ], "patient health literacy" [ 14 ], or "clinical health literacy" [ 63 ]; the second as "public health literacy" [ 35 ]. Nutbeam [ 52 ] refers to the opposing medical and public health views on health literacy as respectively a "clinical risk", and a "personal asset" approach, and points out that they are rooted in the different traditions of clinical care, and adult learning and health promotion, respectively. As both perspectives are important and useful to enable a better understanding of health communication processes in clinical and community settings, any definition of health literacy needs to integrate both views.

senses.label: `public health literacy` - the population tradition, framed as a `PERSONAL ASSET` approach and rooted in adult learning and health promotion rather than clinical care
senses.head: `public health literacy`
senses.gloss: the population tradition, framed as a `PERSONAL ASSET` approach and rooted in adult learning and health promotion rather than clinical care
senses.evidence: One perspective is that they refer to a series of individual cognitive skills and abilities applied in a medical context; the other perspective sees a broader range of competencies applied in the social realm. The first is referred to as "medical health literacy" [ 5 ], "patient health literacy" [ 14 ], or "clinical health literacy" [ 63 ]; the second as "public health literacy" [ 35 ]. Nutbeam [ 52 ] refers to the opposing medical and public health views on health literacy as respectively a "clinical risk", and a "personal asset" approach, and points out that they are rooted in the different traditions of clinical care, and adult learning and health promotion, respectively. As both perspectives are important and useful to enable a better understanding of health communication processes in clinical and community settings, any definition of health literacy needs to integrate both views.

senses.label: `literacy` (the head noun) - `FAMILIAR WITH LITERATURE` or `WELL EDUCATED, LEARNED` for most of its history, and only in the late nineteenth century `THE ABILITIES TO READ AND WRITE TEXT`
senses.head: `literacy` (the head noun)
senses.gloss: `FAMILIAR WITH LITERATURE` or `WELL EDUCATED, LEARNED` for most of its history, and only in the late nineteenth century `THE ABILITIES TO READ AND WRITE TEXT`
senses.evidence: It is important to distinguish health literacy from literacy in general. According to the United Nation Education, Science and Culture Organization (UNESCO) during its history in English, the word 'literate' mostly meant to be 'familiar with literature' or in general terms 'well educated, learned'. While maintaining its broader meaning of being knowledgeable or educated in a particular area, during the late nineteenth century it has also come to refer to the abilities to read and write text.

senses.label: `health literacy` - DECLARED TO HAVE NO AGREED DEFINITION, AND THE CONSEQUENCE NAMED: `there is NO CONSENSUS ABOUT THE DEFINITION of health literacy or about its conceptual dimensions, WHICH LIMITS THE POSSIBILITIES FOR MEASUREMENT AND COMPARISON.` The absence is not reported as untidiness - it is reported as the thing preventing the field from measuring anything.
senses.head: `health literacy`
senses.gloss: DECLARED TO HAVE NO AGREED DEFINITION, AND THE CONSEQUENCE NAMED: `there is NO CONSENSUS ABOUT THE DEFINITION of health literacy or about its conceptual dimensions, WHICH LIMITS THE POSSIBILITIES FOR MEASUREMENT AND COMPARISON.` The absence is not reported as untidiness - it is reported as the thing preventing the field from measuring anything.
senses.evidence: Although its importance is increasingly recognised, there is no consensus about the definition of health literacy or about its conceptual dimensions, which limits the possibilities for measurement and comparison

senses.label: `taxonomy` - a hierarchical scheme limited to one domain and ONE relationship type, as this paper uses it against `ontology`
senses.head: `taxonomy`
senses.gloss: a hierarchical scheme limited to one domain and ONE relationship type, as this paper uses it against `ontology`
senses.evidence: Taxonomies are simplistic schemes that help in the hierarchical classification of concepts or objects [ 1 ]. They are usually limited to a specific domain and to a single relationship type connecting one node to another. Ontologies share the hierarchical structure of taxonomies. In contrast to taxonomies, however, they often have multiple relationship types and are really designed to provide a formal naming of the types, properties and interrelationships of entities or concepts in a specific discipline, domain or field of study [ 2 , 3 ].

senses.label: `synonym` - in ChemOnt a scoped relation, not an equality: exact, narrow, broad, or related when none of the three fits
senses.head: `synonym`
senses.gloss: in ChemOnt a scoped relation, not an equality: exact, narrow, broad, or related when none of the three fits
senses.evidence: For any ChemOnt term, a synonym can have the identical meaning (exact scope), a more specific meaning (narrow scope), or a less specific meaning (broad scope). In some cases, the synonym can have slightly different meaning, so that it cannot be assigned any of the three aforementioned scope categories. In this case, it is simply called a related synonym.

senses.label: `Direct Parent` - the single most descriptive category; `most descriptive` is explicitly acknowledged to vary by user and context
senses.head: `Direct Parent`
senses.gloss: the single most descriptive category; `most descriptive` is explicitly acknowledged to vary by user and context
senses.evidence: However, the notion of what is most descriptive can vary from one user to another, and from one context to another. For example, a cyclic depsipeptide could be also be classified as a lactam. Because of this ambiguity, ClassyFire also displays a list of Alternative Parents (Fig. 7 ) providing a more detailed description of the chemical.

senses.label: `organic` - in ChemOnt, containing one or more carbon atoms, with a short enumerated exception list rather than a principle
senses.head: `organic`
senses.gloss: in ChemOnt, containing one or more carbon atoms, with a short enumerated exception list rather than a principle
senses.evidence: The top level (Kingdom) partitions chemicals into two disjoint categories: organic compounds versus inorganic compounds. Organic compounds are defined as chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms. Inorganic compounds are defined as compounds that are not organic, with the exception of a small number of “special” compounds, including, cyanide/isocyanide and their respective non-hydrocarbyl derivatives, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbon sulfide, and carbon disulfide.

senses.label: `misclassification` - contested in this paper: an assignment the expert panel rejects may still be correct under the criterion the classifier declares
senses.head: `misclassification`
senses.gloss: contested in this paper: an assignment the expert panel rejects may still be correct under the criterion the classifier declares
senses.evidence: Based on its structure, one could argue that bixin dimethyl ester should be classified as a diterpene; but based on its biology, it should be classified as a tetraterpene derivative or as an apo-carotenoid diterpenoid (CHEBI:53186). Given that ClassyFire is designed to classify compounds on a structural basis rather than a biological or biosynthetic basis, this kind of “misclassification” is completely understandable and is arguably not a misclassification.

senses.label: `validly published` - the ICNP status a name either has or has not; names without it `HAVE NO CLAIM TO RECOGNITION UNDER THIS CODE`, and the status can be granted late or withdrawn on review
senses.head: `validly published`
senses.gloss: the ICNP status a name either has or has not; names without it `HAVE NO CLAIM TO RECOGNITION UNDER THIS CODE`, and the status can be granted late or withdrawn on review
senses.evidence: Classification in turn needs an internationally accepted system of nomenclature to unambiguously assign names to taxa ( 3 ). The cornerstone of the ICNP is the status of taxon names as being validly published; other names have no claim to recognition under this code

senses.label: `effective publication` - the weaker condition that gets a name INTO the register without standing; it is `THE INCLUSION CRITERION` for LPSN, not for the code
senses.head: `effective publication`
senses.gloss: the weaker condition that gets a name INTO the register without standing; it is `THE INCLUSION CRITERION` for LPSN, not for the code
senses.evidence: To improve the coverage, a web form for submission was added to LPSN that allows for anonymous suggestions of taxon names. Synonymy relationships between taxon names and assignments of child taxa to parent taxa (i.e, genera to families, families to orders etc.) can also be suggested. The inclusion criterion is the presence of an effective publication as defined by the ICNP ( 3 ).

senses.label: `nomenclatural type` - `THE ENTITY WITH WHICH A TAXON NAME IS PERMANENTLY ASSOCIATED`; for prokaryotes a living type STRAIN, and an attempt to admit a genome sequence instead was rejected
senses.head: `nomenclatural type`
senses.gloss: `THE ENTITY WITH WHICH A TAXON NAME IS PERMANENTLY ASSOCIATED`; for prokaryotes a living type STRAIN, and an attempt to admit a genome sequence instead was rejected
senses.evidence: The nomenclatural type is the entity with which a taxon name is permanently associated ( 3 ). In the cases of prokaryotic species and subspecies, the nomenclatural type is the type strain. Cultures of type strains thus firmly connect taxon names and genome sequences. Quality-checked ( 17 ) genome and proteome sequences of verified type strains are the starting point of TYGS analyses.

senses.label: `correct name` - LPSN's current judgement, published alongside `THE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH A NAME WOULD BE REGARDED AS THE CORRECT NAME IF IT IS NOT CURRENTLY SO REGARDED`
senses.head: `correct name`
senses.gloss: LPSN's current judgement, published alongside `THE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH A NAME WOULD BE REGARDED AS THE CORRECT NAME IF IT IS NOT CURRENTLY SO REGARDED`
senses.evidence: Comments on taxonomic terminology were added to LPSN for single taxon names where appropriate, as well as comments about the conditions under which a name would be regarded as the correct name if it is not currently so regarded by LPSN. The latter change is supposed to improve the understanding of the difference between nomenclature and classification, which may puzzle many microbiologists ( 35 ).

senses.label: `operational taxonomic unit` - a cluster of reads below a fixed dissimilarity threshold, most commonly 3%; the customary unit of marker-gene analysis
senses.head: `operational taxonomic unit`
senses.gloss: a cluster of reads below a fixed dissimilarity threshold, most commonly 3%; the customary unit of marker-gene analysis
senses.evidence: The analysis of marker-gene data customarily begins with the construction of molecular operational taxonomic units (OTUs): clusters of reads that differ by less than a fixed sequence dissimilarity threshold, most commonly 3% ( Westcott and Schloss, 2015 ; Kopylova et al. , 2016 ).

senses.label: `de novo OTU` - a cluster emergent from one data set, whose boundaries and membership depend on that data set and are undefined outside it
senses.head: `de novo OTU`
senses.gloss: a cluster emergent from one data set, whose boundaries and membership depend on that data set and are undefined outside it
senses.evidence: Many methods for constructing these clusters have been developed, but in all cases de novo OTUs are emergent features of a data set, with boundaries and membership that depend on the data set in which they are defined.

senses.label: `closed-reference OTU` - a property of a reference database: each reference sequence defines and labels one
senses.head: `closed-reference OTU`
senses.gloss: a property of a reference database: each reference sequence defines and labels one
senses.evidence: Closed-reference OTUs are properties of a reference database; each reference sequence in the database defines and labels an associated closed-reference OTU.

senses.label: `consistent labeling` - the property that assignments made independently in different data sets can be validly compared
senses.head: `consistent labeling`
senses.gloss: the property that assignments made independently in different data sets can be validly compared
senses.evidence: If the same reference database is used, closed-reference OTU assignments from independently processed data sets can be validly compared, a property we refer to as consistent labeling.

senses.label: `amplicon sequence variant` - a biological sequence inferred prior to amplification and sequencing error, distinguished to a single nucleotide
senses.head: `amplicon sequence variant`
senses.gloss: a biological sequence inferred prior to amplification and sequencing error, distinguished to a single nucleotide
senses.evidence: ASV methods infer the biological sequences in the sample prior to the introduction of amplification and sequencing errors, and distinguish sequence variants differing by as little as one nucleotide.

senses.label: `attack` (relapse, exacerbation) - `patient-reported symptoms or objectively observed signs typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, current or historical, WITH DURATION OF AT LEAST 24 HOURS, IN THE ABSENCE OF FEVER OR INFECTION`
senses.head: `attack` (relapse, exacerbation)
senses.gloss: `patient-reported symptoms or objectively observed signs typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, current or historical, WITH DURATION OF AT LEAST 24 HOURS, IN THE ABSENCE OF FEVER OR INFECTION`
senses.evidence: The Panel considered again what constitutes an attack (relapse, exacerbation) and defined this as patient-reported symptoms or objectively observed signs typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, current or historical, with duration of at least 24 hours, in the absence of fever or infection. Although a new attack should be documented by contemporaneous neurological examination, in the appropriate context, some historical events with symptoms and evolution characteristic for MS, but for which no objective neurological findings are documented, can provide reasonable evidence of a prior demyelinating event. Reports of paroxysmal symptoms (historical or current) should, however, consist of multiple episodes occurring over not less than 24 hours.

senses.label: `dissemination in time` (2010 sense) - satisfied EITHER by a new lesion on a later scan OR by enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexisting on ONE baseline scan; the 2005 sense required a reference scan at least 30 days after onset
senses.head: `dissemination in time` (2010 sense)
senses.gloss: satisfied EITHER by a new lesion on a later scan OR by enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexisting on ONE baseline scan; the 2005 sense required a reference scan at least 30 days after onset
senses.evidence: The 2005 revision of the McDonald Criteria simplified the MRI evidence required for DIT, basing it on the appearance of a new T2 lesion on a scan compared to a reference or baseline scan performed at least 30 days after the onset of the initial clinical event. In clinical practice, however, there is reason not to postpone a first MRI until after 30 days of clinical onset, which would result in an extra MRI scan to confirm a diagnosis. Abandoning the requirement for an extra reference MRI after 30 days does not compromise specificity, 28 and therefore the Panel, in its current revision of the McDonald Criteria, allows a new T2 lesion to establish DIT irrespective of the timing of the baseline MRI.

senses.label: `opticospinal MS` - a regionally used term that `APPEARS TO BE AN ADMIXTURE OF CONVENTIONAL MS AND NMO` rather than a class of its own
senses.head: `opticospinal MS`
senses.gloss: a regionally used term that `APPEARS TO BE AN ADMIXTURE OF CONVENTIONAL MS AND NMO` rather than a class of its own
senses.evidence: Although the McDonald Criteria are widely used in these parts of the world, there is some uncertainty, especially in Asia, about whether MS and NMO are distinct and if so, how they should be distinguished. As currently applied, the term opticospinal MS appears to be an admixture of conventional MS and NMO.

senses.label: `radiologically isolated syndrome` - MS-appearing lesions found incidentally, for which `A FIRM DIAGNOSIS OF MS BASED ON INCIDENTAL FINDINGS ON MRI ALONE ... IS PROBLEMATIC`; the imaging is present and the diagnosis is withheld
senses.head: `radiologically isolated syndrome`
senses.gloss: MS-appearing lesions found incidentally, for which `A FIRM DIAGNOSIS OF MS BASED ON INCIDENTAL FINDINGS ON MRI ALONE ... IS PROBLEMATIC`; the imaging is present and the diagnosis is withheld
senses.evidence: Many individuals with high lesion loads may have had a protracted subclinical disease course prior to their first clinical event. As a consequence, occasional individuals investigated by MRI for indications unrelated to MS have incidental findings of brain lesions with appearance and topography consistent with MS. Detection of this presymptomatic phase, or radiologically isolated syndrome, is increasingly common. Some of these individuals followed clinically and by serial imaging will develop DIT by MRI, and some have clinical disease-defining events after several years. 86 – 89 However, in the absence of supportive research findings, the Panel concluded that a firm diagnosis of MS based on incidental findings on MRI alone, even with additional supportive findings on evoked potentials or typical CSF findings in the absence of MS-relevant clinical symptoms, is problematic. A future definite diagnosis of MS, however, cannot be excluded and may be likely, depending on the evolution of neurologic symptoms and signs.

senses.label: `yearning` (Criterion B, the one mandatory symptom) - `craving, pining, or longing for the deceased; PHYSICAL OR EMOTIONAL SUFFERING AS A RESULT OF THE DESIRED, BUT UNFULFILLED, REUNION with the deceased`, experienced `daily or to a disabling degree`
senses.head: `yearning` (Criterion B, the one mandatory symptom)
senses.gloss: `craving, pining, or longing for the deceased; PHYSICAL OR EMOTIONAL SUFFERING AS A RESULT OF THE DESIRED, BUT UNFULFILLED, REUNION with the deceased`, experienced `daily or to a disabling degree`
senses.evidence: B. Separation distress : The bereaved person experiences yearning (e.g., craving, pining, or longing for the deceased; physical or emotional suffering as a result of the desired, but unfulfilled, reunion with the deceased) daily or to a disabling degree.

senses.label: `caseness` - not a clinical fact but a constructed standard: a dichotomised item-response-model score on the 12 surviving symptoms, cut at the point of `greatest agreement (kappa = 0.68)` with rater judgement
senses.head: `caseness`
senses.gloss: not a clinical fact but a constructed standard: a dichotomised item-response-model score on the 12 surviving symptoms, cut at the point of `greatest agreement (kappa = 0.68)` with rater judgement
senses.evidence: As illustrated in Figure 3 , PGD “cases” determined by a minimum-threshold “cutoff” PG attribute score of approximately 1.0 had the greatest agreement (κ = 0.68) with cases determined by the rater assessments. An IRM PG attribute score above this minimum-threshold cutoff value became our criterion standard for PGD caseness.

senses.label: `present` (of a symptom) - `rated 4 or 5` on a five-point severity scale; `1, 2, or 3` is absent. The whole apparatus above this line runs on binary items
senses.head: `present` (of a symptom)
senses.gloss: `rated 4 or 5` on a five-point severity scale; `1, 2, or 3` is absent. The whole apparatus above this line runs on binary items
senses.evidence: Based on prior work [23] , [59] , a symptom was considered present if rated 4 or 5, and absent if rated 1, 2, or 3, on its five-point scale.

senses.label: `acute` / `delayed` / `persistent` - PGD subtypes defined purely by WHEN the symptom criteria are met (0-6 mo, 6-12 mo, or both), with no reference to severity or content
senses.head: `acute` / `delayed` / `persistent`
senses.gloss: PGD subtypes defined purely by WHEN the symptom criteria are met (0-6 mo, 6-12 mo, or both), with no reference to severity or content
senses.evidence: Three subtypes of PGD were defined in terms of patterns of meeting diagnostic criteria for PGD at 0–6 and 6–12 mo post-loss: acute = meeting the symptom criteria for PGD at 0–6 mo, but not at 6–12 mo, post-loss; delayed = meeting the symptom criteria for PGD at 6–12 mo, but not at 0–6 mo, post-loss; and persistent = meeting the symptom criteria for PGD both at 0–6 and at 6–12 mo post-loss.

senses.label: `V` code (DSM-IV) and `Z` code (ICD-10) - the two manuals' categories for something that may occasion clinical attention WITHOUT BEING A DISORDER; where bereavement sits in both at the time of writing
senses.head: `V` code (DSM-IV) and `Z` code (ICD-10)
senses.gloss: the two manuals' categories for something that may occasion clinical attention WITHOUT BEING A DISORDER; where bereavement sits in both at the time of writing
senses.evidence: In the DSM-IV , bereavement is classified as a “V” code; that is, an “other condition that may be a focus of clinical attention” [12] . Similarly, in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision ( ICD-10 ) [13] , bereavement is classified as a “Z” code, which refers to “occasions when circumstances other than a disease or injury result in an encounter or are recorded by providers as problems or factors that influence care” [14] .

senses.label: `proven` IFD - histology, culture or a sterile-site specimen. `Can apply to ANY patient, regardless of whether the patient is immunocompromised` - the only one of the three categories that is not restricted by host
senses.head: `proven` IFD
senses.gloss: histology, culture or a sterile-site specimen. `Can apply to ANY patient, regardless of whether the patient is immunocompromised` - the only one of the three categories that is not restricted by host
senses.evidence: The category of proven IFD can apply to any patient, regardless of whether the patient is immunocompromised. The probable and possible categories are proposed for immunocompromised patients only, except for endemic mycoses.

senses.label: `probable` IFD - a host factor AND a clinical feature AND mycological evidence, `proposed for immunocompromised patients only, except for endemic mycoses`. **Expanded in this revision without changing the word**
senses.head: `probable` IFD
senses.gloss: a host factor AND a clinical feature AND mycological evidence, `proposed for immunocompromised patients only, except for endemic mycoses`. **Expanded in this revision without changing the word**
senses.evidence: There is no change in the classifications of “proven,” “probable,” and “possible” IFD, although the definition of “probable” has been expanded and the scope of the category “possible” has been diminished.

senses.label: `possible` IFD - a host factor and a clinical feature with the mycology missing. The category that `attracted controversy` where the other two did not - **defined by an absent measurement**
senses.head: `possible` IFD
senses.gloss: a host factor and a clinical feature with the mycology missing. The category that `attracted controversy` where the other two did not - **defined by an absent measurement**
senses.evidence: While definitions of proven and probable disease have been shown to be reliable in research and attracted little controversy among the group, this cannot be said of the possible IFD category. There is much confusion about the difference between a host factor and a risk factor. As before, a host factor has been defined as a characteristic of individuals clearly predisposed to, and not simply at risk of, an IFD [ 1 ]. For example, while impaired gut wall integrity through surgery or illness may increase the risk of candidiasis, it was not considered specific enough to warrant inclusion as a host factor.

senses.label: `host factor` - `a characteristic of individuals CLEARLY PREDISPOSED TO, AND NOT SIMPLY AT RISK OF, an IFD`. Impaired gut wall integrity raises the risk of candidiasis and is refused as a host factor for not being specific enough
senses.head: `host factor`
senses.gloss: `a characteristic of individuals CLEARLY PREDISPOSED TO, AND NOT SIMPLY AT RISK OF, an IFD`. Impaired gut wall integrity raises the risk of candidiasis and is refused as a host factor for not being specific enough
senses.evidence: While definitions of proven and probable disease have been shown to be reliable in research and attracted little controversy among the group, this cannot be said of the possible IFD category. There is much confusion about the difference between a host factor and a risk factor. As before, a host factor has been defined as a characteristic of individuals clearly predisposed to, and not simply at risk of, an IFD [ 1 ]. For example, while impaired gut wall integrity through surgery or illness may increase the risk of candidiasis, it was not considered specific enough to warrant inclusion as a host factor.

senses.label: `exposure` (endemic mycoses) - `a history of residence in an endemic area, NO MATTER HOW REMOTE, travel to an endemic area, or contact with fomites such as soil or vegetation`. A criterion with no time limit at all
senses.head: `exposure` (endemic mycoses)
senses.gloss: `a history of residence in an endemic area, NO MATTER HOW REMOTE, travel to an endemic area, or contact with fomites such as soil or vegetation`. A criterion with no time limit at all
senses.evidence: Exposure to 1 of these fungi is defined as a history of residence in an endemic area, no matter how remote, travel to an endemic area, or contact with fomites such as soil or vegetation that is derived from an endemic area.

senses.label: `implementation fidelity` - `the degree to which . . . programs are implemented . . . as intended by the program developers`, quoted with two elisions; `SOMETIMES ALSO TERMED `INTEGRITY``
senses.head: `implementation fidelity`
senses.gloss: `the degree to which . . . programs are implemented . . . as intended by the program developers`, quoted with two elisions; `SOMETIMES ALSO TERMED `INTEGRITY``
senses.evidence: Implementation fidelity is "the degree to which . . . programs are implemented . . . as intended by the program developers" [ 1 ]. This idea is sometimes also termed "integrity" [ 1 , 2 ].

senses.label: `adherence` - in this framework, NOT one element among five but the measurement of fidelity itself, with content, frequency, duration and coverage as its subcategories
senses.head: `adherence`
senses.gloss: in this framework, NOT one element among five but the measurement of fidelity itself, with content, frequency, duration and coverage as its subcategories
senses.evidence: The measurement of implementation fidelity is the measurement of adherence, i.e ., how far those responsible for delivering an intervention actually adhere to the intervention as it is outlined by its designers. Adherence includes the subcategories of content, frequency, duration and coverage ( i.e ., dose). The degree to which the intended content or frequency of an intervention is implemented is the degree of implementation fidelity achieved for that intervention. The level achieved may be influenced or affected, ( i.e ., moderated) by certain other variables: intervention complexity, facilitation strategies, quality of delivery, and participant responsiveness.

senses.label: `programme differentiation` - retired from the concept: it `ACTUALLY MEASURES SOMETHING DISTINCT FROM FIDELITY` and is renamed `identification of an intervention's essential components`
senses.head: `programme differentiation`
senses.gloss: retired from the concept: it `ACTUALLY MEASURES SOMETHING DISTINCT FROM FIDELITY` and is renamed `identification of an intervention's essential components`
senses.evidence: Despite being viewed as an element of implementation fidelity by the literature, programme differentiation actually measures something distinct from fidelity. It is concerned with determining those elements that are essential for its success. This exercise is an important part of any evaluation of new interventions. It enables discovery of those elements that make a difference to outcomes and whether some elements are redundant. Such so-called "essential" elements may be discovered either by canvassing the designers of the intervention or, preferably, by "component analysis", assessing the effect of the intervention on outcomes and determining which components have the most impact [ 17 ]. This element would therefore be more usefully described as the "Identification of an intervention's essential components".

senses.label: `content` (of an intervention) - its `ACTIVE INGREDIENTS`: `the drug, treatment, skills, or knowledge that the intervention seeks to deliver to its recipients`
senses.head: `content` (of an intervention)
senses.gloss: its `ACTIVE INGREDIENTS`: `the drug, treatment, skills, or knowledge that the intervention seeks to deliver to its recipients`
senses.evidence: The content of the intervention may be seen as its 'active ingredients'; the drug, treatment, skills, or knowledge that the intervention seeks to deliver to its recipients.

senses.label: `thinness` - the named defect of primary studies that report no fidelity data, which stops a review from telling heterogeneity from noise
senses.head: `thinness`
senses.gloss: the named defect of primary studies that report no fidelity data, which stops a review from telling heterogeneity from noise
senses.evidence: Similar issues affect secondary research: the common lack of data on implementation fidelity provided by primary research studies, known as "thinness", prevents those working on systematic reviews and meta-analyses from gauging possible heterogeneity between studies, with the result that data may be pooled or aggregated inappropriately [ 13 , 14 ]. Consequently, the internal validity of a review may be adversely affected, and, thus, the credibility and utility of that research may be thrown into question.

senses.label: `Type III error` - concluding that a programme failed when what failed was its implementation
senses.head: `Type III error`
senses.gloss: concluding that a programme failed when what failed was its implementation
senses.evidence: It is only by making an appropriate evaluation of the fidelity with which an intervention has been implemented that a viable assessment can be made of its contribution to outcomes, i.e ., its effect on performance. Unless such an evaluation is made, it cannot be determined whether a lack of impact is due to poor implementation or inadequacies inherent in the programme itself, a so-called Type III error [ 11 ]; this is also addressed by the thesis of comprehensiveness [ 12 ].

senses.label: `species` (GTDB sense) - a cluster around a single representative genome, entered by ANI and alignment fraction to that representative; NOT a claim about a discontinuity in nature
senses.head: `species` (GTDB sense)
senses.gloss: a cluster around a single representative genome, entered by ANI and alignment fraction to that representative; NOT a claim about a discontinuity in nature
senses.evidence: Each GTDB species cluster is defined by a single representative genome and species assignments are established by considering the ANI and AF (alignment fraction) of genomes to these representatives as previously described ( 5 ).

senses.label: `rank normalized` - higher ranks set by relative evolutionary divergence so that a genus in one phylum is comparable with a genus in another
senses.head: `rank normalized`
senses.gloss: higher ranks set by relative evolutionary divergence so that a genus in one phylum is comparable with a genus in another
senses.evidence: In order to taxonomically organise this large and growing genome dataset, the GTDB uses relative evolutionary divergence (RED) to delineate higher-rank taxa and average nucleotide identity (ANI) to delineate species clusters ( 4 , 5 ). Use of these quantitative criteria for circumscribing taxa allows for automated classification of new genomes ( 6 ), ensures all genomes are classified from species to domain, and normalizes the definition of taxonomic ranks across the bacterial and archaeal domains.

senses.label: `fuzzy species` - a species with one or more genomes at >=95% ANI to a genome in another species; 2.2% of those examined. The complement, `discrete`, is 89.5%
senses.head: `fuzzy species`
senses.gloss: a species with one or more genomes at >=95% ANI to a genome in another species; 2.2% of those examined. The complement, `discrete`, is 89.5%
senses.evidence: In terms of species, 2.2% can be described as fuzzy as they have one or more genomes with an interspecific ANI value ≥95% and 89.5% can be described as discrete as they contain no genomes with an interspecific ANI value >94% (Figure 4F ). Encouragingly, this indicates that GTDB species clusters are largely discrete, but this result should be interpreted with care as most bacterial and archaeal species lack genomic representation based on even conservative estimates of the number of prokaryotic species in nature ( 36 ).

senses.label: `placeholder name` - an alphanumeric string standing in for a Latin name, carried by 77.0% of GTDB species clusters and never replaced by another placeholder
senses.head: `placeholder name`
senses.gloss: an alphanumeric string standing in for a Latin name, carried by 77.0% of GTDB species clusters and never replaced by another placeholder
senses.evidence: Finally, to preserve name continuity, we do not replace alphanumeric placeholder names with other placeholder names, even when names (mostly introduced in early releases) are unwieldy, e.g. CG2-30-70-394 which is used as a genus, family, order, class and phylum name.

senses.label: `Balanced ANI Score` - `0.5 x (ANI score) + 0.5 x (quality score)`, the rule deciding when the genome a species name points at may be swapped
senses.head: `Balanced ANI Score`
senses.gloss: `0.5 x (ANI score) + 0.5 x (quality score)`, the rule deciding when the genome a species name points at may be swapped
senses.evidence: GTDB representatives are updated according to two primary principles: (i) representatives should be assembled from the type strain of a species whenever possible, and (ii) representatives should only be replaced by equivalent assemblies of demonstrably higher quality (Figure 3B ). These two principles are quantitatively defined by the Balanced ANI Score (BAS) which is 0.5 × (ANI score) + 0.5 × (quality score), where the ANI score is 100 – 20 × (100 – ANI to current representative) and the quality score is defined by the criteria given in Table 1 . An existing representative is only replaced by a new or updated genome if it has a BAS ≥ 10 above the BAS of the current representative. This achieves the goal of taxonomic stability by requiring a new representative to be of increasingly higher quality (as defined by the quality score) the more dissimilar it is from the current representative (as defined by the ANI score).

senses.label: `horizontal pleiotropy` - a variant affecting the outcome through a pathway OTHER than the risk factor. `A VIOLATION OF THE INSTRUMENTAL VARIABLE ASSUMPTIONS`
senses.head: `horizontal pleiotropy`
senses.gloss: a variant affecting the outcome through a pathway OTHER than the risk factor. `A VIOLATION OF THE INSTRUMENTAL VARIABLE ASSUMPTIONS`
senses.evidence: Pleiotropic effects —the effects of a genetic variant on multiple biological pathways. These can either affect the outcome through another trait or pathway to the one under investigation, known as horizontal pleiotropy, or affect other traits through the risk factor of interest, known as vertical pleiotropy. Horizontal pleiotropy is a violation of the instrumental variable assumptions because the effects of the genetic variant on the outcome are not exclusively through the risk factor; this is problematic for Mendelian randomisation studies. Vertical pleiotropy is in fact the essence of Mendelian randomisation—showing that one factor influences a downstream outcome—and is in general not problematic 1

senses.label: `vertical pleiotropy` - a variant affecting other traits THROUGH the risk factor. `IN FACT THE ESSENCE OF MENDELIAN RANDOMISATION ... and is in general not problematic`
senses.head: `vertical pleiotropy`
senses.gloss: a variant affecting other traits THROUGH the risk factor. `IN FACT THE ESSENCE OF MENDELIAN RANDOMISATION ... and is in general not problematic`
senses.evidence: Pleiotropic effects —the effects of a genetic variant on multiple biological pathways. These can either affect the outcome through another trait or pathway to the one under investigation, known as horizontal pleiotropy, or affect other traits through the risk factor of interest, known as vertical pleiotropy. Horizontal pleiotropy is a violation of the instrumental variable assumptions because the effects of the genetic variant on the outcome are not exclusively through the risk factor; this is problematic for Mendelian randomisation studies. Vertical pleiotropy is in fact the essence of Mendelian randomisation—showing that one factor influences a downstream outcome—and is in general not problematic 1

senses.label: `instrumental variable` - `variables that are associated with the risk factor of interest, that are NOT RELATED TO CONFOUNDERS, and that AFFECT THE OUTCOME ONLY THROUGH THE RISK FACTOR`; need not be genetic
senses.head: `instrumental variable`
senses.gloss: `variables that are associated with the risk factor of interest, that are NOT RELATED TO CONFOUNDERS, and that AFFECT THE OUTCOME ONLY THROUGH THE RISK FACTOR`; need not be genetic
senses.evidence: Instrumental variables —variables that are associated with the risk factor of interest, that are not related to confounders, and that affect the outcome only through the risk factor. An instrumental variable can be any trait (not necessarily a genetic variant) that meets these criteria, but the nature of genetic inheritance means that genetic variants are often plausible instrumental variables

senses.label: `weak instrument bias` - what happens with variants `that ONLY EXPLAIN A SMALL PROPORTION OF THE VARIATION in the risk factor, coupled with a small sample size`
senses.head: `weak instrument bias`
senses.gloss: what happens with variants `that ONLY EXPLAIN A SMALL PROPORTION OF THE VARIATION in the risk factor, coupled with a small sample size`
senses.evidence: Weak instrument bias —can occur in Mendelian randomisation studies when using one or more genetic variants that only explain a small proportion of the variation in the risk factor, coupled with a small sample size

senses.label: `two sample Mendelian randomisation` - instrument-risk-factor and instrument-outcome associations estimated in DIFFERENT samples; buys power, costs two further assumptions
senses.head: `two sample Mendelian randomisation`
senses.gloss: instrument-risk-factor and instrument-outcome associations estimated in DIFFERENT samples; buys power, costs two further assumptions
senses.evidence: Two sample Mendelian randomisation —using two different study samples to estimate the instrument-risk factor and instrument-outcome associations to estimate a causal effect of the risk factor on the outcome. This can be useful when the risk factor or outcome, or both, are expensive to measure. 17 18 It also provides an opportunity to substantially increase the statistical power, by incorporating data from multiple sources, including large consortia 17

senses.label: `MR Egger regression` - allows pleiotropic effects `AS LONG AS THE SIZE OF THESE PLEIOTROPIC EFFECTS IS INDEPENDENT OF THE SIZE OF THE GENETIC VARIANTS' EFFECTS ON THE RISK FACTOR` - a violation permitted under a condition
senses.head: `MR Egger regression`
senses.gloss: allows pleiotropic effects `AS LONG AS THE SIZE OF THESE PLEIOTROPIC EFFECTS IS INDEPENDENT OF THE SIZE OF THE GENETIC VARIANTS' EFFECTS ON THE RISK FACTOR` - a violation permitted under a condition
senses.evidence: MR Egger regression —a statistical technique that allows one or more genetic variants to have pleiotropic effects, as long as the size of these pleiotropic effects is independent of the size of the genetic variants’ effects on the risk factor of interest 19

senses.label: `integration by congruence` - species limits at the INTERSECTION of two or more independent characters. Stringent; risks beta error, false negatives, and a bias toward old species
senses.head: `integration by congruence`
senses.gloss: species limits at the INTERSECTION of two or more independent characters. Stringent; risks beta error, false negatives, and a bias toward old species
senses.evidence: Figure 1 Schematic representation of two approaches of integrative taxonomy . Background yellow, red, and blue colors represent the spectrum of character variation, each dot being an independent evolutionary linage that requires identification and delimitation as separate species. Integration by cumulation (left) identifies species limits with divergence in one or more not necessarily overlapping taxonomic characters (e. g. mtDNA or morphology), whereas the integration by congruence (right) identifies species limits with the intersection of evidence from two or more independent taxonomic characters (e. g. mtDNA plus morphology).

senses.label: `integration by cumulation` - species limits from divergence in ONE OR MORE not necessarily overlapping characters. Permissive; risks alpha error, false positives, and taxonomic inflation
senses.head: `integration by cumulation`
senses.gloss: species limits from divergence in ONE OR MORE not necessarily overlapping characters. Permissive; risks alpha error, false positives, and taxonomic inflation
senses.evidence: Figure 1 Schematic representation of two approaches of integrative taxonomy . Background yellow, red, and blue colors represent the spectrum of character variation, each dot being an independent evolutionary linage that requires identification and delimitation as separate species. Integration by cumulation (left) identifies species limits with divergence in one or more not necessarily overlapping taxonomic characters (e. g. mtDNA or morphology), whereas the integration by congruence (right) identifies species limits with the intersection of evidence from two or more independent taxonomic characters (e. g. mtDNA plus morphology).

senses.label: `unconfirmed candidate species (UCS)` / `deep conspecific lineage (DCL)` / `confirmed candidate species (CCS)` - three states of an undescribed lineage, defined by what the evidence currently supports rather than by the organism
senses.head: `unconfirmed candidate species (UCS)` / `deep conspecific lineage (DCL)` / `confirmed candidate species (CCS)`
senses.gloss: three states of an undescribed lineage, defined by what the evidence currently supports rather than by the organism
senses.evidence: A further developed stepwise working protocol (Figure 2c ) recognizes three subcategories of candidate species [ 8 ]. Groups of individuals within nominal species showing large genetic distances, but without further information, are considered unconfirmed candidate species (UCS) deserving further study. When additional data indicate that these genealogical units are not differentiated at the species level, they are flagged as deep conspecific lineages (DCL). The third category, confirmed candidate species (CCS), applies to those deep genealogical lineages that can be considered good species following standards of divergence for the group under study but that have not yet been formally described and named. For example, confirmed candidate species are sister lineages in syntopy showing no evidence of interbreeding, or allopatric lineages with distinct morphological or bioacoustical character divergences.

senses.label: `candidate species` - `a set of organisms identified as a putative new species`, in the paper's own glossary; named as `Hirudo medicinalis [Ca3 Siddall et al. 2007]`
senses.head: `candidate species`
senses.gloss: `a set of organisms identified as a putative new species`, in the paper's own glossary; named as `Hirudo medicinalis [Ca3 Siddall et al. 2007]`
senses.evidence: Candidate species: a set of organisms identified as a putative new species. Coalescent theory: retrospective model of population genetics that employs a sample of individuals from a population to trace all alleles to the most recent common ancestor. DNA barcoding: the use of short standardized DNA sequences to identify species.

senses.label: `subspecies` - `infraspecific Linnaean category sometimes used to classify allopatric or parapatric populations showing SOME DEGREE OF DIVERGENCE ... NOT CONSIDERED LARGE ENOUGH FOR THE SPECIES RANK`. A rank defined by a quantity nobody specifies
senses.head: `subspecies`
senses.gloss: `infraspecific Linnaean category sometimes used to classify allopatric or parapatric populations showing SOME DEGREE OF DIVERGENCE ... NOT CONSIDERED LARGE ENOUGH FOR THE SPECIES RANK`. A rank defined by a quantity nobody specifies
senses.evidence: Subspecies: infraspecific Linnaean category sometimes used to classify allopatric or parapatric populations showing some degree of divergence--traditionally in morphological traits--not considered large enough for the species rank.

senses.label: `malnutrition` (GLIM) - at least ONE phenotypic criterion (weight loss, low BMI, reduced muscle mass) AND at least ONE etiologic criterion (reduced intake or assimilation, inflammation or disease burden)
senses.head: `malnutrition` (GLIM)
senses.gloss: at least ONE phenotypic criterion (weight loss, low BMI, reduced muscle mass) AND at least ONE etiologic criterion (reduced intake or assimilation, inflammation or disease burden)
senses.evidence: Weight loss, reduced BMI, and reduced muscle mass were categorized as phenotypic criteria, and reduced food intake/assimilation and disease burden/inflammation as etiologic criteria (Table 3 and Figure 1 ). For the diagnosis of malnutrition, GLIM recommends that the combination of at least one phenotypic criterion and one etiologic criterion is required (Table 3 and Figure 1 ). The selection of threshold values for the consensus diagnostic criteria was guided by review of existing approaches used in screening and assessment as was the selection of threshold values for severity grading described below (see Appendix). The selected threshold values for diagnosis of malnutrition are shown in Table 3 . While only the phenotypic criteria are proposed for the severity grading that follows, the inclusion of the etiologic criteria for malnutrition diagnosis is deemed a priority to guide appropriate intervention and anticipated outcomes.

senses.label: `phenotypic criterion` - what the body shows; the only half used for severity grading into Stage 1 (moderate) and Stage 2 (severe)
senses.head: `phenotypic criterion`
senses.gloss: what the body shows; the only half used for severity grading into Stage 1 (moderate) and Stage 2 (severe)
senses.evidence: Phenotypic metrics for grading severity as Stage 1 (moderate) and Stage 2 (severe) malnutrition are proposed. It is recommended that the etiologic criteria be used to guide intervention and anticipated outcomes. The recommended approach supports classification of malnutrition into four etiology‐related diagnosis categories.

senses.label: `etiologic criterion` - why it happened; required for diagnosis, excluded from grading, and kept `to guide appropriate intervention and anticipated outcomes`
senses.head: `etiologic criterion`
senses.gloss: why it happened; required for diagnosis, excluded from grading, and kept `to guide appropriate intervention and anticipated outcomes`
senses.evidence: Weight loss, reduced BMI, and reduced muscle mass were categorized as phenotypic criteria, and reduced food intake/assimilation and disease burden/inflammation as etiologic criteria (Table 3 and Figure 1 ). For the diagnosis of malnutrition, GLIM recommends that the combination of at least one phenotypic criterion and one etiologic criterion is required (Table 3 and Figure 1 ). The selection of threshold values for the consensus diagnostic criteria was guided by review of existing approaches used in screening and assessment as was the selection of threshold values for severity grading described below (see Appendix). The selected threshold values for diagnosis of malnutrition are shown in Table 3 . While only the phenotypic criteria are proposed for the severity grading that follows, the inclusion of the etiologic criteria for malnutrition diagnosis is deemed a priority to guide appropriate intervention and anticipated outcomes.

senses.label: `at risk` - the output of step one, established `BY THE USE OF ANY VALIDATED SCREENING TOOL`; the definition deliberately does not name which
senses.head: `at risk`
senses.gloss: the output of step one, established `BY THE USE OF ANY VALIDATED SCREENING TOOL`; the definition deliberately does not name which
senses.evidence: There was strong consensus that the key first step in the evaluation of nutritional status is malnutrition risk screening to identify “at risk” status by the use of any validated screening tool 12 , 13 , 14 ; some of these tools are noted in Table 1 and the Appendix. This is followed by the second step of assessment for diagnosis and severity grading as described below.

senses.label: the four etiology-based categories - chronic disease WITH inflammation, chronic disease with MINIMAL OR NO perceived inflammation, ACUTE disease or injury with severe inflammation, and STARVATION including hunger and food shortage
senses.head: the four etiology-based categories
senses.gloss: chronic disease WITH inflammation, chronic disease with MINIMAL OR NO perceived inflammation, ACUTE disease or injury with severe inflammation, and STARVATION including hunger and food shortage
senses.evidence: An etiology‐based diagnosis classification is endorsed by GLIM consistent with those suggested previously by the International Consensus Guideline Committee, 1 the AND/ASPEN Guidelines, 7 and the ESPEN Guidelines. The classification includes malnutrition related to chronic disease with inflammation, malnutrition related to chronic disease with minimal or no perceived inflammation, malnutrition related to acute disease or injury with severe inflammation, and malnutrition related to starvation including hunger/food shortage associated with socioeconomic or environmental factors (Table 5 ).

senses.label: `saturation` - four incompatible readings in one literature: a theoretical category fully developed, no new codes appearing, pre-set codes exemplified, or data repeating themselves
senses.head: `saturation`
senses.gloss: four incompatible readings in one literature: a theoretical category fully developed, no new codes appearing, pre-set codes exemplified, or data repeating themselves
senses.evidence: Extending previous literature that has highlighted the variability in the use of saturation (O’Reilly and Parker 2013; Walker 2012), we have scrutinized the different ways in which it has been operationalized in the research literature, identifying four models of saturation, each of which appears to make different core assumptions about what saturation is, and about what exactly is being saturated. These have been labelled as: theoretical saturation, inductive thematic saturation, a priori thematic saturation, and data saturation. Moving forward, the identiﬁcation and recognition of these different models of saturation may aid qualitative researchers in untangling some of the inconsistencies and contradictions that characterize its use.

senses.label: `theoretical saturation` - Glaser and Strauss 1967: no additional data are found whereby the sociologist can develop properties of the category
senses.head: `theoretical saturation`
senses.gloss: Glaser and Strauss 1967: no additional data are found whereby the sociologist can develop properties of the category
senses.evidence: The criterion for judging when to stop sampling the different groups pertinent to a category is the category’s theoretical saturation. Saturation means that no additional data are being found whereby the sociologist can develop properties of the category. As he sees similar instances over and over again, the researcher becomes empirically conﬁdent that a category is saturated. He goes out of his way to look for groups that stretch diversity of data as far as possible, just to make certain that saturation is based on the widest possible range of data on the category.

senses.label: `saturation` as an EVENT - a point that can be recognised and reported
senses.head: `saturation` as an EVENT
senses.gloss: a point that can be recognised and reported
senses.evidence: A key issue underlying the identiﬁcation of saturation is the extent to which it is viewed as an event or a process. Commonly, saturation is referred to as a ‘point’ (e.g. Otmar et al. 2011; Jassim and Whitford 2014; Kazley et al. 2015), suggesting that it should be thought of as a discrete event that can be recognized as such by the analyst.

senses.label: `saturation` as a PROCESS - a matter of degree, an ongoing cumulative judgement that is perhaps never completed
senses.head: `saturation` as a PROCESS
senses.gloss: a matter of degree, an ongoing cumulative judgement that is perhaps never completed
senses.evidence: The question will then be ‘how much saturation is enough?’, rather than ‘has saturation occurred?’7 This is a less straightforward question, but one that much better highlights the fact that this can only be a matter of the analyst’s decision—saturation is an ongoing, cumulative judgment that one makes, and perhaps never completes,8 rather than something that can be pinpointed at a speciﬁc juncture.

senses.label: `data saturation` - informational redundancy, judged at the level of data collection and separated from analysis and from theory
senses.head: `data saturation`
senses.gloss: informational redundancy, judged at the level of data collection and separated from analysis and from theory
senses.evidence: New data tend to be redundant of data already collected. In interviews, when the researcher begins to hear the same comments again and again, data saturation is being reached… It is then time to stop collecting information and to start analysing what has been collected.

senses.label: `concept` (Deleuze and Guattari, adapted) - a multiplicity whose components are `distinct, heterogeneous and, yet, not separable`, and `there is NO CONCEPT WITH ONLY ONE COMPONENT`
senses.head: `concept` (Deleuze and Guattari, adapted)
senses.gloss: a multiplicity whose components are `distinct, heterogeneous and, yet, not separable`, and `there is NO CONCEPT WITH ONLY ONE COMPONENT`
senses.evidence: When defining of the term concept, I follow and adapt the approach of Deleuze and Guattari in their What Is Philosophy? (1991), in which they hold that “every concept has components and is defined by them” (p. 15). These “components, or what defines the consistency of the concept; its endo-consistency; are distinct, heterogeneous and, yet, not separable” (p. 19). It is a multiplicity, but “not every multiplicity is conceptual,” and “there is no concept with only one component” (p. 15).

senses.label: `conceptual framework` (this paper) - `a network, or a plane, of interlinked concepts that together provide a comprehensive understanding of a phenomenon`
senses.head: `conceptual framework` (this paper)
senses.gloss: `a network, or a plane, of interlinked concepts that together provide a comprehensive understanding of a phenomenon`
senses.evidence: Current usage of the terms conceptual framework and theoretical framework are vague and imprecise. In this paper I define conceptual framework as a network, or “a plane,” of interlinked concepts that together provide a comprehensive understanding of a phenomenon or phenomena.

senses.label: `conceptual framework` vs `model` - the first is built on concepts, the second on variables or factors; the paper stipulates the split to stop loose usage
senses.head: `conceptual framework` vs `model`
senses.gloss: the first is built on concepts, the second on variables or factors; the paper stipulates the split to stop loose usage
senses.evidence: To discourage loose usage of the term conceptual framework, I propose basing conceptual frameworks not on variable or factors but on concepts alone. When variables or factors are used, I suggest employing the term model.

senses.label: `conceptual framework analysis` - a grounded-theory technique that `aims to generate, identify, and trace a phenomenon's major concepts`
senses.head: `conceptual framework analysis`
senses.gloss: a grounded-theory technique that `aims to generate, identify, and trace a phenomenon's major concepts`
senses.evidence: Yet, the existing conceptual analysis technique is inadequate for theorizing the concepts that emerge from the text. Therefore, in this article I propose a new technique, which I refer to as conceptual framework analysis, as a grounded theory technique, or tactic, that aims to generate, identify, and trace a phenomenon’s major concepts, which together constitute its theoretical framework.

senses.label: `skeletal framework` (Morse et al.) - characteristics from previous inquiry giving an internal structure and a starting point, which multidisciplinary phenomena usually do not even have
senses.head: `skeletal framework` (Morse et al.)
senses.gloss: characteristics from previous inquiry giving an internal structure and a starting point, which multidisciplinary phenomena usually do not even have
senses.evidence: Despite the extensive literature that provides logical guidelines for qualitatively deriving theories from text and data (Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Harris, 2003; Miles & Huberman, 1994; Myers, 2009; Strauss & Corbin, 1990), there is a lack of a qualitative systematic method for building conceptual frameworks. This is particularly noticeable in the multidisciplinary literature.

senses.label: `news` - as practitioners define it: `I know it when I see it`, `Because it just is!`, a gut feeling that obscures as much as it reveals
senses.head: `news`
senses.gloss: as practitioners define it: `I know it when I see it`, `Because it just is!`, a gut feeling that obscures as much as it reveals
senses.evidence: Asked how they deﬁne news, journalists sometimes reply: “I know it when I see it.” Pressed on why something has been deemed newsworthy, a typical response is: “Because it just is!” (Brighton and Foy 2007, 147). Deﬁnitions relying on such “gut feeling” (Schultz 2007) arguably obscure as much as they reveal about news selection, prompting academics to offer their own explanations, which can involve devising taxonomies of news values. One of the most inﬂuential and frequently cited of these is a paper by Johan Galtung and Mari Ruge (1965), “The Structure of Foreign News”, published more than 50 years ago.

senses.label: `news values` - as the field defines them: a taxonomy of selection criteria identifiable in published output, offered as a tool rather than an explanation
senses.head: `news values`
senses.gloss: as the field defines them: a taxonomy of selection criteria identifiable in published output, offered as a tool rather than an explanation
senses.evidence: Thus, we reiterate that the above news value taxonomy should be seen as a tool for analysis and further research—designed to provoke discussion and, indeed, contestation— not something to be churned out as if it is the last word on the subject. And, whenever the question arises of why a particular story is seen as newsworthy, there will always remain an element of truth to the reply: “It just is!”

senses.label: `entertainment` (2001) - one category holding both light and dark human interest; split here into entertainment and drama
senses.head: `entertainment` (2001)
senses.gloss: one category holding both light and dark human interest; split here into entertainment and drama
senses.evidence: Entertainment encompasses both a dark and light side, which might be better conveyed in two distinct categories. Some of the darker but “entertaining” human-interest stories might perhaps be more accurately labelled as drama. News stories about sport could be added to the entertainment mix alongside show business, while the surprise category ought to contain “unusualness” within its deﬁnition. We also noticed that there were many stories involving large corporations and these might be included within the power elite category.

senses.label: `magnitude` - large numbers of people or potential impact (2001), widened here to include extreme behaviour or occurrence
senses.head: `magnitude`
senses.gloss: large numbers of people or potential impact (2001), widened here to include extreme behaviour or occurrence
senses.evidence: On investigation it became apparent that the term “magnitude” can mean more than merely involving large numbers; it ought to include extreme behaviours or occurrences (a man dying in extreme temperatures in an oven, for example, or a particularly unpleasant crime).

senses.label: `shareability` - likely to generate sharing and comment; `stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry` is the closest the paper gets to a definition
senses.head: `shareability`
senses.gloss: likely to generate sharing and comment; `stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry` is the closest the paper gets to a definition
senses.evidence: Precisely what qualities give one story more shareability than another are hard to pin down, but Janine Gibson (a former Guardian website editor who in 2015 became editor-in-chief of BuzzFeed UK) has noted that the most shared stories tend to be “stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry” (quoted in Newman 2011, 24).

senses.label: `cultural competency` (Cross et al. 1989) - `a set of congruent behaviours, attitudes, and policies that come together in a system, agency, or among professionals` enabling effective work in cross-cultural situations
senses.head: `cultural competency` (Cross et al. 1989)
senses.gloss: `a set of congruent behaviours, attitudes, and policies that come together in a system, agency, or among professionals` enabling effective work in cross-cultural situations
senses.evidence: Cultural competence is a set of congruent behaviours, attitudes, and policies that come together in a system, agency, or among professionals and enable that system, agency, or those professionals to work effectively in cross-cultural situations.

senses.label: `cultural competency` (individual framing) - the ability of INDIVIDUALS to establish working relationships that supersede cultural differences
senses.head: `cultural competency` (individual framing)
senses.gloss: the ability of INDIVIDUALS to establish working relationships that supersede cultural differences
senses.evidence: the ability of individuals to establish effective interpersonal and working relationships that supersede cultural differences by recognizing the importance of social and cultural influences on patients, considering how these factors interact, and devising interventions that take these issues into account [53] (p.2).

senses.label: `cultural competency` (systems framing) - the ability of SYSTEMS to provide care to patients with diverse values, tailoring delivery to their needs
senses.head: `cultural competency` (systems framing)
senses.gloss: the ability of SYSTEMS to provide care to patients with diverse values, tailoring delivery to their needs
senses.evidence: the ability of systems to provide care to patients with diverse values, beliefs and behaviours, including tailoring delivery to meet patients’ social, cultural, and linguistic needs [54] (p. v).

senses.label: `cultural safety` (Nursing Council of NZ 1992) - `a focus for the delivery of quality care through changes in thinking about POWER RELATIONSHIPS and patients' rights`
senses.head: `cultural safety` (Nursing Council of NZ 1992)
senses.gloss: `a focus for the delivery of quality care through changes in thinking about POWER RELATIONSHIPS and patients' rights`
senses.evidence: The term cultural safety first was first proposed by Dr. Irihapeti Ramsden and Māori nurses in the 1990s [74], and in 1992 the Nursing Council of New Zealand made cultural safety a requirement for nursing and midwifery education [32].

senses.label: `cultural safety` (this paper's proposal) - examined bias, ongoing self-reflection and accountability, `AS DEFINED BY THE PATIENT AND THEIR COMMUNITIES` and measured by progress towards health equity
senses.head: `cultural safety` (this paper's proposal)
senses.gloss: examined bias, ongoing self-reflection and accountability, `AS DEFINED BY THE PATIENT AND THEIR COMMUNITIES` and measured by progress towards health equity
senses.evidence: “Cultural safety requires healthcare professionals and their associated healthcare organisations to examine themselves and the potential impact of their own culture on clinical interactions and healthcare service delivery. This requires individual healthcare professionals and healthcare organisations to acknowledge and address their own biases, attitudes, assumptions, stereotypes, prejudices, structures and characteristics that may affect the quality of care provided. In doing so, cultural safety encompasses a critical consciousness where healthcare professionals and healthcare organisations engage in ongoing self-reflection and self-awareness and hold themselves accountable for providing culturally safe care, as defined by the patient and their communities, and as measured through progress towards acheiveing health equity. Cultural safety requires healthcare professionals and their associated healthcare organisations to influence healthcare to reduce bias and achieve equity within the workforce and working environment”.

senses.label: `gambling related harm` (Queensland) - a `range of adverse consequences` in which safety or wellbeing is placed at risk, arising from PROBLEMATIC gambling only
senses.head: `gambling related harm` (Queensland)
senses.gloss: a `range of adverse consequences` in which safety or wellbeing is placed at risk, arising from PROBLEMATIC gambling only
senses.evidence: The Queensland definition describes harm as a ‘range of adverse consequences’, in which ‘the safety or wellbeing of gambling consumers or their family or friends are placed at risk’ and/or negative impacts extending to the broader community. In describing harm as a set of impacts and consequences, the Queensland definition is clear that gambling harms are the outcome of problematic gambling, rather than problematic gambling itself.

senses.label: `gambling related harm` (New Zealand Gambling Act 2003) - `any kind of harm or distress arising from, or caused or EXACERBATED BY, a person's gambling`
senses.head: `gambling related harm` (New Zealand Gambling Act 2003)
senses.gloss: `any kind of harm or distress arising from, or caused or EXACERBATED BY, a person's gambling`
senses.evidence: The New Zealand 2003 Gambling Act definition is broader, describing harm as ‘any kind of harm or distress arising from, or caused or exacerbated by, a person’s gambling’. This definition includes psychological or emotional impacts of gambling, as well as presumably more concrete forms of harm, such as financial loss.

senses.label: `gambling related harm` (proposed here) - `Any initial or exacerbated adverse consequence due to an engagement with gambling that leads to A DECREMENT to the health or wellbeing of an individual, family unit, community or population`
senses.head: `gambling related harm` (proposed here)
senses.gloss: `Any initial or exacerbated adverse consequence due to an engagement with gambling that leads to A DECREMENT to the health or wellbeing of an individual, family unit, community or population`
senses.evidence: Any initial or exacerbated adverse consequence due to an engagement with gambling that leads to a decrement to the health or wellbeing of an individual, family unit, community or population.

senses.label: `legacy harm` - harm that continues or emerges after engagement with gambling ceases; the label exists to mark that harm does not end with the behaviour
senses.head: `legacy harm`
senses.gloss: harm that continues or emerges after engagement with gambling ceases; the label exists to mark that harm does not end with the behaviour
senses.evidence: Legacy harms related to those harms that continue to occur (or emerge) even if the person’s engagement with gambling ceases through changes in their own or someone else’s behaviour, but may also be experienced if a person continues to gamble. The label was chosen to capture the ongoing impact of harm, and to highlight that harm does not cease with the behaviour.
