senses.label: `harm` in ordinary use - `immediately intuitive, implying damage and adverse consequences`, and that intuitiveness is precisely why it went undefined
senses.head: `harm` in ordinary use
senses.gloss: `immediately intuitive, implying damage and adverse consequences`, and that intuitiveness is precisely why it went undefined
senses.evidence: Harm is a term that is immediately intuitive, implying damage and adverse consequences. However, the assumption that it is unnecessary to define the term precisely in relation to gambling is mistaken.

senses.label: `harm` - SLIDING BETWEEN THE CAUSE AND THE EFFECT: `the term harm is often USED INTERCHANGEABLY TO REFER TO THE BEHAVIOUR - NOT JUST THE CONSEQUENCE`. One word covering the gambling and the damage it does, which makes any claim that one produces the other unfalsifiable.
senses.head: `harm`
senses.gloss: SLIDING BETWEEN THE CAUSE AND THE EFFECT: `the term harm is often USED INTERCHANGEABLY TO REFER TO THE BEHAVIOUR - NOT JUST THE CONSEQUENCE`. One word covering the gambling and the damage it does, which makes any claim that one produces the other unfalsifiable.
senses.evidence: To add further uncertainty, the term harm is often used interchangeably to refer to the behaviour - not just the consequence

senses.label: `terminology` (small t) - the units in any specialized knowledge field; `Terminology` (capital T) - the study of specialized language. The disambiguation is carried entirely by the capital letter
senses.head: `terminology` (small t)
senses.gloss: the units in any specialized knowledge field; `Terminology` (capital T) - the study of specialized language. The disambiguation is carried entirely by the capital letter
senses.evidence: As has often been observed, terminology is a word that can either begin with an upper or lower-case letter. When terminology begins with a small t, it refers to the units in any specialized knowledge field. When it begins with a large T, it refers to the study of specialized language.

senses.label: `monosemic reference` - a term distinguished from a general-language word by its single-meaning relationship with the concept it designates, and by the stability of that relationship in texts
senses.head: `monosemic reference`
senses.gloss: a term distinguished from a general-language word by its single-meaning relationship with the concept it designates, and by the stability of that relationship in texts
senses.evidence: One of the basic assertions of General Terminology Theory (Wüster 1979; Felber 1984) is that terms in specialized language are inherently different from general language words because of the monosemic reference between terms and concepts. In other words, the general claim is that a term or a specialized language unit can be distinguished from a general language word by its single-meaning relationship with the specialized concept that it designates,

senses.label: `domain` - in Terminology, either the knowledge area itself OR the categories of concepts within the specialized field, with different consequences either way
senses.head: `domain`
senses.gloss: in Terminology, either the knowledge area itself OR the categories of concepts within the specialized field, with different consequences either way
senses.evidence: Regarding conceptual domains, in Terminology there seem to be two views on the matter, which are not necessarily incompatible with each other. A domain sometimes refers to the knowledge area itself, and other times, refers to the categories of concepts within the specialized field. Evidently, whether a domain is defined as one or the other has dramatic consequences for its internal structure.

senses.label: `terminological knowledge base` (Meyer) - a term bank whose concepts and designations are linked by meaningful relationships, not only generic-specific and part-whole
senses.head: `terminological knowledge base` (Meyer)
senses.gloss: a term bank whose concepts and designations are linked by meaningful relationships, not only generic-specific and part-whole
senses.evidence: When term bases become terminological knowledge bases, as conceived by Meyer, they enhance data because the concepts and designations are linked to each other by meaningful relationships. Although the traditional generic-specific and part-whole relationships are contemplated, there is a greater emphasis on other types of relationships that enrich the resulting knowledge structure, such as cause-effect, object-function, etc. (Bowker & L’Homme 2004).

senses.label: `standardization` - the founding objective of the discipline, and in socioterminology `a chimera since language is in constant change`
senses.head: `standardization`
senses.gloss: the founding objective of the discipline, and in socioterminology `a chimera since language is in constant change`
senses.evidence: According to socioterminologists, standardization is a chimera since language is in constant change. Polysemy and synonymy are inevitably present in terminology and specialized texts, and the use of one term instead of another can reflect the knowledge, social and professional status of a group of users, as well as the power relationships between speakers.
